Preface

Progress in science can be lumpy. Ground-breaking advances, such as the emergence of quantum theory, the development of spectroscopic techniques including IR and NMR, or the widespread adoption of computers in chemistry, catalyse research, and open new fields. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the latest significant advance.

Perhaps, this assessment of AI seems too generous. Can a computational technique really be transformational? After all, in every university chemistry department, there are computers and spectrometers, but in only some is AI used. However, there are signs that AI may have as great an impact in science as it promises to do in society more broadly; this book explores that impact.

We begin with an introduction to some of the core concepts in AI and machine learning, at a level suitable for those who are new to the field (Allen, Chapters 1 and 2). The tutorial that follows outlines some of the most widely used AI methods at the interface of machine learning and medicine (Lawrence, Chapter 3). Subsequent chapters deal with a wide range of topics, including fundamental studies in catalysis (Liu, Chapter 19) and prediction of the properties of materials (Winkler, Chapter 9; Jelfs, Chapter 12; Brgoch, Chapter 13); studies of synthesis design (Stukenbroeker, Chapter 6; Hirst, Chapter 7; Brgoch, Chapter 13); drug design (Hudson, Chapter 11; Speck-Planche, Chapter 16); industrial applications (Curteanu, Chapter 10; Clough, Chapter 14); theoretical areas of chemistry (Marquetand, Chapter 4; Mizoguchi, Chapter 17) and some more technical aspects of the use of AI (Staker, Chapter 15); autonomous chemistry (Stukenbroeker, Chapter 6; Simpson, Chapter 18); and chemical astronomy (Viti, Chapter 8). Several chapters (among them Stukenbroeker, Chapter 6; Hirst, Chapter 7; Brgoch, Chapter 13; Simpson, Chapter 18, and Shankar, Chapter 20) touch upon some of the difficulties that may complicate the use of AI in science and consider how one might circumvent them, while one further chapter (Cartwright, Chapter 5), which also discusses challenges and solutions when using AI in science, is aimed principally at newcomers to the field.

Chemistry research that takes advantage of AI is burgeoning: from a modest number of published papers in 2000, the publication rate had, by the end of 2019, risen 100-fold. Several factors have contributed to this growth:

  • access to increasingly large volumes of data;
  • a continuing rise in computer speed;
  • improvements in the efficiency of AI software;
  • the availability of innovative specialised chips, such as custom neural network chips;
  • the re-purposing of graphics chips as fast surrogate CPUs for AI applications;
  • the refinement of existing AI methods and the development of new techniques;
  • recognition that some types of problems can be more successfully tackled using AI than with more conventional methods of analysis; and
  • the availability of upgraded tools for automatic data extraction from sources of non-standard structure, such as journals, Powerpoint presentations, or laboratory notebooks.

To that list, we add (cautiously) the future availability of quantum computers. The current view is that such computers will be particularly well-suited to optimisation problems, which are widespread in chemistry (What does the lowest energy conformer look like? Which potential drug binds most strongly to the protein? Which synthetic route provides the highest yield?). Chemists can expect to be among the greatest beneficiaries of this new technology.

Chapters within this book, written by leading groups in the field, provide intriguing examples of how AI can be applied in chemistry. They provide a fascinating glimpse into the future of AI in science.

Hugh Cartwright

Victoria, Canada

CHAPTER 1

Computers as Scientists

TIMOTHY E. H. ALLENa,b

a MRC Toxicology Unit, Hodgkin Building, Lancaster Road, Leicester LE1 7HB, UK

b Centre for Molecular Informatics, Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge, Lensfield Road, Cambridge CB2 1EW, UK

Email: teha2@cam.ac.uk

1.1 What Is Computational Science?

Computers excel at many tasks that humans are very bad at (see Figure 1.1). For example, if you have a smartphone with a voice assistant, try asking it what the square root of 32 761 is. For the phone, this problem is very straightforward, and it almost immediately returns the correct answer of 181. If instead, we were to ask a person the same question, they would probably find it very challenging. However, if they get the correct answer as quickly as the phone, we will think they are a genius (or perhaps more likely that they are cheating!). Now, for comparison, try to engage your voice assistant with a knock-knock joke, and it doesn't work. In contrast to the mathematical challenge, the machine finds this social interaction impossibly complicated, but we would think a person a simpleton if he/she is not able to partake in it. Children learn how to make these jokes before they learn to add. This illustrates why computers make such good scientific companions as they help scientists to be better at the things that they are naturally much worse at.

Figure 1.1 Strengths and weaknesses of humans and computers.

Computational science is a scientific field, which uses a computational methodology to answer scientific questions. Computational scientists are most often trying to answer questions in fields such as chemistry, physics or biology using the algorithms developed by computer scientists. This is, in some respects, analogous to an experimental chemist who uses a reaction to make a molecule in the lab, as opposed to the one who proposes that reaction, or a scientist who uses an NMR machine to determine the chemical composition of a biological sample using a procedure devised by an NMR expert. This is not to say that the scientists deploying these techniques, which might be algorithmic, experimental or otherwise, are any less important than their discoverers. The most impactful scientific techniques are those which have long-term applications across multiple fields.

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms, as described later in this book, could be considered as computational science, but chemistry has a long track record in other computational methods too. Numerous computational techniques do not require AI but rather use the power of computers to solve mathematical equations. Many of the most complex problems are in quantum mechanics.

The field of quantum mechanics is just over 100 years old. In 1900, Max Planck1 proposed that energy is absorbed and radiated in discrete quanta (or packets of energy). Albert Einstein2 used quantum theory to explain the photoelectric effect in 1905, which led to the theory that light acts as both a wave and a particle. Louis de Broglie3 extended wave–particle duality to include all types of matter, including, importantly, electrons. Once it was accepted that electrons behave as waves, the hunt began to find a way of describing these waves mathematically. A mathematical model was proposed by Erwin Schrodinger4 in 1925, and this is shown below, in its time-independent form;

(1.1)

where Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator, Ψ is the wavefunction and E is a constant equal to the energy of the system. The mathematics of this equation is far beyond the scope of this chapter, but it is worth noting that finding solutions to the Schrodinger equation is not trivial for any system. At present, the equation cannot be solved exactly for species with multiple electrons. However, with suitable assumptions and high-powered computers, approximate probability distributions can be found, which tell us where electrons are (approximately, as for quantum systems, it is impossible to know exactly where the electron is) and their associated energy levels. Such details are useful in chemistry to help explain how, and why, the reactions happen.

Because of the wealth of detail that quantum calculations provide, the use of computational calculations to explain, predict and even mimic chemical reactions is an extremely important field. Ken Houk's group at UCLA, for example, have been exploring asymmetric chemical catalysis for many years using computational calculations.5 Such chemical reactions are crucial in the manufacture of molecules with chiral centres, and many of which have important biological properties. Chemicals can have handedness or chirality, which can lead to important biological consequences, as some molecules fit into spaces that others cannot. To manufacture such molecules, we must consider which product(s) might be generated by a chemical reaction that could follow several different pathways. Computers can help us predict why certain reactions are more favourable. To do this, we need, among other things, to calculate the energy barrier that exists between the reactants and the products of a reaction. Computers can consider the shapes of molecules in 3D, their interactions with one another and the energies of these systems, allowing the calculation of these so-called activation energies (see Figure 1.2).

Figure 1.2 A common procedure used in the Houk group for the computational investigation of chemical reactions. Reproduced from ref. 5 with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2016.

From among all the chemically reasonable routes from reactants to products, how can we select the one that has the lowest activation energy? This low-energy pathway will often dominate the reaction, and therefore its product should be the one that is experimentally observed. Calculations of the activation barrier can be considered alongside the experimental observations to evaluate the hypothesis and gain insight – does what is expected through the calculations match the observation? If so, the model can provide useful insight into the chemistry of the interaction by providing information about the structure and dynamics of the transition state as chemicals move from reactants to products. Perhaps, is there an unfavourable interaction between two large groups in the unfavoured pathway that raises its energy? Or is there any favourable electronic interaction in the favoured pathway that lowers the barrier? Such insights can be used subsequently to design new and more efficient reactions.

1.2 What Is Artificial Intelligence?

Defining AI is surprisingly challenging. When trying to do so, I often think of the idea of a generally intelligent machine (a machine able to do a wide range of different tasks as a human does) and would, therefore, define an intelligent machine as A machine capable of doing things that humans consider to be intelligent.

Although this may not be entirely satisfactory, it sums up the goal of AI science quite well as humans are the most intelligent species on earth. It also aligns with the well-known Turing test, developed by Alan Turing in 1950. The standard version of this test requires a human interpreter to converse with, and subsequently judge, two other hidden players, of which one is another human and one is a machine. If, after having conversations with both players, the interpreter cannot distinguish between the machine and the human, the machine would be deemed to have passed the test and therefore be considered “intelligent” (within the boundaries of Turing's test of course) (see Figure 1.3).6 In this context, the test is often referred to as “the imitation game”.

Figure 1.3 The Turing test.

Some tasks that we might consider require a degree of intelligence include speech and vision, scientific and medical decision making, and strategic gameplay. We will consider some examples of these tasks in the rest of this section.

AI has been a pursuit of scientists at least since the 1950s. During that decade, there were three important meetings. A “Session on Learning Machines” in Los Angeles in 1955, a “Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence” at Dartmouth College in 1956, and a symposium on the “Mechanization of Thought Processes” at the National Physical Laboratory in the United Kingdom.6 These early meetings tackled many of the problems that still occupy AI researchers today. These include examples of tasks such as pattern recognition,7 understanding of language,8 and playing chess.9 Other, more mechanistic, issues were also discussed, including the imitation of the human brain and central nervous system as the basis for learning machines,7 and the use of iterative learning to ultimately improve computer performance in learning tasks,10 as well as the realisation that powerful machines would be required to address many of these challenging topics.

Let us consider again the definition of AI given earlier. What is it about humans that makes them intelligent? And does answering this help us understand what kinds of things machines need to be able to do to also be considered intelligent?

Humans sense the world around them through vision. They explore the world by moving around it. They can speak to one another and recognise incoming speech. They can also recognise patterns in objects they encounter and events they experience. These goals are all currently being explored in AI, in the fields of computer vision, robotics, speech recognition, natural language processing, and pattern recognition. Let's cover some examples from the history of AI in these different research areas.

In the late 1950s and early 1960s, a number of projects attempted to use pattern recognition algorithms to aid in the identification of target objects in aerial photographs (aerial reconnaissance). Laveen N. Kanal, Neil C. Randall, and Thomas Harley at the Philco Corporation, for example, attempted to screen aerial photographs for military tanks.6,11 A small section of the film was processed to enhance any edges, and the result presented to the target detection system as a 32×32 array of 1's and 0's. This array was segmented into 24 overlapping 8×8 “feature blocks”, and each of which was then evaluated using a statistical test to establish if the block contained a part of the tank.

These tests assessed 50 photos containing tanks and 50 without tanks. This allowed a statistical model to be prepared to discriminate tank-containing feature blocks from non-tank-containing feature blocks using a linear boundary in 64 dimensions. A score was calculated for each image by considering how many of the 24 feature blocks in an image suggested the presence of a tank. This can be considered analogous to how a random forest12 model works (see Figure 1.4).

Figure 1.4 In a random forest model, each “tree” is a different model, and each evaluates the incoming data to make a prediction. The overall prediction from the random forest is a consensus of these.

The performance of the model on the test images was excellent. Every image containing tanks had a score of at least 11 while all images without a tank had a score of 7 or less. In addition, half of the test images were perfectly classified, i.e. a score of 24 for an image containing a tank or a score of 0 for a non-tank image. Given the technological limits of the era (this work was not programmed on a computer, it used analogue circuitry), this is quite remarkable.

Another early project in pattern recognition and computer vision concerned human face recognition. Woodrow W. Bledsoe, Charles Bisson, and Helen Chan developed techniques for facial recognition at Panoramic Research in the 1960s.6,13 In this early work, a human operator extracted the coordinates of facial features, such as the position of the pupils, from photographs. From these coordinates, a set of 20 distances was calculated, such as the width of eyes, and these distances were then stored on a computer to be compared to the same distances in previously unseen photos during the recognition phase. The closest records were returned, using a nearest neighbour14 calculation to make a prediction (see Figure 1.5).

Figure 1.5 In a nearest neighbour model, the new example (blue star) is considered in the same feature space as all examples previously seen (other shapes). The nearest neighbour (double-headed arrow) or more commonly a collection of near neighbours (large circle) are used for the classification of the new case. In this case, the new example fits most closely with the circles.

In 1970, this work was taken further by M.D. Kelly during his PhD at Stanford.6,15 Kelly wrote a computer program, which was able to detect the facial features by itself, for the identification of people, enormously reducing the workload required.

Subsequent work on facial recognition software progressed rapidly. A 2007 National Institute of Standards and Technology report showed the results of testing seven state-of-the-art face recognition algorithms against humans under different lighting conditions.6,16 While all the algorithms performed admirably in a number of case examples, three of the algorithms outperformed the humans in all the test cases. The best of these methods for facial recognition use ML algorithms on extremely large data sets.

One goal of true AI is to produce a machine that can understand written and spoken language. Such a machine would approach, and perhaps pass, the Turing test. Garnering meaning from words and sentences, as opposed to merely being able to recognise their occurrence, is an extreme challenge – as those who are talented enough to have learned a second language will attest. Consider the simple sentence;

  • “I never said he stole my money”

Depending on the emphasis, this sentence can have seven different meanings;

  • I never said he stole my money – Somebody else said it.
  • I never said he stole my money – I didn't say it.
  • I never said he stole my money – I implied it.
  • I never said he stole my money – Somebody did, maybe him.
  • I never said he stole my money – It was only borrowed.
  • I never said he stole my money – It was stolen from someone else.
  • I never said he stole my money – He stole something else.

And this is even before we get to truly crazy sentences such as “Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo” using three meanings of the word buffalo to construct a grammatically allowed sentence from eight repeats of the same word!

To assist computers in this task, we break sentences into parse trees – diagrams that represent sentences and their structure.6 As some sentences have more than one meaning, they also have more than one parse tree. A key breakthrough here was to use probabilities to identify which meaning is most likely in the given context. This, in turn, allows rules to be established as to which combinations of words are allowed in which orders, and hence which meanings are most likely from given sentences. The huge number of rules that would require coding make writing such a rulebook impossible. Luckily, the vast array of written words catalogued through human history make this a perfect task for the algorithms covered in the next section – ML.

1.3 What Is Machine Learning?

ML is a subcategory within the field of AI and specifically pattern recognition. ML algorithms are computer programs that, through the inspection of a data bank, and without explicit instruction from a human programmer, learn to carry out specific tasks. What kinds of questions can these algorithms answer?

Many modern AIs, including ML algorithms, require a large amount of data for their training. They also require well-defined questions, as they do not currently have the capacity for independent thought. This will be further explored in the next section, but I want to delve into a couple of examples from the world of ML to set the scene for this.

Firstly, I will discuss some of my own research, which includes the development of ML algorithms. Chemicals can have a range of effects in the human body. Some of these are desirable (such as the therapeutic effect of a medicine), whereas others are not. Undesirable effects are investigated in toxicology studies, which are required before a new drug can be prescribed, a new hair shampoo released, or a new pesticide used on crops. The primary aim of these studies is to ensure that the new chemicals are safe for humans and the environment, taking into account the amount of chemical that is used (the dose or exposure). Traditionally, toxicology studies were conducted using animal experiments, and an estimated safe dose for humans was extrapolated from these tests. However, animal testing is expensive, time-consuming, unethical, and humans and animals have different biology that can impact the results. Consequently, there is now a major drive in toxicology to look at methods that do not require animals; computational toxicology is one of these areas.

In my research, I aim to understand how the interaction of chemicals with proteins and enzymes in the human body might lead to a toxic outcome. Using computer models, new chemicals can be assessed before any experimentation is carried out. This mechanistic toxicology approach, based on understanding if and how interactions happen that lead to toxic outcomes, is an effective approach to toxicological problems. These rapid and cost-effective computational results can be followed up with targeted in vitro experimental assays on cells to provide further evidence. By making use of advanced new computational techniques, including ML, toxicology can become a more efficient, ethical, and reliable science.

To construct any kind of computational model, experimental data are required. Luckily numerous biological experiments on cells have been conducted, with widely disseminated results. Databases such as ChEMBL (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/)17 and ToxCast (https://www.epa.gov/chemical-research/toxicity-forecasting)18 collate much of this data and are open source. This data can provide the basis for models.

Initial modelling approaches included the use of structural alerts, coded fragments of molecules that are found more commonly in experimentally active molecules than inactive ones.19,20 While this procedure is relatively simple, it is popular among toxicologists as it allows them to easily identify the parts of a molecule that have caused it to be considered active by the computer. The procedure is extremely transparent. Furthermore, the toxicologists can also look at other molecules containing the fragment in a process known as read-across, in which the experimental results for an existing chemical are used for a new, untested, chemical when an argument can be made that the two molecules are similar enough. In the structural alert approach, a computer program is used to identify the common chemistry in the training data to be built into a model. If a new chemical contains a known active chemical feature, it is predicted as active by the algorithm (see Figure 1.6).

Figure 1.6 The use of 2D structural alerts to classify novel molecules to predict their biological activity. Reproduced from ref. 20 with permission from Oxford University Press, Copyright 2018.

In a second modelling approach, quantum chemistry calculations were used as discussed earlier in the computational science section. Data were obtained for the Ames mutagenicity assay, and this was modelled by considering the activation energy for the reaction between the chemical toxicants and methylamine.21 The methylamine is a substitute for DNA in the calculation, as the Ames assay measures mutagenicity, and one way a chemical can be mutagenic is via a direct chemical reaction with DNA. Several experimentally tested chemicals were considered, and their activation energies were calculated computationally. The results showed a good correlation with the experimental results – with higher activation energies being calculated for Ames negative compounds and lower ones for Ames positive compounds (see Figure 1.7).

Figure 1.7 Calculated activation energies can be used to classify molecules as Ames positive, negative, or unknown. Reproduced from ref. 21, https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jcim.8b00130, with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2018.

This is as expected: the Ames negative compounds have high activation energies and hence cannot react with DNA to cause mutations under normal biological conditions. The research allowed us to establish activation energy thresholds for chemicals that were likely to be Ames positive, negative, and unknown (in the middle, uncertain area) that can be used in the future to classify new chemicals.

ML neural networks are also used. These have involved the use of the TensorFlow algorithm in Python 3 to classify molecules in a similar fashion to structural alerts (see Figure 1.8).

Figure 1.8 Neural networks can be used to make predictions of molecular biological activities.

Open source receptor-binding data are used to train neural networks to classify molecules as binders or nonbinders. These networks are extremely powerful predictors and show a high level of prediction accuracy, outperforming the structural alerts. The networks are also able to provide a confidence estimate of how well a new molecule matches what it knows to be a binder or a nonbinder, which can be treated as a measure of certainty in the prediction.

A disadvantage of using ML algorithms in toxicology is the difficulty in understanding why a specific prediction has been made. Unlike structural alerts, a trained neural network does not point out the parts of the new molecule that make it active. This is a challenge we have been looking to overcome using similarity calculations and examining which molecules the network “thinks” about in the same way, to identify chemical analogues during the prediction process.

A second, exciting ML example dates from the beginning of 2019.22,23 DeepMind, a leading AI research lab, and Blizzard Entertainment, a computer game development company, released a video demonstration on YouTube of AlphaStar, an AI, battling against professional human gamers in the game StarCraft II. DeepMind already had experience in building AIs to play games against humans in both Chess and Go, but StarCraft II is an entirely different challenge and shows how powerful AIs have become, and how much scope there is for them in the future.

Why is StarCraft II a more complex game than Chess or Go? Well, StarCraft II is a real-time strategy (RTS) game, meaning that players do not take turns, but are instead expected to strategically outwit their opponents and execute their moves in real time. In addition, StarCraft II is more complex than Go or Chess, with considerably more potential moves available at any given time and more moves to be made per game. Finally, the players have imperfect information, as they cannot directly observe the whole game area at all times, so it is very challenging to analyse what other players might be doing. This is obviously very different from Go and Chess where the players can always observe the whole board. As a result of these factors, success in an RTS game can be seen as a step towards a more general AI, which is able to solve a variety of problems like a human.

It is worth noting for context that in this demonstration, StarCraft II was slightly simplified to assist the training and operation of the AlphaStar algorithm. Only a single game map was considered (whereas human players are expected to play across a variety of different maps) and only a single faction, Protoss, was used (whereas RTS games tend to have a number of different factions to play as, all with their own strengths, weaknesses, and suitable strategies). This made the game slightly easier for AlphaStar to compete with the human professionals, in terms of the complexity of the full StarCraft II experience. That said, AlphaStar was also handicapped in the demonstration. A computer might be expected to have an advantage over a human player by being able to make faster moves during the game. Unlike a human player, AlphaStar does not have to click or press buttons to execute its commands. DeepMind limited AlphaStar to a number of actions-per-minute lower than that of a typical StarCraft II professional player.

AlphaStar itself is a neural network ML algorithm. The algorithm observes the game space, and its imperfect information, in a manner analogous to a human player and then makes decisions on what moves to make. While it perceives information, AlphaStar uses a neural network called a long short-term memory (LSTM)24 to make decisions (see Figure 1.9).

Figure 1.9 A simple graphic showing an LSTM neural network. An LSTM is a combination of four machine learning algorithms (shown in blue boxes). These algorithms can be thought of as a cell that makes the overall decision. These use the current input, previous output, and previous cell state to decide; (i) what previous information to forget (forget gate layer), (ii) what needs to be remembered (new memories) and where this information goes (input gate layer), and (iii) what current decision should be made (output decision). The current cell state and current output are then used again as the process restarts itself. This ability to remember and forget makes LSTMs great at tasks involving continuous thinking, such as games and language recognition.

LSTMs are ideal for tasks when decision-making changes with time, as it allows AlphaStar to remember its previous decisions and thought processes to impact its current move. The LSTM then makes a decision to execute an action at a specific location, i.e. to build units or attack the opponent. Finally, AlphaStar considers how the overall game is going in terms of a win prediction to feed into its strategy. For example, if AlphaStar thinks it is winning, it is more likely to attack and try to finish off the opponent. This is one of the most difficult things for a human player to do, and hence it is very impressive that AlphaStar is able to consider this.

So, before the demonstration, AlphaStar needed to be trained to play StarCraft II. Its training began with an initial setup phase where human vs human games were used to extract the basic moves of StarCraft for AlphaStar to imitate. Once the algorithm had these basic moves, it was used as the basis for the AlphaStar League, an internal competition between different algorithms to establish the strongest ones. In each iteration of the League, the strongest algorithms were kept and slightly altered and the weakest discarded (which is the sort of approach used in the AI technique known as genetic algorithms). This allowed the algorithms to discover new strategies and attempt a variety of different tactics. Over many iterations, the best algorithms win out, and these are the ones that played against the professional players in the demonstration. Through the seven-day training procedure AlphaStar was put through in the AlphaStar League, it was estimated that it had played the equivalent of 200 years of StarCraft II for a human pro!

Now, I don't want to spoil the demonstration for those of you who have not seen it, but I can say that AlphaStar performed admirably against human professional players, and the pros and commentators who took part in the demonstration were impressed with the AI. During its training League, AlphaStar was also able to invent new strategies that would be considered unconventional for a human player to choose and sometimes it made in-game, real-time decisions, which baffled experienced commentators but turned out to be excellent choices. I cannot recommend checking out the demonstration highly enough.

CHAPTER 2

How Do Machines Learn?

TIMOTHY E. H. ALLENa,b

a MRC Toxicology Unit, Hodgkin Building, Lancaster Road, Leicester, LE1 7HB, UK

b Centre for Molecular Informatics, Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge, Lensfield Road, Cambridge CB2 1EW, UK

Email: teha2@cam.ac.uk

A variety of machine learning (ML) algorithms exist, and a range of key methods are discussed elsewhere in this text. All ML algorithms draw on the power of computational mathematics to spot and exploit patterns in data. As a result, the machines can be considered as mathematical pattern spotters rather than true learners. That said, the kinds of algorithms that have been developed in computer science to exploit this ability are extremely powerful and can be applied to a great number of problems, which is one of the key reasons for the current level of excitement around ML.

In this chapter, I will describe the general procedure that can be used to build an ML algorithm and describe how it is trained. Here, we will be specifically considering artificial neural networks (ANNs), but many of the issues raised are common to a variety of ML algorithms. To help guide the discussion, two examples are considered throughout – an image classification task to recognise hand-drawn numbers, and a quantitative prediction task, where molecular solubility values are predicted from chemical structure.

2.1 Framing the Question

Computers excel at answering certain types of question but are poor at answering others. Therefore, an essential first step in using ML is to consider the type of question that we are asking the computer.

A common misconception about artificial intelligence (AI) and ML exists – the current methods are not what we would call general intelligence. In other words, they cannot reliably perform tasks outside the range of knowledge on which they have been trained, nor they can display human-like problem solving ability across multiple layers of thought. For example, they cannot break down a problem into smaller steps and then solve each of those individually to reach a conclusion. Rather, current ML algorithms are far better at solving specific problems that are well framed by their human creators. One way to consider if your question is suitable is to consider the “features” and “labels” associated with it (see Figure 2.1).

Figure 2.1 A (very) simple machine learning algorithm.

Simply put, ML features are the inputs and the labels are the outputs. To give an example, in an image classification task, the features are derived from the image and its label describes what the image is. If a question has clearly defined features and labels that are logically linked, even if these links are complicated, it is potentially a suitable area for ML. ML algorithms have shown a remarkable, and rapid, ability to recognise and classify images, now readily demonstrated online. There are simply too many images on the internet to have humans classify every one, so software is trained on a subset of images that have been labelled by humans. In my work, I train ML algorithms to predict the biological activity of molecules. The molecules are the features, and their biological activity is the label. These features and labels are logically linked, as the chemical structure of a molecule determines its ability to bind to an enzyme or disrupt a membrane. Hence, this question is also suitable for ML.

Many computer scientists are confident that AI will, in due course, start to show general intelligence and be able to handle complex questions and provide correspondingly complex answers. At that point, genuinely interesting conversations with a machine should be routine – breaking through the famous Turing test. For now, though, we use what we have at hand. After all, asking my chemistry-based algorithms to classify pictures wouldn't work at all, and the same is true for asking a machine trained to identify images to predict the activity of new molecules. The questions must be carefully considered, and the machines should be used for the purpose for which they were built.

2.2 Gathering Data

A key aspect of ML is the requirement for large quantities of high-quality data. No algorithmic procedure can overcome issues with training data quality. A prediction is of questionable value if it is made by an algorithm that was trained on unreliable or poor-quality data. If, for example, you are trying to build a model to predict the outcome of a chemical reaction, you want the experiments to have been performed by well-qualified scientists who follow good laboratory practice and use new reagents of high purity. If the data are quantitative, you want that information to be measured precisely with equipment that was recently well-calibrated. It may also be desirable that laboratory conditions such as temperature and pressure were consistent, or at least recorded, while all the experiments were being conducted. Obviously, the chances of a single dataset conforming to all the above statements are extremely low. Even when the experimental procedure was of high quality, some uncertainty in the data is almost unavoidable; dealing with this uncertainty is challenging. Data points can be checked manually for consistency, considering the experimental procedures used, the lab in which the experiments were run, and reputation of those running them, but this quickly becomes an overwhelming, and extremely tedious, task.

The volume of data required for hungry ML systems may also be substantial. Generally, ML algorithms require more data points than traditional applications of statistics, such as quantitative structure–activity relationships, because the former are more complex in their mathematical construction. However, all methods benefit from larger data sources as this allows their application to be better assessed across a larger number of scenarios. Luckily, modern techniques, such as high throughput screening (HTS), allow for many data points to be generated relatively quickly. HTS uses robotic and automated experimental procedures to allow large numbers (sometimes on the scale of millions) of experiments to be performed rapidly and consistently. These procedures are popular in drug discovery where the assessment of the ability of new potential drugs to activate or inhibit biological targets can yield their binding coefficients and assess their likely therapeutic activity. Taken together, a balance often is to be sought between having a large number of data points for ML model construction and using only the highest quality data available to ensure that the algorithms produced can be trusted.

A final important consideration is how machines perceive data. As humans, we perceive information in a variety of ways, which we often take for granted. Current computers are not so lucky, and we need to feed data into machines in a way they can understand. This often involves reducing data into strings of numbers that machines are excellent at handling. Consider the example of interpreting images of handwritten numbers, a classic example that has been tackled in ML numerous times. Humans can easily recognise the numbers in Figure 2.2. But to feed these images into a machine, we need to break down each image into pixels and affix a value to each pixel, denoting its grayscale value in the image (see Figure 2.3).

Figure 2.2 Handwritten figures are instantly recognisable to the human eye.

Figure 2.3 A handwritten number can be broken down into computer-readable values. In this example, a 12×12 grid is applied over the number to generate 144 values ranging from 0 to 1 depending on the amount of black in each one.

But how is this relevant to chemistry? All chemists are familiar with chemical structures presented in a similar manner to the one in Figure 2.4. Instead of a drawing, the chemist could describe the main features of the chemical over the phone, or in an email, but such descriptions are perhaps less precise than we would like, and certainly not precise enough for ML. “Chemical fingerprints” are often used to overcome this problem. Chemical fingerprints consider the presence of chemical features in a molecule and convert these into “on” bits in a bitstring. This can be done using features that would be easily identifiable to a human, such as the presence of a particular atom or functional group in the MACCS keys, or using a circular fingerprinting algorithm. Extended Connectivity Fingerprints (ECFPs) are one class of these, and they can be quickly calculated computationally based on individual atom environments (see Figure 2.5).

Figure 2.4 A hand-drawn chemical structure which a human chemist can easily interpret. A human chemist may recognise this molecule as paracetamol.

Figure 2.5 The paracetamol molecule broken down into a set of identifiers, which can be computationally “folded” onto a bit string of a predefined length.

The user selects a radius, and each atom environment, along with its neighbours within that radius, is converted by the computer into an integer identifier. The user also selects a length for the output fingerprint, and the computer hashes the identifiers onto a fingerprint of the fixed-length that the user selected. This is useful for ML as the algorithm will always output the same length string, providing consistency no matter which molecule has been entered. Extended connectivity fingerprints are commonly used in medicinal chemistry and to evaluate the similarity between two molecules by considering the number of “on” bits the molecules share in a procedure such as a Tanimoto similarity calculation. They are not perfect, however, as decoding an ECFP to find the parent molecule is not possible as various different functionalities can be hashed onto a single bit. This is known as a bit collision (see Figure 2.6).

Figure 2.6 For larger molecules and shorter bit string lengths multiple identifiers can be folded onto the same bit, leading to a collision and a loss of chemical information.

Once a database has been obtained for the machine to be trained on, an appropriate algorithm can be chosen for the task and set up for training.

2.3 Setting up the Algorithm

Artificial neural networks are a subclass of ML algorithms based on the workings of animal brains. When you or I learn new information, connections are made between biological neurons in our brains that allow subsequent recall. Connections between biological neurons are known as biological synapses, and they pass the signal across from one neuron to another, given sufficient electrical “push” to get the signal across. These electrical signals jumping through our brains allow us to think and learn, and these are the reasons our brains “light up” in certain areas when we are considering new chemical problems, experiencing pain, or falling in love. Neuroscientists can measure these electrical signals using a technique known as electrophysiology to identify which neurons or set of neurons are active under specific conditions.

Artificial neural networks mimic this process using artificial neurons and artificial synapses (henceforth simply neurons and synapses). The neurons are organised in layers and can be considered as placeholders for numbers. The synapses connect each neuron with all the neurons in both the preceding and the following layers with a mathematical relationship. The first layer of neurons is known as the input layer, the last is the output layer, and any layers in between are the hidden layers (see Figure 2.7).

Figure 2.7 A simple neural network showing the input, output and hidden layers of neurons connected by synapses.

Data are fed into the network through the input layer, and predictions or decisions are revealed by the output layer. In our image classification task, each pixel is assigned a number according to its grayscale. This list of numbers constitutes the inputs. The outputs would be labels associated with the numerical value each image represents (see Figure 2.8). In chemistry, we may wish, for example, to train a neural network to predict the intrinsic solubility of chemicals based on their chemical structure. The chemical structure in the form of a chemical fingerprint can be entered as our list of features, and our labels would be experimentally measured intrinsic solubility values.

Figure 2.8 How different features are generated from handwritten numbers and chemical structures.

Before training can commence, a few important decisions have to be made, specifically concerning the architecture of the network being constructed. Neural networks have one or more hidden layers, each containing a number of neurons. How do we know how many layers to have? How many neurons should each layer consist of?

The answers to these questions are not trivial. In fact, an ML engineer will often consider a number of different network architectures to establish which is best, using trial and error. Generally, more complex tasks, with larger input and output layers, high scientific complexity, and large training datasets will require deeper (more hidden layers) and wider (more neurons per layer) networks. This is not always true though, and shallower and narrower networks train more rapidly and, therefore, are faster to reach a solution. These networks are also less prone to overfitting, a phenomenon we discuss later. Because of this, ML engineers try to abide by Occam's razor, the idea that simpler solutions are more likely to be correct than complex ones. In ML, the search for Occam's razor involves trying a number of parameters and choosing the simplest set which provides a good model.

Once the numbers of neurons and hidden layers have been set, it is time to consider what the synapses between neurons do. I have already mentioned that the synapse is a mathematical relationship, and the simplest of which could take the form:

(2.1)

which in ML is conventionally written:

(2.2)

where w is the weight, and b is the bias. During training, the ML algorithm changes the weight and bias values with each training step in a way that, one hopes, helps it to “learn” patterns in the data provided. However, if all the synapses are linear functions, then the network will be unable to learn. Almost every meaningful problem to which we might wish to apply ML is non-linear, but this cannot be represented by a linear combination of linear functions. To overcome this issue, at each neuron, there are two processing steps: the sum of all incoming synapse signals is calculated, and then the result is put through an “activation function” to determine the output from the neuron. The use of a non-linear activation function is a key reason neural networks can learn and predict non-linearity in data. Some examples of activation functions used in neural networks include the Sigmoid, Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU), and TanH functions (see Figure 2.9).

Figure 2.9 Three widely used activation functions, Sigmoid, ReLU and TanH.

The number of useful activation functions is modest, so the choice between them is often performed using trial and error. Sometimes, the same activation function is used for each layer in the network, while other times different functions are chosen. All allow the network to learn non-linearity in the data, which is the most important consideration.

2.4 The Training Procedure

We have framed our question, selected our data, made it readable by a computer, and set up our network architecture. We are almost ready to press the button and watch our network train. But how does this work?

The first thing to consider is how does the network know how well it is performing. In classification tasks like recognising a handwritten number, the answer is straightforward – if the predicted label (produced by the network given the input) matches the observed label (the label attached to the input in the dataset), then the prediction is correct. Otherwise, it is incorrect. This is modelled computationally using a cost (or loss) function. The simplest cost functions tally how often the network is wrong and add up the cost associated with each wrong prediction. In this case, a perfect predictor would, therefore, score zero, and our objective during training is to minimise the cost function.

Now you might see why training is iterative. When trying to find the best possible model, the algorithm will choose a set of weights and biases and calculate the cost function. This gives a measure of how it is performing, allowing it to make changes to the weights and biases. It can then recalculate the cost function and try again. Each iteration is one training step towards a machine that has “learned” patterns in the data it is given.

Now consider how the value of the cost function changes as we adjust the weights and biases within our network. If we consider only having one parameter (w), we could prepare a plot like Figure 2.10. In this problem, there is a well-defined minimum where the cost function converges, and the slope is 0. Calculating the cost function for every possible value of w to find the minimum is impractical, and the situation is even worse as the number of internal parameters increases. A technique called gradient descent is used to overcome this issue. Initially, an arbitrary starting value for w is chosen, and the cost function calculated. The gradient descent algorithm then calculates the gradient in the cost function curve at this point, telling the ML algorithm which direction is closer to the optimal solution. Where there are multiple weights and biases to consider, the gradient is a vector of partial derivatives with respect to these parameters. The gradient descent algorithm then takes a step in the direction of maximum negative gradient to reduce the value of the cost function as quickly as possible. The weights are updated, more training data run through the network, and a new value of the cost function is calculated (see Figure 2.11).

Figure 2.10 The variation of the cost function with a single changeable parameter (w).

Figure 2.11 Variation of the cost function during training.

By repeating this process, the cost function closes in on the minimum. Over the course of the training procedure, which may contain tens, hundreds, or thousands of training steps, the cost function is reduced to a minimum, and the network is trained. Once training is complete, the network will be evaluated to see how well it performs.

The image recognition task example is a classification task, with the algorithm aiming to correctly identify the number. In cases such as these, a given prediction is either correct or incorrect. In this type of classification task, the percentage of correct predictions is known as accuracy and, as you might expect, the best ML classifiers will have the highest accuracy values. For example, consider our predictions for several hand-drawn number 1s, shown in Figure 2.12.

Figure 2.12 Outcomes from a hypothetical predictor on some hand-drawn numbers, a score for each prediction, with correct predictions being assigned a 1 and incorrect predictions a 0, and a calculated accuracy for these predictions.

In our solubility prediction network, the prediction produced by the network is a number that can be compared to experimentally measured values. The closer these values, the better the predictions are; root mean square error (RMSE) is one way to measure this, and lower RMSE values indicate better models.

(2.3)

where θpred is the predicted value, θexp is the experimental value, and n is the number of values for which predictions are made. In this example, RMSE becomes the basis for the cost function, and the lowest RMSE gives the best model.

2.5 Overcoming Flaws

Once a model has been constructed, it is time to see how it performs. We have already discussed how classification tasks can be evaluated using accuracy, and quantitative prediction tasks can be evaluated using RMSE. An issue here is how to best make these evaluations.

The data used to train the model is known as the training set. As has already been mentioned, the best training sets contain a large number of reliable data points. But any measure of network performance calculated using the training set has an obvious flaw – the model has already seen these examples and learned from them. Hence, it can be considered as a memory task rather than a predictive task. This means that the machine is not learning how to make intelligent predictions about new examples, but it is simply regurgitating information it has already been given. Therefore, to reliably assess performance, we need to use examples from outside the training set to make this evaluation.

A common way to do this is to use a test set – a subset of the entire database that has been held out of the training procedure. Splitting data like this is called the holdout method. Often a ratio of 80% : 20% or 75% : 25% is used, with the larger set used as the training set. While any split can be used, it is worth noting that making the training set too small will make it difficult to train the model and making the test set too small will make validation unreliable (would you trust a model that scored 100% on a classification task in the test set if the test set only included one example?). Sometimes a third set is also used, called the validation set. In this case, the model is trained on the training set, evaluated to ensure optimal training on the validation set, and finally tested on the test set. This helps to ensure that the final model produced is not biased by samples in the test set.

Now that we have a training set and a test set, and we can evaluate model performance on both sets to see how the model performs. Often this is the point at which a major flaw in training becomes apparent – overfitting. Overfitting is the result of a model that, having been trained to such an extent that it learns all the tiny quirks and peculiarities in the training set, shows optimum performance on the training data, but fails to learn general rules and relations in the training data, so works poorly on the test data.

In Figure 2.13, the model is attempting to classify the circles and triangles into different classes. It is possible to draw a mathematical function to perfectly classify the training set data with an accuracy of 100%. Initially, this model looks ideal, but when the test set is considered, many of the data points are placed in the wrong class, and accuracy here is only 50%. Hence, the model is overfitted. What we can do is to recalculate our model with a simpler mathematical function to avoid overfitting (see Figure 2.14). With this model, training accuracy drops noticeably to 83%, but test accuracy increases to 70%. When models are not overfitted, they tend to have closer performance on both the training and the test sets.

Figure 2.13 An overfitted model classifying circles and triangles. This complex model shows good performance on the training data (left-hand plot) but poor performance on the test data (added in darker colours on the right-hand plot).

Figure 2.14 A better model classifying circles and triangles. This simpler model shows poorer performance on the training data (left-hand plot) but improved performance on the test data (added in darker colours on the right-hand plot).

This is great, so how do we take it into account in our ML algorithm? A common strategy is early stopping. This is based on the idea that during early iterations of the training procedure, the algorithm learns the more general features of the training data. While during later iterations, more minor details, relating to just a few or possibly a single training example, are learnt.

Consider Figure 2.15. During early training, the algorithm is learning the general features of the dataset, and as a result, training and test accuracies improve. After a certain number of iterations, however, this trend ends and while the training set accuracy continues to increase, the test set accuracy drops off. In this example, if training was stopped early overfitting would be avoided.

Figure 2.15 The variation of training and test set accuracy with the number of iterations.

Another way to prevent overfitting is to alter the cost function by adding a term to it (the regularisation term) to penalise complexity in the neural network.

Model complexity can be considered as a function of the weights of all the synapses in the neural network. Synapses with high weight values are considered to add more complexity to a model than those with low weights. L2 regularisation is a procedure used to quantify this in the regularisation term, by summing the squares of all the weights in the network.

(2.4)

where wi is the weight value for synapse i among a total of n synapses in the network. The effect of regularisation can be tuned by multiplying the regularisation term by a constant, known as the regularisation rate. The regularisation rate must be high enough to prevent overfitting, but not so high that it prevents the model from learning. After all, a model, which is so simple that it cannot learn from the data, is of no use whatsoever. The ideal regularisation rate allows the model to learn on the training set, but also produce correct predictions when applied to previously unseen examples, either in the test set or real world.

When the regularisation term is added to the cost function it now looks like this:

(2.5)

where Loss (Data|Model) represents the loss associated with the original cost function (i.e. how well our predictions match the observations), L2 regularisation represents the L2 regularisation term shown above, and λ is a constant called the regularisation rate, which controls how much regularisation is used in the model training – too little and the model will be overfitted, too much and the model will be too simplistic to accurately reflect the observed data.

Overfitting is not the only issue that can be encountered during training. Let us consider again the issue of gradient descent towards a minimum value of the cost function (see Figure 2.16).

Figure 2.16 A simple cost function with only one minimum.

In this case, we only have one minimum in the cost function surface, which is convenient. However, most surfaces have multiple minima (see Figure 2.17). As I am sure you have already figured out, this could lead to two trained networks with different statistical performances (see Figure 2.18), depending on where on the surface training begins and how large the taken training steps are. This is obviously an issue, as one of these is not the global minimum and hence not the best possible network.

Figure 2.17 A more complex cost function with multiple minima.

Figure 2.18 On this surface, two descents can find different minima, depending on the start point. Only one is the global minimum – the lowest possible value of the cost function, and hence the best possible model.

As a result of this, it is a common practice to repeat training several times – in the same way, you might repeat an experiment – to ensure that the global minimum is found and that the calculation can be trusted.

2.6 Deploying the Algorithms

So, you've gathered appropriate data and constructed and trained an ML algorithm, taking into account the dangers of data set bias and overfitting. What's next? Well, hopefully, you've constructed a model worthy of being applied to further external data from the real world. In our example models, it might involve classifying further written digits on scanned forms for data entry or predicting physicochemical properties for evaluation during new chemical development.

Just before you head out to change the world, I want finally to go a little further into the subject of model validation and touch on a couple of examples that I think offer valuable lessons.

In computational science, validation can be a touchy subject, and everyone has their favourite and least favourite statistical performance metrics (and during model development, your favourite will likely become the one which paints your model in the best possible light), but they all have strengths and weaknesses. In our hand-drawn numbers classification task, we assigned each prediction as either correct or incorrect, and this allowed us to calculate the accuracy of our predictions. For binary classification tasks, where the actual answer is yes or no, predictions can be classified using a confusion matrix (see Figure 2.19).

Figure 2.19 A confusion matrix for binary classification.

In a classification task, it is common to calculate the number of true positives (TPs), false positives (FPs), true negatives (TNs), and false negatives (FNs). From these, a variety of statistical measures can be calculated including

Sensitivity (also known as true positive rate or recall), the probability an experimental positive is correctly classified;

(2.6)

Specificity (also known as true negative rate or selectivity), the probability an experimental negative is correctly classified;

(2.7)

Positive predictive value (PPV, also known as precision), the probability a predicted positive is experimentally positive;

(2.8)

Negative predictive value (NPV), the probability a predicted negative is experimentally negative;

(2.9)

These metrics each consider half of the predictions made, so these should always be considered in pairs. However, sometimes one being high and the other being low is acceptable, depending on the modelling scenario. For example, consider if you are searching for a rare bird in a jungle, and you have trained a model to predict the location of the bird within a certain area. A model with high PPV would be useful as it reduces the chance of a wasted expedition to try and locate the bird! A high NPV does not really matter in this case as you do not really care where the bird is not. Let's consider another example where you need to test a large number of water samples to detect, which are contaminated. Your machine can test the samples and predict if they come from contaminated sources. In this scenario, it is extremely important to have a high NPV, as otherwise, this could result in tainted water sources going uninvestigated. A high PPV is desirable, but if you must conduct further tests on some water sources that are safe, that is less bad than having contaminated sources remaining untreated.

Some other statistical measures help with data imbalance, including

Balanced accuracy, which averages the sensitivity and specificity, helping to account for small data imbalances between the positive and negative classes;

(2.10)

Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), a measure of model quality, provides a value between −1 and 1. 1 indicates a perfect model, −1 an entirely incorrect model (i.e. every prediction is exactly wrong), and 0 a model thatassigns labels at random. MCC can be used even when classes are very unbalanced;

(2.11)

Finally, a popular measure of model performance in ML is to use the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and calculate the area under it (AUC) (see Figure 2.20).

Figure 2.20 A ROC curve shows how the true positive rate (sensitivity) varies with the false positive rate (specificity). The AUC is to the right of the dotted line; a higher AUC is associated with higher model performance.

This is far from an exhaustive list, and when evaluating models it is best to consider multiple measures of quality to ensure that you are not biased by favouritism. By using good validation practice, you can ensure that you produce good models, and by validating them on additional data when that becomes available you can measure how well they perform in the real world. After all, this is the ultimate objective of any ML model.

One final note is based on ML algorithms and their place within the world of AI. Earlier I considered defining AI as “A machine capable of doing things that humans consider to be intelligent”. This definition suggests that within AI, there is far more than just ML algorithms and neural networks. A great many tasks that require intelligence do not require neural networks to solve them. Consider the computer game minesweeper: with relatively little effort a decent computer player could be programmed, but it would take many hours to train a neural network to learn that game, and the result may not be better. Ultimately, care must be taken when computational approaches are chosen to assist us with scientific problems.
