CHAPTER 5

Machine Learning in Science – A Role for Mechanical Sympathy?

HUGH M. CARTWRIGHT( 0000-0003-0949-2657)

Department of Chemistry, Oxford University, OX1 3QZ, UK

Email: Hugh.Cartwright@chem.ox.ac.uk

5.1 Introduction

The phrase “Mechanical Sympathy” has an interesting origin: it was coined by Jackie Stewart, a British racing car driver. You don't need to be an engineer to enter motor racing, he argued, but knowing about engines can make you a better driver. In other words, to get the best out of something, don't be just a passive consumer.1 As a three-time winner of Formula 1 motor racing championships, perhaps he had a point.

Might “Mechanical Sympathy” be helpful in Artificial Intelligence? Here, we argue that it could.

5.1.1 A Little History

The earliest scientific applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) were Expert Systems (ESs). Incapable of independent learning, the ES was a crude tool by today's standards, requiring pump-priming with rules:

  • “IF the pH is greater than 7, THEN the solution is alkaline”
  • “IF there is strong infrared absorption near 1760 cm−1, THEN suspect a carbonyl group in the molecule”

Human experts were required to determine which rules should be included in the knowledge base. Despite being time-consuming to construct, in a few fields, such as the interpretation of mass spectral fragmentation patterns, their performance hinted that computers might match, and eventually surpass, human scientific reasoning.2

The subsequent development of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), on which this chapter focusses, was a key step in the evolution of AI; in contrast with the ES, these needed no instruction. Despite this clear step forward, computational chemists were initially unimpressed; they continued to concentrate on quantum mechanics and crystallography, using algorithms so greedy for CPU cycles that they sucked up half of all computer time in many Universities in the 1960s and 1970s.

It proved impossible to ignore AI indefinitely though. Like a computational Swiss Army knife, AI evolved to encompass a multitude of tools. Today's “narrow AI” can tackle only one type of problem at a time – spectral interpretation or robotic control perhaps – but its range of application is broad. Intrigued by the promise of fast, intelligent interpretation of data, chemists have been adopting AI enthusiastically.3–7

What could possibly go wrong?

Quite a lot, in fact.

5.1.2 Challenges

This chapter addresses the challenges that await physical and life scientists when they stick a toe into the warm water of AI. Though intended primarily for those who have limited prior experience with AI in science, it may be helpful also for those with greater familiarity.

The challenges discussed below have the potential to seriously compromise an AI application, which sounds alarming. Would it not in that case be safer for scientists to set AI aside and limit themselves to “conventional” methods of analysis? The answer is undoubtedly no. AI is becoming pervasive in society for a good reason – it works – and it promises to be equally successful in science.

So, this chapter is not a warning sign (“Use AI at your own risk”). Instead, it is an information booth (“Look within”). Practical issues do arise when scientists use AI for the first time; here are suggestions of what to look out for.

But this seems perverse; why are suggestions necessary? After all, if AI is so “intelligent”, why should its use present difficulties? For a clue to the reasons, consider the following:

You may be surprised to learn that this is a complete, functioning computer program.8 Written in the wonderfully eccentric language apl (A Programming Language), it executes an example of John Horton Conway's iconic Game of Life,9 which formed the basis of Cellular Automata.

It is not hard to see why apl programs earned a reputation for brevity and incomprehensibility. You could run them from a command line, but would need a “real” programmer to create them or explain how they worked.

For a period in the late 1960s and into the 1970s, apl prospered in science, but it faced a formidable competitor. Though much less compact, programs written in FORTRAN were easy to understand, avoiding the opaqueness that characterised apl; furthermore, FORTRAN programming was in the skill set of many physical and life scientists. Organisations such as QCPE10 offered FORTRAN programs (weighty boxes of punched cards delivered – free of charge! – around the world), which non-computer scientists could use unmodified. Organic chemists became instant near-experts in Molecular Orbital calculations.

As FORTRAN flourished, apl withered; the few available AI programs were underpowered, limited in scope, and quirky, so provided little competition. Fast forward to 2020, FORTRAN is out of favour, and apl has been relegated to a niche role. By contrast, AI is immeasurably more powerful than in its earlier incarnations and, with the benefit of new software, it is easier to use than the arcane programs of a decade ago.

If powerful and rather more friendly AI software has left apl and FORTRAN in the dust, where is the problem? Paradoxically, the danger is ease of use: the more user-friendly the software becomes, the more tempting it is to just feed in one's data and “see what happens”. And even when running the software is not necessarily simple, it is often still possible to use whatever default parameters are set within the software, and then accept the results if they seem “reasonable”. Most AI programs will generate output, no matter how absurd the input, but confidence in that output requires an understanding of the limitations of the software that we use.

We need to know what is going on under the AI hood.

A bit of Mechanical Sympathy would be perfect.

Let's dive in.

5.2 Problems and Solutions

5.2.1 How Many Samples do I Need to Train an AI?

The favourite tool of nuclear physicists is the Large Hadron Collider at CERN in Switzerland,11 which can generate 1017 bytes of data (enough to fill 100 000 1Tb hard discs) in about three minutes. So much data are produced that, after real-time filtering, nearly all are thrown away;12 only the most promising are retained for detailed analysis.

Chemists rarely generate data at such speed, but large-scale databases (including PubChem,13 the Inorganic Crystal Structures Database,14 Reaxys, SciFinder and ChEMBL15) do exist; some are central to applications discussed in this book.

How many samples are needed for training? It might seem that the more data we use, the better the outcome. But it is not quite that simple.

Comment When ANNs first found their way into science, some researchers used their entire experimental dataset for training; the quality of the network was then tested using samples from the same set.16 This might have seemed a good idea at the time, but you probably already realise that it was not. Double-dipping into the dataset is akin to testing a pianist who has learnt sight-reading using half a dozen pieces of music, by asking them to sight-read one of the pieces they already know. Training and testing are separate tasks: samples used during training cannot be re-used for testing.

Some samples in the dataset must, therefore, be held back for testing; how many? Experience suggests that a division of the dataset into 75% for training and 25% for testing often works well; if a validation step (Section 5.2.5) is used, a 70 : 20 : 10 split for training, validation, and testing is reasonable. However, these splits are based on experience, not theory, so these are not immutable.

How large should the database itself be? The more complex and numerous the relationships between features and observables are (see Box 5.1), the more data are required from which the network can learn. In simple problems, such as determining the concentrations of three coloured dyes from the absorption spectra of multiple solutions that contain them, only a few underlying relationships link concentration to absorption (one per dye, if Beer's law holds) and a small database is sufficient; but most problems for which an ANN might be considered are more complicated and require far more data.

Box 5.1 A Little Terminology.

The role of an ANN is to find relationships that link features (also known as descriptors, predictors, attributes, feature vectors or fingerprints) to observables (also known as targets, ground truth or labels). For example, if the aim was to find the composition of novel solvents for organic materials, the training data might consist of various known solvents whose features included their molecular weight, molecular dipole, synthetic feasibility, pH, number of carbon atoms etc., while the observables could be the solubility of different organic solids in those solvents.

Training takes place in a series of cycles (or epochs), during each of which the network is shown the entire training set once.

The difference between the known values of the observables and those generated by the network is the test or validation error (or loss function).

The search for efficient synthetic routes (discussed elsewhere in this book) is typical of a complex problem in which an ANN may be of use. The yield of a chemical reaction depends on the identity of reagents, presence of catalysts, solvent, temperature and pressure, reaction phase and other factors, so there are many relationships that contribute to the links between features and observables. A suitable database will be very large.

For some complex problems, the database may, in fact, be so large that training becomes unreasonably lengthy, even after a portion of the database has been reserved for validation and testing. It may then be necessary to use Data Reduction (Section 5.2.4) to slim down the database prior to training.

At the other extreme, some databases are too small, a problem that is more common in chemistry than in many other sciences. To fill in the gaps, additional data might be generated through further experiments, by lifting information from unstructured sources such as journal publications using data mining or by accessing previously unused databases. Google Scholar,17 a powerful tool for searching scientific publications, has recently been complemented by Google Dataset Search.18 This executes rapid searches by keyword of many thousands of commercial, non-commercial, government and other websites, a process that can be helpful in locating previously unrecognised databases.

Another potential option when the database is small is Transfer Learning,19,20 commonly used in image recognition. We first train a network using a large pool of data related to the topic in which we are interested. The trained network then becomes the starting point for a shorter period of training, using samples from the small database. The purpose of this secondary training is to tweak the previously determined network weights; in essence a network trained to solve one problem is tuned to solve a second. The procedure is efficient, making use of databases that might otherwise be too small for effective learning, and can also be beneficial if a database is unbalanced. Neural Turing machines and imitation learning provide further ways to make effective use of small datasets.

A final comment on dataset size: if the dataset is small, you might think that one way to use it to best advantage would be to:

(i) train the network, reserving as usual a portion of the dataset for testing;

(ii) then return the test data to the dataset and use those samples to finish training.

Superficially this is attractive; it seems to resemble Transfer Learning, mentioned above. The 20–30% of the data that the network was not shown during training might contain useful information, so why not give the network this extra information to “top up” its learning?

The problem is that a final polishing of the network using the test set could lead to a better model, but we cannot be confident that it will do so, as there is no way to test the updated ANN. If there is bias in the test data, for example, the model may degrade rather than improve: we have no means of detecting this. Equally, without an independent check of performance, we might terminate training too early, or allow it to run for too long, leading to an under- or over-trained model. Avoid feeding test data back into the dataset to try to improve the model; it is never wise.

5.2.2 We Are Combining Databases; Do Difficulties Await?

Babies enter a rich, chaotic world and immediately start to make sense of sounds, shapes, lights, and tastes. It would save time if AIs could emulate this,19 learning from random, unrelated pieces of data; but that's not how AIs work. The difference between a successful application and a failure may be the care with which data are curated. What does that involve?

Comment Without proper data curation, our approach is “hope for the best”. This is a poor strategy; in fact, it is not a strategy at all. If we just throw data into a Machine Learning (ML) pot to see what happens, we should prepare to be disappointed, especially if the data are complex, recorded over long periods, subject to significant noise, or derived from multiple sources.

Data collection is just the first step in curation. Not all data are in accessible, well-maintained databases; some might be buried in journals, presentations, figures, tables, lab notebooks, poorly documented experiments, or even diaries. Tools such as ChemDataExtractor21 can interrogate unstructured sources, but the data that they yield are often in a format incompatible with data obtained elsewhere. Data must be classified and authenticated, labelled, checked for relevance and unreadable entries, possibly reformatted, and archived in a form suitable for future use – all these are curation tasks.

Information can also be biased (see Box 5.2), intentionally or inadvertently;22,23 whatever the origin, bias can slow learning and diminish its effectiveness. Data from cheap, quick and easy experiments can be more generously represented in databases than data from more challenging, but information-rich, experiments. As one would anticipate, researchers contribute results mainly from their own field, so this too leads to data being plentiful in some areas, weaker in others. Bias may also arise when data from commercial sources are partially redacted, to prevent competitors from learning about areas that might be commercially sensitive. Even failed reactions could be revealing, so these might be omitted or obfuscated. These effects work against the generation of a successful ML model, which requires that data cover all areas of the search space roughly evenly.

Box 5.2 Bias.

Both the composition of a database and the way that samples are chosen from it can bias learning. Here are some examples:

  • Overrepresentation within the database of data that are easy to obtain, while data that are more challenging to collect, but nevertheless potentially valuable, are poorly represented.
  • Overrepresentation within the database of data from one's own specialised field compared to other relevant fields.
  • Deliberate withholding of pertinent data from the database for commercial reasons, or to prevent others from gaining a research advantage.
  • Selection of only a portion of the dataset for learning by excluding samples that might not support what you wish to prove.
  • Weighting all samples equally, even though some are known or suspected to be less reliable.
  • Selection of samples from a dataset in a non-random fashion; for example, without sufficient evidence to justify the choice, choosing only data from particular years, or data only from research groups you are familiar with or who work in particular countries.
  • Selection of databases without adequate justification for using some and omitting others.

Curation is like digging the garden in the spring, a tedious but unavoidable task before the more gratifying one of harvesting. The process of actually feeding data into an ML application must wait upon curation, a task that may take far longer than training, but one that is nonetheless vital.

5.2.3 We Use a Chemical Reactions Database to Predict Synthetic Routes, but We Are Making Little Progress. What Might Be Going Wrong?

Given high-quality, diverse data, we feel ready to start our ML. But even well-curated databases can contain holes.

Comment Marquee science projects, such as predicting the composition of materials with pre-specified properties,7 creating a room temperature superconductor,24 or the computational design of synthetic routes,25 are technically challenging, industrially important, and commercially valuable.

For such projects, a large dataset is essential. This is the so-called Curse of Dimensionality:26 as the number of independent features required for effective learning grows, the number of samples needed for training increases roughly exponentially with the number of features. Consider the design of synthetic routes: from Organic 101 you may recall what products to expect when two organic chemicals are mixed, but in planning a viable, high-yield synthetic route this level of knowledge is completely inadequate. Machine-readable, fully contextualised data with “above the arrow” information such as solvents, catalysts, temperature, time, the order of addition of reagents etc. are essential. It is not uncommon to find that some of this critical data are not reported for reactions in the literature, severely limiting the value of the data.

Negative data are not as troublesome as unreported data, though; in fact, negative data can be valuable. An ANN cannot learn from data it never sees, but it can utilise negative results.27 Reactions that fail, have a low yield, or are extremely slow are far less likely to appear in the literature than successful reactions,28 but the knowledge that a reaction is not viable allows us to rule out proposed synthetic routes that involve it. If data on failed reactions are missing, it may be possible to estimate them using maximum likelihood methods,25 or an external analytical model. Alternatively, speculative data for failed reactions may be created for reactions that could be considered to be plausible, but can reasonably be supposed to be failures.29,30

5.2.4 Our Database Is so Large That Training Will Take Forever. What Can We Do?

The perfect dataset is comprehensive yet compact, noise-free, machine-readable, evenly spread across the search space, and in a consistent format. Real datasets contain noise, redundancies, duplicates and errors, and may be in a mix of formats (data in both metric and imperial units perhaps, or in numerical and text form). Even worse, some databases may be so bloated that training becomes virtually impossible.

Comment Curation is not a sharply demarcated process; it overlaps with preprocessing, during which we massage information in the database to improve the prospects for learning.

A simple and common type of preprocessing is the scaling of data. If features to be fed into an ANN have very different magnitudes, the larger values may dominate learning, so that features whose values are always small act as little more than noise during the learning process. In principle, the ANN itself is capable of scaling down large values so that they do not dominate learning. However, when large values feed into a sigmoidal activation function, there is only a feeble dependence of output on input, as the activation function plateaus at large input values. Learning is then slow and can be ineffective. Scaling reduces this effect by bringing all feature values into approximately the same range.

Scaling is straightforward, but a more critical challenge arises when a database is so large that it is almost unusable. Some of the largest databases in chemistry comprise molecular data; Reaxys, for example, contains data on more than 100 million compounds. Each molecule may be characterised by hundreds of features, including molecular weight, logP values, number of chiral centres, molecular polarity, and molecular volume. The inclusion of very large numbers of compounds and numerous features in a database provides great flexibility; data can be added to the database without needing to know which features might be of value in some future application, so a comprehensive database encourages wide applicability. Unfortunately, it can also make the database unwieldy.

The molecular features that are key in an application may lie alongside hundreds of other features, which are irrelevant or redundant, so some way of either identifying those key features or cutting back the dataset can be essential. Features of low information content can be identified using a Genetic Algorithm,31 and then discarded before training begins. Alternatively, Principal Component Analysis (PCA)32 can be used to create a new set of linearly independent “components”, each of which represents a blend of the dominant features of the data and is associated with an eigenvalue which quantifies the variability in the data that the component encapsulates. The eigenvalues can be used to determine how many components should be retained: components with large eigenvalues are used, while those with small eigenvalues are discarded. (You will recognise that there may be a grey area between the components that we deem to have “large” eigenvalues and so are kept, and the components that are unlucky enough to have “small” eigenvalues, so are candidates for removal.)

As a side benefit, this culling of components with small eigenvalues can help reduce noise. If the signal-to-noise ratio in the dataset is high, most noise should be concentrated in components with small eigenvalues, so removal of these will lessen their influence, while leaving the meaningful features largely untouched. The PCA procedure does unavoidably blend a degree of noise into the sample features though, so some noise is retained in the large eigenvalue components; some information also is lost along with noise by discarding components with low eigenvalues. In addition, the components that are retained do not have a simple physical interpretation.

Nevertheless, data reduction is valuable; it improves efficiency by reducing the size of the dataset, so training should be faster. It may also limit distortion arising from misleading or erroneous data, as the overall effect of a small number of faulty samples within a large dataset may be no greater than the background noise, so will largely be concentrated in the components with small eigenvalues. Finally, a reduction in the number of features diminishes the chances of overfitting and leads to a simpler model. Although the choice of how many components to keep is a matter of judgement, both experience and the eigenvalues themselves provide useful guidance.

5.2.5 How Do I Set the Parameters?

AIs process data, not meaning; whether they predict the composition of a superconductor or the probability that the Yankees will win the World Series next year, their mode of action is roughly the same. Flexibility and ease of use are among their attractions, but the latter can be a trap: if you train a network “blind”, using the default parameters, sub-optimal or even meaningless results are likely. How should the parameters be set for the best chance of success?

Comment Successful AI applications require more than just high-quality data. The values of several parameters (known as hyperparameters) affect how well an ANN learns, and as these parameters interact in complex ways, it can be difficult to determine the optimum value for every one of them.

Of the parameters in an ANN, the connection weights, which comprise the network's memory, are the simplest to deal with. In fact, we do not need to deal with them at all, for these are under the control of the network itself, and are updated during training.

Although the numbers of input and output nodes are nominally under user control, in practice these numbers are determined from the dataset. One input node is required for every feature (such as each wavelength in an IR spectrum at which the absorption has been measured), and an output node for every observable that the network will predict (the presence or absence of absorption peaks associated with different normal modes of vibration, for example).

The most crucial of the remaining parameters, all of which can be set by the user, are those that define the network geometry. The number of hidden layers and number of nodes per layer determine how many connection weights there are, and this in turn determines how complex a problem the network can solve. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have many layers, so these can tackle more complex problems, but in the neural network world, bigger is not necessarily better. Large networks are prone to overfitting, in which not just relationships but individual samples from the dataset and noise are learnt, diluting network generality. Choices also must be made of the type of activation function to be used, the learning rate and momentum factor and how the data will be split between training, test and validation sets (see Box 5.3).

Box 5.3 Validation.

It might seem that training is completely independent of the test set. The test set is used for just a single purpose: to measure the quality of the trained network; it is never used to update network weights.

However, even though testing appears to be “at arm's length” from training, this hides a problem. Training and testing are not truly independent because the test set determines when training should be halted. In this way, the performance of the completed model depends on the composition of the test set. If a different test set were used, training might have continued longer, or be brought to a halt earlier, thereby influencing the extent of learning.

To address this issue, it is common to use a validation set. Like the test set, validation samples are picked at random from the dataset. As the network is trained, its performance is monitored using the validation set, not the test set. When the validation error reaches a minimum, training is stopped and at that point the network is shown the test set; it is the error on this test set that we use as a measure of the network's quality.

Provided that neither the network nor the database is very large, this process can be repeated with different values for the hyperparameters, and different validation sets. One can then choose the values for the hyperparameters that gave the best overall performance.

With several parameters to be set, how should we proceed? First, we should be aware that for many straightforward problems a single hidden layer in the ANN is sufficient. Small networks train rapidly and are good generalisers, so, even though choices must still be made about geometry and learning parameters, a trial-and-error approach is usually feasible. Small networks are also less likely to learn noise in the data or learn specific examples from it because all the connection weights are needed to describe relationships in the data. A small network with one hidden layer is therefore often an appropriate starting point.

When the data are more complicated, more than a single hidden layer may be required. Although network design is then more difficult, we are not completely in the dark. If PCA has been used for data reduction, the number of principal components that have been retained will be known, and this can be used as a guide to network size. Nevertheless, although the number of parameters to be set is not large, they interact in ways that can be difficult to predict, so a logical approach is helpful. Evolutionary methods, in particular the Genetic Algorithm,31 have proved to be a popular tool for finding networks of high quality. Their principal disadvantage is that they must be effectively integrated into the ANN, as it is rarely feasible to run a Genetic Algorithm optimisation of a neural network by hand.

A further option is offered by expanding or pruning networks.33 In the first method, a network that is likely to be too small is trained, and a test set used to assess its performance. A single node is then added to a hidden layer, and the newly enlarged network trained from scratch and re-assessed. Further nodes are added and training repeated until performance (as judged by the test set) shows the network starting to learn noise and examples. The size of the “ideal” network is in this way determined.

We might instead consider an inverse procedure, in which we start with a network thought to be too large, and then repeatedly train, assess, and prune the network, removing one node at a time, until performance begins to deteriorate noticeably. Of the two methods the former is more practical, because the networks being tested are smaller than the optimum, and therefore train rapidly, while in a pruning scheme the discarded networks are all too large, so train more slowly.

You may have spotted a difficulty though: for networks of two or more layers, we must decide which layer is altered each time the geometry is updated. Although in deep networks individual layers may be used to recognise different features of the data, this is rarely feasible in two- or three-layer networks, so an element of trial-and-error is almost unavoidable unless an evolutionary algorithm is used.

5.2.6 How Has My AI Learnt Something That Is Not There?

You have written an ANN program to recognise cats. Keen to avoid bias, you train it with an equal number of images of black cats, white cats and ginger cats, then test the trained network on some fresh pictures of cats and dogs. The ANN consistently identifies dogs as non-cats – that's encouraging – but strangely it sometimes correctly identifies an image as a white cat, but later misidentifies exactly the same image as a black cat. What is going on?

Comment This sounds like a minor, tolerable irritation; most AI tools are not correct 100% of the time,19 so we must be prepared to accept the odd mistake. But there may be deeper problems.

ANNs used on time-based data, such as the progression of illness in an acutely unwell patient or the online control of a chemical flowshop, typically have a feedback (or recurrent) structure. This gives them a temporal memory; in other words, they can learn sequences. Our cat problem has arisen because the ANN has learned from both the training data and from how the data were presented. In our eagerness not to bias training, we have shown it a white cat, a black cat, a ginger cat, a white one, a black one, a ginger one, a white one, … and so on. The algorithm has unwittingly been fed extra information:

“if you see a white cat, the next image will be a black cat”

and has learnt from it.

In time series, a knowledge of how one data point relates to its neighbours is vital information, but if you never analyse such series you might feel that you can ignore the issue of presentation.

But there is a fundamental problem here. Databases are frequently organised in a logical fashion (or even in an illogical, but nevertheless ordered, fashion); molecules might appear in the order of increasing molecular weight, all chemical reactions involving amino acids might be collected together, drugs might be listed in the order of decreasing effectiveness, or all data derived from research groups in a particular country might be grouped together. One might note in passing that even if the database as a whole does not display this degree of ordering, some level of organisation is quite common. Data uploaded to a database are often unintentionally biased – an incoming chunk of data might all be from the same research group perhaps, or all relate to the same group of reactions or the same drug testing program – the database may then contain regions that are not representative of the whole unless the entire database is periodically randomised. If samples are not drawn from the dataset in a truly random fashion, learning can be affected; this is a potential problem even for a standard feedforward algorithm. The solution is simple: just select samples genuinely at random during training.

5.2.7 My Trained AI Tested Beautifully; Now It Produces Rubbish

When a creative person “thinks outside the box” we may be impressed by the result. When an AI does the same, we can expect trouble.

Your PhD student, whose project was to use AI to predict phase diagrams, has given up Chemistry to become a merchant banker. Figure 5.1 shows data from her most recent experiment,34 which was almost finished when she left to make her fortune.

Figure 5.1 The mole fraction of propanol in the vapour phase above a propanol-water mixture as a function of composition. Points at low propanol mole fraction (<0.1M) are missing.

You'd like the complete diagram, so you plug in the experimental data that she has already measured and use her AI to predict the rest of the figure. Are you feeling confident about the result?

Comment Before we tackle your student's problem, take a look at Figure 5.2, which shows how height varies with age for a group of schoolchildren.

Figure 5.2 Variation of height with age for 100 children.

Let's train an ANN with the data, and then ask it how tall a typical seven-year-old child is. “About 118 cm” it responds.

This seems right; how about a typical 75-year-old? The ANN is confident once again: 580 cm (about 19 feet) is its estimate. Of course, the mistake is ours, not that of the ANN. The network has done as instructed, learning how age (the feature) determines height (the observable). However, even though the trained network answers our queries, the reliability of the answers that it provides diminishes the further away the question takes it from the boundaries of the dataset. Its estimate of the height of a 14-year-old might be reasonable, as it has seen data relating to children close to that age, but a 75-year-old is so far from any data that it has been trained on that its conclusions are meaningless.

Returning to our scientific example, the full set of experimental data is shown in Figure 5.3.

Figure 5.3 The mole fraction of propanol in the vapour phase above a propanol-water mixture as a function of composition. All points, including those shown at low propanol mole fraction, are experimental data.

It is clear that we cannot reasonably expect the AI to adequately predict the four points in black in Figure 5.3. if the only data that it had access to during training was the points shown in Figure 5.1. Confidence in the ANN's responses to questions that lie outside the bounds defined by the information in the database must be low, an observation that may be forgotten when working with very large databases, as we may not even know precisely what the limits are. We conclude that we should be cautious about accepting the output of an ANN unless we have evidence that the data from which it has learnt suitably cover the range of samples in which we are interested.

5.2.8 My AI Solved the Challenges in Box 5.4; How Did It Manage It?

Box 5.4 What is the next number in each of these series?

  • Series A: 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 8, ….
  • Series B: 6, 6, 7, 9, 8, 6, …

[Not sure of the answers? They follow later.]

If our AI solved the problems, did it use brilliance or luck? There is no use in asking for an explanation; AIs don't show their working.

Comment Explanation is fundamental; in the absence of solid justification, predictions are persuasive only when they are consistently right. Without evidence, a correct prediction might be a stab in the dark, or reliable just within some limited domain.

This is not to say that inexplicable science is valueless. Quantum theory does not provide an explanation for wave-particle duality, yet still is part of the bedrock of science. Nevertheless, if we are offered a startling conclusion without explanation by an AI we might reasonably be cautious.

Though the “knowledge” of an ANN is encoded in its connection weights, an individual weight does not “mean” anything. The weights are not even unambiguous: ANNs of identical geometry trained on the same data can converge on completely different sets of weights and yet still yield similar predictions. It is the combination of weights with network geometry that relates features to observables, but the mathematical relationships encoded within the trained network are far from constituting a coherent explanation.

It is difficult to discern what small networks are telling us with their connection weights, so we can expect that deep networks will present even greater challenges. Their multiple layers combine deep power with deep impenetrability. The performance of DNNs in challenges such as playing Go and in protein folding are impressive, and we may be prepared to tolerate inadequate explanation because of their power. Nevertheless, in safety-critical tasks, such as control of commercial aircraft or nuclear missiles, we should be wary of using methods whose conclusions we cannot interrogate. Even in non-safety-critical applications in science, we should not feel that DNNs are the gold standard (see Box 5.5). On many types of problems, they perform no better than smaller networks and are even more difficult to interpret.

Box 5.5 Some Limitations of Deep Learning Networks.

  • The networks are complex, with many weights, so a large quantity of training data is required.
  • Training is lengthy, so substantial computer power is needed.
  • In common with other ANNs, DNNs currently have a poor ability to explain their “reasoning”.
  • DNNs are unable to integrate prior knowledge; for example, they cannot at present explicitly take into account physical laws such as those that govern the electrostatic interaction between two ions (though they may be able to learn about such laws from the data).
  • There is evidence that trained DNNs can sometimes be misled by showing them data that differ only marginally from the data on which they have been trained (for example, using adversarial images).
  • They are poor at dealing with hierarchical knowledge, a form of information that humans can readily understand and use.

In passing, we should also note that ANNs are not alone in being difficult to interpret. Support Vector Machines project data into high-dimensional space, of which we can only visualise a small portion. Support Vector Machines are no better at explaining what they have done than are ANNs.

Even in non-safety-critical applications, explanation would be helpful. If a black box model cannot be interpreted, it cannot be manually expanded or improved. We cannot pick apart the ANN model and stitch in additional pieces, nor can an ANN learn how to complete a task and then instruct a human on how to carry out the same task efficiently. Future generations of AI tools will not only be good at doing what we cannot, such as calculating how proteins fold, but also good at what we can, for example driving a car. If we are to make the best use of an AI which has learnt skills that humans are familiar with, it will be essential that we can understand how it reached its decisions and learn from them (even be taught by them).

There are ethical considerations too. There is no “morally correct” way to fold a protein or determine whether a black hole lies at the centre of a galaxy, but we can imagine situations in which the decisions of an AI may be both difficult to predict and hard to justify. Suppose an autonomous car suddenly finds itself in a situation in which a collision is inevitable, an accident that will cause injury to you as the passenger (and to the AI itself), or instead to multiple pedestrians. If the car has no ethical compass – and can we at present imagine how it would learn such a thing? – it may prioritise its own, and your, survival over that of many other humans. We could run trial accidents with virtual cars and people to see how the AI reacts, but would we be comfortable with the idea that, after training in such a virtual world, the AI may have developed its own ethical guidelines and yet still be unable to articulate them?

Critical situations arise in other fields such as the control of chemical plants. As AIs control progressively larger sections of a complex plant, our need to understand how decisions are made will grow stronger. The development of AIs that can explain themselves to humans will be an essential requirement as they become ubiquitous.

5.2.9 My AI Thinks that Basketball Players Cause Global Warming

Figure 5.4 demonstrates that high salaries for players in the NBA (National Basketball Association) cause global warming. Other factors that raise the temperature of the earth include a drop in the number of elephants in Norway, and the increasing cost of rubber boots in Belgium.

Figure 5.4 The link between the average salary of basketball players and global mean temperature rise.35,36

Except, of course, that they don't.

Comment AIs have ability but no intelligence. They can reveal correlations – statistical measures that describe the degree to which two sets of values are related – but ANNs cannot determine whether correlation indicates causation, where the change in one variable is directly responsible for a change in another. Meaningless correlations, for example between the population of Scandinavian elephants and global temperature, constitute the problem of “false discovery”.

False discovery took on particular significance in the middle of the last century. The rate of lung cancer was rising (the illness was so rare at the start of the 20th century that many physicians would see no cases during a lifetime in practice), but the cause of the rise was unknown. In 1950, Bradford Hill and Richard Doll, having previously theorized that exposure to tarmac or car fumes might be responsible, published findings that suggested that smoking cigarettes was to blame instead.37

The response of cigarette manufacturers was predictable: outright denial. Lung cancer was not caused by smoking, they argued, but by an unidentified heritable factor that made some people unusually susceptible to lung cancer; the same factor made people prone to addiction to tobacco. The smoking↔lung cancer correlation was there, but the link was this unknown heritable factor, not smoking. Genetics (had it been the real explanation) was what is known as a confounding variable; a factor that affects two completely separate elements – in this case lung cancer rates and tobacco addition – that are not linked causally to one other. Years passed before the companies admitted that their introduction of a confounding factor was not based on any meaningful data and that smoking did indeed cause lung cancer.

As we see with NBA player salaries and global warming, the values of two properties may be correlated without a linking mechanism. Surprisingly, the reverse can also be true: one factor may directly affect another and yet not be correlated with it. An example is a thermostat, which maintains a constant temperature in a house. As the outside temperature falls, the thermostat runs the heating for longer and the heater burns more gas. As the temperature in the house is virtually constant, there is a negligible correlation between the temperature of the thermostat and the amount of gas consumed, even though the thermostat causes the change in gas consumption.

Correlation (also called association) is not causation. But how can we distinguish one from the other? Teasing out the difference can be complex. Bayesian networks,38 already used in speech recognition, weather forecasting, and other areas, are a potential solution for some problems. These are more open to scrutiny than most types of ML, so in favourable cases, it is easier to disentangle correlation and causation.

There is not enough space here to delve into Bayesian methods, and, though useful, they are by no means an infallible way of detecting causation. The message is that if your ML application seems to suggest that two parameters are correlated, be cautious in assuming that one must cause the change in the other. Scientific input to back up the conclusion of the ANN is necessary.

5.2.10 Results from my AI Suggest that my Data Contain only Noise, but I Think there Might be Something Real present. How can I Tell?

Almost all scientific datasets contain noise. Some noise may be averaged out as the ML learns, but what if that noise is not noise at all and learning is destroying the signal?

Comment As they orbit their star, planets beyond our solar system may pass between the star and the earth, causing a brief drop in the amount of starlight reaching us. Astronomers use the change in intensity during these transits to infer the presence of a planet.39 As planets are so much smaller than stars the changes are slight, so the alteration in the signal may be swamped by the background variability of the starlight. How can we deal with this?

A potentially useful approach is PCA, which we met in Section 5.2.4. The eigenvalues that a PCA treatment of a dataset yield tell us how much variability in the dataset each eigenvector represents. If the dataset contained nothing but noise, the values of the eigenvalues would be expected to decrease in a roughly monotonic manner. If there are genuine, albeit small, signals in the data, this should be reflected in one or more eigenvalues whose size sets them apart from eigenvalues which just represent noise.

If we know what the signal might look like, instead of training the ANN using raw data, we can train it using examples of the signal. Astronomers are keen to detect amino acids in interstellar space as possible indicators of life elsewhere in the galaxy. Traces of amino acids have been found within meteorites, and so it is reasonable to infer that these molecules might also exist in interstellar space, but they are difficult to detect because their concentration is apparently very low. An ANN can be trained on a set of laboratory spectra of amino acids and then fed experimental spectra from astronomical observations to look for the very weak signals which might suggest the presence of these molecules. The reverse process, in which an ANN is trained using experimental astronomical observations and then shown the spectrum of a sample amino acid is likely to be less successful because of the incorporation of large amounts of noise into the model. Neither approach is trivial to execute because of the extreme weakness of the astronomical signals (if indeed they are there at all). Nevertheless, AI methods show promise in interpreting weak signals such as these.

5.2.11 My AI Was Fine Until I Found Some Extra Data to Give It; Why Did the Data Make It Worse, Not Better?

Narrow AI is good at learning one thing but struggles to go further.

Comment We train an AI until learning is maximised as measured by performance on a test set. If training is later resumed, using additional, previously unseen data, what was learnt before may be slowly forgotten, as new information begins to overwrite the old (but see Transfer learning in Section 5.2.1); loss of prior learning is especially likely if the new data lie in a very different area to the old. An algorithm trained to recognise dogs will gradually lose that ability if subsequently it is trained with further images that include only other animals.

Deep learning avoids some of these problems, as a DNN can be constructed with constrictions that may force different layers to learn different aspects of the data. Even then, if a trained network is flooded with fresh data that lie in a new area knowledge will degrade. A DNN can play Chess, play GO, or fold a protein, but cannot do all three tasks.

5.2.12 My AI Struggles Even Though It Has Plenty of Data

Being able to calculate the error or loss function is an absolute requirement for an ANN; without access to the values of observables, an ANN cannot learn. Before learning starts, we must define a goal; this may be quite simple to express, recognising fractures in X-rays perhaps, or predicting the composition of ultrahard materials. But the ANN needs a goal in scalar or vector numerical form, not a general and woolly wish list. Defining goals can be challenging; some problems are ill-formed. What does this mean?

Comment The goal of an ill-formed (or ill-defined) problem is unclear or difficult to quantify. The most common reason is that the overarching goal comprises many sub-goals, with little chance that all of them can be satisfied simultaneously.

Suppose that we decide to use AI to devise a new polymer film, which will act as a temporary skin for people who have suffered serious burns. We require that the product should be effective, non-toxic, retain its properties long enough that the skin underneath it can properly recover. There are other possible criteria too: it should be straightforward to apply so that it could be used in an emergency by untrained personnel; it should not bind to the recovering skin; it should be cheap to produce, have a long shelf life, be easy to synthesise, and promote healing. The list of goals is long, and we might at first believe this to be an advantage: the more goals there are the more precisely the ideal product can be defined. By giving the ANN very specific guidance about these goals surely it can home in on precisely the right formulation? The reality is just the opposite.

There are both practical and ethical problems in using our AI in this example. Recall that an ANN attempts to minimise the difference between its actual output for a sample and the desired output. For all samples in our dataset, we must, therefore, start by determining the observable(s) by combining the many contributing factors, each separately weighted to reflect their relative importance. But “relative importance” is a matter of judgement. How should ease of use of the product be balanced against complexity and safety of the production process? What level of toxicity is acceptable: if one person dies while 99 are saved is that acceptable? What about five deaths, or ten? Suppose that the product would save lives but is so expensive that it would draw funds away from other crucial health services; how do we judge whether the new polymer skin is, overall, beneficial, taking into account the negative effects elsewhere arising from loss of funding? Or – even more problematic – suppose that the polymer skin might work well for people with one particular blood group and not at all for those with a different group; would it be appropriate to fund development and deployment of a product of benefit to only a minority of the population?

Left to its own devices, we cannot expect that the ANN will be able to optimise every observable independently. Instead, it might propose a product that is both extremely effective and extremely costly, or one that is cheap, easy to use, and toxic. Consequently, before we attempt to train the network, we must make these judgements ourselves, possibly on very limited data. Ill-formed problems are not unusual; they are often among the really complex problems that we would most like to solve. As AI increases in power, many more such problems will become amenable to attack. The technical challenges of constructing an ANN, which can tackle such problems are minor compared to the larger questions of how multiple goals should be combined. Even when ethical issues do not complicate the issue, there are no simple answers here.

5.2.13 The Problem: My AI Is Just Odd

AIs can produce curious results, even when they behave as designed.

Comment AI is barely out of its diapers, so we should not be surprised when applications don't always turn out as planned.

Consider what may happen when the great majority of cars are autonomous. The cars must assure the safety of both passengers and pedestrians, so if a pedestrian suddenly steps off the pavement in front of a car, it must stop, and move only when the pedestrian is clear. If another pedestrian then steps into the road, the car must stop again. What will be the likely consequence in cities with many cars? Pedestrians will quickly realise that it is safe to step into the road, no matter how heavy the traffic. Before long, traffic flow will come to a halt. The ultimate in safe roads, perhaps, but the demands for policing of pedestrian behaviour using methods such as face-recognition technology may become overwhelming.

Unexpected behaviours will not be confined to the roads. Consider an AI whose role will be to control an industrial plant in which chemicals flow into an open tank, react, and then leave through an outlet pipe. If the tank overflows, safety will be compromised, so the AI must learn to adjust the rate of liquid inflow to prevent this happening. We train it on a virtual model of the plant, using a loss function which penalises the AI whenever liquid overflows from the tank. It should soon learn how to keep the liquid level within safe limits, but we might not anticipate that it will learn that the simplest way to do this is to turn off the liquid flow entirely. Safe it is, efficient it is not.

In simple, readily interpretable units such as a chemical flow system, it is possible to spot and correct unwanted behaviour at an early stage. The more control that AIs have, however, the more complicated and inscrutable their behaviour will become; it will then be imperative that any system put in place can be demonstrated unambiguously to behave in a reliable and logical way.

5.2.14 It Is Going Pear-shaped. What Can I Do?

In this final section, we look briefly at a further selection of problems you might encounter with your ANN.

5.2.14.1 The Network Is Not Learning

Check the data. If there is little sign of learning, test the ANN using a well-studied, small dataset, such as the Iris.40 Learning for this dataset should be nearly complete within at most a few dozen cycles; if it is not, the data may be being read incorrectly, or the network is not working correctly. Could the ANN be reading the data column by column instead of row by row, or vice versa? If the data are being read correctly, and you are able to inspect the network weights, feed a single sample through and recheck the weights by hand after backpropagation to see that they have updated as intended. It's tedious, but this is a thorough way to find programming errors.

Check the activation function. Step functions do not work for meaningful problems; if you are using one, change it to a sigmoid function like tanh or ReLU.

Check the data labels. Perhaps samples in the dataset are being read correctly, but are mislabelled, so the observables do not relate to the samples to which they are attached. Check the labels in a portion of the dataset by hand. If they seem correct, train a small network using just this checked set and see if testing shows that learning is improved.

Is there anything there to learn? The data may contain nothing that links input to output. This is more likely if you are using a large dataset and have selected a subset of sample features and/or observables for training. Stop the training, expand the dataset by around 20%, adding samples that contain only random data, then train again from scratch. If performance is no worse the datasets may contain no information that the network can use.

Check the network geometry. The network may be too large. If so, it may memorise each sample in the dataset individually and not discover any relationships, thereby avoiding learning the rules needed to identify any test samples. Start training with a small network and a modest number of samples. If there is evidence of learning, gradually increase the number of samples to prove that there is data that the network can learn.

5.2.14.2 My Network Learns Very Slowly.

Are you too eager? Training an ANN can be slow. Typical networks require hundreds or thousands of epochs to learn effectively, even more if the dataset is very large. Check to see how the validation error is behaving. If it is improving, and performance on the test set is doing the same, keep going.

The samples are very noisy If the samples are noisy, use a larger dataset, if one is available, to diminish the effect. If the signal is comparable to the noise, learning will be slow and may be ineffective. Try using PCA to shrink the dataset and see if removing the components with the smallest eigenvalues reduces the noise. PCA is not magic though – it becomes progressively less effective at removing noise as the signal to noise ratio decreases and the signal gets swamped in noise.

Is it possible to identify samples within the dataset that are more reliable than the rest (experimental data from a well-respected lab, perhaps)? Try learning from these samples to see whether performance improves. But beware – such a procedure will introduce bias because you are selecting from a favoured portion of the dataset that you believe will serve your purpose best.

Poor links between input and output. The database may contain useful information, but the features you are feeding in may be linked only poorly to the output.

Unbalanced data. The dataset may be biased towards a subset of poor-quality samples. Perhaps they overwhelm other samples whose features have far smaller values; consider whether the entire dataset could benefit from scaling or whether individual samples could be weighted. If there are many samples of one sort and far fewer samples of others consider whether the dataset could be supplemented, or trimmed without too much loss of information, to even it out. Again, though, be aware of the danger of introducing bias when removing or weighting samples.

5.2.14.3 The Loss Function Diminishes During Training, and the Testing Error also Falls. I Expected that a Rise in the Error on the Test Set Would Indicate When to Stop Training, but This Rise Never Comes

Inappropriate sampling of the database. How are samples drawn from the dataset for training and testing? You already know that these must be taken at random, but the division into the training set and the test set must be made before training begins and then left unchanged. If you instead choose a set of training samples at random, train for one epoch, and test with the samples left over, then draw another set of random samples to train on during the next epoch and use the (new) samples left over the testing you are in effect using the whole dataset for training (see Figure 5.5). As you test with the samples that the network has previously seen, you can expect testing performance to continue to improve with time, even though this improvement is not meaningful.

Figure 5.5 The variation of the loss function (solid line) and testing error (dotted line) as the ANN learns. The testing error has continued to decline as learning proceeds, even though it should reach a minimum and then start to rise (dashed line).

5.2.14.4 During 20 Epochs, Performance on the Test Set Improves Very Little, and Then It Starts to Get Worse. Does This Mean That My Network Has Learnt All It Needed to Know in Just 20 Passes Through the Dataset?

Network problems. If training appears to be complete in 20 epochs, consider one of the following: (i) yes, learning is over, but the problem is so straightforward you didn't need an ANN anyway; (ii) you are being too impatient – the problem may be tough and training needs more time; (iii) the network is far too large for the number of samples you have, so the network is learning individual samples (the number of samples should be substantially more than the number of connection weights); (iv) training is not working. Perhaps the learning rate is far too high or low. Or the connection weights have been given initial values that are very large, so the algorithm needs a long time to drag these down into a range at which learning can progress effectively.

Dataset problems. The samples you have used for training and testing may cover different sets of relationships, so what the network learns from the training set is of minimal value in predicting results for the test set. Check whether your dataset has been ordered in some fashion and you are not using random sampling from the entire dataset.

5.2.14.5 I Think That My Network Is Overfitting; What Should I Do?

Consider regularisation. The ideal network encapsulates all the rules in the dataset, but nothing else. The larger the network, the more likely it is that it will learn noise and individual samples, so a reduction in network size is likely to be helpful. Try adding a regularisation term41 to the cost function in order to penalise complexity. Use the smallest number of descriptors that seem necessary to fully describe the dataset. If you have run PCA on the samples and found that there are just a few components with large eigenvalues and the rest are small, you should not be using a very large number of features.

5.2.14.6 After Training, I Compared the Network Weights with Those My Colleague Got Using the Same Dataset; They Were Completely Different. Who Is Right?

See Section 5.2.8. There is probably nothing wrong. If you and your colleague were asked to propose solutions to the equation a+b=16, she might suggest a=5, b=11, while you offer a=b=8. You are both correct because – trivially – an infinite number of solutions exist. Similarly, the ANN can encode relationships in its weights in an unlimited number of ways. You should not expect the connection weights in two networks to be the same, even if network performance is similar.

5.3 Conclusion

The analysis of scientific data can be challenging at any time, but analyses that incorporate AI methods bring with them a slight air of mystery. The connection weights in an ANN are open to inspection, but the understanding that we can draw from those weights is limited. One might compare that with the simplicity of a mathematical procedure such as fitting a line through a set of experimental data points.

This lack of interpretability will continue to be a key issue as the use of ML methods in science expands. While we can manually check the coding of programs to reassure ourselves that the software works as intended, checking that an AI program has reached a justifiable solution is harder. Subsequently being able to understand how it arrived at that conclusion is tougher still.

Fortunately, AI algorithms are evolving. The need for software that can offer some form of explanation is well recognised, and tools that are both smarter and more capable of explanation are under development.42 It is reasonable to suppose that in due course our algorithms will not be limited to giving a reliable, but explanation-light, analysis of a dataset, but be able to curate datasets, select a suitable ML method, choose optimum values for all the relevant parameters without input from the user, and, once training is over, explain what they have found in terms that we can understand.

In the meantime, as we wait for fully explainable AI, it is important to have an understanding of what goes on under the surface and be able to diagnose the problem when things do not work out. A little Mechanical Sympathy may help ensure that your algorithms have the best chance of generating a meaningful model.

And, in case you are wondering about the solutions to the problems in Section 5.2.8, check out Box 5.6.
