CHAPTER 6

A Prediction of Future States: AI-powered Chemical Innovation for Defense Applications

TYLER STUKENBROEKER( 0000-0002-7889-7183)* AND JONATHAN CLAUSEN( 0000-0002-1628-7136)

Strategic Analysis, Inc., Arlington, Virginia, USA

*Email: tstukenbroeker@sainc.com

6.1 Introduction

The U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) is a unique consumer of chemicals in several ways. First, as an employer of 2.9 million soldiers, civilians, and reservists, it has an unmatched need for pharmaceuticals, adhesives, fuels, coatings, and other chemical products. Second, many of these products are utilized outside of normal supply chains, whether at a forward operating base in Afghanistan or on an aircraft carrier in the Pacific. Finally, the use case for some of these products can be dynamic and unconventional. Missions may require items to be customized on the fly to meet the needs of a warfighter. For instance, a medicine may need to be produced without the use of refrigeration, or perhaps an obscurant is required that will effectively mask a specific environment.

Traditional chemical discovery and manufacturing capabilities rely on manual human planning that requires specialized knowledge and training. To conduct chemical synthesis using an ever-expanding toolbox of reactions, reagents, and methods, a highly trained chemist or engineer is required. This is not feasible for many military settings and situations, as the need may arise on short notice, in a remote area with little infrastructure, or in the absence of expert personnel. These constraints are even more restrictive when novel chemicals are required—to the point that developing new compounds for defense occurs in a relatively small number of laboratories where discoveries may take years or decades to reach the warfighter. The ability to automate chemical planning and discovery would have a dramatic impact on DoD's ability to carry out its mission.

The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) makes pivotal investments in breakthrough technologies for national security.1 This has given rise to ground-breaking defense and civilian technologies such as GPS, self-driving cars, night vision, and of course, the internet. DARPA recognized that the same type of large-scale, collaborative effort which led to these breakthroughs was needed to address chemical automation, and launched the Make-It program in 2015 to automate the synthesis of any molecule.2 The program drew from the DARPA Battlefield Medicine program,3 which built a continuous flow chemical system for the on-demand production of 15 different active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) molecules. Make-It sought to push this to the extreme: hardware that could be automatically configured to carry out any organic synthesis route that could be done in a laboratory or chemical plant. However, it became clear that this represented only part of the challenge—more daunting was the development of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms that could devise the best route and conditions for the synthesis of organic molecules.4 Make-It revealed the challenges of applying AI to the molecular domain. A new DARPA program launched in 2019, Accelerated Molecular Discovery (AMD),5 seeks to address this by integrating AI models with experimental systems for autonomous molecular design. Other U.S. government agencies, such as the National Institutes for Standards and Technology, the National Institutes of Health, and National Laboratories, have also recognized the potential for integrating experts from the AI community with those in materials6 and therapeutics7 discovery, suggesting that though currently on the vanguard, such collaborations may soon become routine.

This chapter will discuss progress in computer-aided synthesis planning (Section 6.1), challenges acquiring and working with chemical data for machine learning (Section 6.2), potential solutions to these challenges (Section 6.3), and their integration into the research workflow (Section 6.4). It is not intended to be a comprehensive review but rather a survey of the emerging challenges and opportunities (particularly those of the DoD) through the lens of recent research. The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the authors and do not reflect the policy or position of DARPA, the DoD, or the US Government.

6.2 The Synthesis Search Engine: Automating Synthetic Planning

In this section, we discuss algorithms that leverage machine learning (ML) in the context of other discoveries and demonstrations in the field. First, ML-driven optimization of known reactions is presented (see Section 6.2.1). The remaining sections deal with the synthesis of novel compounds, starting from single reactions (see Section 6.2.2) and then complete retrosyntheses (see Section 6.2.3).

6.2.1 Optimizing Known Routes

Most experiments carried out in chemistry laboratories are not novel reactions. Researchers are typically repeating a reaction from the literature or a laboratory notebook for the purpose of synthesizing a compound for further use. The main concern, therefore, is not what product will form but how efficiently it can be generated. There are many conditions which can be altered: time, temperature, and solvent, to name a few. Chemists can use heuristics and past experience to guess the optimal values, but the number of parameters makes the optimization procedure better suited for statistical algorithms. Indeed, design of experiments (DoE) approaches have been demonstrated which can find the optimum conditions with a minimum number of experiments using algorithms such as stable noisy optimization by branch and fit (SNOBFIT).8

In 2017, Zhou et al. demonstrated an ML approach to DoE optimization.9 A reinforcement learning system was designed using a recurrent neural network to optimize concentration and temperature for several reactions (see Scheme 6.1). The system outperformed non-ML algorithms by requiring 71% fewer steps to identify optimal conditions. By pairing the system with a droplet-based screening platform, optimal reaction conditions could be determined in about 30 minutes for the four reactions tested (see Scheme 6.1). We expect to see continued integration of ML algorithms into reaction optimization systems such as those in use in academic10,11 and pharmaceutical labs.12,13

Scheme 6.1 Reactions investigated by Zhou et al.9 Reproduced from ref. 9, https://doi.org/10.1021/acscentsci.7b00492, with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2017.

Given the long history of ML for optimization in fields such as power management,14 manufacturing,15 logistics,16 and telecommunications,17 it is not surprising that these types of algorithms can help scientists optimize reactions. However, the ability to screen non-discrete variables such as solvent or catalyst requires more specialized chemical knowledge to be integrated. Ahneman et al. demonstrated the possibility of this approach by employing a random forest to predict yields using a variety of palladium catalysts for a cross-coupling reaction.18 Using high throughput reaction screening data, they were able to predict which catalysts would best pair with particular substrates.

The Ahneman work highlights the value of pairing ML with reaction screening. The greatest impact of this combination, however, could lie beyond studying a single system. For an individual laboratory, it may not be worthwhile preparing small amounts of compounds to improve a suboptimal (e.g., low yielding, poor e-factor, hazardous) reaction. In this way, the existing route or a reference to the original procedure is propagated in literature, leading to suboptimal routes being used repeatedly. But with just a few of these tools, distributed across laboratories working in different areas of chemical synthesis, improved conditions could be determined and propagated across an entire field, resulting in significant aggregate savings of time, energy, and materials. As an example, consider 2-iodoxybenzoic acid (IBX), a commonly used oxidation reagent first prepared in 1893 by Hartmann and Meyer (Scheme 6.2).19 Historically, the poor solubility of this reagent has limited its use to a few solvents. Countless chemists toiled away using high-boiling DMSO until 2002 when Moore reported that the reaction was effective in more facile solvents.20 Though it may not have been worthwhile for a single chemist to screen different solvent systems, the cumulative benefit across the field was substantial. The problem is likely more pronounced for less common reagents, where the incentive to publish improved preparation or methodology is further diminished.

Scheme 6.2 Structure of 2-iodoxybenzoic acid (IBX).

Flexible flow chemistry systems are becoming more common for scalable synthesis, even at the laboratory level. When combined with ML algorithms, these systems can perform on-the-fly optimization of temperature, concentration, and flow rate in a continuous or discrete manner. Thus, ML and automated hardware are a way to lower the barrier of process optimization for small-scale syntheses. Combined with proper documentation and data sharing (see Section 6.3), this will lead to continuous improvements in efficiency and encourage the adoption of greener solvents and reagents.

6.2.2 Predicting Reaction Outcomes

Compared with reaction optimization, prediction of chemical reactivity is an area with little precedent. This problem is fundamentally more challenging because of the many ways that two or more molecules can interact. Consider the human approach to predicting reactivity:

  1. Identify the reactive sites (atoms) on the reactants
  2. Determine possible types of reactions that could occur
  3. Evaluate the possibility and extent of a certain reaction

AI systems that follow this approach generally utilize reaction templates described below. Other approaches may not separate these tasks explicitly and are categorized as non-template methods, described subsequently.

Template based: The choice of molecular representation (see Section 6.2.4) will both affect and depend on the approach to generating and evaluating candidate transformations. Graph-based representations are widely used in both rule-based and ML approaches to compare the molecule against reaction templates and subsequently identify applicable reactions and the reaction center (see Figure 6.1). One approach pioneered by Coley and co-workers21,22 applied 1700 templates extracted from the US patent database, and then used a neural network to rank the likelihood of products generated. This demonstrated the feasibility of ML for forward prediction; however, the method suffered from the high computational cost of, for each template, determining if the molecular graph contains a subgraph isomorphic to the template. To mitigate this, both Segler23 and Coley24 used a neural network to suggest a template, rather than comparing directly to each one.

Figure 6.1 Application of reaction templates in the forward and reverse direction, with increasing numbers of adjacent bonds included. Reproduced from ref. 22, https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.accounts.8b00087, with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2018.

Template-based approaches include fundamental tradeoffs between coverage, accuracy, and speed. This is evident when specifying the complexity of the reaction core. Templates which only contain the bond-forming/bond-breaking atoms lack the crucial context of electronic and steric effects elsewhere in the molecule. However, more complex templates that include adjacent fragments will take longer to compute and may over-specify a transformation. Another tradeoff is the number of templates used. It would not be possible to consider every transformation; therefore, models are usually limited to examining hundreds or thousands of templates. Often this parameter is expressed as the cumulative percentage of reactions from which templates were learned. Unfortunately, it seems clear that even good coverage of well-known reactions (e.g., including templates for 99% of the reactions in Reaxys) is not sufficient for complex retrosynthetic analysis across broader organic chemistry. Analysis of the “network of organic chemistry” performed by Szymkuć found a power law relationship between the number of times a reaction is found in the literature and its ranking based on that frequency.25 Such a relationship indicates that a few outliers (i.e., rarely used reactions) can have a significant impact on the overall statistics; in this case, the network of known organic chemical reactions. Szymkuć contends that this requires the enumeration of many thousands of chemical rules (∼80 000 for Chematica program),26 something that proves challenging for both machine-extracted rules and human-encoded ones.

Template-free: In contrast to direct template matching, one could compute directly on the molecular SMILES string, treating the reaction as a translation task between products and reactants (see Figure 6.2). This approach, which uses an encoder-decoder model called sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq), was explored separately by Nam,27 Liu,28 and Schwaller.29 A few surprising results stood out. First, the models were able to generate valid SMILES strings of products as outputs a majority of the time, without explicit specification or filtering. Second, the models showed a large performance gap between forward and retro prediction. Liu's model, which operated in the reverse (retro) direction, was not able to outperform Coley's template-based model. However, the best overall performance was reported for Schwaller's seq2seq model, which predicted reaction products in the forward direction and included an attention layer. Attention models, which allow the algorithm to focus on particular parts of the input, have the added benefit of providing some explainability, something that template free-models normally lack compared with template-based ones. The impact of including attention also suggests that model architecture is an important area for future investigation. Indeed, Yang30 showed that in addition to the representation used, the neural network architecture is of critical importance to the property prediction task.

Figure 6.2 Attention-based seq2seq model as implemented by Pande.28 The input is a SMILES string of a molecule, here methanol, which is passed to sequential recurrent neural networks, an encoder and decoder, which output a SMILES string of the predicted reagents. The attention mechanism allows the model to focus on particular characters (usually atoms) in the input. Reproduced from ref. 28, https://doi.org/10.1021/acscentsci.7b00303, with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2017.

6.2.3 Performing Retrosynthesis

The ultimate goal for CASP is to reliably produce multi-reaction synthesis plans for any molecule, known or novel. For a human chemist, this process is ostensibly considered in the retrosynthetic direction, from a target toward buyable starting materials. But given that reactions are taught (and occur) in the forward direction, the chemist is necessarily performing a holistic evaluation of pathways that simultaneously considers both the value of a certain reaction for building the target of interest and the likelihood it will yield the desired product. It is challenging to create algorithms for such a nuanced task, and though seq2seq suggests that there could be important distinctions, the differences in the predictive power of algorithms performing the forward versus retro tasks have not been thoroughly explored.31

The large number of reactions available to make each molecule creates an exponential explosion of possible routes at each step. Consider the tree structure whose root is a target molecule and leaves are buyable substrates. The average number of different five-reaction syntheses from a target can be 1016 by some estimates.25 Therefore, to predict a retrosynthetic route for a target, ML algorithms are needed to identify and navigate promising portions of these tree structures without needing to exhaustively explore them. Such an algorithm must be able to determine and prioritize transformations which lead to synthesizable molecules and ultimately buyable starting materials. The criteria by which a model makes such prioritizations are referred to as a cost or reward, depending on whether the quantity should be minimized or maximized. In general, the notion of cost or reward can include many factors that one wants to optimize, such as monetary costs of starting materials, reaction yields, time of reaction, environmental factors, or reaction complexity.

Describing complexity is deceptively challenging. Using an intuitive relationship—more complex molecules are more expensive to make—one could simply consider the differences in length of the SMILES strings for reactants and products as a proxy for the cost of a reaction.25 Another approach is to consider structural features, assigning each a predetermined complexity cost. However, molecular complexity, as perceived by humans, is an unreliable metric for navigating chemical space. Greedy application of complexity heuristics one might use for evaluating a transformation may lead to synthetic shortcuts being overlooked. A perfect example of this is the use of protecting groups. Their installation increases the number of bonds and atoms but only transiently; their effective use should be seen as a decrease in cost by a well-performing model. Many of the most elegant syntheses in organic chemistry contain transformations that initially appear unintuitive, inefficient or counterproductive, but ultimately set up highly efficient reactions.

A measure of complexity is necessary to impart expert-level chemical intuition on retrosynthetic algorithms. Conveniently, Coley was able to leverage the existing machine-coded reaction dataset to develop SCScore, a prediction of the number of reactions required (some of which may temporarily increase bond or atom counts) to synthesize any molecule from starting materials.32 By learning a holistic notion of synthesizability from data, the SCScore metric is useful to not just guide retrosynthetic analysis, but also to prioritize drug candidates for synthesizability or identify complexifying reactions for chemical library construction.

While SCScore provides a useful heuristic, it does not specify a policy for choosing which transformations will make up the optimal synthetic route. This can be achieved through reinforcement learning. This approach learns an optimal decision-making policy that will accept short-term loss in order to maximize long-term reward. Following training, the policy may be executed to determine the optimal route along a retrosynthetic tree. Segler23 demonstrated the effectiveness of reinforcement learning for retrosynthesis using the Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) method, made famous by the success of DeepMind's AlphaGo algorithm in learning the complex game Go.33 Briefly, their implementation learns a decision policy by using MCTS (see Figure 6.3) to perform simulated “playouts” of a small subset of possible routes within the full reaction trees of various targets, records the ultimate outcome (success or failure in reaching buyable starting materials), and notes it for each reaction in the branch which was played out. The learning process balances between playouts of the most successful routes and exploration of unseen ones, and results in a policy that may be used to successfully predict valid retrosyntheses of molecules not seen during training.

Figure 6.3 Monte Carlo Tree Search. For retrosynthesis, nodes represent compounds and lines represent reactions. Selection finds a promising node that has yet to be explored. Expansion is applying templates or some other strategy to generate candidate precursors. The playout uses retrosynthetic steps to try and reach starting materials. The success or failure to do so is determined and propagated up through the parent nodes and the process is repeated.23

Schreck34 published a similar method for learning policies using deep reinforcement learning (see Figure 6.4). In comparison with the greedy application of a SMILES-based complexity heuristic, both Waller23 and Schreck achieved significant improvement in the number of molecules for which a full retrosynthetic path could be found in reasonable time.

Figure 6.4 Reinforcement learning for determining cost functions, as implemented by Bishop34 Reproduced from ref. 34, https://doi.org/10.1021/acscentsci.9b00055, with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2019.

Ultimately, retrosynthetic algorithms must consider more information to provide a real-world estimate of synthetic cost including imperfect reaction yields and the cost of purification. It is even more challenging to estimate costs that depend on the sequence of the reactions, such as switching solvents between reactions.

6.2.4 Assessment

The elements of a CASP system—reaction optimization, forward prediction, retrosynthesis—can each be addressed as separate problems. But, the Make-It program revealed how interconnected each aspect is. To deliver a full end-to-end solution, the retrosynthetic algorithm must consider how many templates are used to define the branching number and determine cost, based on the solvents and reagents needed. It remains uncertain how much these tasks should even be dictated. Research on seq2seq models suggests that properly specified ML models can, in some cases, perform these tasks in a concerted manner, perhaps at the expense of explainability.

Assessing the performance and value of a model is also not a straightforward task. Ground truth within reaction databases is frequently used to determine a “top 1” or “top 5” prediction accuracy for forward reactions (i.e., the fraction of time that the algorithm predicted the correct product within its top X results). However, there is no comparable metric for multistep retrosyntheses. Generated routes can be compared with published ones, but it is expected that they will differ based on small parametric differences in the model, or even offer improved routes to those known. Attempts have been made to baseline against human experts.23 One could envision a “chemical Turing test” wherein passing means that chemists cannot distinguish between a route generated by a machine or by legendary synthetic chemist E.J. Corey. But this may be biased toward reactions which chemists are comfortable with, rather than those which are most efficient. The ultimate validation is carrying out the proposed synthesis, which is slow and expensive. New ways to test novel routes through rapid experimentation or in silico are needed to provide feedback for these systems.

6.2.5 Adoption

The Make-It program aims for a push-button system that will evaluate any molecule, tell the user if and how it can be synthetized, and, provided the proper starting materials, produce it autonomously. However, reaching that vision, or even making progress toward it, requires that these tools have demonstrable uses in the near term. Make-It technologies are already being adopted by partners in industry and government to address real challenges. An early success from the program was Chematica software developed by Grzybowski and coworkers.35 This rule-based expert retrosynthesis system was challenged by MilliporeSigma (formerly Sigma-Aldrich) to provide routes to targets which for which previous synthesis attempts had failed. Chematica provided routes to all six targets that MilliporeSigma chemists were able to successfully perform within the constraints of the challenge. MilliporeSigma subsequently purchased Chematica and is now marketing the software under the name Synthia™ and using it internally to expand their product catalog.

In all cases, user experience is critical to adoption; a system is only as useful as it is usable. Usability involves not just the user interface design (e.g., legible reaction schemes, easy stereochemical inputs) but also the ability to prioritize the most useful information for display. For instance, early in the development of CASP systems in Make-It, the search output would often highly rank very similar results, essentially offering the same route over and over again with minor variance. Later iterations of the software were designed to provide diverse routes and group similar ones when presenting them to the user. Another practical consideration is the computational requirements of such systems. Even for CASP systems that employ expensive template matching and large libraries of transformations, a single retrosynthetic step can usually be performed in a fraction of the time it would take a human. However, the bottleneck for system performance is the explosion of possible routes, requiring large amounts of memory to store. In systems developed under Make-It, routes to reasonably complex drug-like molecules can be computed in 6–60 seconds on a multi-core desktop computer.24

One might characterize current CASP software as an early version of a “synthesis search engine.” Just as Google and Bing have become necessities for navigating the vastness of the internet, CASP enables chemists to similarly navigate reactivity space. All the systems described above allow chemists to easily link to source materials, saving countless hours of gathering and reviewing papers, pouring over the literature for a key reference. A reaction, which might be common in one field, is rare in another, such that it takes a discipline-agnostic software to suggest to a chemist to use it. We predict that current CASP systems will continue to increase in complexity, applicability, and performance. Today's systems are a stepping stone toward AI-powered chemical awareness.

Finally, it should be noted that these algorithms can be adapted to co-examine multiple targets, identifying a minimal set of starting materials for a library of compounds. They can even be parallelized to perform a meta-analysis of the entire reaction corpus to guide reaction development toward the most impactful new transformations. For a large organization like the DoD, which purchases a diverse range of chemicals, such tools could identify common building blocks and intermediate compounds in order to streamline production and reduce costs.

6.3 Data Challenges for Statistical Learning in Chemistry

Quantitative structure–activity relationships (QSAR) were first reported in 1961, launching the field of cheminformatics.36 Early work relied mostly on correlating physical properties such as logP with a biological outcome. Eventually, fragment-based and quantum mechanical descriptors started to be incorporated and in the early 2000s, neural networks were used for property prediction.37 In 2014, the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH), Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and Food and Drug Administration (FDA) sponsored Tox21, a challenge to predict the performance of thousands of molecules in toxicological assays. The entries showcased a wide range of ML techniques for prediction of toxicity, including random forests, deep neural nets, support vector machines, and others.38

Despite the popularity of statistical methods for cheminformatic modeling, however, ML was not embraced by synthetic chemists. The Make-It program, launched in 2015, attempted to leverage many of the underlying QSAR techniques to retrosynthesis and forward prediction. Doing so illuminated several challenges that will need to be overcome for complex tasks such as property prediction and molecular design. While in some sense these challenges are universal across ML applications, they have aspects unique to experimental sciences and chemistry in particular. This section will focus on the challenges of integrating chemical data to statistical learning systems.

ML algorithms thrive in domains where data are abundant, or at least easy to produce, and relevant to the task at hand. Advances in computer vision (CV) and natural language processing (NLP)—prototypical examples of ML's success—are aided tremendously by the ubiquity of digital data online and the efforts of a community that has been focused in these areas for decades. Such data are produced by the public at no cost and carefully curated and annotated by the research community into standard, high-quality collections to further model development and provide common references and benchmarks (e.g. ImageNet,39 CoNLL Shared Tasks,40etc.).

This is in stark contrast to the chemical sciences, wherein data are comparatively expensive to generate and often treated as valuable intellectual property that should be safeguarded rather than shared. Data published in academic journals are publically available but must be aggregated to provide sufficient training data typical for ML. These composite datasets are (1) biased, (2) inaccessible, and (3) narrow, challenges which will be discussed in that order.

6.3.1 Data are Biased Toward Successful Experiments

Journals prioritize confirmatory studies in which a hypothesis was supported by the experimental data. A project for which the experimental data are not explained by the hypothesis is deemed a failure, forever relegated to a lab notebook. This model has drawn criticism for incentivizing data and statistical manipulation.41 But a widespread and arguably more serious effect is the bias it generates in scientific databases toward positive results (see Figure 6.5). With few exceptions, chemical reaction databases contain only successful reactions, i.e., reactions which have significant yield of the reported product. Negative results, such as no reaction, or an unwanted one, are seldom reported. This makes using supervised learning classifiers difficult as these require explicit positive and negative labels for each class.

Figure 6.5 Aggregate yields reported in Reaxys. Figure courtesy of K. Jensen, presented in part at the Make-It Industry Forum, October 2019.

This challenge was encountered in the Make-It program. Coley trained supervised models on the Reaxys database to predict the reactants yielding a target product (see Section 6.1). Without examples of failed reactions or side products in the training data, however, the models were not able to classify reactions as plausible. Both Segler23 and Coley21 overcame this by generating “synthetic” negative examples to provide additional class labels. Coley identified reactions that had over 50% yield and surmised that no other products (including expected ones) could be present in the product mixture. Waller applied the same strategy and further supplemented the negative data pool by randomly sampling amongst scrambled reactant-product pairs to give 70 million false pairings. This enabled reasonably good performance to be achieved on the Reaxys data; however, this should be considered something of a stopgap measure. Most valuable to the model are the reactions which would be expected (by some human heuristic) to give one product, but instead gave another. Fortunately, these occur all the time in the course of chemical research; unfortunately, they are rarely published or otherwise disseminated.

6.3.2 Existing Data are Unreliable and Non-standardized

As cheminformatics gained popularity, databases emerged containing some combination of formulae, structures, physical properties, and biological activities. These data are routinely used to train and validate QSAR models for a variety of drug discovery and materials applications. In addition to the biases described above, the data are likely to suffer from a more fundamental problem. A recent study audited just the structures in six large databases and found that up to 3.4% of entries contained an inaccurate structure, such as a misplaced chlorine atom or swapped hydroxyl and methoxy.42 The authors found that this level of error had significant impact on the accuracy of models trained on the data. Yet publications often report model performance without any experimental validation—just train:test splits that would fail to uncover systematic issues with the data.

If databases are unreliable, one might look to scientific journals to obtain primary source data. Chemistry literature is a particularly appealing source of knowledge for ML because, unlike reaction databases, it occasionally describes reactions and conditions that were ineffective in addition to those that were successful. To the extent that negative results are disclosed in the chemical literature, it is usually via discussion in the text, which in turn may reference figures and tables which are necessary to fully understand the specifics. Humans are able to understand this information readily, but the nuances of language and unconstrained diversity of figures and tables inhibit automated interpretation by machines. Though significant progress has been made in NLP and CV techniques in general, relatively little effort has been expended applying these techniques to the chemistry domain. As a result, most publicly available NLP and CV models, having been trained on more general domains, struggle when applied to chemistry data's unique vocabulary and syntax.

Finally, one must fundamentally trust the published data. Though publications may be peer reviewed, most experiments are not reproduced by other laboratories because tenure-seeking faculty are incentivized to demonstrate and publish novel discoveries. Even when that is not the case, an experiment may be too expensive or complex for another lab to reproduce, or the detailed procedure is not made available. As evidenced by Figure 6.5, which shows disproportionate numbers of experiments reporting yields rounded to the nearest 10, it is clear that published results do not always reflect accurate reporting of real experimental data. How and where this impacts the viability of models and subsequent predictions should be considered very carefully.

6.3.3 Data are Relevant to a Narrow Collection of Tasks

A fundamental assumption of supervised learning, though seldom met in practice, is that the data on which a model is trained are from the same distribution as the data on which the model will be tested. Effectively extrapolating to data that are dissimilar to the training data, though aided by such methods as encoding first principles and continual learning, is still an open research topic in the machine learning community.43 In chemistry, however, the most valuable predictions are those involving molecules, reactions, or properties for which little experimental data exist from the distribution of interest (i.e., predictions outside the training set). Therein lies the challenge.

The highly competitive nature of pharmaceutical research, while important for innovation, generates large caches of proprietary data, much of which is never used but also not released for fear of enabling a lucrative discovery by a competitor. But even if this could be overcome (vida infra), the data would reflect the large imbalance between aggregate pharmaceutical R&D and other chemical industries—a disparity that extends to publically available data as well. In 2018, the R&D budget for the top 15 pharmaceutical firms was $100 billion,44 compared with just $11 billion45 for the top 15 chemical firms in other sectors. This naturally leads to databases oriented toward the pharmaceutical industry and its applications. Virshup46 illustrated this by performing an analysis of the popular PubChem and ZINC databases. First, the entirety of the drug-like small molecule universe (estimated ∼1060 molecules, originally described by Lipinsky47) was mapped uniformly to 90 thousand “bins,” or neurons, using a self-organizing map according to Tanimoto similarity of their fingerprints. It was then shown that 98% of PubChem compounds were assigned to just 2% of the neurons, mostly characterized by compounds with low molecular weights and few rings. Various conclusions can be drawn from this result, but the facts are the following: (1) much of the small molecule universe is unexplored, and (2) that which has been explored is not representative of the whole.

This data disparity extends to the property space as well. Wu et al.48 recently aggregated a collection of property datasets to establish benchmarks for various property prediction tasks. While some datasets contain property information for many compounds (for example, PubChem BioAssay (PCBA) has biological activity of over 400 000 compounds), data on other properties are less abundant (lipophilicity values on 4200 curated compounds from ChEMBL). Data quantity is not a sufficient condition for model quality; however, in many cases, it is a necessary one, particularly for complex deep learning models with many parameters and when the generation of new data cannot be controlled by the model's developer. Figure 6.6 illustrates the performance of several different models based on training set size.

Figure 6.6 Importance of large datasets and the performance variation between several different models for property prediction. Adapted from ref. 48 with permission from the Royal Society of Chemistry.

This incongruence between the data available and the tasks attempted suggests that, without generating task-specific data, ML will be heavily reliant on exploiting existing knowledge rather than exploring new chemical space, and most successes for ML in chemistry will be restricted to these areas in which the community is already heavily invested. This is particularly challenging for properties of specific DoD interest, as the community of researchers that produces such data is so small.

6.3.4 There Is No Standard Representation of Chemistry Data for Machine Learning Models

Even supposing that the ideal data for an ML task in chemistry can be acquired, the format in which it should be presented to the model is not obvious. Until recently, NLP and CV relied heavily on manual feature engineering as a preprocessing step to transform the raw data into a form that would be ingested by the model. The standard practice was computing multiple features such as the context-free grammar parse of a sentence, or the scale-invariant feature transform of an image and then using feature selection techniques to determine which features to include.

Though still a component of ML learning pipelines, the importance of feature engineering was diminished with the advent of deep neural networks. Many current deep neural network models instead take some more fundamental representation of data as an input, such as a one-hot vector for each word in a corpus or a convolution of neighboring pixels in an image, from which successively more salient features are automatically derived as part of the model's training process. The advantage of this technique is that, loosely speaking, these representations are more information complete than engineered features, in that they contain essentially the same information from the raw data that an oracle (in this case, a person) would use to make a decision.

Chemistry's oracle is nature, having sufficient information to resolve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for multi-electron systems to arbitrary precision. It is impossible to provide all such information to an ML model in a classical computer,49 so the question becomes: what is the appropriate abstraction of the information nature has available, and how should this abstraction be represented? There is almost certainly no single answer to this question; the appropriate representation will vary depending on the chemistries involved and the ML task attempted.

Molecular representations typically fall into two broad categories: fixed representations, analogous to the engineered features described previously which do not vary depending on the task (e.g. molecular descriptors and fingerprints), and learned representations which are developed in the context of the model's task.50 Examples of each are shown in Figure 6.7.

Figure 6.7 Examples of different molecular representations.

An example of a fixed representation is the two-dimensional, atom-bond skeletal formula familiar to many people. It corresponds directly to a molecule's atom and bond arrangement and can be interpreted as an undirected graph. A text-based representation, which is familiar to human chemists but perhaps less interpretable, is SMILES, which are alpha-numeric strings that represent the graph-connectivity of a molecule. Molecules may be represented by expert-defined descriptors, hundreds of which can be calculated by the popular Dragon software.51 Extended connectivity fingerprints52 are determined by a hashing function that incorporates local topological information of the molecule. One attractive feature of these is that they are easy and quick to generate using off-the-shelf tools such as RDKit and easy to customize for particular applications. Waller's retrosynthetic algorithm (see Section 6.2) used fingerprints to suggest transformations that would be applicable to a given target. Such fixed representations have long been used, in various forms, in many QSAR approaches.50

Learned representations in chemistry are a relatively recent advance and are typically produced by operating on the graph structure of the molecule. Duvenaud53 developed the first such implementation using convolutions over arbitrary molecular graph structures for various property prediction tasks. A similar approach was adopted by Coley for the forward reaction prediction task in the Make-It program.54

The literature is not consistent on whether fixed or learned representations are preferred for prediction tasks in general. In predicting binary assay outcomes that indicate whether a certain compound, for example, binds to a specific receptor, inhibits some pathway or induces toxic effects, Wu finds that learned representations tend to be more successful,48 while Mayr suggests that fixed representations perform better.55 Yang suggests that the discrepancy likely arises from differences in evaluation protocols and further demonstrates the benefits of hybrid representations that combine convolutions and descriptors.30 The advantages offered by a hybrid representation illustrate a broader point: different application spaces lend themselves to fundamentally different representations. Much like the datasets discussed above, work in this area has been steered toward the prediction of therapeutic properties, and the particulars of what fixed features to include or how to produce learned features will likely vary when applied to predicting different properties such as vapor pressure or heat of formation. One focus of the DARPA AMD program is developing and evaluating molecular representation across varied application spaces to provide better understanding of these questions.

6.4 Realizable Solutions to Data Challenges

Data are the lifeblood of an AI-powered laboratory. In Section 6.3, we discussed how ensuring the objectivity, accessibility, and relevance of data are the most significant constraints on model performance when applying ML to chemistry. The particulars of how to address these issues depend on the source of the data, be it from one's own lab, external sources (e.g., databases or other labs), simulations, or extracted from the scientific literature. Here, we highlight several solutions various researchers and organizations have implemented to address these data shortfalls.

6.4.1 Automation and Standardization of Experimental Data Collection

A chemist has the most control over the experiments performed in their own laboratory, with their own equipment, and under their own protocols. It is therefore the most natural place to effect change in the way data are generated. We present here three objectives for laboratory workflow which are fundamental to improving data utility, objectivity, and accessibility.

  • Objective 1: Recording Data in a Machine-Readable Format The push for digitization of data and experimental protocols is not new. Electronic lab notebooks (ELNs) initially appeared in the 1990s.56 However, the adoption of such tools has been slow for a myriad of reasons,57 including concerns about the cost of software, data security, and legal issues. Usability, however, remains the largest challenge. Chemists may struggle to enter the nuances of a chemical reaction scheme58 or be forced to adopt an unfamiliar organizational scheme. ELNs must strike a balance between being generalized enough to be used by different types of chemists but powerful enough to account for the nuances of each field.
  • Attempts to develop a universal ELN continue. But, lamentably, even if a highly usable, widely applicable system were available, there is no guarantee it would be adopted by researchers who may have entrenched preferences and habits. It may ultimately be more successful to recast the ELN as an auxiliary observer, automatically documenting an experimental procedure and recording the data. The Ley59 lab has explored the use of computer vision for monitoring experiments through video and natural language processing for ingesting written text and converting it into standardized, machine-readable formats.60 Similar approaches rely on integrating analytical instrumentation into digital repositories. However, the APIs provided by manufacturers of such instrumentation often produce data in proprietary formats different for each instrument. Exporting the data to open source formats for preservation or integration into statistical models is time-consuming and may not maintain the original data resolution. Pressure on manufacturers from the research community to be more open with their APIs would likely require a community-wide effort combined with stiff industry competition.
  • A program called ASPIRE at the NIH National Center for Translational Science (NCATS), which seeks to combat opioid abuse and find safer options for pain management, includes a specific challenge to develop “next-generation, open source electronic laboratory notebook[s] that would serve as an electronic synthetic chemistry knowledge portal and allow for … unbiased data collection during the synthesis planning, execution and analysis.”7 Designs will be selected which integrate with ML models and analytical tools to provide a complete chemical discovery workflow.
  • Objective 2: Standardized, Algorithmically Generated Experimental Protocols. Capturing all possible details about an experiment is one way to ensure faithful, reproducible data. Another is to create protocols and experimental plans that enforce standardized execution. The University of Washington's (UW) Biofabrication Center61 launched the software Aquarium which monitors sample inventory and specifies preparations but leaves manual operations and complex observations to be performed by a laboratory technician.62 This enforces not just standardized data collection but also standardized experimental design, which will help increase the accessibility to ML models. The UW effort is part of the DARPA Synergistic Discovery and Design (SD2) program, which takes a data-driven approach toward model building across a wide variety of domains.63
  • Objective 3: Hands-free Execution of Experiments: Robotic experimentation offers cost savings and safety improvements, but an additional driver of laboratory automation is the ability to generate unbiased, fully documented datasets. Eliminating the manual execution of more tedious tasks such as pipetting, heating, mixing and instead relying on automated tools allows more experiments to be conducted, more data to be acquired, and also improves the reproducibility and specificity of that data. Large-scale realization of laboratory automation is exemplified by the development of “cloud labs,” which are quickly becoming viable options for biological experimentation, where robotic automation has had a large head start versus chemistry. One example is Transcriptic, which allows for biological assays to be run without a human in the loop.64 Another is Emerald Cloud Lab, which offers all the capabilities of an organic synthesis lab, including solid handling, rotovapping, purification and many different analytical capabilities.65

The first two objectives align with a larger goal for scientific data generation and stewardship, which is adoption of the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) Data Principles by data producers and publishers.66 While not an objective in and of itself, the FAIR principles are recognized as a necessary condition for innovation and discovery using AI in chemistry.67

6.4.2 Sharing Data Across Laboratories

An exciting aspect of lab automation is the ability to decentralize research. This approach requires rapid, clear communication between data scientists and experimental labs. These collaborations are commonplace today but are usually ad hoc, 1:1 partnerships that operate via “data dumps” from one group to another. This occurs even within research groups, where a graduating student leaves poorly annotated and disorganized data. In either case, the data scientist or model builder must spend a great deal of time cleaning the data, a process that may introduce errors in interpretation. In the future, we expect data sharing to move from small specific collaborations to massive, public datasets that are continuously added to and utilized by many groups. Publicly available datasets such as PubChem or BindingDB, as well as commercial ones such as CAS and Reaxys, continue to grow,68 but problems with data format and accuracy create new bottlenecks.

An alternative to these resources is data produced directly from research groups in conjunction with a publication, something that some journals now require using consistent data standards.66 The best path toward FAIR data in chemistry will be a combination of these approaches: decentralized release of data from many data producers, in consistent and useful formats, combined with the data management tools of centralized databases. Though the adoption of FAIR principles has many proponents, adherence is not yet common practice in the community.

Another early step toward making existing data more FAIR is Google's Dataset Search.69–71 This search engine allows users to search for datasets that might otherwise be difficult to find, as most search engines will not index the internal records in a hosted database. For now, the tool requires that data providers annotate their datasets with an open metadata format, and it does not provide a way to access the data other than linking to the host site. In the future, this or other tools may integrate an API that allows models to directly utilize multiple datasets and even automatically search for them.

Ultimately, however, even combined datasets from academic and government laboratories may not match the scale of those held by companies and organizations that are unable to share their data for competitive or privacy reasons. A number of workarounds have emerged to harness this propriety data, ranging from privately funded “open innovation” consortia, to tightly controlled partnerships.72 One potentially scalable model is that of Accelerating Therapeutics for Opportunities in Medicine (ATOM) consortium, which relies on Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) as a trusted intermediary to aggregate, manage, and securely analyze data provided by members from the pharmaceutical industry.73 This set-up allows members to benefit from both shared data as well as the uniquely powerful computing capabilities and expertise provided by LLNL. At MIT, an alternative framework is employed by the Machine Learning for Pharmaceutical Discovery and Synthesis Consortium. Here, the ML models are developed jointly but are deployed in-house to be trained separately on companies’ proprietary data.74,75 This allows for collaborative development of tools and models but does not benefit from pooled datasets.

A different approach to utilizing non-public data is altering it to conceal the specifics but still inform ML models. Homomorphic encryption76,77 allows computation without ever decrypting the data or having access to the decryption keys. Another example is data obfuscation.78 Here, data are augmented with new samples or random noise in such a way that effective ML models can be trained on the data, but sensitive information related to individual samples or groups of samples obscured. Further research is needed in this area to make these techniques more robust, easy to implement, and better-performing.

6.4.3 Leveraging Experiments Described in Scientific Literature

Compared with large, structured databases, chemical literature contains disorganized and unstructured data. Even for data explicitly stated in tables and figures, the formatting and structural representations are not easy for machines to interpret. Olivetti and McCallum have demonstrated two promising approaches for accessing knowledge within materials literature sources. In 2017 the group published an unsupervised technique to extract synthesis parameters for 30 different oxide systems from a corpus of 640 000 journal articles.79 More recently, they constructed a dataset of 230 synthetic procedures annotated by domain experts with labeled graphs that express the semantics of the synthesis sentences, which may be used for shallow annotation of unseen text.80 These techniques circumvent the major hurdle of manually annotating large datasets that are commonly encountered when applying NLP methods to novel domains. The Optical Structure Recognition Application (OSRA)81 is one of the better-known systems for classifying images of molecular structures, though it assumes that the images have already been extracted from the articles. Staker82 recently developed end-to-end deep learning solutions for both segmenting molecular structures from documents and predicting chemical structures from the segmented images.

The community is also working to make the machine-readability of journals an intrinsic design goal by developing easily accessible metadata at the time of publication.83 It is currently focused on enhancing discovery by search engines, but if it was adopted broadly and extended to describing text and figures, this could obviate the need for sophisticated NLP and CV extraction techniques.

6.4.4 Generating Data Through Simulation

Some data are impractical to gather experimentally, either because of cost or the limits of analytical equipment, and are therefore more efficient to acquire through molecular dynamics (e.g., a model predicting binding affinity84) or quantum mechanical simulations such as density functional theory (DFT). However, the time and computational resources required for such simulations present another opportunity to leverage ML. Gilmer85 developed an ML model, trained on the QM9 database, which was able to approximate quantum mechanical quantities such as HOMO and LUMO values with comparable accuracy to DFT in hundredths of a second – over 300 000 times faster than simulation-based DFT methods. A directed-bonds variant of the message-passing neural network architecture developed by Gilmer was shown by Yang30 to be applicable to a wide range of property prediction tasks. Not only are these tools valuable themselves, but the rate at which these estimates are computed makes it feasible to provide accurate approximations to downstream models.

ML predictions were used to prioritize further simulation and experimentation by Gómez-Bombarelli for the discovery of efficient molecular organic light-emitting diodes.86 Simple fragments were combined in a donor–acceptor configuration to create 1.6 million structures—far too large a pool to screen with quantum simulation. Therefore, molecular fingerprints were generated and analyzed by a neural network to prioritize candidates for quantum calculations. Initially, the model was trained on calculated values for 40 000 randomly selected structures. To improve the model for prediction of the most efficient structures, it was periodically retrained during the screening. The virtual screen eventually generated five candidates that were synthesized and demonstrated favorable properties.

6.4.5 Closed-loop Integration of Data Generation and Predictive Models

To the extent that the technologies above are in use today, the generation of data and the development of models which leverage them are largely independent. We believe the most promising approach to ensuring that there exists objective, accessible, and highly relevant data for a particular ML task is to integrate data generation and predictive model components into a closed loop workflow. Recently, methods have been demonstrated43 which enable the models themselves to use Bayesian optimization or other active learning techniques to identify the next experiment, simulation or data query to execute based on the model's hypothesis. Most importantly, this is done with the explicit objective of acquiring the optimal data to inform that specific model and improve its performance. The model's hypothesis is then updated with the new data, and the process repeats.

There are several impacts of this paradigm. First, data from experiments designed in this way are more informative to the model than experiments conducted outside of the loop, and therefore less data are needed to produce accurate models. Indeed, they are maximally relevant in terms of the optimization function used to select the next experiment. This enables rapid development of models for domains where little data exist, and a means to intelligently navigate the astronomically large unexplored chemical space to extend into new domains. Second, the data are complete and objective, in the sense that all experimental conditions can be specified and controlled, and results can be preserved regardless of whether they confirm the hypothesis. The format can be specified to ensure accessibility of the data to models. Last, such a laboratory workflow may evolve from automation to autonomy—not only relieving the chemist of the drudgery of manually executing many aspects of an experiment, but also of deciding what experiment to execute and what its parameters are. Consider that robotic automation serves as the hands of a chemist, and AI tools as the mind of one. In the most sweeping conception, this laboratory would be able to discover and synthesize compounds supported by a minimal number of technicians and guided by scientists who would need only provide the chemical search space and the desired properties. The automated system would provide fully documented data collection and traceable conclusions.

6.5 Initial Demonstrations of the Self-driving Laboratory

The term self-driving laboratory (SDL), coined by Aspuru-Guzik, describes an AI-powered lab, which can generate hypotheses and test them without human intervention.87 This closed-loop aspect elevates an automated lab to an autonomous one. The conceptualization of the SDL aligns with the human chemist workflow—planning, experiment, analysis, and optimization—but the implementation of it is likely to streamline research in unforeseen ways. Where a human may have biases toward a certain type of reaction or analysis, the machine is agnostic toward these things, as its choices are entirely data-driven. Given the complexities of implementation, it is challenging to deliver quantitative measures of the advantage of the SDL. Nevertheless, several case studies within material science have yielded results that imply the benefits of this approach. Two are discussed here.

Nikolaev et al. utilized an AI planner built using a random forest/genetic algorithm to optimize conditions for carbon nanotube growth.88 The authors were successful in increasing the growth rate throughout 600 sequential, autonomous experiments, and suggested that this type of autonomous experimentation (termed ARES) could be applied to other materials fields including metal oxidation, additive manufacturing, and chemical vapor deposition without much difficulty.

An investigation by Xue and coworkers discovered nickel-titanium shape memory alloys.89 These flexible materials, which recover their shape upon heating, can be characterized by the thermal hysteresis (ΔT) required to cause the effect. To find alloy compositions, which had minimal ΔT, researchers tested several regression models and applied an efficient global optimization (EGO)90 selector algorithm to suggest new candidate compositions. After nine experimental cycles, the system found an alloy with ΔT=1.8 K, the lowest ever demonstrated. The key to success was the ability to balance exploration and optimization in the selector.

These examples and many others have demonstrated the promise of self-driving laboratories for material synthesis and discovery91–94—yet examples within chemistry are difficult to find. Comparison to the materials science experiments suggests that the main challenge is adopting design algorithms to non-continuous chemical space. Innovative strategies to transfer the self-driving laboratory tools to chemical space are needed.

The Cronin lab has worked on this problem using an experimental workflow called the Chemputer, which integrates closed-loop reaction screening and AI models together with the ability to ingest data from databases or NLP sources.95 The system autonomously explored the reactivity of a defined set of molecules by performing a series of experiments, examining and classifying the product as reactive or unreactive, and using a support vector machine to predict the reactivity of untested pairs. The goal of the system was to find new reactivity, rather than to optimize a particular property. In a demonstration, the system discovered several novel multicomponent reactions.

To truly reproduce the traditional molecular design process within an autonomous workflow requires models that can emulate human creativity. The models discussed so far have primarily been discriminative models, which estimate a conditional probability p(y|x). Given an observation x (e.g., some molecular representation), the model predicts the probability of a property y (toxicity, solubility, etc.). Performance, and to a lesser degree interpretability, are of primary importance in determining representations for such discriminative models. Generative models, in contrast, attempt the more complex task of estimating the joint distribution p(x,y) of observations and properties, from which new observations with desired properties may be described by computing p(x|y). Generative models such as variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks have gained popularity for generating novel speech, text, and imagery, and have also recently been applied to inverse molecular design.96 In this application, the viability of the inverse design candidate is also of utmost importance, as ultimately the candidate must be synthesized. This has been approached by imposing constraints on the topology of the generated molecular graphs,97 and enforcing a Chomsky type-2 grammar that encodes chemical knowledge upon a string-based representation of a molecule.98

The ability to generate completely novel structures is one of the most exciting possibilities enabled by improvements in ML algorithms for chemistry. Recently, a new kinase inhibitor drug was discovered by a generative model.99 Using an autoencoder approach, Zhavoronkov and coworkers used reinforcement learning to find an inhibitor of kinase implicated in fibrosis. The ability of the AI system to generate and prioritize candidates led to the discovery and validation of a nanomolar binder in just 46 days, compared to a typical timeline of 10 years or more and billions of dollars.100,101 This demonstration study represents arguably the boldest step yet toward replicating human chemical intuition, while critical commentary suggests its limitations.102 The DARPA Accelerated Molecular Discovery program will push these boundaries to explore wider swaths of chemical space and integrate them into closed loop workflows for a variety of DoD and other applications.

6.5.1 Implications of Autonomous Research

The ability for laboratories to design and synthesize novel molecules offers a future where vaccines are created in hours, vehicle coatings can be easily customized to specific climate, and affordable, customized catalysts neutralize greenhouse gases. But as AI enters the laboratory, it is wise to consider the ancillary impacts as well. It is impossible to design autonomous systems without recognizing the possible impact on employment. In most cases, scientific automation has served to expand experimental throughput rather than replace bench chemists. And the power of ML has led to huge increases in data science jobs. Yet, both have led to a shift in the types of skills required for researchers, and combining both these trends is expected to accelerate that shift. In the future, researchers will need to be capable coders, able to interpret ML results and comfortable manipulating structures on a computer.

It is not unusual for chemistry PhD students to learn these skills, but usually it is by necessity. In the future, they must be integrated into the core educational curriculum. Performing ibuprofen synthesis in microfluidics or building an ML model to predict binding could all be implemented into students’ laboratory curricula without sacrificing the core chemistry ideas or requiring large investments in new equipment. It will, however, require that educators become familiarized with these new fields. The National Science Foundation, the American Chemical Society, and other organizations can help with this by providing educational seminars and materials; these can also be leveraged to benefit chemists working in industry who will also need to gain proficiency in these skills. Despite these changes, we believe that AI will support and empower scientists to be more efficient, creative, and prolific.

Outside of core research, other related areas will be disrupted. Chemical safety and environmental regulation must adapt to future discovery paradigms. Traditionally, regulatory approval for a new drug application required a standard battery of tests. Today's FDA is increasing in flexibility, something the new research paradigm outlined above could help support. Research within the FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) has embraced the use of QSAR models for predicting toxicity and other outcomes based on a candidate drug's structure.103 As such models become more common for discovery as well as the regulatory approval, it will enable toxicity and other assessments to be performed at earlier stages of development, avoiding costly drug regulatory failures and shortening approval time for patients. In a similar way, the ability for AI prediction of reaction byproducts and compound stability could lead to more streamlined assessment of a particular manufacturing route.

A compelling question is, if computers are inventing the molecules, who owns the intellectual property (IP)?104 Currently, many computational tools are used for drug discovery, but they require enough human guidance such that they are not the source of IP. They might be considered the writer's pen, which has no claim to the author's copyright on their text. But if AI algorithms generate molecules autonomously, should the person who coded the algorithm maintain some part of the intellectual property? License agreements will need to address this. Imagine an open-source tool, which would rapidly generate high-quality drug candidates using publicly available data, analogous to Google's open-source AI tools for generating paintings or music. Would it be a race to submit them to the trademark office? Or, if no IP were granted, would we begin to see novel drugs without patent?105 Legal policy and business structure stand to be greatly impacted by the development and adoption of these tools. These factors must be considered alongside, not after, the development of automation and autonomy in the chemical sciences.

6.6 Conclusion

In 2016, Malaria killed 445 000 people106 and drug-resistant bacteria killed 700 000.107 For targets such as these, the moral obligation to leverage science against human suffering aligns with the national security interest to prevent global unrest sparked by pandemics. Yet, neither area attracts a fraction of the pharmaceutical investment that cancer or central nervous system illnesses do.108 We believe that DoD is well positioned to lead the way. In August 2018, the FDA approved the first prophylactic drug for malaria in more than 18 years, which was developed at the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research.106 Other DoD laboratories are developing cutting edge bulletproof plastics,109 improved thermophotovoltaics,110 and safer lasers.111

In the private sector, successes such as these would be followed by dramatically increased investment, drawing from large profits. This is not the case for government labs, which have relatively static budgets and do not reap the benefits of massive licensing deals. Yet, we have the opportunity to enhance the important work being done at these laboratories by providing AI tools to the researchers in them. The DARPA programs discussed here, as well as many other programs supported by the agency's $2 billion AINext campaign,112 will create tools to make laboratories working on areas such as soldier health, munition performance, or jet fuel safety, operate more efficiently, providing benefits to the warfighter, the nation, and our allies. DoD investment to integrate ML and automation will both serve as a force multiplier for those researchers and de-risk the adoption of these tools for chemical and biological researchers in academia and industry.

CHAPTER 7

Machine Learning for Chemical Synthesis

ALEXE L. HAYWOOD,a JOSEPH REDSHAW,b THOMAS GAERTNER,c ADAM TAYLOR,d ANDY M. MASONd AND JONATHAN D. HIRST( 0000-0002-2726-0983)*a

a School of Chemistry, University of NottinghamUniversity ParkNG7 2RDUK

b School of Computer Science, University of NottinghamJubilee CampusNG8 1BBUK

c TU Wien (Technical University of Vienna), Faculty of Informatics, Information Systems Engineering InstituteFavoritenstraße 9-111040 ViennaAustria

7.1 Introduction

Synthetic chemistry is at the heart of medicinal and materials chemistry. Anticipating how molecules will react (forward synthetic planning) and how a molecule can be synthesised (retrosynthesis) rely on the expert knowledge and experience of a synthetic chemist. Repositories such as Reaxys and SciFinder contain millions of compounds, reactions, references, and bioactivities. These repositories allow chemists to search through vast regions of chemical space to fill in any gaps in their knowledge. Reaction precedents on analogous structures and/or reaction types to molecules with no reported synthesis routes can be retrieved. Although integrated tools enable the search results to be filtered, analysing the information to make informed decisions is a manual process that requires the intellect and time of an expert synthetic chemist.

Automating retrosynthetic analysis, the recursive breakdown of a target molecule until reactant precursors are reached that are commercially available, would significantly reduce the time taken to plan chemical syntheses. The concept of using a computer to plan synthetic routes was first proposed around 50 years ago.1 The history of CASD tools has been reviewed in detail,2–5 from the pioneering work of E. J. Corey in the development of Logic and Heuristics Applied to Synthetic Analysis (LHASA)6 to contemporary commercially available programs. Thus far, chemists are yet to implement these tools when planning synthetic routes to new molecules. A survey was completed in 2017 (13 chemists in two companies)3 to determine what chemists expect from CASD tools. The following were identified as the most important aspects to include: (i) user-friendly, (ii) provide supportive literature examples, (iii) define possible bonds to be broken, (iv) lead to commercially available reactant precursors, (v) recognise conflicting reactivity and suggest protecting groups, and (vi) prioritise results. While aspects (i) to (v) can be implemented regardless of the chemist's area of expertise, prioritising results is a challenge. Chemists working in different parts of the chemical industry have different priorities when designing reactions. Their criteria for a suitable reaction could be based on cost, greenness, reaction conditions (such as temperature or catalysts), and so on. Therefore, CASD tools need to be flexible and rank pathways based on the criteria provided by the chemist.

Forward synthetic planning is the prediction of products given the reactants, reagents, and a set of reaction conditions. Experiments, which are predominantly used to identify reaction outcomes, are expensive, time-consuming, and require experienced chemists. It would therefore be beneficial for computational tools to identify the major product, any side-products, and validate retrosynthetic predictions. Optimising reaction conditions, such as catalysts and solvents, is also an important part of synthetic planning. Changing a set of reaction conditions, even slightly, could result in the formation of a different major product or a failed reaction. Integrating CASD with high-throughput screening and robotic equipment holds much promise for the future of reaction optimisation.

Advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning methods and availability of big data have provoked renewed interest in CASD. In this chapter, we will outline sources and representations of reaction data, give a brief description of machine learning methods focused on synthetic chemistry, and provide detailed approaches to CASD with contemporary examples and comparisons.

7.2 The Nature of the Chemical Data

7.2.1 Data Sources

Large amounts of data are required for training machine learning algorithms. Typically, supervised learning methods (see Section 7.3) are used in this area; these require labelled data. This means the ground truth associated with each input is required, whether that be the reactants, products, or yield data. Reactions are often extracted from reaction databases, cleaned, and re-written in a machine-readable format.7,8 The lack of a conventional approach for data extraction has resulted in different types of information, managed in different ways, used as the input to the machine learning methods. Databases are noisy and can contain duplicate and even erroneous reactions. These should be removed in the cleaning process. Recorded reactions that generated multiple products can be managed in two ways. The highest yielding (i.e. major) product can be kept and the others discarded,8 or the reaction can be split into multiple single-product reactions.9–12 Atom-to-atom mapping is often required in retrosynthesis and forward synthetic planning tools, usually to identify reaction centres. Atom map indices are used to label all atoms in the reactant species that are mapped to the atoms in the product species as shown in Figure 7.1. Reactions with incorrect or incomplete indices should be removed. Other reaction information, for example stereochemistry, has historically been difficult to incorporate due to sparse availability, difficulty in encoding into the molecular descriptors, or difficulty in incorporating into the model.

Figure 7.1 An example of an atom mapped reaction.

Reaction data reported in scientific journal publications and patents can be accessed through commercial repositories, such as Reaxys and SciFinder. Synthetic chemists use these tools to retrieve relevant experimental procedures, chemical literature, and patents. However, extracting large quantities of reaction data for data analysis or to train machine learning models requires a specific licence. Although rare, academic research groups have extracted ∼12.5M single-step reactions from Reaxys and built models for forward reaction prediction,13,14 retrosynthetic route design14,15 and the prediction of reaction conditions.16 Nonetheless, to compare models an open-source dataset is required where access is not an issue.

Open-source patent data from the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) is the alternative dataset of choice when commercial licences are not available. US patents from 1976 to September 2016 were parsed by Lowe.17 Reactants, products, reagents, solvents, quantities of molecules used, yield, temperature, time, preparation and workup steps were extracted using text-mining.18 This common benchmark dataset contains ∼1M single-step reactions. Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILES)19 strings (see Section 7.2.2) represent the molecules in each atom mapped reaction. The USPTO dataset is useful for building synthetic design models, as it consists of many popular chemical reactions, particularly ones used in medicinal chemistry. Subsets of the dataset have been pre-processed and split into training, validation and testing sets. The USPTO_MIT subset of ca. 480K reactions has been used in reaction prediction.20 For the retrosynthesis task, the filtered dataset of 50K reactions (USPTO_50K) have been classified into ten reaction types (see Table 7.1).21 This enables models to be compared based on individual reaction types. The USPTO dataset contains prophetic examples which are predicted experimental methods and results that have not been carried out.22 Prophetic examples are allowed in US patents as long as they are not written in the past tense. Models based on patents that include prophetic examples should be considered with caution, as synthetic routes may not have been predicted based on experimentally valid examples.
