Reaction data published in journals and patents are biased toward high yielding reactions; low yielding and failed reactions are rarely reported. The latter may include reactions where all of the starting material remains or reactions leading to the formation of unexpected products. Supervised learning models built on published data are therefore limited, as counter-examples are required in training for optimum performance. The absence of failed data has been overcome by generating negative examples. Here, reaction templates (see Section 7.4) are used to generate chemically plausible “wrong/false” products.13,15,23

Electronic Laboratory Notebooks (ELNs) are used in the pharmaceutical industry by chemists to document their experimental procedures, conditions, and notes. They also store other useful data including yields and spectra. ELNs contain failed reaction data and hence can be utilised to enhance supervised learning models, without generating artificial negative data. The restricted reactant space covered in ELNs contains common reactions used by chemists. The reactions are considered to be of high quality, reproducible, and reliable. Unfortunately, ELNs are not accessible to the public, nor in commercial databases due to confidentiality reasons. However, with access, the reaction data within ELNs has been used to build reaction prediction24 and retrosynthesis models8,24 as well as to predict reaction conditions.25

7.2.2 Molecular Descriptors

For a machine learning algorithm to learn from chemical structures, those structures must be represented in a way that an algorithm can process. Molecular descriptors are based on the structural, physiochemical, electronic, or topological nature of molecules. The type of descriptor used affects the performance of the algorithm as it has to capture the relevant information required.

One-dimensional descriptors represent molecules as a list of structural fragments. They are fast, easy to calculate, and simple to compare. An example is molecular fingerprints. These are vectors composed of binary digits that correspond to the presence or absence of specific substructures. This encoded information only defines one-dimensional features of the molecules. Molecular fingerprints can also contain two-dimensional information relating to atom connectivity by encoding the neighbourhood of each atom. Three-dimensional conformer information can also be encoded. A type of fingerprint called Morgan circular fingerprints has been used to predict reactant precursors by comparing the similarity of target molecules with products in a knowledge-base.9 A reaction fingerprint, calculated by the difference between the sum of the products and the sum of the reactants fingerprints, has been developed to classify reaction types.26

Two-dimensional descriptors encode the topology (i.e. connectivity) of a molecule. For example, molecular graphs contain nodes that correspond to the atoms, and edges that correspond to the bonds that connect the atoms. The nodes are labelled by atom type and the edges are weighted based on bond type. Molecular graphs are fast to compute and easy to interpret, as molecules with identical graphs are identical molecules. Another type of two-dimensional descriptors are line notations that describe a molecule as a sequence of characters. The most widely used line notation is SMILES and its extensions, SMARTS (SMILES arbitrary target specification) and SMIRKS (a reaction transform language). SMILES strings are defined as follows.

  • Atoms are written as their atomic symbols.
  • Single, double, triple and quadruple bonds are written as “-”, “=”, “#” and “$” respectively, although single bonds are usually omitted.
  • Atoms in aromatic rings are encoded using lower case letters.
  • Reactions can be written by splitting the reactants, reagents, and products with a “>” symbol.

For a single molecule, multiple SMILES strings may be valid, as the string can start from any atom within the molecule. This should be accounted for when building models, by either canonicalizing the SMILES strings or building a model that understands which different SMILES strings are equivalent. SMARTS strings are an extension of SMILES which include additional logical operators to allow searching for generic substructures. SMIRKS are another extension that describes generic reaction transforms. These line notations can be used as a direct input to machine learning algorithms.27–29

Another type of descriptor employs properties found using quantum calculations. Examples include NMR shifts, electrostatic charges, HOMO/LUMO energies, vibrational frequencies, and intensities. Quantum chemical calculations have been used as descriptors in the prediction of yield.30 However, density functional theory (DFT) calculations are computationally expensive.

7.3 Machine Learning Methods

Machine learning algorithms can be divided into many categories depending on the given task. This section will concern itself with two of the most popular, namely supervised and unsupervised learning. In supervised learning, the relationship between input-output pairs is modelled, to build a predictive model. The input data can be represented with various valid descriptors, examples range from a vector of numeric values to molecular graphs (see Section 7.2.2). Supervised learning models process the input data and return output data as a numerical or binary value. The key aspect of supervised learning is that the values of outputs are already known and can be used as examples to guide the learning process.

If the output data is a continuous or quantitative value, modelling its relationship with an arbitrary set of inputs is known as regression. Defining X={xi}Ni=1 as the set of N input data points, Y={yi}Ni=1 as the set of corresponding output data points and F as the unknown relationship between the two, regression estimates F based on the evidence that yi=F(xi) for i=1,…, N. The unknown function, F, does not have to represent a direct relationship between the input and output; it could represent a probability distribution over input-output pairs. However, the methods to infer F are the same and it is these that we are concerned with. Standard regression techniques assume that F belongs to a set of functions of similar structure and can therefore be parametrised based upon this structure. For example, one could assume that F is linear and parametrised by a vector β, thus yi=βTxi for i=1,…, N. However, this can be restrictive if the relationship being modelled is not sufficiently described by the assumed form. To overcome this, many machine learning approaches make no such assumptions and, instead, infer F solely based upon the supplied data.

One popular approach to regression would be to use an artificial neural network (ANN). This is a model that can approximate an arbitrary relationship between the input-output pairs and is defined by a matrix of parameters W called the weights. During the learning process, the ANN uses the “Backpropagation” algorithm31 in conjunction with a gradient-based optimisation scheme (for example, gradient descent) to produce an estimate F̂ of F that minimises the error in its predictions. Each prediction ŷi is a function of the input xi and the weights W, so ŷi=F̂(xi, W). Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss function (which quantifies how accurate a prediction is) with respect to each weight. The gradient-based optimisation scheme then utilises this information to adjust W so that the error in prediction between ŷi and yi is reduced. This process is repeated numerous times to allow the ANN to learn a set of weights that best describe the relationship. A more mathematical, yet still approachable, introduction to ANNs can be found in the review by Higham and Higham.32

We have described a method to model the relationship between input and output data, where the output is a real number. Another supervised learning problem considers the output as a binary value i.e. yi=1 or yi=0. This is known as classification. Whilst ANNs can also be used for classification, another effective model is the Support Vector Machine (SVM).33 SVMs classify through the use of a hyperplane (a generalisation of a straight line to any number of dimensions) that best separates the dataset. If a data point resides on one side of the hyperplane, it is classified one way. If it lies on the other side of this hyperplane, it is classified the other way. This can be formalised by writing any hyperplane as the set of points x satisfying wtx−b=0. Thus, any hyperplane is defined by w and b, which are identified by training an SVM classifier. Assuming the input data is linearly separable (it can be divided into two non-intersecting sets with a hyperplane), training an SVM selects two parallel hyperplanes of the form wtx−b=1 and wtx−b=−1 by minimising the cost function shown in (7.1).

(7.1)

The constraint yi(wtxi−b)≥1 ensures that both hyperplanes separate the data whilst also maximising the distance between them, which is usually referred to as the margin. To maximise the margin, it is necessary that each of the two hyperplanes must pass through at least one of the data points. Such data points are known as “support vectors”, hence the model's name. The SVM determines the hyperplane that “best separates” the data by maximising the margin. The resulting classifying hyperplane takes the form wtx−b=0 and lies exactly halfway between the two. Figure 7.2 illustrates this. A new data point x̂ is classified as 1 if wtx̂−b≥0 and −1 if wtx̂−b≤0. The previous description was based on the assumption that the input data are linearly separable, but this often is not the case. To account for this case, one needs to incorporate slack variables into the SVM formulation. These variables allow certain data points to reside on the wrong side of the best separating hyperplane by adding a penalty to the cost function, as shown in eqn (7.2).

(7.2)

Figure 7.2 An example of a set of linearly separable data points. Also shown is the optimal hyperplane that separates them. The highlighted points are the support vectors.33

Here, the slack variables ξi are greater than zero if a data point xi resides on the incorrect side of the hyperplane. A penalty of is added to the cost function to account for this. C is a user-defined parameter that balances the number of incorrectly classified points against the best fitting hyperplane. A more thorough treatment of this can be found in the article by Bennett and Campbell, which also includes the extension to non-linear decision surfaces.34 Furthermore, a number of other algorithms can be used to perform classification and these have been the subject of many reviews.35,36

Unsupervised learning is an approach in which we are only provided with input data and the aim is to find global (describing a property of the whole dataset or distribution) patterns within this. We distinguish this from data mining, which is a similar area of research that is more concerned with local (describing a subset of the whole dataset) patterns in the data. With no prior knowledge of the pattern, the method identifies them by searching for and exploiting commonalities within the data. A standard approach to this task would be to partition the data into sets of “similar” data points, or clusters. A clustering algorithm therefore creates a number of clusters and each data point is uniquely assigned to the cluster that it is most similar to. A simple, yet effective, algorithm to perform such a task would be k-means.37 Initially, k data points are randomly selected to be the cluster centres. Each cluster is formed by the subset of data points closest to the respective cluster centre. The cluster centres are recalculated as the mean of the points assigned to the cluster. All data points that are not cluster centres are reassigned to their closest cluster and this process repeats until the clusters no longer change. Whilst it can be used for classification and regression (see Erman, Arlitt and Mahanti38), the process of identifying clusters is mainly used to better understand the dataset in question. Although k-means is guaranteed to find a clustering of the data points into k clusters, it is up to the practitioner to determine if anything meaningful can be inferred from the clustering. Another popular unsupervised learning algorithm is Principal Component Analysis (PCA). This is a dimensionality reduction algorithm that reduces a set of possibly correlated variables into a set of linearly uncorrelated variables called the principal components. Each principal component is calculated in such a way that it retains as much variance as possible. The first principal component retains the largest possible variance and all subsequent components retain the largest possible variance given that they are orthogonal to the previous principal components. This results in a set of variables that best represent the data; PCA is commonly incorporated into data visualisation. By plotting the first two principal components, one can visualise a low-dimensional representation of the original dataset. This is one of the more traditional algorithms to perform dimensionality reduction. We point the reader to the review by Maaten, Postma, Herik for an overview of more recent approaches that aim to overcome the limitations of traditional PCA.39k-means is one of the simpler clustering methods and we encourage the reader to inspect the review by Fung for a more thorough overview of clustering methods.40

Having chosen an algorithm and built a model, the next point of concern is to evaluate how well it performs. Whilst performance can be measured in a number of meaningful ways, a key issue is to understand how well it generalises. Analogous to how a school teaches its pupils a topic and then tests them on related, but unseen questions, we “teach” the model using a set of data and test it on similar, but previously unseen data. This allows us to assess whether the model has learnt anything useful and evaluate how well it has learnt. In such analyses, one first splits the dataset into a training and test set (a 70:30 split is common). A model is built using only the training set and is used to make predictions on the test set. The key idea here is that the model has never before seen the test set, so it is using the knowledge it has learnt from the training data to make its predictions. This approach allows us to state the generalisability of the model to unseen data points. However, this may not be an accurate assessment of generalisability, as it is dependent on which data points belong to the train and test set. K-Fold Cross Validation (K-Fold CV) is a procedure to overcome this. Instead of splitting a dataset into a train and test set once, K-Fold CV performs the split K times. Initially, it divides the dataset into K sets (or folds) of approximately equal size. It takes the first fold to be the test set and the remaining K−1 folds to be the training set. The model is trained on the training set and makes predictions on the test set. This process is repeated using each fold once as the test set (ensuring that each data point belongs to the test set once). Figure 7.3 illustrates this. A score that evaluates how close the model predictions are to the actual values can be calculated for each train/test split, from which an average can be taken to get an overall score. Further details about K-Fold CV, as well as a number of other methods to estimate model accuracy and generalisability, can be found in the study by Kohavi.41 Although K-Fold CV is a quick and easy way to reduce over-estimation of model accuracy, the data is split into K sets randomly. Therefore, it could lead to an unreliable over-estimation of model performance if there is a distributional shift in the data. If the training and test sets are very similar, machine learning models can exhibit high accuracy due to memorising the training set (overfitting the data).42,43 In the case of synthetic route design (see Section 7.4), care needs to be taken in the construction of training and test sets. In particular, one should be mindful that if highly similar reactions are present in both the training and test set, one may make an overly optimistic estimate of the generalisation achieved by the algorithm. Conversely, if the test set reactions are too dissimilar to those in the training set, one will be trying to make predictions beyond the scope of what one might reasonably expect the algorithm to learn.

Figure 7.3 An example of how K-Fold Cross Validation works. Here, K=5.

Now we can quantify how good our model is, it is worth considering how to pick the best model from a set of models. Generally, we should only compare models performing the same task e.g. two regression models. Let's assume we have the results of K-Fold CV for two different regression models. The next step in picking the best model would be to use a statistical test to determine whether the difference in performance is solely due to chance. One such test is the t-test, with a null hypothesis of “the difference in the means is equal to zero”. This test can be used to evaluate whether the difference between the means of two datasets is statistically significant, and we could easily apply it to the results of our two K-Fold CV procedures. Performing such a test would allow us to accept or reject the null hypothesis. As α is defined as the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is in fact true, the test indicating a rejection of the null hypothesis implies that we are (1−α)×100% certain that the difference in the means is not zero. Taking alpha to be 0.05, another way to state this is that the probability of observing these two K-Fold CV results and their difference being due to chance is 0.05. This is an important point because things would change if we were to compare three models, which would involve three separate hypothesis tests. Assuming our confidence for each test is α, the probability of one of the differences due to chance is now 1−(1−0.05)3=0.1426 and is approximately three times as likely. To account for this, we use the Bonferroni Correction which states that, when testing N hypotheses, our confidence for each test must be equal to . This is one of many corrections that are applicable to multiple hypothesis testing, see the paper by Goeman and Solari44 for a wider overview and the article by Demšar45 for a thorough treatment of many statistical tests related to machine learning.

7.4 Synthetic Route Design

Designing synthetic pathways can be divided into two categories that are inverse processes. The first category, forward reaction planning, requires prior knowledge of reactant precursors to predict possible products of reactions. Retrosynthesis is the second, working backwards from a target molecule, predicting possible bond disconnections to obtain simpler reactant precursors. This step happens recursively until commercially available reactant precursors are reached. The overall synthetic pathway of a target molecule is a series of reaction steps. Single-step retrosynthetic design is far more complex than forward reaction prediction as there is no single correct answer. This is due to functional groups present in the output (reactants) being absent from the input (products). In the example Buchwald-Hartwig reaction shown in Figure 7.4a, the halide leaving group is not present in the product. Multiple precursors and different reactant types may be plausible for a single bond disconnection. For example, the C–N bond in the target shown in Figure 7.4 can be synthesised by a Buchwald-Hartwig reaction with various halides or a Chan-Lam reaction. Without defining the reaction type, multiple bonds could be disconnected, particularly in larger molecules. In reaction prediction, all relevant functional groups are present in the input (reactants). This significantly reduces the number of possible reaction types that may occur and hence reduces the number of possible outputs in comparison to retrosynthesis.

Figure 7.4 An example of forward synthetic planning (a) and retrosynthesis route design (b) and (c).

The most prominent approach to synthetic route design is the use of pre-defined heuristics to encode reactions. Heuristics, also known in this context as reaction templates, define a single chemical transformation from reactant(s) to product(s), or vice versa. Basic reaction templates contain the atoms and bonds involved in bond-making/breaking (the reaction centre) and any neighbouring atoms that may influence the reaction. Additional information may not be included due to data availability and inconsistency.8,23 More complex templates can include reaction conditions, reactivity conflicts, protection requirements as well as stereo-46 and regioselectivity.47,48 In multi-step retrosynthesis, the aim is to find the minimal number of reaction templates that need to be applied to a target molecule to reach commercially available reactant precursors. There is an inevitable trade-off between generalisation and specificity when defining reaction templates. If the templates are too generalised, the model will not be able to perceive any potential reactivity conflicts and may result in improper use. On the other hand, overly specific templates result in poor generalisability to unseen molecules.

Reaction templates are written in a user-friendly syntax, usually specific to the developers. Early programs manually hand-coded reaction templates.49 This method suffered from three major issues: (1) Expert synthetic chemists with years of experience were required to code each reaction. (2) This labour-intensive task was not scalable to a large number of chemistries and incomplete template libraries covering a limited scope of reaction classes were often a result. (3) The complexity of reactions is not straight-forward due to reactivity conflicts and dependencies on reaction conditions and hence was difficult to codify. Despite these limitations, the commercially available program Synthia (formally Chematica) has proved that, with sufficient time investment, hand-coded reactions can be used successfully for the retrosynthesis prediction task.47,48,50 A more efficient and less time-consuming process for defining templates is to extract reaction data automatically from the literature. Providing the reactions in the dataset are atom mapped, the reaction centre can be identified.8,15,46,51–54 Tools, such as the Reaction Decoder Tool (RDT), are available to calculate atom map indices if they are not known.52,53 A toolkit has also been developed for handling stereochemical information when defining reaction templates.54 It is far easier to maintain automatically extracted template libraries and they have been employed in reaction prediction14,55 and retrosynthesis.14,15,56

Contemporary template-based methods consist of two components: a pre-defined template library and a scoring function. These components can be combined in two different ways. The first is to exhaustively apply all possible reaction templates to obtain potential reactants or products and then rank the generated candidates.23 The second is to rank the reaction templates and only apply the most relevant templates to the input molecule to generate candidate species.14,15,46 ANNs have been applied to both candidate and template ranking.14,15,23 The similarity-based approach is slightly different to contemporary methods, as there is no pre-defined template library. This method is used exclusively in retrosynthesis. The target molecule is compared to the products in a knowledge base, reaction templates are extracted from the most similar reactions and are applied to the target to generate reactant candidates. The similarity of the candidates is compared to the precedent's reactants and used in combination with the product similarity score to rank the reactant precursors. This similarity-based approach differs from purely template-based methods as it is fully data driven.

Although template and similarity-based methods are easily interpretable, as they align with the way a synthetic chemist thinks, they have several limitations. The constant maintenance of template libraries is time-consuming and can be challenging when including new chemistries. Automatic extraction of templates from datasets is heavily dependent on atom-mapped reactions, which are not always completed or correct. Also, common atom-mapping tools are based on predefined expert rules. Reaction templates only focus on the local environment of reaction centres and, therefore, important groups in the global environment may be missed. Template-based methods are not able to make accurate predictions outside of their template library and hence cannot discover novel chemistries.14 However, these methods are useful in aiding synthetic chemists with everyday retrosynthesis tasks.

The alternative to template-based methods is template-free methods. These methods are fully data driven and trained end-to-end without the construction of predefined reaction heuristics. Therefore, template-free methods are scalable to large datasets at a fraction of the computational cost and are generalisable to novel chemistries. To date, template-free models have either been graph-based or sequence-based. Graph-based models follow the same two-step procedure as those that are template-based in that reaction centres are identified to generate reactant precursors or products, depending on the task. Predictions generated from this approach are easily interpretable as the approach is analogous to that of a synthetic chemist. Reaction centres have been identified to generate product candidates using a convolutional neural network on molecular graph descriptors.20,55 Graph-based models have only focused on reaction prediction and not retrosynthesis.

Sequence-based models have a different approach to the above-mentioned methods. Here, the problem can be thought of as a machine translation task, whereby a language (e.g. English) is entered into a model that translates the text into another language (e.g. Spanish). When applied to reaction prediction and retrosynthesis the molecules can be represented by text notation, such as SMILES strings (see Section 7.2.2). In reaction prediction, the reactant SMILES strings are translated into a product SMILES string and vice versa for retrosynthesis. Sequence-to-sequence models have an encoder-decoder architecture consisting of two recurrent neural networks and an additional attention mechanism.10,27,29 In this type of model each token in the SMILES string is assumed to be related to its neighbour and hence influences the nature of the neighbouring token. For each SMILES token, these models will only learn the local surrounding tokens and not tokens that are far away in the sequence. A transformer-based architecture has been adapted for the machine translation task.57 These models differ from sequence-to-sequence models, as they do not contain recurrent neural networks. They have a fully attention-based encoder-decoder architecture. As the recurrent component is missing, the model is able to correlate individual tokens in the SMILES string regardless of their location. Unlike the sequence-to-sequence models, transformer models are able to capture long range interactions between tokens. Transformer models have shown success in both forward reaction prediction28 and single-step retrosynthesis.11,12,24,58 Sequence-based models have some advantages over two-step graph-based models. They do not require atom-mapping, atom features nor any chemical knowledge. The global environment of the molecules is also implicitly incorporated into the model. The major drawback to sequence-based methods is SMILES invalidity. The models do not directly learn the terminology of the SMILES notation, so these cannot be guaranteed to predict valid SMILES. The attention mechanisms present in all the template-free methods discussed enable the models to be interpreted. Attention weights of the atoms (i.e. the SMILES tokens) can be used to identify which aspects of the input species influence the output species.

The performance of synthetic route design models is a balance between accuracy, reliability, and adaptability. Model accuracy can be calculated as the percentage of test set predictions where the ground truth was ranked within the top-n per cent of the predicted molecules for the given target. For example, the top-1 accuracy is the percentage of predictions where the correct molecule was ranked in the top-1 per cent. A model should be able to estimate the reliability of its predictions. The calculation of confidence scores should be implemented into model evaluation to identify when the model is likely to fail.24,28 It is important to know how adaptable a model is. A model may have high accuracy scores, but can it generalise across chemical space? For example, if trained on patent data can it accurately predict synthetic routes to molecules in ELNs that cover a different range of chemical space?24 These are important points to consider when evaluating synthetic route design models.

7.4.1 Retrosynthesis

7.4.1.1 Single-step Retrosynthesis

A combination of template-based and template-free models have been developed for the single-step retrosynthesis task. A target molecule is entered into the model which then disconnects a bond and generates possible reactant precursors. A benchmark dataset of 50 000 reactions extracted from US patents, herein named the USPTO_50K (see Section 7.2.1),21 has been used to train and test single-step retrosynthesis prediction tools (see Table 7.2). A template-based model was built by Liu et al. as a baseline model.10 The reaction templates consisting of the reaction centre, neighbouring atoms, and the reaction class were automatically extracted from the training data. For each target molecule, all templates in the same reaction class were applied to generate reactant candidates that were subsequently ranked. The similarity-based approach described previously, another type of template-based method, outperformed the baseline and the template-free sequence-to-sequence model developed by Liu et al. in every reaction class.9,10 The similarity-based model does not focus on finding only the major product but ranking all possibilities. As a result, it has the highest top-5 per cent accuracy of 81.2% when the reaction class is known prior. This approach is limited beyond the scope of the knowledge base and will always disfavour creative disconnections.

Sequence-based, template-free models (Transformer – Lin et al.,12 SCROP,11 MT24 and Transformer – Karpov et al.58) with a transformer architecture can overcome these limitations and have shown to be state-of-the-art even when the reaction class is unknown (see Table 7.2). As previously mentioned, a drawback to these methods is the prediction of invalid SMILES. The standard transformer architecture does not learn the grammar of the SMILES notation. Therefore, a predicted SMILES string may be grammatically invalid, but the grammatically correct version may be the ground truth. The self-corrected retrosynthesis predictor (SCROP) has an additional component to the other transformer models.11 Once a reactant SMILES is predicted, a transformer-based syntax predictor is used to automatically correct the SMILES string if it is not syntactically plausible. The addition of the syntax predictor improves the SMILES invalidity rate (see Table 7.3), remaining under 2.0% for the top-5 per cent of SMILES strings. The SMILES invalidity rate of the SCROP11 model is also lower than the Seq2seq10 and Transformer – Lin et al.12 models. The Molecular Transformer (MT24) model does not report a SMILES invalidity rate for comparison. The SCROP11 model achieves the highest top-1 accuracy of 59.0% when the reaction class was known.

All models were trained and tested with prior knowledge of the reaction class (apart from MT24 and Transformer – Karpov et al.58) which is useful if a particular reaction is of interest. However, it is more realistic that the reaction class is unknown. Model training and testing of the Similarity,9 Transformer – Lin et al.,12 SCROP,11 MT24 and Transformer – Karpov et al.58 models were performed without prior knowledge of the reaction class. Removal of the reaction class resulted in a drop of 11-16% in the top-1 per cent accuracy (see Table 7.2). All the transformer-based models have comparable top-1 accuracies.

7.4.1.2 Multi-step Retrosynthesis

The aim of CASD software is not only to predict the reactant precursors of a target molecule but also to break down the precursors recursively until they are commercially available. This multi-step retrosynthesis task can be thought of as a synthesis tree. A synthesis tree will have a branching factor - the number of possible steps that can be taken from a particular molecule - and a depth - how many steps until the path is terminated. Pathway termination will occur if the precursors found are commercially available or if a predefined depth constraint is reached. For retrosynthesis, the branching factor is usually large and the depth low. The number of possible synthetic routes drastically increases with the number of steps in a pathway (depth). CASD tools require intelligent algorithms to identify the most promising branches and avoid exhaustive calculation of all possibilities. Unfortunately, choosing the optimum predicted reaction at every step may not lead to the most efficient pathway. The effect of each decision will not be known until the cost of the entire pathway is calculated. This cost could be related to the price of starting materials, the number of steps, waste generated, greenness, ease of product purification, sustainability, safety hazards, or environmental hazards. CASD tools generate synthesis trees to minimise a cost function that is often user-defined.

Commercially available CASD programs include InfoChem's ICSYNTH,46 Wiley's ChemPlanner™ (formerly ARChem Route Designer)51 that has integrated into CAS’ SciFindern and Synthia™ (formerly Chematica), a trademark of Merck KGaA.47,48,50 These programs are based on reaction templates. Synthia™ contains a template library of ca. 60 000 reaction templates, hand-coded by expert synthetic chemists. Along with reaction transforms, the templates also encode possible incompatibility groups, protecting groups and reaction conditions. ICSYNTH and ChemPlanner™ automatically extracted templates, consisting of the reaction centre and neighbouring atom/groups, from reaction databases. ICSYNTH also provides software to generate template libraries from in-house data that can be used independently or alongside the supplied libraries. Scoring functions, based on user-defined criteria, evaluate each synthetic step and guide the search to commercially available substrates. Synthia™ and ICSYNTH filter the predictions to remove any unwanted structures. Additional heuristics are defined in Synthia™ to penalise non-selective reactions, strained intermediates, and unlikely structural motifs. In ICSYNTH, the predicted structure is compared to a predefined list of unacceptable structures. ChemPlanner™ uses a similar approach to filter out functional group incompatibilities. Synthia™ and ChemPlanner™ account for regiochemistry and electronic effects. Synthia™ can also handle stereochemistry and steric effects. Each program generates synthesis trees with references to supporting literature and the cost of starting materials.

Segler and Waller have published their neural-symbolic model, composed of three neural networks (expansion policy, in-scope filter and rollout phase) combined with Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) to guide the multi-step retrosynthesis search.15 Reaction templates were extracted from 12.4 million reactions published before 2015 in Reaxys. The expansion policy and in-scope filter together are known as the expansion procedure, which is based on a knowledge base of 301 671 reaction templates containing reaction centres. The expansion procedure was applied to each target molecule to predict the reactant precursors for a single step. Here, the target molecule was represented by fingerprints and inputted to the expansion policy to prioritise the reaction templates. The top k templates were applied to the target to generate reactant candidates. The in-scope filter classified the reactions as feasible or not, to filter out any unfeasible reactions. The rollout policy, based on 17 134 reaction templates (containing reaction centres and neighbouring atoms), calculated tree position values. The expansion procedure and the rollout policy are incorporated into the MCTS algorithm to forms the 3N-MCTS model. Predicted pathways generated by the model for drug-like compounds could not be distinguished from literature routes according to a double-blind AB test. While the 3N-MCTS model can account for stereochemistry, it does not consider the prediction of reaction conditions in pathway generation.

7.4.2 Reaction Prediction

Retrosynthetic routes, either predicted by chemists or machine, are not guaranteed to be experimentally feasible. To validate the routes, one option is to test all the possibilities experimentally, which requires experienced synthetic chemists, a substantial amount of time, and high costs. An alternative validation technique is forward reaction prediction. Here, the reactants, reagents and possibly reaction conditions are known, and the aim is to predict possible products. It is important to include reaction conditions in the model as slight changes in solvent or temperature can result in a large change in yield or the formation of a different major product. Quantum chemical calculations can be used to identify the major product, but the calculations are computationally expensive and limited to smaller molecules. Machine learning and artificial intelligence can be applied to large systems at a low computational cost.

The benchmark dataset for reaction prediction is the USPTO_MIT dataset (Section 7.1) composed of ca. 480K reactions.20 State-of-the-art in reaction prediction are template-free models (see Table 7.4). The graph-based Weisfeiler-Lehman Difference Network (WLDN55) model outperformed the sequence-to-sequence (S2S27) model with an increase of 5.3% top-1 per cent accuracy. The WLDN model identifies the reaction centre from a reactant pool consisting of reactants, reagents and solvent species using a Weisfeiler-Lehman Network, a type of graph convolutional neural network. Another graph convolutional neural network (WLDN) then ranks the candidate products generated by focused enumeration. A sequence-based transformer model, the Molecular Transformer (MT28), outperformed the graph-based model (WLDN) by 4.8% in the top-1 per cent accuracy. The reported accuracies are for the USPTO_MIT dataset that was pre-processed to distinguish between reactants and reagents, prior to model training and testing. Removing the distinction results in lower model accuracy, 5.6% lower for the WLDN model and 1.8% for the MT model.

To assess the adaptability of the MT model, the MT and WLDN models were trained on the USPTO_MIT data and tested on reaction data within ELNs from Pfizer.24 The two datasets cover different regions of chemical space, which ensures the elimination of control bias from analogous reactions in the reported model accuracies. The MT model predicts the correct molecule within the top-1 per cent 69.0% of the time when predicting outside of its trained chemical space (see Table 7.4). The transformer-based architecture is currently the highest performing model type for both forward reaction prediction and single-step retrosynthesis.

7.4.3 Optimising Reaction Conditions

Identifying reaction conditions requires the expert knowledge and experience of a synthetic chemist. A reaction may be carried out under a variety of reaction conditions, but the most common conditions selected are those used for similar reactions that proved to be successful. Selection based on similarity can be insufficient, as reaction outcomes are influenced by a number of reaction parameters. Reaction conditions are therefore challenging to anticipate, especially because small changes in reaction parameters can result in quite different reaction outcomes or failed reactions. Chemists are required to find a combination of catalyst(s), reagent(s), solvent(s), temperature and pressure that work. Predictions from CASD programs and reaction prediction methods can only be validated experimentally if corresponding reaction conditions are also predicted. Therefore, incorporating condition prediction into such tools is crucial.

The prediction of reaction conditions is an under-explored area that has mainly focused on the optimisation of a single reaction condition or single reaction class. A binary classification model has been implemented for the prediction of the type of catalyst and solvent used in Michael additions.59 A similarity-based approach was employed for the identification of catalysts for catalytic hydrogenation reactions, a type of deprotection reaction. The greatest interest has been in catalyst prediction and optimisation. Catalysts are important as they can increase rates of reactions and, in asymmetric catalysis, allow for the selectivity of one stereoisomer. Efforts to predict the selectivity of asymmetric catalysts have the potential to change how catalysts are designed, when one stereoisomer is favoured.60–63

It is desired that reaction condition prediction tools allow for the prediction of all reaction conditions. A neural network has been built to predict catalyst(s), solvent(s), reagent(s) and temperature for a range of chemical reactions, which can be applied on a large scale.16 The combination of machine learning with an automated synthesis and testing module is the future of reaction condition optimisation.64 Computer-assisted synthetic planning and a robotic flow chemistry platform have been built for the execution of predicted synthetic routes to small molecules. This is a step closer to fully automatic synthetic chemistry.

7.5 Real-life Applications

CASD programs (see Section 7.4.1.2) that predict multi-step synthetic pathways to molecules may have high validation scores, but chemists will remain cautious until there is evidence supporting their true value. Applications thus far are primarily focused on drug-like targets and bioactive molecules.

InfoChem, in collaboration with AstraZeneca, has evaluated the performance of ICSYNTH (see Section 7.4.1.2) to act as an idea generator.46 The ability of the program to predict routes to medicinal targets, present in AstraZeneca's commercial drug projects or the literature, was assessed. Predicted pathways were compared to the literature, brainstorm proposals and in-house experience of chemists working on the projects. Without prior knowledge of the brainstorm proposals, ICSYNTH rediscovered known chemistries, returned brainstorm suggestions and provided new unreported synthetic routes. Due to its unbiased nature, it also identified an unconventional transformation that leads to a non-intuitive solution to a problem.46 ICSYNTH is able to generate ideas to complement synthetic chemists.

In a case study, synthetic routes proposed by ChemPlanner™ (see Section 7.4.1.2) were verified experimentally.65 Synthetic routes to medicinally relevant targets were compared to routes developed by chemists. ChemPlanner™ identified almost all routes designed by chemists, although not all were identified as the best routes due to the scoring functions within the program. Alternative routes with fewer steps and lower costs were also suggested. Therefore, ChemPlanner™ can assist synthetic chemists in designing synthetic routes, saving them time and money.

Synthia™ (see Section 7.4.1.2) uses network theory, high power computing, AI, and expert chemical knowledge to design retrosynthetic pathways.47 It can design novel synthesis routes to medicinally and industrially relevant targets. The program found synthetic routes to the selection of eight commercial bioactive substances and natural products.47 The target products were chosen where previous attempts at synthesis were low yielding, not scalable, or failed. The predicted pathways were evaluated experimentally. Synthia™ designed routes that improved yields and saved money and time. It also designed a successful pathway to one of the targets that had no known synthetic routes. An extension of Synthia™ enables one to avoid patented routes.48 It is important not to breach existing patented routes when designing pathways to novel molecules. A bond preservation method identifies bonds, which are essential to patents and prevents their disconnection in retrosynthesis. To validate this method, three commercial drugs linezolid, sitagliptin, and panobinostat were evaluated by Synthia™. Predicted pathways were generated with and without the patent bond constraints. Without constraints, Synthia™ suggested similar routes to the patents. However, by selecting the bonds that are not to be broken, the program could navigate around them and identify alternative routes.

7.6 Conclusions

In the pharmaceutical industry, progression from early-stage drug candidates to preclinical trials is performed in the quickest and the most cost-efficient manner. Synthetic chemistry has facilitated both drug discovery and development. Medicinal chemistry is a significant part of drug discovery, the aim being to design and synthesise novel small drug candidates for testing medicinal chemical hypotheses. For a single biological target, many analogues of lead compounds are synthesised on a small scale for screening, to identify structure–activity relationships. Medicinal chemists require reliable synthetic pathways that will deliver material for test quickly. Consequently, medicinal chemists are biased towards robust reactions when designing routes to novel molecules.66 The use of artificial intelligence and machine learning in CADS programs removes this personal bias in its predictions and therefore can broaden the medicinal chemists’ toolbox.

Process chemistry is the key in drug development, whereby active pharmaceutical ingredients are scaled up and reactions are optimised. Process chemists usually work on a single target molecule, as opposed to many analogues. Synthetic routes to target molecules are optimised to meet SELECT (safety, environmental, legal, economics, control, and throughput) criteria.67 Synthetic accessibility of molecules is one of the several criteria that influence which compounds are selected to be synthesised in medicinal chemistry and is an important concept in process chemistry. It is desirable to know whether a compound is synthesisable prior to performing the reactions experimentally. The closest to knowing is to predict synthetic pathways with high confidence. CASD programs could assist medicinal and process chemists in accelerating synthetic planning timelines, reducing the number of steps in a pathway, reducing costs, and suggesting alternative, unconventional pathways.

There are clear advantages for synthetic chemists to incorporate CASD into their everyday working lives. However, poor model interpretability has created suspicion among synthetic chemists. As a result, there is limited implementation of the tools. The so-called black-box tools will not be accepted unless they can be justified by literature or preferably, experimentally. Early and strong engagement with synthetic chemists will facilitate more rapid development of CASD with wider acceptance and uptake from the community.

There are other challenges that also need to be addressed to achieve advancement in CASD. Reaction data and code sharing are at the top of the list. Open-source large datasets containing counter-examples are required for training algorithms to perform optimally. Reaction data need to be of high quality and reproducible, containing no prophetic examples. There is a call for open sharing of machine-readable data and to define publication standards in order to incorporate this. Open sharing would allow for fair benchmarking of different methods. Rigorous validation methods for the assessment of model generalisability need to be established to ensure that reported results are not misleading.

CASD programs are aimed to assist synthetic chemists in the decision-making process for designing pathways. They are not intended to replace synthetic chemists; chemical intuition is still needed. The combination of robotics with CASD is the future of automated reaction optimisation. Such units would improve productivity in synthetic laboratories but will not replace the bench chemists.

CHAPTER 8

Constraining Chemical Networks in Astrochemistry

SERENA VITI*a,b AND JONATHAN HOLDSHIPa,b

a Department of Physics and Astronomy, University College London, Gower Street, London, WC1E 6BT

b Leiden Observatory, Leiden University, PO Box 9513, NL-2300 RA Leiden, The Netherlands

*Email: serena.viti@ucl.ac.uk

8.1 Introduction

The space between the stars, the interstellar medium (ISM), is far from empty. The ISM is populated with interstellar clouds and filaments, made of gas (∼99%) and dust (∼1%). These clouds and filaments are the birth sites of stars.1,2 Modelling the physical and chemical processes leading to the formation of stars and, hence, planets is a highly non-linear, very time-dependent, problem, involving a multi-layered interconnection between the physics and the chemistry of the gas and the dust. Despite the many advances driven by state-of-the-art telescopes, we are still far from solving the ‘star formation problem’: stars form in molecular filaments or clumps, cold (∼10 K) and relatively dense (>104 particles cm−3) regions of the interstellar medium, where most of the gas is molecular. These regions also contain higher-density cores. The first two stages of the formation of solar-like systems involve highly non-linear physical and chemical processes that are hard to corroborate by astronomical observations alone. In the first stage, some cores can become gravitationally unstable and initiate star formation. This collapse is controlled by the presence of molecules, which cool the gas and allow gravity to overcome hydrostatic equilibrium. During this pre-stellar core phase, due to the high density and low temperatures in the cores, species from the gas phase ‘freeze’ onto the dust grains present and form an icy mantle. The gas and surface compositions during these two stages exhibit a complicated time dependent, non-linear chemistry that strongly depends on the physical environment.3 Little experimental information is available for the interstellar ices. What is the unprocessed ice composition? What are the efficiencies of the viable surface reactions? And how do the energetics of the ISM (cosmic rays, UV radiation, shocks) influence the processed ices?

Examples of key issues involve even the simplest molecules: the CO molecule sticks efficiently to surfaces at temperatures below ∼25 K and is abundant in the ices. Some of this CO can be converted to other species, and the observation of CO2 and CH3OH in ices4 suggests that this processing does occur. H2CO, CH3OH, and glycolaldehyde are involved in the surface hydrogenation of CO, and determining their chemistry in star-forming regions is vital for studies of prebiotic chemistry.5 Some ices return to the gas phase when the gas temperature rises above 20 K. At lower temperatures, non-thermal desorption processes can still return molecules from solid to gas-phase.6 However, these non-thermal mechanisms ‘compete’ with the freeze-out. Gas-phase chemistry is better constrained than surface chemistry; nevertheless, many uncertainties still remain on the formation and efficiencies of routes for some of the most complex species (routinely called Complex Organic Molecules or COMs by astronomers) observed in space.7,8 In summary, the composition of the gas and icy mantles varies according to a time-dependent process, which is highly dependent on the conditions of the gas and dust in any particular cloud.

In the second stage, i.e. when the protostar is born, the gravitational energy is converted into radiation and the envelope around the central object, the future star, warms up. The molecules frozen on the grain mantles during the previous phase acquire mobility and likely form new, more complex species. When the temperature reaches the mantle sublimation temperature of ∼100 K, the molecules in the mantles are injected into the gas, where they react and form new, more complex molecules. Simultaneously, a fraction of matter is violently ejected outward in the form of highly supersonic collimated jets and molecular outflows. When the outflowing material encounters the quiescent gas of molecular cloud, it creates shocks, where the grain mantles are (partially) sputtered and the refractory grains are shattered. Once in the gas phase, molecules can be and are observed via their rotational lines. Again, as during the first stage, the interaction of gas and dust, and hence the gas composition, varies within very short timescales (less than one hundred years), and the effects of chemistry and dynamics are interlocked in a complex non-linear fashion.9

In both stages, molecules provide an essential tool for the analysis of the chemical and physical conditions of star- and planet-forming regions. Each stellar or planetary evolutionary stage is characterized by a chemical composition, which, if properly interpreted, leads to the determination of the physical processes of its phase.

This brief description of the multi-million years of star formation cycle highlights our challenge: the interconnection and non-linear correlation of the many parameters with each other or with extra, unknown ones, makes determining and specifying the parameter network within chemical models a highly challenging task.

Of particular importance is the reliability of the chemical reactions datasets. Databases of chemical reactions and rate coefficients for both gas and solid-phase reactions are the key input to all chemical models. While there are some gas-phase databases online, in reality each research group creates a personal version of such databases, especially as there is no accepted standard for databases; in addition, there is no database containing a complete set of solid-phase reactions. We explore the completeness and reliability of such databases in the next section.

8.2 Completeness and Reliability of Chemical Reactions Databases

Typically, chemical models of the ISM in use today employ databases of mainly 2-body (sometimes 3-body) chemical reactions; these contain long lists of gas and solid-phase chemical reactions. In the gas-phase, for each reaction, three constants are provided that are then used to calculate the rate coefficient. The first constant (usually α) represents the rate at 300 K and the other two constants (β and γ) give the temperature scaling of that rate. For photo-reactions, an equivalent set of constants gives the rate in an unshielded interstellar UV field and the extinction dependence of that rate. These three constants will have their own associated uncertainty. Depending on the physical conditions, between 20 and 50% of the reactions may not have been experimentally studied. In some cases, chemical reaction rates are therefore highly speculative.

For reactions occurring on the dust grains, the pathways, efficiencies, and branching ratios are even more uncertain than for the gas-phase reactions, due to the lack of experimental data. Surface reactions are, therefore, highly speculative and consequently are often not included in astrochemical models.

Reducing the degree of uncertainty for all the reactions would require an unfeasibly large number of laboratory experiments. Yet, chemical models fully rely on these databases, making their accuracy a prime problem for Astrochemistry. In the next two sections, we will describe elaborately the two categories of databases: gas-phase and surface reaction networks.

8.2.1 Gas-phase Networks

All the astrochemical models developed through the years calculate the abundances of hundreds of species involved in thousands of chemical reactions. Gas-phase reactions are the backbone of chemical networks as they are the primary routes for the formation and destruction of most molecules. Hence, a poor understanding of the rate coefficients can lead to large errors in the abundances of the main molecules observed in the ISM.

The range of kinetic temperatures and gas densities over which we need accurate rate coefficients will depend on the region of space that we need to model, but it can be from 10 K to >1000 K and from 100 to 1014 particles cm−3, respectively. Chemical reactions, under these conditions, can be studied in the laboratory or theoretically. However, each experiment, or study, takes at least a few months to complete. Often then, rate coefficients are estimated from other already known rate coefficients. More importantly, even if every reaction were to be experimentally or theoretically investigated, it would be impossible to do so under the whole range applicable to the ISM and many extrapolations are therefore performed. Measures have been taken by the community to compile databases where some quality assurance is performed. For example, the Kinetic Database for Astrochemistry (KIDA)10 is a public gas-phase network, which provides all the rate coefficients from various sources and evaluates their accuracy where possible. We refer the reader to10 for a detailed explanation of this network. However, even the best efforts at transparency and completeness such as KIDA fall short of providing the user with a complete, accurate, and reliable gas-phase network that includes all the possible species involved in the complex chemistry routinely observed in the ISM. This is especially true for complex organic molecules, which are species that contain 6 or more atoms, are present in the ISM mostly with low abundances and yet are key for our understanding of prebiotic chemistry in space.7 Gas-phase networks including the formation and destruction of COMs are far from complete11,12 and astrochemical models have been struggling to explain the observed abundances of COMs. While most current models tend to favour grain surface over gas-phase chemistry in COMs formation, several studies have now shown that COMs may indeed form in the gas phase but that, due to the incompleteness of gas-phase networks involving COMs, the relative contribution of gas-phase versus surface reactions cannot be quantified.

8.2.2 Grain-surface Networks

There is no doubt that dust grain chemistry plays a pivotal role in the formation of key abundant species observed routinely in the ISM e.g. H2O, CH3OH, and NH3 which are primarily formed through solid state chemistry.13,14 Although debate exists on whether gas-phase reactions contribute to the formation of COMs, it is clear that the latter are at least partly formed on the surface of the grains.7,8,15

We know that dust grains act as ‘catalysts’ meaning that – on their surface – surface reactions and energetic radiation can synthesize molecules as complex as prebiotic species16,17 starting from very simple molecules (e.g. CO and N2) and atoms (H, C, O, N, S etc.) deposited from the gas when the temperature of the medium is close to 10 K. In the last couple of decades, many experiments have been performed to evaluate surface chemical reactions (see the review in ref. 18).

Molecular hydrogen was the first molecule to be studied on dust surfaces.19 Many experiments since then have been performed to study the formation of more complex molecules e.g. ref. 20–22 as well as the ice morphology and ice mantle mechanisms e.g. ref. 23 and 24. However, all these experiments are performed within a constrained range of laboratory conditions, which differ from those found in the ISM: for example, atomic fluxes, ice temperatures, ice morphologies, and mixture ratios, energetic processes in the laboratory will differ from those found in the ISM. Hence formation, desorption and destruction routes and rates for surface molecules as derived from experiments may not always be exhaustive to the needs of the chemical modellers. In other words, experimental data for interstellar ices are limited, as the experimentation process is neither simple nor fast. As a consequence, most chemical models either include very simple surface reaction networks or ones where most of the reactions are essentially guesswork.

8.3 A Bayesian Approach

In astrochemistry, it is not common to use Bayesian methods as a means of deriving posterior probability distributions (PPDs) for model parameters from observations. The first study to do so9 used Bayesian inference to derive parameters such as the gas density and cosmic-ray ionization rates within a dark molecular cloud from observations of species in the gas and ices using chemical models. This study particularly highlighted the nature of the problem at hand, namely that astrochemical problems are typically non-linear, ill-posed inverse problems where solutions may not be unique or may not depend continuously on the observational data. In one study,9 a Bayesian approach based on the use of the Metropolis–Hastings (MH) algorithm (an example of a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm) was adopted and they used a simplified version of UCLCHEM (a time-dependent gas–grain chemical model, now open source: https://uclchem.github.io/) to explore a nine-dimensional parameter space for molecular clouds. They ran two identical sets of eight MCMC chains differing only in the way the prior distribution information was set, with the first set having a non-informative prior information in the form of an acceptable range of possible values for observed ices, while in the second the prior include all the observational constraints from observations, including gas-phase abundances. Of particular relevance to this review, it is interesting to see how the different prior distributions have affected the resulting Posterior Probability Distributions (PPD) for one of their dimensions: the branching ratios for some key chemical reactions pathways e.g. those that control how much of the oxygen that freezes on the grains turns into H2O or OH. With noninformative uniform prior, the high-density regions of the PPD cover excessively large sections of the distribution, meaning that the branching ratio could not be constrained enough. With informative priors, the high-density region in the PPD is reduced and gives a clear indication that the production of water over OH is favoured. This example showed for the first time in Astrochemistry that branching ratio parameters can be successfully estimated through Bayesian MCMC methods.

A more recent work25 used the above methodologies as a proof of concept in an attempt to infer rates of reactions for a limited surface network, and in doing so provided the means to derive reduced networks in the context of observational constraints. In this work, a simple chemical model was developed that considers only the solid state chemistry in the ice mantles of dust grains in a dark molecular cloud. The simplified model is a time-dependent single-point model that generates a time series of solid-phase molecular abundances as a function of the physical conditions of the molecular cloud and the chemical parameters of the defined chemical network. This network only included surface reactions and mainly hydrogenation of common gas-phase species. We report these reactions in Table 8.1.

Obviously, the reactions included are not exhaustive of all the possible combinations: the criteria used to choose which reactions to include were based on (i) simple hydrogenation until saturation e.g. reactions 4 and 5 and (ii) reactions that have been found to be efficient, or even dominant, routes to forming a species e.g. reactions 21–24 to form methanol. For this toy model, gas-phase reactions were ignored, but the depletion of the gas phase on the surface was parameterized.

They find that when observational constraints directly constrain the abundance of a species involved in a reaction, the range of likely values for the rate of that reaction can be sufficiently narrowed for use in chemical models. Therefore, this method represents a method by which reliable reaction rates can be obtained for use in modelling until laboratory measurements or theoretical work supersede them.

Although this approach has many strengths, it requires a large amount of computational power. In both of the above examples, the chemical model used for the inference was greatly simplified in comparison with a typical model used to interpret observations. Where the model itself is not the subject of the inference (as it is in the work of ref. 25), we might use machine learning to map from model inputs to outputs in order to do more efficient parameter inference on the input parameters.

8.4 Machine Learning Techniques for Complex Networks

Ultimately, chemical modellers need to be able to rely on complete and accurate chemical reaction networks. Reducing the degree of uncertainty for such networks requires cutting edge Artificial Intelligence techniques combining Artificial Neural Networks, Bayesian Inference methods, and advanced Monte Carlo sampling algorithms. While we are still quite a way from achieving these, ML techniques have now started being used in Astrochemistry.

A neural network was used to emulate a full chemical model.26 By creating a training set from the outputs of a full model (UCLCHEM†) for a wide range of input physical parameters, they were able to train a neural network to predict these outputs. This allows for the computation of chemical abundances required to interpret observations in milliseconds rather than the minutes of CPU time required to run a full chemical model. Consequently, computationally intensive parameter inference can be performed using a close approximation of a full chemical model without taking an infeasible amount of CPU time.

Such neural networks would have uses beyond the direct interpretation of observations. Many radiative hydrodynamical simulations use highly approximate radiative-chemical treatments to provide the cooling rates for the simulated gas. This is a necessity when a full chemical model would add to the computational burden of an already intensive model. However, evaluating a neural network is generally a small task and as such, more accurate chemistry could be inserted into physical models in the form of pre-trained neural network emulators.

The use of machine learning techniques on chemical networks could be of particular importance for the reduction and accuracy of networks of complex organic molecules, in particular those that are as yet undetected in the ISM. For example, the ‘holy grail’ for astrochemists is to find amino acids in space. Amino acids are important organic compounds that play a key role in the formation of proteins. In the protein production process, amino acids join together to form polymer chains, which represent the structural units of proteins. It is believed that the formation of amino acids may indeed have occurred in the ISM, as they have been firmly detected in meteorites.27 This is supported by laboratory experiments where amino acids are found to form on the surface of model dust grains by UV-photon and ion irradiation of suitable precursor molecules under astrophysically relevant conditions.28,29 Despite great efforts towards their detection, a firm detection of amino acids in the ISM is still – unfortunately – eluding us.

One possible solution to this is to use ML tools to identify weak signals from the amino acids in spectroscopic telescope data. When detecting molecules, strong peaks in the spectra from an observed object are identified by matching their frequency to known emitting frequencies of molecules. If the emission is weak it may not be detected by a human, or the statistical significance of many weak lines may be missed. A classification model trained to categorize spectra as containing a particular molecule or not, based on the spectral noise and the emission profile at various frequencies, could give confident detections in cases that a human would miss. In the case of previously undetected molecules, such as amino acids, a training set can be produced by creating many synthetic spectra. Further, such an analysis could be performed on thousands of targets with little effort which has made it an interesting prospect for the exo-planetary community aiming to identify molecules in planetary atmospheres.30

Another solution is to focus our search by determining the optimal conditions for observing amino acids. It is likely that, if present, such amino acids must form on the mantle of dust grains. It is therefore essential we determine the optimal conditions under which simple amino acids, such as glycine and alanine, can form on the dust icy mantles and can subsequently be released into the gas phase.

Key prerequisites for understanding how and where glycine and alanine form are the determination of the surface reactions that lead to their formation as a function of (i) kinetic temperature; (ii) gas density, (iii) structure of the gas, (iv) presence and abundance of other molecular species on the ices, and (v) UV and cosmic ray ionization rates, among other factors. To date, no large-scale predictions of the formation routes of glycine and alanine have been made, as a function of the parameters above.

A possible method to achieve this may be based on advanced and cutting edge techniques developed in the information sciences, ML and statistical disciplines. It should be possible to devise and apply a combination of statistical and ML techniques to perform large scale chemical models, involving large datasets of gas- and surface-phase chemical reactions to derive the physical and chemical conditions under which every surface chemical reaction is viable. A technique worth investigating is probabilistic graphical modelling, a branch of ML that studies how to use probability distributions to describe a particular problem whose ‘model’ has many uncertainties.

Ultimately, for any well-defined species set (COMs, amino acids, ice species etc.), we need to be able to simultaneously investigate the paths and efficiencies of their formation and destruction over a large physical (densities, temperatures, radiation fields, and cosmic ray ionization rates) and chemical (rate coefficients) parameter space, and discover if, where and under what conditions these species are abundant in space.

8.5 Conclusion

Machine Learning and probabilistic methods for solving typical astrochemical problems is a fast-growing field. As larger chemical reaction networks and more complex models are being employed in astrochemistry, the need for intelligent data mining algorithms will increase. It is clear that there are large uncertainties, as well as lack of information on formation and destruction routes, in gas and especially surface reactions and rate coefficients. To date, these uncertainties have only been tackled by laboratory experiments and quantum mechanical calculations. However, the complexity of the reaction networks, the lack of much prior information in the form of observed ices, and the length of each laboratory experiment, make a parameter exploration (in terms of gas densities, gas temperatures, UV, and cosmic ray fluxes for example) unfeasible. Initial ‘experimentation’ with ML algorithms has been proven to be an efficient avenue to tackle this challenge.
