CHAPTER 9

Machine Learning at the (Nano)materials-biology Interface

DAVID A. WINKLERa,b,c,d

a La Trobe Institute for Molecular Science, La Trobe University, Bundoora 3046, Australia

b Monash Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Monash University, Parkville 3052, Australia

c School of Pharmacy, University of Nottingham, Nottingham NG7 2QL, UK

d CSIRO Data61, Pullenvale 4069, Australia

Email: d.winkler@latrobe.edu.au

9.1 Machine Learning Overview, Challenges, and Opportunities

Currently, machine learning (ML) is one of the most exciting computational techniques in science, technology, and medicine. The reason for the excitement is that, unlike traditional computer programs that have to be programmed precisely with every operation required to achieve a goal, ML methods can learn from examples in a similar way to humans. The same ML program can be trained to model and predict many different types of experiments and scenarios and can take into account heterogeneous data types like experimental conditions, physical and chemical properties, and processing history of samples.1 ML models can generate models of continuous properties like water solubility, biological activity, and materials strength, but also categorical data (good/bad, active/inactive, nontoxic/moderately toxic/very toxic etc.). Newer types of ML can also generate very good features, i.e. mathematical representations of intrinsic properties of molecules, materials, images etc. that generate improved models, as the quality of features is paramount when constructing ML models.2

Not surprisingly, artificial intelligence (AI) methods, largely ML, are generating a lot of new and potentially disruptive science across broad research and application domains.3 There is an exponential increase in the number of publications that employ ML; many of these are in top-level journals, like Nature, Science, Cell and PNAS and their families of journals. However, ML is not new. The first neural network, the perceptron, was developed in 1958. A simple statistical modelling antecedent, quantitative structure–activity (or property) relationships (QSAR/QSPR), arose in chemistry at a similar time. Shortly after, neural networks were used to model relationships between chemical structures and other molecular and physicochemical properties of organic molecules and some useful property, especially biological effects. There was a steady progress in this field, but several important roadblocks hindered more rapid progress and wider application of these ML methods. The main issues were very limited computational technologies, lack of data to train ML models, a lack of clarity on how to generate mathematical entities that encode useful information, lack of understanding on how to reduce the dimensionality of ML modelling problems (feature selection), and even long-standing academic arguments on the best way to measure how predictive an ML model is.4 Despite these limitations, a lot of useful research was conducted in this period; the method generated new drug candidates and predicted their possible toxicities and metabolic liabilities, and many of the limitations of low availability of computational resources were eased as computing power underwent spectacular development in subsequent decades.

At the moment, there is a happy coincidence of (or perhaps a deliberate push towards) advanced development in computational technologies and algorithms (e.g. deep learning (DL)), automation and robotics generating very large data sets suitable for training ML models, and development and/or application of a much broader range of powerful ML algorithms with unprecedented capabilities. What has also changed in chemical applications of ML is that we have found very good solutions to many of the vexing roadblocks in the QSAR/QSPR method (a model for ML in chemistry). Deep learning methods such as autoencoder/decoder, adversarial, and convolutional neural networks, for example, have simplified the problem of generating mathematical descriptors to train ML models. Indeed, these methods can now take simple representations of molecular entities (e.g. SMILES strings, linear text representations of organic molecules) and generate relevant descriptors internally. We have also adopted powerful new descriptors like fragment and signature descriptors5 that generate very good models. Unlike older and more arcane descriptors (e.g. those generated by descriptor generating packages like Dragon6), they are much easier to interpret in terms of molecular interactions and mechanisms. There is now a much wider use of efficient sparse feature selection methods (e.g. LASSO) that remove poor and uninformative descriptors, making models faster to train, easier to interpret, and more predictive.

These developments have driven a substantial expansion of ML into new areas such as forward and retrosynthetic reaction prediction,7 prediction of thermodynamic and dynamic stability of materials, prediction of protein structures from sequence,8 prediction or properties and performance of porous and 2D materials,9 for energy applications, and many others.10 Very recently, these techniques are being applied to autonomous evolutionary design of robots,11 neatly completing the circle where robotics have allowed the generation of large amounts of data, which is then used to train models that can generate new robot architectures. This chapter will not discuss these applications as many are well covered in other chapters in the text.

Data availability has grown massively with rapid developments in robotics, automation, and omics technologies. Copious and diverse data representative of the domain of the problem being studied are essential for data-driven modelling methods like ML and DL. However, the size of possible accessible materials space (∼10100, essentially infinite) clearly shows that experiments alone, no matter how fast or well planned (e.g. using design of experiments), cannot cover such spaces adequately. More efficient methods are required to identify ‘islands of utility’ in the vast sea of materials possibilities. This strongly suggests that ML methods need to couple synergistically with evolutionary algorithms that can explore very large search spaces very efficiently. This will be discussed in detail later in this chapter.

9.2 Scale and Importance of Problem/Special Issues with Complex Materials

Like ML and big data, the fields of materials science, regenerative medicine, and biomaterials are undergoing unprecedented expansion. They are taking advantage of new automated methods of synthesis, characterization, and testing of materials.12 Much of the most interesting research is occurring at the boundary between materials and biology e.g. biomaterials, tissue engineering, stem cell control, implantable and indwelling devices, nanoscale smart delivery systems, 2D materials for wearable sensors, robotics, and prosthetics.

However, ML modelling of complex materials has special problems compared to small organic drugs or drug-like molecules. Nanomaterials exhibit distributions of shapes and sizes, their surfaces change dynamically depending on the environment in which they are embedded, and the materials are often not well characterized. Similarly, polymers are also not well characterized, they are polydisperse, crosslinked, their structures are not precisely known etc. There is a strong need for systematic studies on how properties of these materials affect the behaviour of systems constructed from them. Clearly, characterizing complex materials mathematically for use in training ML models is problematic. Materials-specific descriptors are largely not available or if they are, are quite arcane and uninterpretable. However, new DL methods such as encoder-decoder networks and general adversarial neural networks will significantly improve this deficiency, as they can generate internal descriptors ‘on the fly’ from chemically simple representations.

There are massive opportunities provided by contemporary ML technologies. They are providing, for the first time, the opportunity to tackle scientific, medical, social, and technological problems that have been out of reach due to their complexities. We now describe several areas in materials science where ML has provided novel solutions to very complex problems. The aim is to show how ML is now being used; the focus is on applications that are useful and interesting rather than those that are cutting edge but obscure.

9.3 Machine Learning Examples in Materials

We provide a few examples of where ML has been used to solve important problems in the energy and environmental arena. This section, which is brief because it is covered by others, shows recent research into ML modelling of porous and 2D materials properties.

Porous materials like metal organic frameworks (MOFs), zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs), and covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are attracting much interest because of their diversity, tunability, and potential energy-related applications such as carbon capture, hydrogen and methane storage, electrocatalysts for carbon dioxide electro-reduction and water splitting reactions and related applications. There are millions of porous materials that could be synthesized that reside in large porous materials databases; however, it is not known which of these are stable and synthesizable. For every reported successful synthesis of an MOF, there are undoubtedly hundreds or thousands of failed reactions that have been attempted. ML could use knowledge of successful and failed reactions to predict and optimize the syntheses of new MOFs. MOF synthesis involves the self-assembly of metal ions and organic linkers in a 3D periodic network. However, our understanding of this self-assembly process is still too poor to predict which combinations will be able to be synthesized or which synthesis conditions will be optimal. Moosavi et al. recently used ML to capture chemical intuition from a set of successful and unsuccessful experiments to synthesize a metal–organic framework.13 They used a random forest ensemble learner to evaluate the importance of variables in the synthesis of a MOF made from copper ions and 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylic acid, thereby generating a material with unprecedented surface area. Moghadam et al. subsequently applied ML to predict the mechanical stability of MOFs that are suited to their applications.14 They first conducted high-throughput molecular simulations for 3385 MOFs containing 41 distinct network topologies, which were then used to train an ML model to predict the mechanical properties of MOFs. Their model trained using five accessible descriptors, could rapidly estimate the bulk moduli of new or existing MOFs, which are representative of the critical pressure these materials can withstand under typical operating conditions, a valuable tool for the MOF community.

In the energy applications area, Thornton and co-workers reported the use of ML to design zeolite catalysts for CO2 reduction.15 They employed statistical and machine learning (QSPR) modelling techniques to identify quantitative relationships between the zeolite structural characteristics and the adsorption properties for CO2 and hydrogen simulated by accurate but computationally demanding grand canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) calculations. Robust structure–property relationships were found that linked structural descriptors such as pore size, surface area and void fraction to zeolite performance. Useful catalysts were identified from the computational screening of >300 000 zeolite structures. Several of the top candidates were very promising energy-efficient templates for catalysis with predicted performance 50% higher than conventional reactors.

They subsequently showed how ML can be used to leverage GCMC calculations of hydrogen adsorption by nanoporous materials to identify their performance limits.16 Hydrogen is an attractive transportation fuel with zero carbon emissions, but it is difficult to store. MOFs have shown promise as physical adsorbents of hydrogen. They exploited the Nanoporous Materials Genome, containing over 850 000 materials, and GCMC calculations results used to train an ML model to explore the limits of hydrogen storage. The also incorporated limited evolutionary optimization that used ML models of the fitness of materials to accelerate the discovery of higher performance examples in successive rounds of optimization. Figure 9.1 shows the results of selected GCMC calculations used to train neural net models of the fitness landscape for nanoporous materials, and improvements in performance over three optimization cycles. Maximum net capacity at room temperature was achieved with pore sizes of around 6 Å and void fractions of 0.1, while at cryogenic temperatures pore sizes of 10 Å and void fractions of 0.5 are optimal. The top candidates were commercially attractive cryo-adsorbents, with promising storage capacities at 77 K and 100 bar of 40 g L−1, a promising alternative to liquefaction.

Figure 9.1 Selected GCMC calculations (grey filled circles), ML predictions (light grey points), and experimental data (black points) for net deliverable energy as a function of void fraction at 77 K, cycling between 100 and 1 bar, for the complete genome (∼850 000 porous materials). GCMC calculations were used to train neural net models of the fitness landscape for nanoporous materials that were used to generate improvements in performance over three optimization cycles. Experimental data are from the literature, the dashed line represents the predicted bare tank performance, and the solid dark line is the fitted Langmuir model. Reproduced from ref. 16, https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.chemmater.6b04933, with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2017.

2D materials are another very strong research area of contemporary research. These materials are essentially 1 atom thick; layered materials derived from them exhibit novel and useful electro-optic properties. They are also being developed as components of wearable and implantable electronics such as continuous sensors. Their properties can be predicted using computationally expensive quantum chemical calculations. Recently a flurry of papers has shown that ML models can be used to predict properties of large libraries of 2D and layered 2D materials orders of magnitude faster than QM calculations, with similar accuracy.

There are ∼2000 2D materials known or predicted to be synthesizable, and they exhibit a wide diversity of potentially useful properties. For example, a recent study17 identified 1825 2D materials that could be exfoliated from known inorganic compounds. Hybrid layered 2D materials (two layers of different 2D materials) are of great interest for photovoltaic and photonic applications, as they have much larger scope for being tuned in application-specific ways. Known 2D materials can theoretically generate ∼2 million bilayer structures, and around a billion trilayers. Clearly, such a massive number of hybrid materials cannot be generated and tested experimentally and, even though DFT calculations can predict their properties, the computational demands make it also infeasible to predict the properties of more than about a hundred materials. ML methods can be used to leverage a relatively small number of accurate DFT calculations of hybrid 2D materials properties into a much larger material space. For example, Tawfik et al. reported the prediction of the interlayer distance and band gap for almost 1500 bilayer heterostructures. Their models could predict the interlayer spacing for hybrid materials in a test set with a mean error of 4% and an RMSE of 0.2 eV for the band gap. Use of hybrid DFT and ML methods allow predictions to be made for large numbers of materials much faster than those from DFT calculations alone.

9.4 Machine Learning Examples in Nanomaterials

Materials in nanoparticulate form often exhibit useful (but also potentially detrimental) biological properties compared to the same material in the bulk phase. This is largely due to the extremely high surface to volume ratio of small particles compared to larger ones. Materials surfaces interact directly with biology so are very important. Nanomaterials have shown great promise in delivering drugs and gene therapies to target tissues in the body, and as imaging agents for diagnosis. ML methods have been used quite widely to understand the relationship between nanoparticle physicochemical properties and how they affect biology. Computational models of nanoparticle behaviour are very difficult to devise for several key reasons: nanoparticles exhibit a distribution of sizes and shapes, so are more difficult to characterize than small molecules; they are much larger than molecules, so it is not clear how to encode their chemical properties in meaningful ways; in biological systems they become coated by complex layers of proteins (the corona) that significantly affect the types of biological responses that they generate; experiments to map their distribution in vivo, uptake through lungs, GI tract, and skin are very difficult; and although in vitro assays are easier they often do not correlate well with in vivo responses.

ML methods can simplify some of these difficulties and they do not require a complete understanding of mechanisms involved in nanoparticle biological responses. They have been an important element in understanding the potential adverse biological properties of nanomaterials used commercially. The aim is to use ML models as part of a ‘safe-by-design’ paradigm to generate commercially useful materials with minimal adverse effects. For example, Le et al. described an experimental and computational approach for the development of nanoparticles that are safe-by-design.18 They generated a library of 45 ZnO nanoparticles with varying particle size, aspect ratio, doping type, doping concentration, and surface coatings and measured cell damage in human umbilical vein endothelial cells or human hepatocellular liver carcinoma cells. They successfully generated quantitative and predictive ML models mapping nanoparticle properties to cell viability, membrane integrity, and oxidative stress. Figure 9.2 shows the results of ML models for these potentially adverse biological effects of nanomaterials as function of the size, shape, core material, doping, and coating type.

Figure 9.2 Performance of ML models for LDH level (a measure of cell membrane integrity, right) for a range of ZnO-based nanomaterials with different sizes, shapes, core materials, doping, and coating types (left). Reproduced from ref. 18 with permission from John Wiley and Sons, © 2016 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim.

The most important factors driving cell damage were the concentration of nanoparticles the cells were exposed to, the type of surface coating, the nature and extent of the ZnO core doping, and the aspect ratio of the particles. Oksel et al. also reported several ML models of nanoparticle biological properties and recently described the application of random forest ML methods to modelling nanoparticle properties.19 They found RF methods generated models that were easier to interpret in terms of ranges and limits of nanoparticle properties that most influence any adverse effects of nanomaterials.

As ML methods are data-driven, one of the main issues with them is obtaining sufficient high-quality experimental data to train them. This is particularly difficult with nanomaterials, as there are still relatively few high throughput synthesis and characterization studies on these materials, and they are more difficult to study experimentally. This urgent need was identified in recent reviews on the application of ML methods to predicting the adverse properties of nanomaterials20,21 and in a paper calling for more systematic studies of these properties.22

Amphiphilic, self-assembling nanomaterials such cubosomes and hexosomes are a promising class of drug delivery materials (see Figure 9.3). However, they are tricky to design as the types of nanophases they assemble into can be dependent on the temperature, time, drug loading and drug physicochemical properties, amongst others. Only specific nanophases are useful as delivery vehicles. Predicting the effects of these complex parameters on the resultant nanophase was considered intractable until recently. Le at al. showed how ML methods can accurately predict which of several (sometimes coexisting) nanophases will form for a given set of conditions.23,24 They validated their ML models predicting nanophases by a subsequent de novo synthesis of loaded amphiphilic nanoparticles and experimental determination of the resulting nanophase using small angle x-ray scattering on the Australian synchrotron (see Figure 9.4). The predictions were 90% accurate. They subsequently showed how ML models could accurately predict the time evolution of nanoparticulate amphiphilic drug delivery systems.25

Figure 9.3 Amphiphilic, self-assembling nanomaterials, such cubosomes and hexosomes, adopt many kinds of nanostructures, not all of which are suitable as drug delivery vehicles. Here, we show example structures of the inverse-bicontinuous diamond QIID (Pn3m), gyroid QIIG (Ia3d), and primitive QIIP (Im3m) cubic phases. Reproduced from ref. 23, https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/mp3006402, with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2013.

Figure 9.4 ML models predicting the existence of individual phases (inverse-bicontinuous diamond QIID (Pn3m) cubic (blue, to the left of Figure 9.4A and B), hexagonal HII (yellow, filled circles), gyroid QIIG (Ia3d) cubic (red), primitive QIIP (Im3m) cubic (purple, to the right in Figure 9.4C and D), and fluid isotropic FI (brown)) for a range of new drugs incorporated in the nanophases. Amphiphiles used to generate the nanoparticles were (A) phytantriol and (B) monoolein nanoparticles. These particles were loaded with new drugs at 25 and 37 °C. Circles indicate incorrect predictions for the nanophases determined subsequently by small angle X-ray scattering at the Australian Synchrotron. The predictions were 90% accurate. This showed how ML models could accurately predict nanophase behaviour as a function of amphiphile, drug type, drug loading, and temperature. Reproduced from ref. 23, https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/mp3006402, with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2013.

siRNA can also be used for therapeutic purposes and ML has been used to design siRNA libraries and more effective materials to deliver these highly charged molecules. A 2011 review described the various ML methods used to assist with the rational design of siRNA sequences and delivery systems.26 For example, Huesken and coworkers trained a neural network on 2182 randomly selected siRNAs targeted to 34 mRNA species using a high-throughput reporter gene system.27 The ML model predicted the activity of 249 siRNAs in an independent test set with a modest r2 value of 0.44. This ML model was used to design a genome-wide siRNA library consisting of two siRNAs per gene. This collection of 50 000 siRNAs identified genes involved in the cellular response to hypoxia. The dramatic increase in the capability of ML methods subsequently has reignited interest in this important area. The prediction of efficacy of siRNA sequences for gene silencing has improved significantly and ML methods are making much better predictions on the efficiency of nanoparticulate gene delivery systems. For example, more recently Han et al. used deep learning methods to improve the accuracy of prediction of siRNA efficacy. Their DNN extracted hidden features from sequences and thermodynamic properties. The model predicted siRNA efficacy slightly better, with an r2 value of 0.53. Subsequent experiments showed that their model was more accurate than several other siRNA prediction methods. Anderson's team at MIT reported the effects of a small library of nanoparticles synthesized from lipid-modified aminoglycosides and siRNA.

9.5 Machine Learning Examples in Biomaterials and Regenerative Medicine

Biomaterials are an important element of regenerative medicine that promises hitherto inaccessible treatments for injury and disease. Biomaterials can replace damaged tissues, stimulate the growth of nerves, provide environments for implanted cells in cell therapies aimed at generating essential hormones such as insulin, replace bone damaged by accidents or disease, precisely deliver drugs and gene therapy agents to diseased tissues, and hide otherwise biologically incompatible implanted components such as pacemakers and cochlear implants from the body's immune response. Given the almost infinite variety of chemically accessible materials to choose from, it is essential to conduct experiments to select them using high throughput techniques, and to employ powerful computational methods such as ML and evolutionary algorithms to extract design rules from large data sets and to explore materials space as efficiently as possible. To date, the materials most widely used for these purposes are polymers and nanomaterials.

Given the rapid growth in implantable and indwelling medical devices, it is particularly important to design or discover materials that resist bacterial attachment and biofilm formation, and those that reduce or eliminate the foreign body response (FBR) that often causes device failure. FBR to an implanted device generates a fibrous capsule that insulates the device or implanted cell therapy from the body, compromising function. Clearly, materials surfaces and interfaces are often the main drivers of biological response, so the ability to analyze, modify and model the chemistry and topography of surfaces is very important for the development and optimization of new biomaterials. However, interactions between surfaces and biology are poorly understood at the molecular and mechanistic level.

ML methods have been used to model the propensity of polymers to support the growth of pathogenic microbes. Clever generation of large arrays of different polymers using dip pen and inkjet printing methods has provided the means for measuring the responses of diverse cell types to the polymers. Building on the seminal work from the Langer group at MIT, Hook et al. described this experimental technique in a recent publication.12,28 They found relationships between the degree of attachment of three important hospital pathogens, Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and uropathogenic Escherichia coli, and surface chemistry (as determined by experimental surface analysis) for several hundred diverse polymers. Subsequent ML modelling of these data using surface analysis data as descriptors, or computational generated molecular descriptors for the monomers, resulted in robust and predictive models of pathogen attachment.29 A subsequent study showed how a single ML model could simultaneously predict the attachment of all three pathogens,30 making it much simpler to conduct virtual screens of thousands of accessible but not yet synthesized polymers to identify those with low general pathogen attachment (summarized in Figure 9.5).

Figure 9.5 A single ML model simultaneously predicts the attachment of three important hospital-acquired pathogens,30 Measured and predicted attachment (estimated using the log of the GFP fluorescence, logF) of the multi-pathogen attachment model employed computed molecular descriptors. Reproduced from ref. 30 with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2018.

As ML models of biomaterials (and drugs too) have historically been trained using efficient but rather arcane (hard to understand) descriptors, they subsequently showed how a specific type of molecular fragment descriptor could generate models that were easier for experimental materials scientists to interpret.31 A similar ML modelling approach was used to find relationships between the attachment of stem cells to polymer libraries.32,33 More recently, ML methods have been used to model a library of 141 homopolymers and 400 diverse copolymers for their abilities to support attachment, proliferation, and differentiation of human dental pulp stem cells.33 In this study, a Bayesian regularized neural network with a sparsity inducing Laplacian prior was used to model the three stem cell responses separately. Computational models were generated, relating polymer properties to cellular responses. The models correctly predicted the attachment of stem cells 92–95% of the time, proliferation 85–92% of the time, and differentiation 82–85% of the time. The models also identified several key functional groups that support specific cell responses.

Surface analysis methods like time of flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) and Raman spectroscopy are very important for understanding how biomaterials interact with biology. This is because the surfaces of bulk materials and nanomaterials are the primary sites of contact with cells and other biological entities. ToF-SIMS impacts materials surfaces with atoms or clusters of atoms to fragment the constituent molecules, providing a kind of fingerprint that is specific to the materials surface. Surprisingly, analysis methods for the large data sets that surface analysis methods generate have involved relatively simple statistical methods like principle components analysis (PCA). When used as mathematical descriptors that encode surface chemistry, ion peaks from ToF-SIMS, for example, are also very useful for generating quantitative relationships between surface chemistry and biological responses.12,28 Recently, we and others have employed more sophisticated informatics and ML methods to analyze these data sets and have shown that much more information can be obtained this way. For example, a recent study found that self-organizing maps (SOMs), a specialized form of neural network used for nonlinear clustering of complex data, are more effective at extracting information from data from ToF-SIMS experiments on polymers than principal components analysis (PCA), which is commonly employed.34,35Figure 9.6 shows how SOMs can distinguish between nylon samples with very similar chemical structures, a task that PCA cannot achieve. The nonlinear neural network clustering methods could detect small quantities of materials such as antibodies better than traditional methods but could also discriminate between materials with high degrees of chemical similarity.34,36

Figure 9.6 Discrimination between nylon samples with very similar chemical structures using Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs). The 10×10 supervised Kohonen network (SKN) was calculated for positive ion ToF-SIMS data. False-colouring is used to clarify sample locations on the network according to their sample group – see online version of the figure: (red, Nylon-6; green, Nylon-11; navy, Nylon-12; cyan, Nylon-6(3)T; pink, Nylon-6/6; yellow, Nylon-6/9; and dark green, Nylon-6/12). This ML model had a 98% class assignment accuracy. Reproduced from ref. 34 with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2018.

We and others have also shown the importance of using modern sparse feature selection methods to remove chemical features from models that do not drive biological responses. These methods remove (set to zero) any features that are less relevant to the biological response using a variety of mathematical methods; the most widely used are the LASSO regression and multiple linear regression using an expectation algorithm and a sparse Bayesian prior.37,38 This makes models more interpretable, and also improves the predictive power of them because optimally sparse models generalize the best to new data. These methods have been very effective in identifying small numbers of genes in gene expression microarray data that correlate with biological responses. Tens of thousands of genes on a microarray can be reduced in a context-dependent way to a handful of those most relevant. For example, Autefage and co-workers used gene expression data from experiments in which mesenchymal stem cells were driven down the osteogenic (bone) pathway by strontium ions leaching from an implanted biomaterial. These implants have been shown to slow the loss of calcium in bone, reducing fractures and osteoporosis. Subsequent analysis using sparse feature selection identified a small number of related fatty acid and steroid biosynthesis genes as being important in osteogenesis. Subsequent experimental testing of these predictions using qPCR, lipid raft and gene expression measurements validated the importance of these hitherto unknown pathways for strontium-induced differentiation of MDS down the osteogenic pathway.39 In another study, stem cells were caused to divide symmetrically or asymmetrically using a variety of chemical and physical methods. In symmetric division, they divide into two stem cells and in asymmetric division they divide into one stem cell and one progenitor cell. This division process was a long-standing unexplained problem in stem cell biology. Subsequent analysis of the gene expression microarray profiles identified 5 potential markers for the symmetry of stem cell division. Experimental validation using fluorescent antibodies for these gene products shows that these genes were indeed markers of symmetry of division (see Figure 9.7).40 Some of these markers are now sold commercially by Asymmetrex.

Figure 9.7 Experimental validation using fluorescent antibodies for these gene products shows that these genes were indeed markers of symmetry of division. The top row shows the positions of cell nuclei marked by DAPI stain, the lower panels show the marker H2A.Z that only identifies one of the two cells when asymmetric division has occurred (lower right two panels) and both cells when symmetric division occurs (lower left two panels). Reproduced from ref. 40 with permission from Elsevier, Copyright 2015.

9.6 Materials for Cell Therapies, Bioreactors, and Implantable Cells

Cell therapies (implanting of therapeutic cells into the body) are important medical interventions e.g. bone marrow transplants for leukaemia (current) and islet cells for diabetes (future). Key to the success of these therapies is the ability to culture large quantities of cells in artificial bioreactors.41,42 Materials science and ML methods are playing increasingly important roles. For example, ML methods successfully modelled the relationships between bioreactor parameters such as initial cell type and seeding density, cytokine concentrations, reactor types, media etc. on subsequent cell fold increases (how many times the initial seed concentration of cell increased).1 This study by Winkler and Burden modelled the increase in total number of cells and 5 different stem cell or progenitor cell types belonging to the haematopoietic (blood) differentiation pathway. Data from over 300 bioreactor experiments were successfully and quantitatively modelled using MLR and sparse Bayesian neural network methods. Apart from predicting the fold increase for each cell type within a factor of two (three for nucleated cells), their sparse feature selection methods also identified the most important chemical factors and bioreactor parameters driving each type of cell expansion, very useful information for controlling the specific types of cells the bioreactors generate.

9.7 ML and Evolutionary Methods

Although ML is attracting most of the attention, as we stated in the Introduction, the estimated 10100 possible accessible materials mean that even the most optimistic predictions of the capabilities of high throughput experimentation and ML modelling suggest that these methods cannot possibly explore more than a minute fraction of this effectively infinite space unaided. Evolutionary algorithms (EA) are one of the most efficient ways to explore very large search spaces. It is therefore logical that evolutionary methods be employed to explore materials spaces better to discover entirely novel materials and to optimize those already discovered. There have been a limited number of studies on using evolutionary methods to ‘evolve’ materials, primarily catalysts and phosphors, as these represent ‘low hanging fruit’, more easily represented as materials ‘genomes’. Applications of evolutionary methods to bioactive compounds and materials discovery are only now emerging, and progress is summarized in recent reviews.43,44

White light LEDs that have made possible energy-efficient lighting potentially lowers greenhouse gas emissions. These devices rely on phosphors, often made by high-temperature sintering of rare earth oxides. Phosphors are useful to demonstrate how materials ‘genomes’ are generated and the basic operation of in silico simulated Darwinian evolution. Phosphors can be very simply presented by a ‘genome’, for example, a vector containing the relative mole fractions of each rare earth oxide component. After sintering, phosphor brightness and colour are measured (equivalent to species fitness in Darwinian evolution) and the best phosphors are ‘bred’ to generate a new and higher fitness population of phosphors. Mutation operations such as elitism (passing on the best phosphors into the next generation unchanged), changing the concentration of one rare earth (point mutations), and splitting the genomes of two phosphors and combining the parts into new ones (crossover operators) are applied to the fittest materials in a given cycle of evolution. This evolutionary loop is iterated for a number of cycles, until a specified performance level is reached, or the algorithm fails to generate improved examples. In this way, Sharma and co-workers45 steadily improved the fitness (brightness and colour) of mixed metal oxide seven-dimensional library (MnO–Na2O–Li2O–MgO–ZnO–CaO–GeO2) by evolution to find a promising green phosphor for use in backlit liquid crystal display applications. (see Figure 9.8). They synthesized only a few hundred phosphors but explored a much larger space of phosphor composition to find locally optimum materials.

Figure 9.8 By iterating around this evolutionary loop for five cycles, Sharma et al. improved the fitness of the phosphors (brightness and green colour). The upper and lower panels are replicates. Consequently, it is very likely that the next disruptive technology to be adopted by materials scientists after ML will be genetic technologies. This is likely to play out in two ways: more efficient searching of materials spaces using high throughput experiments coupled with EAs, and even more effective searching using synergistic combinations of ML and EA. The latter involves building ML models of the fitness landscape from experimental data in successive initial rounds of high throughput experiments and using these to replace experimentation in later stages of the search. It has been shown that such ‘adaptive’ evolution (an in-silico equivalent of the biological Baldwin Effect) allows systems to evolve more quickly than those that do not use it.46,47

Evolutionary methods also make possible, for the first time, the possibility of autonomous discovery methods, fully automated invention machines with no ‘human in the loop’. In broad terms, such a machine would consist of a general purpose synthesis robot, automated characterization instruments for quality control and to measure a specified fitness, an evolutionary program that could select the fittest members of an initial population of molecules or materials and mutate them into a new population, and a method for specifying the new molecules to be synthesized to the robotic synthesizer. Several groups are developing autonomous chemists and autonomous materials scientists. Some of these are focused on automating organic synthesis,48 and others materials discovery.49 There is major work towards universal organic synthesis machines, a prerequisite for an autonomous organic chemist, at the Max Planck Institute for Colloids and Interfaces in Potsdam. The US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) has funded several international initiatives. to help remove barriers to autonomous synthesis systems. The research teams are pursuing both hardware and software solutions for automation.50 MIT is using preloaded cartridges to automate synthetic steps such as heating, mixing and separating chemicals.51 They trained an ML model on millions of reactions from the Reaxys database and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. The ML model learned to apply retrosynthetic transformations, identify relevant reaction conditions, and to estimate reaction feasibility. It was taught to generalize from specific known chemical reactions to new substrates. A team at the University of Glasgow led by Prof. Lee Cronin have developed a Chemputer, a modular desktop-sized robotic synthesizer that compiles text-based synthetic instructions into machine instructions to drive synthesis robots costing £25 000–30 000 (US$33 000–39 500) each.52 This approach has successfully synthesized generic versions of common drugs in an order of magnitude faster than conventional manual synthesis methods. His online platform, Chemify, allows chemists to download Chemputer assembly instructions.

9.8 The Path Forward

ML is passing through at least the second of the well-known hype cycles. Claims of ML's capabilities are often exaggerated, but it is clear that there are also many examples across broad fields of science, technology, medicine, manufacturing, and business of spectacular outcomes. ML is a disruptive technology that will change the world as we know it in the next few decades. It has the potential to remove much of the tedious, repetitive, and sometimes dangerous work of chemical and materials researchers, freeing them up for more creative endeavours. The main roadblocks to future development are:

  • the ability to describe complex materials mathematically to train ML methods,
  • a paucity of data to train deep learning models,
  • a better understanding of how to reduce bias in ML models learning from examples,
  • development of chemical synthesis languages that will completely specify reactions to improve reproducibility and allow robots to be programmed with synthesis information,
  • development of synthesis machines with broad applicability (e.g. by breaking down molecule or materials syntheses into a finite number of unit operations),
  • and optimal synergy between automation, ML, and evolution.

ML and AI will also generate profound changes to the workforce, with even intellectual jobs such as accounting, law, and some aspects of medicine being impacted. As foreshadowed, the combination of AI, ML, robotics, and evolutionary methods will potentially unleash new ways of doing science that can accelerate our understanding of materials properties, their interactions with biology, and the discovery of novel molecules with highly novel and useful properties. As well as robots helping design and synthesize new molecules and materials, we are likely to see materials evolving collaboratively with robot morphologies and controllers to generate new fit-for-function robots,11 another neat ‘closing of the loop’ in technology.

CHAPTER 10

Machine Learning Techniques Applied to a Complex Polymerization Process

SILVIA CURTEANU( 0000-0002-5281-1265)

“Gheorghe Asachi” Technical University of Iasi, Faculty of Chemical Engineering and Environmental Protection “Cristofor Simionescu”, Iasi, Romania

Email: silvia_curteanu@yahoo.com

10.1 Difficulties in Chemical Process Modeling

In chemical reactions engineering, there are many processes and systems for which the physical and chemical laws that govern them are not known, or limited, or only uncertain knowledge is available. In such cases, either phenomenological models cannot be developed or those models are subject to significant errors because of the approximations included. Empirical modeling, based on experimental data, then becomes a viable tool, with a real chance of providing accurate models. Artificial neural networks, belonging to the machine learning (ML) domain, fall into this category, operating on input–output data in a “black box” fashion.

In complex, highly non-linear, chemical processes, in addition to the difficulty of obtaining a mechanistic model, further problems arise related to solving the mathematical models, which are often represented by systems of differential equations. Modeling the output–input dependence using neural networks represents a possible way in which one might avoid the problem of solving intractable mathematical models.

Another major difficulty in controlling the quality of products in a chemical synthesis is the lack of “online” measurements for some variables and the substantial delays that may accompany other measurements.

Further difficulties in process modeling exist in the complex field of polymerization processes. Polymer products often contain numerous specially added materials to enhance their use characteristics. The most widely used process for obtaining these materials is discontinuous polymerization, which is also useful if it becomes necessary to change the production specifications for the manufacture of polymers with different properties. Discontinuous operation is a dynamic process, with reaction conditions often varying in a fairly wide range. Consequently, both data collection for modeling and configuring the reactors present problems.

In contrast to discontinuous processes, continuous polymerizations benefit from the availability of significant amounts of data and the possibility of making precise adjustments to process conditions, corresponding to narrow operating ranges of the key adjustable parameters.1

One of the most important features of free radical polymerization is the significant increase in viscosity that occurs as the reaction proceeds, especially in homogeneous systems such as mass and solution polymerizations. Under these conditions, the heat transfer, associated with the appreciable exothermicity of the reaction, becomes a difficult factor to control. From a kinetic point of view, the viscosity changes cause the initiation, propagation and, especially, the termination steps of the chain reaction(s) to become diffusion-controlled. These phenomena are defined in terms of cage, glass, and gel effects; they represent the most difficult part of a polymerization process to model.

Another problem related to polymerization reactions is the possibility of multiple solutions. Differences in operating conditions (such as feed concentrations, temperature, pressure, or catalyst addition rates) can lead to the same type of polymer (same molecular mass, density, and composition), but with different productivity.

Ensuring the quality of product is a much more difficult task in polymerization processes than in conventional reactions involving small molecules, because the morphological and molecular properties of a polymeric product strongly influence its physical, chemical, thermal, rheological, and mechanical properties, as well as the final applications of the polymer. From this point of view, the development of mathematical models that can predict the quality of the polymer from a knowledge of the operating conditions in a polymerization reactor is usually the key to obtaining an efficient and high quality production and improving the operation of the plant.1 Many researchers have conducted detailed studies on the mechanistic modeling of polymerization reactors. However, a complete mechanistic model would contain a very large number of differential equations, the solution of which would require considerable time. In addition, the values of many kinetic parameters that appear in the model may be unknown or difficult to determine precisely. Furthermore, development of the model, especially for diffusion-controlled reactions, under discontinuous or semi-discontinuous operating conditions, is extremely difficult when several polymers of different product specifications are manufactured in the same installation.

Developing a kinetic model for free radical polymerization is not an easy task, especially when polymerization takes place at high temperatures and pressures. These difficulties are not only due to the complex reactions that occur simultaneously in the reactor but also to the limited understanding of the physical and chemical phenomena related to the mixtures including polymers.

An alternative to mechanistic modeling is provided by empirical modeling, which requires less knowledge specific to the process than is needed for phenomenological modeling. Empirical modeling requires data (measurements) on the variables considered to be representative for the behavior of the process and for the quality or properties of the product or system. Statistical regression techniques and neural networks have been increasingly used to build empirical models.

10.2 Phenomenological Modeling of the Free-radical Polymerization Process

This section is necessary before approaching the application of ML techniques in free radical polymerization for at least two reasons. First, the difficulties related to establishing and solving the mathematical model of the process, as well as problems related to the accuracy of the modeling, are demonstrated here. Second, the mechanistic models inserted here may constitute data generators required for techniques based on ML.

Among the polymerizations that take place through free radicals, the polymerization of methyl methacrylate (MMA) and styrene (St), similar in many aspects, but with specific features, were chosen as examples. We will try to show the usefulness of ML techniques to overcome the difficulties of classical modeling, but also to make a significant contribution to the accuracy of the results. Also, it is not difficult to demonstrate that a user who may not be familiar with these techniques (such as a chemical engineer) can readily manipulate them to obtain the predictions (s)he needs, especially when the software products are provided with a graphical user interface. It should be noted that most of the software products used in the case studies presented here belong to the author of this chapter (and to her group) and some of them being patented.

In a free radical polymerization reaction, a phenomenological model starts from the kinetic scheme of the process; for MMA this scheme is:

Assuming the steady-state and that no monomer is consumed in the initiation stage, one obtains the following equations based on the above kinetic scheme.2

where x is the conversion of monomer; λk and μk are the moments of macroradicals and dead polymer, respectively, that give the molecular weight distribution (k=0, 1, 2); ε takes into account the volume variation during the reaction; M0 represents the concentration of monomer at time t=0, and f is the efficiency of the initiator. The system composed from eqn (10.1)–(10.8) was obtained with the moment method, detailed in ref. 3.

A major feature of homogeneous free radical polymerization is the significant increase in viscosity of the reaction mass as the reaction progresses (as monomer conversion increases). Under these conditions, a deviation from the normal kinetic behavior and changes of mass and heat transfer in the reaction medium are observed.

The highest sensitivity to the increase of viscosity is presented by the rate constant of the termination step, kt. The severe reduction of the mobility of the macroradicals due to the increase of viscosity causes a decrease in the value of kt, resulting in a self-acceleration of the reaction (the gel effect or Trommsdorff effect).

Normally, when polymerization is conducted at low temperatures, at a certain level of conversion, a transition state is reached, and the temperature corresponding to this moment is called the glass transition temperature. The rate constant kp decreases before the monomer is completely consumed. This is the glass effect in radical polymerization, being also the effect of the viscosity increases.

Finally, at high conversions, due to the increase in viscosity, the efficiency of the initiator also decreases, appearing as the so-called cage effect.

Therefore, one of the specific problems of free radical polymerization is that it is diffusion-controlled, which leads to the manifestation of gel, glass, and cage effects. Process modeling is directly affected by these because, as Figure 10.1 shows, the above mathematical model formulated in terms of moments (master curve) fails to reproduce the experimental data.

Figure 10.1 Master curve and experimental data obtained at 50, 70, and 90 °C for MMA conversion.

From a certain value of conversion, called the critical conversion (corresponding to the deviation of the experimental data from the kinetic curve of Figure 10.1), significant structural changes occur in the reaction mass due to the transition to diffusion control. To obtain a realtsic model we require a means of capturing these changes in a mathematical formalism.4

The most widely used model that considers the variations of propagation and termination rate constants (gel and glass effects) was proposed by Chiu et al.5
