The main criteria in evaluating a mathematical model are accuracy of results and ease of handling. The ideal case corresponds to the quantification of the phenomenology of the process (physical and chemical laws that govern the process) through mathematical relations. However, in many cases in models of diffusion-controlled effects, empirical constants are needed to match the experimental data or these models are entirely of the black box type. Thus, the use of artificial neural networks for free radical polymerization can be considered as a favorable alternative; the advantages it presents overcome the so-called deficiency of their empirical character. A third possibility is to combine two types of models, phenomenological and empirical, as will be described later in this chapter.

10.3 Artificial Neural Networks Applied to Polymerization Processes

Given the difficulties of modeling the polymerization processes mentioned in section 1, Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) prove to be useful predictive models in a wide range of applications in the field of polymer engineering. They possess the ability to learn what happens in a process without quantifying the physical and chemical laws of the system. Therefore, they are recommended modeling tools in the case of complex non-linear processes for which phenomenological understanding is limited.

The manipulation of the ANNs applied to the modeling of polymerization processes implies collecting training data from experiments or by simulation on mechanistic models, setting up the training and validation data sets according to the type of neural network, determining the architecture and parameters of the network (training) and, finally, evaluating the generalization capacity of the neural model when the network produces results for data that are not included in the training set. This last step really establishes the quality of the model, namely its generalization ability.

The input variables in an ANN are chosen depending on the process, either based on the experience and knowledge of the engineer, or by applying a sensitivity analysis that allows the parameters to be ranked according to their importance. The outputs correspond to the purpose pursued, being correlated with the input variables.

The quality of a neural model depends on the quantity of data available for modeling, on their representativeness, on the uniformity of their distribution in the investigated space, and on the methods used to develop the neural model. This last consideration refers to the choice of the best type of model depending on the process subject to modeling and the training method with the highest chance of leading to an optimal or near-optimal model. Regarding the quantity of data, a significant number of data samples is recommended, more important than their number being a relatively uniform coverage of the domain to which they belong. A larger amount of data and, consequently, a longer training time, is required in the case of complex, strongly non-linear systems. Obviously, the accuracy of the experimental data is a key factor in determining the accuracy of the modeling results.

Developing the topology of a neural network is a critical and sometimes difficult step, especially when it comes to determining the optimal network architecture. In addition to trial-and-error, different techniques have been tested, of which evolutionary algorithms have proven to be the most efficient variants.

Concerning the polymerization processes, one can solve problems such as estimating the reaction characteristics (conversion, reaction yield) depending on the working conditions (time, temperature, concentrations of reactants, etc.), predicting the final properties depending on the initial compound structures and/or reaction conditions, identifying the optimal working conditions that lead to pre-defined structures or characteristics of the reaction, identifying the structures that will generate pre-established final properties (molecular design), or determining the most influential input parameters.

Numerous articles in the specialized literature cover modeling, optimizing, predicting and controlling some parameters from polymerization reactions using various ML techniques, of which, in particular, individual neural networks or hybrid soft-computing techniques are notable. Noor et al.7 present a number of important issues related to the application of ANNs in polymerization reactions including vinyl acetate polymerization, continuous copolymerization processes, gas-phase olefin polymerization, continuous free-radical polymerization of styrene in a tubular reactor, free-radical polymerization of MMA, semibatch polymerization, and polymerization of nylon-6.6 in a twin-screw extruder reactor. The first part of Curteanu's article8 is a review that also associates neural networks with polymerization processes. Fernandes and Lona9 provide a brief tutorial on the use of ANNs for polymerization processes, a tutorial which contains a number of practical considerations regarding neural network selection and training.

10.3.1 Types of Applications Based on Neural Networks in Polymerization Reaction Engineering

When using neural networks, some considerations are the type of network to be employed, how this relates to different types of applications and different processes, determination of the best network architecture, and how they might be included in different soft-computing configurations.

ANNs have proven to be suitable tools for direct and inverse neural network modeling, monitoring (soft sensors), and control procedures. In addition to these applications, two types of approaches can be highlighted: 1) determining how the process performance (efficiency, yield etc.) or the properties of the final product (chemical, physical, mechanical, optical, surface properties etc.) depend on the reaction conditions; and 2) analysis of quantitative structure property/activity relationships (QSPR/QSAR) in an attempt to correlate structural descriptors of compounds with their physico-chemical properties and biological activities.

In Direct modeling, a correlation is derived between the output values of one or more variables and a series of input variables that significantly influence the outputs. For example, Chan and Nascimento10 model olefin polymerization in high pressure tubular reactors using feedforward neural networks. The selection of the best network topology was based on a sensitivity analysis relating the mean square error to the number of intermediate neurons.

For a chemical reactor, optimization involves determining the reaction conditions that lead to suitable values for properties that are required in the final product or to a maximum efficiency of the process. Inverse neuronal modeling can respond to the first optimization variant and, even if it is not easy to perform, compared to the classical procedures that require the existence (determination) of a good mathematical model and the selection of an optimization technique, it is an acceptable alternative.11 Fernandes and Lona9 designed a neural network that determines the operating conditions (comprising monomer and comonomer feed rates, catalyst feed rates, surface gas velocity, and porosity) of gas-phase ethylene polymerization in a fluidized bed reactor leading to the desired properties of the copolymer (molecular mass, polydispersity, composition, and production). Another example related to the synthesis of polyacrylamide-based hydrogels by inverse neuronal modeling consists in determining, in an easy manner and with good results, the initial reaction conditions which lead to a pre-established reaction yield and maximum swelling degree.12

In many processes in chemical engineering, “difficult-to-measure” variables are estimated using “easy-to-measure” variables, based on a two-way correspondence between them. One solution to such a problem is the use of inferential models or soft sensors represented by neural models. For example, Zhang and co-workers13 apply inferential software sensors for a batch reactor in which MMA polymerization takes place. The molecular mass of the polymer is estimated based on online measurements of reactor temperature, jacket inlet temperature, jacket outlet temperature, monomer conversion and coolant flow rate. Gonzaga et al.14 describe the implementation of a virtual sensor (soft-sensor) in the polyethylene terephthalate (PET) production process. The sensor, based on an ANN, is used to estimate the viscosity of PET, using both online and redundant measurements. Thus, an efficient strategy for controlling this industrial process is designed, with neural networks overcoming the disadvantages of difficult measurements.

Another type of application is represented by the use of ANNs for the identification of systems and design of controllers, through the inclusion of neural models in optimal control strategies. Wei et al.15 proposed an optimal control strategy for a propylene polymerization process, integrating a simplified mechanistic model based on a polymer property estimator and a feedforward neural network model based on a predictive control model for melt index. Lifgtbody and Irwin16 present a neural network modeling application designed to improve the control of a polymerization reactor, highlighting the problem of precise control of polymer viscosity based on delayed measurements. A non-linear predictor consisting of a feed-forward neural network is used to remove limitations that arise from delays in measurements.

10.3.2 Different Types of Neural Network Models Used in Modeling of Polymerization Processes

Neural networks can be divided into two broad categories: static, which includes feedforward neural networks and dynamic, which includes global recurrent, local recurrent, Elman and dynamic filter networks. Static neural networks are suitable for short-term predictions and are relatively easy to develop and train, while dynamic ones are recommended for long-range prediction models.

Feed-forward (multilayer perceptron) neural networks are often used for modeling chemical processes, and their universal approximator qualities give very good results in most cases. One or two hidden layers containing a reasonable number of neurons are usually sufficient. But, in some cases, other types of networks have proven effective in modeling chemical engineering processes, exceeding the performance of feed-forward networks. In this section, this will be illustrated, contrasting with the examples included in the previous sections which relate mainly to the multilayer perceptron.

A feed-forward network that models styrene polymerization under semi-batch and non-isothermal conditions has been reported by Curteanu and Petrila.17 This approach demonstrates the usefulness of ANNs in modeling a complex process, under special operating conditions, semi-discontinuous and non-isothermal. The supplementary addition of initiator or monomer at certain stages of the reaction (dependent on critical conversion) contributes to the control of polymer molecular mass and, therefore, its properties. The same effect is obtained in non-isothermal conditions, represented by increasing temperature steps. Simple neural networks were used, of feed-forward type with two intermediate layers, the same models being valid for different operating conditions; differences are achieved by the way the models are used, not by changing their structure. Figure 10.3 shows the dependence of the monomer conversion on intermediate addition of an initiator, and Figure 10.4 shows the molecular mass of the polymer resulting from the application of a non-isothermal program.

Figure 10.3 Monomer conversion obtained with a feed-forward neural network with intermediate addition of 5 mol m−3 of initiator, I0 =15 mol m−3, before the gel effect (continuous line); dotted curve I0=15 mol m−3 and dashed curve I0=20 mol m−3.

Figure 10.4 Polidispersity index obtained with a feed-forward neural network for five step increasing temperature: 80, 90, 95, 100, 110 °C.

Recurrent neural networks have the advantage that they provide long-term predictions, which are useful for many processes in chemical engineering. For example, in discontinuous processes the aim is to optimize the quality of the final product (this is a frequent requirement of the polymerization processes). Therefore, precise, reliable long-term predictions are essential in such cases.

Tian and co-workers18 present the development of a recurrent neural network model for an emulsion copolymerization reactor in which the essential parameters are the average numerical molecular mass (Mn), the copolymer composition (C), the polymer conversion (X), and the temperature profile (T). Dynamic modeling assumes that these quantities occur not only at the output, but are added to the inputs by values at previous times, because these previous values influence the final results. For example, a neural network developed for modeling Mn has inputs T (t−1), T (t−2), X (t−1), X (t−2), Mn (t−1) in which t is time.

Jordan-Elman neural networks are recurrent neural networks that supply MLP with context units, representing processing elements that remember past activity. Context units provide the network with the ability to extract temporal information from the data.19 An example is the modeling of the synthesis and swelling behavior of polyacrylamide gels with inclusion polymer.20 To evaluate the quantitative influence of the reaction conditions on the yield and swelling degree, neural networks of different types were used, of which Jordan-Elman networks proved to be the most efficient.

Curteanu and co-workers21 used modular neural networks to predict the liquid crystal property of poly (siloxane-azomethine) based on a series of molecular and structural descriptors including fully extended length, diameter of the structural unit, and the dipole moment. This type of neural network uses several MLP networks in parallel, combining their results. There is no total interconnectivity, so the number of weights is smaller, and the structure benefits from some flexibility due to the diversity of ways in which an MLP can be segmented into modules. The applied method provides very good results, thus proving the utility of neural networks in classification problems, in particular for quantifying the structure–property relationship.

Using as a case study the polymerization of styrene carried out in a CSTR, Haiyan et al.22 applied a novel method for modeling and controlling the molecular mass distribution of the polymer. Their technique is based on combining the orthogonal polynomial feedforward neural network (OPFNN) with a recurrent neural network (RNN), resulting in what the authors call a gray-box model. Satisfactory results are obtained when the molecular mass distribution of a polymer is difficult to accurately model with classical tools.

An alternative to the use of individual neural networks is represented by stacks of neural networks, which, in many cases, leads to an increase in the performance of neural models, as it combines different neural networks that capture different aspects of the modeled process. An additional advantage of using different neural networks arises because of the various possibilities of combining the outputs of the individual networks, as well as varying the number of networks included in the stack. The flexibility of the stacking technique represents an advantage of these types of models that give real chances of increasing the accuracy of the results.

Zhang et al.13 used stacks of neural networks to evaluate the properties of a polymer by estimating polymer quality variables from process measurable variables. For each set of data, a neural model is designed which, subsequently using PCA (Principal Component Analysis), is aggregated into a stack. In a further example23 neural network stacks were used to model the synthesis of multicomponent hydrogels based on polyacrylamide. The swelling degree of the product and reaction yield were correlated with working conditions, which included the quantities of monomer, initiator, cross-linking agent, inclusion polymer, time and temperature. The performance of the stack model (see Figure 10.5) compared favorably with that of individual neural networks.

Figure 10.5 Neural network stack applied to modeling of the polyamide–hydrogel synthesis.

When choosing between phenomenological modeling and black box techniques such as ANNs, several factors should be taken into account. Phenomenological modeling has the advantage that it is based on the physical and chemical laws that govern the process, but, in most cases, the approximations they include lead to inaccurate results. On the other hand, empirical modeling, conducted through an appropriate procedure, can provide precise results, and yet does not clarify the process phenomenology. The two classes of methods represent viable modeling alternatives, with applicability depending on the process and the purpose pursued. Following the previous discussion, the utility of hybrid neural models that include a simplified (approximate) phenomenological model and one or more neural networks whose role is to correct the outputs of the phenomenological model or to model difficult parts of the process is evident. Such hybrid modeling offers the possibility of extracting the best features of both approaches, phenomenological and empirical, which leads to precise results.

In the polymerization processes, there are many parts or variables that are difficult to model: the effects of gel, glass and cage, reaction rates, kinetic constants, fluid and flow behavior, physical properties, etc. As a result, these processes are good candidates for hybrid neural modeling, especially for on-line advanced model-based control design strategies.24 Some examples are given below.

Tian and co-workers1 approach the discontinuous polymerization of MMA with a hybrid model composed of a simplified phenomenological model (that ignores the gel effect) and stacks of recurrent neural networks (that correct the residuals of the mechanistic model). A similar strategy is applied by Nascimento et al.25 to the finishing stage of nylon-6.6 polycondensation in a twin-screw extruder reactor. Within the hybrid model, the information on the final amino and carboxyl groups comes from a mechanistic model; subsequently, these results are used to calculate the relative viscosity with a neural network model. Another example of a hybrid model is designed for an industrial polyethylene process.26 The mechanistic model part in this example is developed to predict the temperature in the reactor, the conversion and the distribution of the polymer molecular mass. For this latter parameter, important for the evaluation of the end-use properties of the polymer, no satisfactory results are obtained through a classical modeling based on fundamental material and energy balances. However, the empirical component represented by neural networks of feed-forward type, added to the phenomenological model, makes it possible to obtain precise predictions for the distribution of the polymer molecular mass. Vega et al.24 developed a hybrid-neural model for a loop-tubular polymerization reactor for polystyrene production. An approximate mechanistic model was combined with neural networks that have the role of modeling reaction rates and, in addition, correcting the final errors in modeling.

10.4 Soft-computing Hybrid Configurations Applied to Polymerization Processes

Neural networks can be combined with other ML tools, leading to the development of improved performance methodologies, with possibilities in a variety of different applications: modeling, optimization or automatic control. The most commonly used combinations include ANNs and evolutionary algorithms or neural networks and fuzzy systems. Obviously, the number of soft – computing techniques that can be combined is not limited to two.

For example, evolutionary algorithms can be used to 1) optimize the architecture and parameters of a neural network, 2) estimate the optimal set of parameters at the input of a neural model, or 3) optimize the processes modeled with neural networks.

Regarding the first option, several researchers argue that evolutionary methods are more effective in determining the topology of neural networks,27,28 than other techniques such as trial and error, empirical or statistical, fuzzy inference, and constructive or destructive methods.

An evolutionary algorithm searches a population of chromosomes whose genes encode the elements of a neural network, looking for the best (adapted) individuals who satisfy an objective function (known as the fitness function). The mechanism that determines the search progress is based on the genetic operators of selection, recombination and mutation. Such a problem is identified with a multi-objective optimization in which the space of the solutions consists of different topologies of the neural networks from which the algorithm will select the best one. The process is iterative, after each step the better solutions being maintained29 with, in some variants, the solution of highest fitness being protected so that it cannot be lost. The use of neuro-evolutionary techniques applied to the design of neural networks is presented in more detail in ref. 30.

An example is fluorescence modeling31 of the polydimethylsiloxane/silica composites containing lanthanum, which was performed using a methodology based on ANNs, individual or aggregated in stack, designed with a genetic algorithm (GA). The GA, applied here to determine the topology of neural models, has proven to be an efficient, flexible method, leading to a near optimal configuration with high probability.

Differential Evolution (DE) is another commonly used evolutionary algorithm that can be applied to global search within the space of a typical feed-forward neural network. Curteanu et al. applied DE to the design of a neural network that modeled the free radical polymerization of styrene.32 The good results provided by this algorithm suggest that this method is an efficient one.

Another example,33 in which a hybrid model consisting of a simplified phenomenological model and a neural network developed using the DE algorithm, addresses the free radical polymerization of styrene. What is noteworthy in this approach is the different ways in which two sub-models connect. The best variant that leads to accurate predictions for monomer conversion and molecular mass of the polymer is assumed to have been accomplished by executing the following steps: 1) for each combination of variables, the moment when the gel effect appears was automatically determined; 2) until this critical moment, the phenomenological model was applied; 3) after the critical moment, an optimal neural model was designed by applying the DE algorithm.

The optimization of discontinuous polymerization processes raises problems related to the proposed objectives, the decision variables, the mathematical solving method, the model that will be included in the optimization procedure, and the specific aspects of the multi-objective optimization, within which the objective function is formulated – either scalar or vectorial. The difficulties related to the development of the mathematical model were discussed in the previous sections. The disadvantages of traditional optimization methods are well recognized:34 1) convergence to the optimal solution depends on the choice of the initial solution, so is not guaranteed; 2) most algorithms tend to block in suboptimal solutions; 3) the efficiency of an algorithm depends on the specificity of the problem addressed.

In addition to these difficulties, polymerization processes generally involve multi-objective optimization, which, in turn, brings new problems. Formulating a scalar objective function that involves the weighted combination of several objectives allows the use of simple algorithms for solving, but the results depend significantly on the values of the weights and there is a risk of losing optimal solutions. The use of an objective function formulated as a vector has the advantage of providing the Pareto set of optimal solutions.

As a result of these advantages, techniques based on evolutionary algorithms are gaining ground. They provide a means to overcome the difficulties outlined above, both because of the principles on which their functioning is based and their flexibility in handling different variants or parameters that improve their performances.

An ANN+GA combination, with a scalar multiobjective function, has been applied to optimize a polysiloxane synthesis process.35 Within this methodology, the neural model evaluates the dependence of the conversion and molecular mass of the polymer on reaction conditions: temperature, time, amounts of catalyst and co-catalyst. The objective of the optimization was to maximize conversion and to obtain a molecular mass with an imposed value. A simple GA was used which, besides optimum values of the decision variables (reaction conditions), also calculated the weights with which the two objectives were scalarly combined.

A similar problem, but based on a more elaborate variant of machine learning, was applied to determine the reaction conditions (temperature, catalyst concentration, reaction time, and initial composition) that lead to maximizing the conversion and obtaining a desired molecular mass in the synthesis of dimethyl-methylvinylsiloxane copolymers.36 The variation in time of the main reaction parameters was modeled with a feedforward neural network that subsequently calculated the fitness function for the GA, conceived in the elitist non-dominated sorting GA (NSGA-II) variant. The objective function was in vector form, so that the result of the optimization problem is represented by the non-dominated Pareto front containing optimal values for the decision variables.

Neuro-fuzzy hybrid systems combine the advantages of the two types of techniques, namely the explicit, easy to understand knowledge of fuzzy systems with the implicit knowledge, acquired by a neural network through learning. An example for this type of machine learning method is the online monitoring of the melting index, an important variable that determines the quality of the product obtained in the process of propylene polymerization.37 The soft sensor consists of two variants: adaptive fuzzy neural network and adaptive fuzzy neural network associated with support vector regression, added for parameter tuning.

The same problem of melting index prediction of polypropylene38 uses another association of algorithms: neural networks, particle swarm optimization and simulated annealing. Modeling is performed with the RBF neural network; its parameters are optimized with a modified swarm optimization particle variant and combined with simulated annealing, thus overcoming the disadvantages of the two individual optimization methods.

Leon and co-workers discussed the use of several machine learning techniques in predicting the liquid crystal property of copolymers with mesogenic groups in the main chain, depending on a series of molecular and structural descriptors.39 A comparison was made between the results obtained using feedforward neural networks and categorization algorithms, such as decision trees, nearest-neighbor and Bayesian induction, implemented in some variants: C4.5 pruned, C4.5 unpruned, random tree, random forest, naive Bayes, nearest-neighbor, k-nearest-neighbor and non-nested generalized exemplars. The best results were provided by neural networks and a k-nearest-neighbor method. The observation that the efficiency of the method is primarily related to the choice of the set of input parameters that determine the liquid crystal property was important.

10.5 Machine Learning Techniques Applied to Methyl Methacrylate Free Radical Polymerization

In this section, we will illustrate the application of different machine learning techniques to MMA modeling and optimization. Previously, the phenomenological modeling was presented based on the kinetic scheme of the reaction and the quantification of diffusion-controlled effects. We also highlighted the difficulties of phenomenological modeling, along with the advantages of methodologies that include artificial intelligence tools. To the examples mentioned so far, a more complete example will be added, involving a process for which different variants of modeling and optimization (different machine learning techniques) are compared and graded, with the well-defined purpose of improving the results.

In a discussion of direct and inverse neural modeling of MMA,10 direct modeling follows the correlation between the monomer conversion, the molecular masses of the polymer and the viscosity of the reaction mass with time, monomer concentration and temperature. Inverse modeling, as an optimization variant, provides the reaction conditions that lead to the predetermined values for conversion and molecular masses. As ML techniques, feed-forward neural networks are used, with one or two hidden layers, determined by trial-and-error. The networks have one or more output variables, being designed as separate models for conversion, molecular mass or viscosity, or a single model with three outputs, given that input variables that have a significant influence on all three outputs can be chosen.

An interesting example is shown in Figure 10.6 in which the monomer conversion obtained with the MLP neural model (3 : 9 : 3 : 1), the phenomenological model, and the experimental validation data are compared. The neural network better captures the behavior of the system.

Figure 10.6 Conversion of the monomer in the MMA polymerization obtained with MLP neural model (3 : 9 : 3 : 1) (continuous line), phenomenological model (dotted line), and experimental validation data (○).

The results of these procedures have as reference values T and I0 provided by the complete kinetic model. It should be noted that INN values are very close to the reference values, the method thus proving superior to the classical optimization variant.

A hybrid model40 has proved to be very efficient for MMA modeling, the improvement being especially evident in the distribution of molecular masses. In this approach, a simplified phenomenological model that does not include quantification of the diffusion-controlled effects was combined with neural networks in different ways: 1) The errors resulting from applying the phenomenological model, with higher values as conversion increases, have been corrected with a feed-forward neural network; 2) The ANN was used as a model for the gel and glass effects, providing the mechanistic model with adequate (correct) values for the rate constants of propagation, termination and transfer to the monomer, these being influenced by diffusion; 3) The two models were used alternately, first the phenomenological model, then the neural network, starting from the so-called critical conversion – the point at which the effects of diffusion become significant.

For the first method, Figures 10.7 and 10.8 show how the residuals of the approximate phenomenological model were corrected for gravimetric polymerization degree (one of the variables that is difficult to model) with a neural network of feedforward type in the training and validation stages.

Figure 10.7 Training results of a feed-forward neural network obtained at different temperatures and initiator concentrations for the residuals of gravimetric average polymerization degree; continuous line – training data; ○ – neural model.

Figure 10.8 Validation results of a feed-forward neural network for the residuals of gravimetric average polymerization degree; continuous and dotted lines – simulation data; ○ – neural network predictions.

For the third case, Figure 10.9 illustrates the successive use of the two models, highlighting the very good match with the reference data.

Figure 10.9 Monomer conversion obtained in MMA polymerization with a hybrid model composed from a simplified phenomenological model (●) and neural network (○); continuous line – complete phenomenological model.

Applying one of the three mentioned variants, respectively using a hybrid model, the results obtained in MMA modeling are much better than when individual or even stacked neural networks are used.

Optimization of the MMA polymerization process can be illustrated by some examples in which phenomenological or neural models, traditional optimization or evolutionary algorithms have been used, but what is more interesting in relation to the improvement of the optimization procedure's performance is how different methods can be combined.

A first example41 starts from the use of a complete phenomenological model for discontinuous polymerization of MMA (presented in section 2), a scalar formulated multi-objective function that includes minimizing reaction time (t), minimizing the polydispersity index (Q), and realizing imposed values for conversion (x) and polymerization degree (DPn). The decision variables were the initial concentration of the initiator (I0) and the temperature (T), represented by several isothermal steps. For optimization, three methods were applied, and their results were compared: a classical method based on sequential quadratic programming (SQP), a GA, and a hybrid technique (HM) that combines SQP and GA: GA provides initial values for SQP. The comparison showed the validity of all three methods, because, in a multi-objective optimization, the result is a compromise between the partial objectives; thus, depending on the situation and the priority objective, different results can be chosen. Taking into account aspects such as ease of handling, the accuracy of results, as well as the timing of the procedure, the hybrid method seems to be the recommended one.

Another optimization strategy applied to MMA polymerization40 uses neural networks and GAs. The process is modeled with a feedforward neural network developed and trained with a GA to ensure a near optimal topology. Subsequently, the method of solving consists of applying a GA that, besides the optimum values for decision variables, calculates the weights of the objective function, which overcomes the difficulty of a scalar objective function. The aim of the optimization was to minimize the polydispersity index, to maximize monomer conversion and obtain a preset value for the numerical average polymerization degree. The broader aim of the approach was to develop a general methodology for modeling and optimization, based on machine learning techniques, which could be easily adapted to other complex, non-linear processes. Figure 10.10 shows some details of this methodology.

Figure 10.10 Optimization procedure based on a neural model and genetic algorithm.

The predictions provided by neural networks are typically of great practical utility, being able to supplement or replace experiments that may be costly in time, material, and energy. In view of the way that these models work, the prediction time, and the accuracy of the results, they are recommended for online optimal control procedures. A further advantage is presented by the various possibilities offered by neural network types, structure, or by the possibility of combining with other instruments to form efficient hybrid configurations.

CHAPTER 11

Machine Learning and Scoring Functions (SFs) for Molecular Drug Discovery: Prediction and Characterisation of Druggable Drugs and Targets

I. L. HUDSON,*a S. Y. LEEMAQZb AND A. D. ABELLc

a Mathematical Sciences, College of Science, Engineering and Health, Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT), Melbourne, Victoria, Australia

b Robinson Research Institute, Adelaide Medical School, University of Adelaide, Adelaide, South Australia

c Department of Chemistry, Adelaide Node Director Centre for Nanoscale BioPhotonics (CNBP), University of Adelaide, Adelaide, South Australia

*Email: irene.hudson@rmit.edu.au

11.1 Introduction

The chemical structure of a drug molecule affects its physicochemical properties and biological activities. Lipinski's1–4 Rule of Five (Ro5) revolutionised the way scientists grappled with exploring the molecular landscape. The introduction of the Ro5 sparked a lot of debate within the scientific community as to the best way to divide the chemical space using molecular parameters (MPs) and other factors. To date, many different rules, filters, and models have emerged that attempt to partition molecules and targets based on a variety of different parameters and factors, with some proving more effective than others. The Ro5 is a filter based on four simple molecular properties (MPs): lipophilicity (a molecule's ability to dissolve in fats or lipids) measured as the octanol/water partition coefficient (logP)≤5, molecular weight (MW)≤500 Da, number of hydrogen bond donors (HBD)≤5, and number of hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA)≤10. These cut-off points were founded on the results from Pfizer's high-throughput screening, which indicated that molecules with lower MW that were more hydrophilic (larger polarity) were more likely to be successful at progressing to the next stage of drug development.5 Lipinski advanced these results by indicating that molecules that violated two or more of Ro5's rules were much less likely to have the properties for successful development as an orally bioavailable medicine.6,7 This has had a large impact on the direction and nature of exploration methods used in the pharmaceutical industry, even though the Ro5 filter can only be applied to drugs that use passively transported absorption methods.5 Despite this, the Ro5 classification is still a commonly used measure of a molecule's druggable potential.

Numerous pharmacologically active molecules, however, have failed to reach the market or have a problematic route of administration due in part to their inherent chemical structure. Some light was recently shown on the reasons surrounding this deficit with chemists now focussing on new drugs with improved potency.8 This was further confirmed by Rafferty9 given his discussion of the discrepancy between drug exploratory techniques taught to those in industry and academia. Drug candidates that exhibited poor physico-chemical properties were considered more likely to be lost to attrition due to poor AMDET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity) properties and pharmacokinetics. It was thought that by reducing the number of potential drug candidates that are lost to attrition during pre-clinical development, more time and resources could be invested in developing candidates that progress to the later stages of the discovery process.

Further to Lipinski's work, recent studies have explored the physico-chemical parameters of molecules that are most important to the druggable classification. A number of researchers have reported that lipophilicity is an important MP as it contributes to a number of other parameters such as solubility, permeability, promiscuity, and selectivity of a compound.10 Its measurement has also sparked debate as to which calculation (distribution coefficient (logD) or Lipinski's originally proposed logP) most accurately captures its molecular value.5,11,12 In a study,13 it was reported that, although logP is a useful descriptor of lipophilicity, it does not account for the ionic variation that molecules possess when exposed to different biological pH values. Many of the drugs currently available on the market possess ionic qualities,13 which supports the use of logD. However, to date, there remain studies that have used logP as a measure for lipophilicity. Further investigation of the more appropriate measure of lipophilicity and its effect on accurately determining drug-like classification was recently reported.11,12,14–16 These studies showed that logP values switch magnitude in relation to MW across the druggable status of a molecule. To account for this change, that exists due to the interaction between pH values and ionic levels, logD was proposed as a more accurate biological measure of lipophilicity.11,12

Efforts by chemists and data scientists to reliably expand areas in the chemical space that are likely to yield viable drugs have been constant and growing. Indeed, recently, there has been a significant momentum to develop drug candidates beyond the so-called drug-likeness space, outside the Ro5 space,3 to the so-called beyond Ro5 (bRo5) space, or “middle space”,17 and the expanded Ro5 (eRo5)17 to tackle difficult targets – with particular focus on up-to-the-minute therapeutic candidates and targets.8,18 Recently many disease targets have been classified as “undruggable” due to their lack of oral bioavailability.19–21 Generally, such targets have binding sites, which are large, highly lipophilic, flexible, highly polar and featureless. An ongoing major issue in drug discovery is to select compounds for difficult targets that have higher MW and are more lipophilic.22 It has been suggested that significant expansions in the range of so-called druggable chemo-space for MW, polar surface area (PSA), logP, HBD and HBA, can provide oral clinical candidates for difficult targets.17 Recent analyses of candidate molecules have shown that the bRo5 space allows for increased likelihood of discovering orally active and cell permeable compounds and has highlighted their ability to modulate difficult targets.23 Definitions of the molecular cutpoints (or cut-offs) per MP used in the vector describing “druggability” for such expansions of chemo-space are given in Table 11.1.

We refer the reader to two reviews. First is an earlier review of computational tools to set up a suitable formulation strategy for bRo5 compounds and molecular requirements for different targets. These authors suggested that enabling a formulation strategy for the prediction of ‘formulate-ability’ may increase the number of orally tractable targets.24 Second is the recent review of chemical and pharmaceutical approaches to help overcome structure-related problems and achieve acceptable ADMET properties, this via chemical modifications and pharmaceutical technology applications to improve improving drug-likeness25 (see also the recent review by Hudson16).

In recent years, machine learning has played an increasing role in determining the robust classification of druggable molecules.26 In particular, research has shown that recursive partitioning (RP), Random Forests (RFs),27 support vector machines (SVMs),28 and Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs)5 have been commonly employed in this arena.16,29–38 Classification methods such as RP, naïve Bayesian,39 and SVM34 approaches have been used to categorise small molecules, into druggable and non-druggable compounds. In ADMET evaluation40 naïve Bayesian methods were shown to provide more accurate results than RP and SVM.39 In contrast, SVM showed very good classification results compared with other classification methods in early pharmaceutical research.41

High throughput docking of small molecule ligands (candidate drugs) into high-resolution protein structures is now standard in computational approaches to drug discovery.42 High throughput docking does well in correctly identifying the binding modes of ligands, but associated scoring functions have poor success rates in predicting binding affinities.43 Interestingly, a hybrid Self Organising Map ANN approach was recently suggested as a computational tool for the evaluation of docking experiments of calpain ligands (small drug molecules) for the treatment of cataracts.44,45 These authors showed the value of adding chemical–physical structure for improved identification of good candidate drugs for the classification of calpains for the treatment of cataracts. More recently Hudson et al.14 studied the performance of SVM and RP methods based on 10 physico-chemical MPs, to successfully classify small molecules (ligands) with low or high violator scores (defined by an optimal cutpoint, C=5, as based on skew normal mixtures46 and on logit models. RP and SVM were then used to classify the high-score molecular violators from the low-score ones (<5). They also showed that SVM used in combination with simple molecular descriptors provided a reliable assessment of a scoring function of counts of violations of MPs which were suggested earlier by Hudson et al.47 to partition molecular chemo-space into so-called druggable versus non-druggable molecules.

We refer the reader to a summary given in Table 11.2 of a selection of machine learning (a subset of artificial intelligence (AI)) studies for druggability prediction based on physico-chemical MPs. Noteworthy also is that while AI and the more recent development of deep learning (DL) are not new, recent advances in high-performance computing, the availability of large annotated data sets required for training, and the development of novel frameworks for implementing deep neural networks, have led to an unprecedented acceleration of the field of both pharmacogenomics and molecular (network) biology. We refer the reader also to a recent review of DL methods in drug discovery16 and a review on machine learning methods used for predicting drug-likeness of molecules and their disease or organ category.26

As implied above, lead discovery or lead optimisation involves testing the structure–activity relationship of compounds, after which selected compounds are synthesised and screened experimentally. Analysis of the structural and physico-chemical properties of compounds has been shown to increase a candidate molecule's probability of activity for a specific target, as well as the molecule's eventual survivability through preclinical development. As such there have been a number of investigators that have sought to improve Lipinski's Ro5 filter by means of additional MPs and to create different violation cut-off points for each MP.14,15,48 Numerous physico-chemical properties,49–52 including Lipinski's Ro5,3,6 the latter known as the rule of thumb, have been applied to improve ADMET properties.10,40,53 It is important to note that the type and the length of the molecular descriptor vector influences the details of the chemical representation, and the choice of the feature set is driven by the expected depth of description. A recent study14 studied the viability of scores involving the original 4 variables of Lipinski's Ro5 and an additional 6 MPs (PSA, number of rotatable bonds (ROT), number of rings (NRING), number of halogens (Halogens), number of N and O atoms (NATOMs), and logD). They compared the best cutpoint, C, for a rule violations testing C=3, 4 or 5 and it was determined that the most effective cutpoint that optimised drug-like classification was less or equal to 5 violations.14 A list of main ADMET based rules of druggability is given in Table 11.1.

The aim of this chapter is two-fold: (i) to propose computational methods to identify druggable disease targets and (ii) to establish which of ANN or RF procedures and which scoring functions best partition disease target space. This has not been formally established for the data set studied earlier,14 which showed indirectly that molecules with more than 5 violations were empirically associated with specific disease targets, but this study did not test machine learning methods using the actual target scores associated with the 172 disease targets, as was recently performed in Hudson et al.15 and extended to encompass Principal Component Analysis (PCA) based metrics of the targets in this chapter. Recent preliminary work by Leemaqz et al.,54 using SVM and RPs directly on the median scores of molecules associated with specific disease targets, showed the superiority of SVM over RP to partition targets with a median logD based score of 4 or more. In this chapter, we extend this work to ANN and RF analyses and use both the non-PCA constructs (based on raw data) and find corresponding PCA constructs based on both the MPs and the targets. We use cutpoints which are aligned with the cutpoints as reported in Hudson et al.14,15 and in part modify the cutpoints of Leemaqz et al.54

The score function evaluated in this chapter for both the raw and the PCA based MPs and based on the target median scores comprises the 4 traditional parameters of the Ro5,1–3 plus 5 extra MPs PSA, ROT, NRING, NATOMs, and either logP and logD. Recently, logD was suggested as a preferable predictor for permeation11,12 compared with the more traditionally used Lipinski's permeation coefficient logP.13 Hudson et al.14,47 developed druggability rules for molecules (scores counting violations) that account for physico-chemical properties, and derived novel cutpoints for each of the 10 possible MPs (which included both logP and logD, as candidates). These cutpoints, reported in Table 11.1, were based on a mixture clustering discriminant analysis approach,55 and were shown to be in substantial agreement with recent cutpoints reported for a subset of MPs14,42 (Table 11.1). We use these MP cutpoints14,47 in this chapter to derive a scoring function of violations per molecule and for each of the targets, testing cutpoints C=3, 4 or 5.

11.2 Data and Methods

11.2.1 Data and Druggability Scoring for Molecules and Disease Targets

We analysed 1279 small molecules from the DrugBank database,56 a unique bioinformatics and chemo-informatics resource combining detailed drug (i.e. chemical, pharmacological, and pharmaceutical) data with drug target (i.e. sequence, structure, and pathway) information, containing 6711 drug entries (a candidate molecule is shown in Table 11.3.). In total, there were 105 Ro5 non-compliant molecules, 681 with oral and 598 with non-oral delivery modes. In this study, 172 targets representing 1279 molecules were found and the median score value obtained for the molecules in the given target; with 99 targets predominantly oral and 73 non-oral in terms of modes of delivery.

Table 11.3 DrugBank3.0 information on one candidate molecule (DB01048 Abacavir).

Specifically, we investigated the MP score functions based on recent filter scores,14 where molecules with violations of less or equal to 4 (or 5), were considered a druggable molecule. The score function per molecule sums the number of violations based on 8 or 9 MPs modelled. The filter scores were created as follows for each MP: lipophilicity logP≤1.9, hydrophobicity logD≤3.5, MW≤305 daltons, HBD≤4, HBA≤10, PSA≤140 angstroms, ROT≤7, ring numbers≤2, and NATOMs≤40 (see Table 11.1). Note the cutpoint for logD of 3.5 is smaller than 5.5 as suggested earlier.13 In this chapter, we test models including either of logD or logP as lipophilicity variants and apply ANN and RF methods to test models to classify the score based partitions for both the raw MP data or raw target median data along with corresponding derived PCA based dimensions (Dim) of both targets and MPs.

11.2.2 Description of the MPs and Targets by Score Function Strata

Table 11.4 shows the description of the MPs analysed, stratified by score logD for cutpoints C=4 or C=5, where the MP parameter set excludes logP, as logD was found to be optimal. In addition, the number and percentage of molecules within the Ro5, bRo5, and eRo5 regions in chemo-space, as defined in Table 11.1, are given in Table 11.4, as are the number and percentage of molecules recently identified as good druggables via skew normal mixture analysis.14 This latter study, summarised in this chapter, identified 928 and 351 molecules with score ≤4 and >4, respectively (Table 11.4). Of the 928 low score violator molecules, 86.2% were also identified as good druggables by skew normal mixtures.14 Whereas of the 351 high score violator molecules only 53% were identified as good druggables by skew normal mixtures. While 1174 molecules follow the Ro5, only 34 (3%) of these molecules satisfied the eRo5 criteria, of which 11 molecules were outside the Ro5 region, 6 of which (18%) had a low score (≤4), with 82% being high scoring >4 violators (see Table 11.4). In the full data set 614 molecules were found to be in the bRo5 space, all of which satisfied the Ro5 criterion, 23% had a score ≤4 in contrast to 77% exhibiting high scores >4 (see Table 11.4).

11.2.3 Statistical and Program Approach

11.2.3.1 PCA Analyses of the Molecular and Target Data

It has been appreciated for some time that chemical space visualisations invariably need to reduce the dimensionality inherent in the process of comparing molecular structures. This is often achieved via algorithms such as PCA and recently through t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding.57 To visualise the distribution of the molecules, and primarily the targets in chemical space, we performed a PCA58 on the set of physico-chemical descriptors described above (see also Table 11.1). PCA is a statistical method for variable reduction that allows multidimensional data to be visualised using two- and three-dimensional plots, which incurs minimal loss of information from the original dataset. As detailed by Hudson et al.14 it is well known that several of the molecular descriptors analysed in this chapter are correlated, in which case PCA is appropriate. PCA implements a linear transformation to rotate the matrix of variables onto a set of orthonormal axes that then define the dimensions of greatest variance for the dataset.59 The resultant axes are called principal components or dimensions (Dim) and represent linear combinations of the original variables (descriptors). The matrix rotation preserves Euclidean distances and maximises the fraction of total variance from the original dataset on each successive principal component. Via this transformation, the first principal component (PC1 or Dim1) retains the greatest fraction of variance from the original dataset, the second principal component (PC2 or Dim2) contains the next largest fraction, and so on. In this way, an n-dimensional dataset (in our analysis n=10) can be visualised using an m-dimensional plot of principal components (where m<n) with minimal loss of information. The PCA was performed to find new and reduced dimensions based on both the MP data and on the target medians data.

11.2.3.2 ANN and RF Approach

The dataset was partitioned into 70% and 30% for training and testing purposes, respectively, to avoid model overfitting. The success of the model was determined by assessing the area under the curve (AUC) of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, a measure used to predict model accuracy.60 For replication, all models were created using a seed of 44. RF models were based on 10-fold cross validation on the training partition with a repetition of 5. As RF is considered an accumulative model algorithm, the only tuning parameter used was the number of trees. The averaged model across the specified number of trees was then assessed on the testing data. ANN models were created using a 10-fold cross validation on the training partition and repetition of 5, with models assessed via the training partition. All possible variable set scores were scaled and centred before being integrated in the model. The final model was created using a tune grid containing decay (to avoid overfitting via regularisation) parameters between 0.1 to 0.5 by a value of 0.1 and size parameters (the number of hidden nodes in the network) between 1 to 10 used. Each of these steps was conducted across each of the different score functions: score C logP and score C logD, for C=3, 4 or 5. This ensured the best machine learning method was identified and the most effective score function, whether based on raw data or the PCAs. RStudio, an integrated statistical software package, was utilised to complete all analyses. In particular, the Husson et al. FactoMineR package61 in RStudio was used to complete all PCAs. The Kuhn Caret package62 was used for all classification and the Beck et al. NeuralNetTools63 used for the visual plots and ROC analyses for the neural network models.64

11.3.1 PCA Results

Table 11.7 and Table 11.8 report the eigenvalues of the target-based PCA and the PCA loadings, respectively, for the 8 parameters analysed (the logD model, which excludes logP, and the latter is shown to be less optimal than logD). Taken together, the first three principal components (Dim1, Dim2, and Dim3) retain 89.24% of the full 8-dimensional target data (see Table 11.7). The PCA component loadings given in Table 11.8 aid in the assessment of the influence of the original 8 parameters on the distribution of the targets and are displayed in the loading plots of (Dim2 vs Dim1) and (Dim3 vs Dim1) in Figure 11.2. The distribution of the target violators with score 4 (>4) versus the non-violator targets in two-dimensional space is shown in the PCA plot of Dim2 vs Dim1 in Figure 11.3.

Figure 11.3 PCA plots of Dim2 vs. Dim1 for the target median data. Quadrants: A=top right, B=top left, C=bottom left, and D=bottom right.

As seen in Table 11.8, the variables that contributed most to Dim1 were MW, HBD, HBA, PSA, and NATOMs. logD contributed most to Dim2, and ROT and NRING contributed the most to Dim3. We conclude that Dim1 explains flexibility, Dim2 explains lipophilicity, and Dim3, due to the negative relationship between ROT and NRING, represents cell permeability.

The distribution of the score >4 targets is shown to be more spread along Dim1, and the range of the targets with score ≤4 seems more pronounced on Dim2 (see Figure 11.3). Positioning of compounds along Dim2 is governed largely by logD (and by high values of PSA, HBA, and HBD), which influence compounds in a positive (upward) and negative (downward) direction, respectively (Figures 11.2 and 11.3). In addition, logD influences the positioning of targets negatively (leftward) along Dim1 and positively (rightwards) by (MW, NATOM, and ROT) along Dim1. A larger portion (70%) of the targets with high scores >4 cluster in the upper right (quadrant A) of the PCA plot (Figure 11.3, see also Table 11.9) and to a lesser extent (22%) are in the lower right region (quadrant D), 6 of which (75%) are oral targets (see Table 11.9). For the non-violator targets with scores ≤4, 35% and 37% cluster in the upper left (quadrant B) and lower left (quadrant C), respectively – with equivalent percentages being oral or non-oral low score targets in each quadrant B and C (see Figure 11.3, Table 11.9). PCA analysis successfully identified a group of disease targets with a specific score function range and position of ADMET descriptors in different quadrants. Indeed Table 11.9 confirms a significant association between the score 4 logD classes and the quadrants for all targets (P<0.0001) and also for targets stratified by both score 4 status and oral status (a significant score 4 status by oral status interaction effect, P<0.0001).

11.3.2 Machine Learning Classification Results

The AUC and 95%CI of each machine learning model (RF and ANN) for both the raw MPs data and the raw disease target data across score functions (with varying cutpoints and model variations, founded on whether logD or logP were included in the model) are given in Table 11.10. Based on earlier work,14,15 only score 4 or 5 cutpoints were tested for the MPs, and only scores 3 and 4 reported for the raw target data (see Leemaqz et al.54). The corresponding RF and ANN AUC and 95%CI values based on the PCA constructs for MPs and the targets are given in Table 11.11.

11.3.2.1 Results of the Analyses Based on the PCA of the MPs and the Raw Target Data

Table 11.10 reports the RF and ANN models on the raw target data and demonstrates that RF performed better than ANNs for the score 3 variant models, but that the ANN score 4 logD model was optimal overall, with AUC (95% CI) of 0.89 (0.77, 1.00). The neural network plots for the 4 models based on the raw target data for the score C logP and score C logD (C=3 and 4) partitions are given in Figure 11.4. Table 11.11 shows that overall the ANN classification was superior to the RF models for score 3 and score 4 logD models, with the ANN target based PCA with partition C=4 achieving best classification, with AUC (95% CI) of 0.92 (0.81, 1.00). Similarly, for the molecular parameter PCs, the ANN method performed better than RF classification, with the score 4 logD being optimal with AUC (95% CI) of 0.95 (0.87, 0.94) (see Table 11.11). Figure 11.5 displays the ANN plots for the drug target PCA constructs based on score 4 logP and score 4 logD models. Figure 11.6 shows the RF plots for the drug target PCA constructs based on the score 3 logP and logD variants.

11.3.2.2 Mapping Variable Importance from ANN Analyses to the PCA Loadings of the Target Data

For the superior ANN score 4 logD model based on the raw target data given in Table 11.10, the corresponding variable importance measures, in decreasing order of magnitude, were attributable to PSA, logD, NRING, HBA, MW, NATOMS, ROT, and HBD with a corresponding variable importance vector of 21.65, 19.53, 13.18, 11.48, 11.06, 9.5, 7.52, and 6.08, (see also Table 4 of Hudson et al.14). This revealed the stronger contribution in the ANN classification of both PSA and logD, compared to MW as is traditionally assumed. From Table 11.8, which reports the PCA loadings of the PCA dimensions founded on the target data studied in this chapter, we note that the variable importance measures above, mirror, in part, the sequence of high absolute values of the PCA loadings on the variables (see Table 11.8) for the dimensions as follows: adding strength to the value and interpretation of the PCA dimensions to classify targets into high versus low scorers as shown in Figure 11.3:

  • Dim2: PSA (loading=−0.24), logD (0.61), NRING (0.45)
  • Dim1: HBA (0.41), MW (0.41), NATOM (0.39)
  • Dim5: ROT (−0.37), HBD (0.60).

11.4 Conclusion and Discussion

This chapter demonstrates how PCA and score functions of violations can be used to identify the hidden pattern of druggable molecules and disease targets. Our novel PC analytic MP and target constructs showed that molecules and targets lie in particular locations (quadrants) in molecular space and as stratified by our scoring function cutpoints. Overall violations above 4 mirrored poor targets, which could be plainly differentiated and located in reduced PCA dimensional space (see Figure 11.3) as can also be seen in both the 2D raw MP and 2D target data maps (see Figures 11.7 and 11.8) which, in addition, delineate the bRo5 and eRo5 regions. We found that in the full data set analysed, 614 molecules actually lie within the bRo5 space, all of which satisfied the Ro5 criterion, of which 23% had a score ≤4 in contrast to 77% exhibiting high scores >4. While 1174 molecules follow the traditional Ro5, only 34 (3%) satisfied the eRo5 criteria, of which 11 molecules were outside the Ro5 region, 6 of which 6 (18%) had a low score (≤4), while 82% were high scoring >4 violators.

Figure 11.7 Molecular parameter 2D maps: black=Ro5 (with extension) region, blue (to the right of the Figure)=bRo5 region, and red (lighter colours to the left of the Figure)=eRo5 region.

Figure 11.8 Target median data 2D maps: black=Ro5 (with extension) region, blue (to the right of the figure)=bRo5 region, and red (lighter colours to the left of the figure)=eRo5 region (points in the plots are medians for each target).

The RP and ANN rules to classify the high score target and the low-score molecular violators, based on both MPs and the PCA constructs, confirmed the value of logD's inclusion in the scoring function, validating Zafar et al.11,12 and supporting the recently established cutpoints.14,15 Overall, the RF models and ANNs showed different variable importance profiles. The ANN models performed better than RFs, and the use of logD rather than logP was confirmed. Earlier work15 had also shown that the most important MPs that influence classification, determined by RF methods, were MW, NATOM, logD, and PSA. By contrast, the ANN target models indicated that PSA and logD were highly important, more so than the traditional parameter MW. Overall, our score 4 partitions using logD were better at classification as shown in all RF and ANN analyses.

Our simple scoring functions of counts of violations partitioned chemospace well, identifying both good and poor druggable molecules and targets. Moreover, ligands with 4 or more violations, were shown to be associated with specific disease targets, e.g., Anti- Bacterial, Antineoplastic, Antihypertensive and Anti-allergic, within which most molecules had a non-oral delivery mode. The Anti-Bacterial target drugs (score 4=6) were shown to have high values for all MPs, consistent with the results of Giordanetto et al.,65,66 who reported that compounds that fall into the bRo5 space (higher MW and PSA) include the Anti-bacterial target. Interestingly, the value of HBA, HBD, and PSA were also high for Anti-Bacterial target drugs (10, 3.5 and 180.82, respectively) with these descriptors representing important hydrogen bond or electrostatic features. We note that these descriptors also displayed high loadings in PCA space. Target drugs with a low median score were e.g., Adrenergic, Dietary, Analgesics, Anaesthetics, Adjuvants, Anti-convulsants, Antimetabolites and Antidepressants, most of which were non-oral. Notably, the Dietary target drugs had low values for the molecular descriptors, with a lowest score 4 of 1.0, lowest median MW and also negative medians for both logP=−2.45 and logD=−2.81.14,15

Two decades have passed since the Ro5 piloted the concept of “drug-like” properties. A recent examination of oral drug parameters approved before and after the original Ro5 analysis has demonstrated that while some parameters such as calculated logP and HBD have remained constant, cutoffs for parameters such as MW and HBA have increased substantially over the past 20 years, thus bringing into question whether MW is a “drug-like” property.67 Understanding the internal relations in the chemical database remains a key feature for the exploration of the chemical space to further develop new substances with predefined properties. Visualisation of the target chemical space by mapping from multidimensional descriptor space into a reduced dimensional space is still a challenging task in chemo-informatics and computational medicinal chemistry. Deep learning (DL) algorithms and neural networks now offer ways forward. For example, a parametric Stochastic Neighbour Embedding t-SNE approach, which yields a neural-network-based function to map new portions of data, has been suggested recently to aid the interpretation of structurally conditioned biological properties of chemical compounds.68 Likewise, the exploration of chemical space by core analysis,69 feature optimisation in high dimensional chemical space by DL,70 and chemical space exploration guided by DL68 have been indicated as new approaches. We refer the reader also to a recent review on DL methods in drug discovery16 and a comparative analysis of machine learning algorithms for the prediction of potential druggable drugs by DrugMiner.34
