CHAPTER 12

Artificial Intelligence Applied to the Prediction of Organic Materials

STEVEN BENNETT( 0000-0001-6285-910X),a ANDREW TARZIA( 0000-0001-8797-8666),a MARTIJN A. ZWIJNENBURG( 0000-0001-5291-2130)b AND KIM E. JELFS( 0000-0001-7683-7630)*a

a Department of Chemistry, Imperial College London, Molecular Sciences Research Hub, White City Campus, Wood Lane, London W12 0BZ, UK

b Department of Chemistry, University College London, 20 Gordon Street, London WC1H 0AJ, UK

*Email: k.jelfs@imperial.ac.uk

12.1 Introduction

Functional organic materials are prevalent in many fields, including electronics,1 porous materials,2 polymers,3,4 and ionic liquids.5 We define the scope of organic materials here as materials formed from small or polymeric molecules constituted of only light elements. We do not include pharmaceutical drugs and biological materials as these are covered elsewhere, although we will note similarities in the problems faced and the approaches that can be used to tackle them. The discovery of new materials has previously been dominated by serendipity, but there is now a clear need to accelerate their discovery to help tackle the problems facing humanity, such as climate change and the depletion of the Earth's natural resources. The focus of this chapter is the application of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to accelerate the discovery of new organic materials by assisting in the prediction of their structure and properties and guiding their optimisation for target applications (see Figure 12.1).

Figure 12.1 A schematic summary of the materials discovery workflow in the age of AI, which is driven by the data from (a) curated databases and the scientific literature. From the available data, (b) complex and multivariable structure–property relationships can be inferred using AI. Here, brute force structure generation and/or prediction may feed into property predictors or inverse design may be applied, which predicts top candidates for a target property prior to structure prediction. The (c) resultant search space can then be explored experimentally using AI-designed experiments (d) to efficiently explore phase space, leading to optimised materials, as well as improvements to material databases, search spaces, and the preceding AI models through feedback mechanisms.

Organic materials often offer advantages over their inorganic counterparts in their improved sustainability, increased processability, reduced toxicity of the final material, and often lower cost, all of which are crucial to the scale-up of material production. Furthermore, organic compounds are relatively easy to modify through a vast array of robust synthetic routes, allowing for the fine-tuning of material properties. For example, in the development of semiconductors and other electronics, there is currently a push to replace inorganic, silicon-based materials with organic materials.6 From a modelling perspective, one major difference between organic materials and their inorganic counterparts is that they are normally a combination of separate molecules, be it small molecules or polymers, rather than a single entity. As such, one can in principle represent an organic material either as an isolated molecule, ignoring, perhaps beyond a mean-field approximation, the effects of the environment of the molecule, such as intermolecular packing in the case of solids, the solvent in the case of dissolved molecules, or even interfaces, or treat the whole condensed system. There are many clear examples in the literature for systems where a ‘molecular representation’ is employed. However, for this representation to be accurate and effective, the material's properties need to be dominated by that of the individual molecules. For example, for porous molecular cage materials, because the individual molecule's structure defines the solid-state pore topology, the potential for molecular separations can be determined from the single molecule.7 Similarly, for conjugated polymers that form amorphous solids, a comparison between DFT calculations on isolated polymer chains and experimental photoelectron spectroscopy on polymeric solids8 suggests that isolated polymer chains might be a good representation of the solid for predicting their optoelectronic properties. Conversely, for polymers of intrinsic microporosity (PIMs),9 where intermolecular voids arise from the inherent poor packing of the polymer chains, a molecular representation will be clearly inadequate for predicting the emergent porosity, and a ‘condensed-phase representation’ is required. The choice of representation is relevant to both the generation of training data and the kind of descriptors used for machine learning. As will be discussed in more detail below, for some properties, computational limitations mean the only (efficient) way of calculating them is inherently molecular, while completely different types of descriptors are used for molecules and condensed phases.

The search space for new organic materials does not only include the chemical space of the constituent molecules, which is estimated to consist of 1060 molecules,10 but must also consider different ways of assembling individual molecules into materials, their resultant bulk properties, and the effect of experimental variables such as synthetic protocol.11 With previous knowledge in a field, an experimental chemist can decrease this search space significantly. However, an inherent bias towards small changes within ‘known’ regions of phase space is a hindrance to a thorough exploration of phase space for the optimal material for an application. Computational methods and algorithms offer cheaper and more complete ways of searching phase space for the optimal materials.12 A crucial aspect of exploring phase space using computational methods is the ability to predict the material properties of interest for each candidate accurately. Here, it is common to replace the complexity of multiple length and timescales with simplified models that are defined by existing structure–property relationships.

Computational optimisation has been applied in the field of drug discovery for many years because clear structure–property relationships exist.13 In the case of early computer-aided drug discovery, only the molecular structure, which was used to calculate simple molecular properties (for example Lipinski's rule of five),14 was necessary to advance the drug discovery process. Similarly, in the field of crystalline, inorganic materials, the existence of well-defined structures simplifies the determination of structure–property relationships, because in many cases the relatively well-defined electronic structure of the crystalline material contains the required information about the properties of interest.11,15 However, because weak non-covalent interactions mostly define the bulk structure of many organic materials, the link between structure and organic material properties is not always clear. Therefore, the development and understanding of structure–property relationships is a complex, multiscale and multivariable problem. Given sufficient data, AI can be applied to understand multiscale structure–property relationships and remove the need for approximations and simplifications, which significantly advances the ability to predict material properties. Such a capability will drive the implementation of inverse design procedures, which determine the optimal candidate materials and efficiently explore the material search space based on the optimisation of material function, without the need to test a myriad of possible candidates.16,17

It is possible to apply AI approaches to all aspects of a modern materials discovery pipeline, from candidate generation and data extraction to analysis and property prediction, offering the opportunity to drastically speed up the discovery process without a significant loss of accuracy. Additionally, AI presents a pathway toward the automation of materials discovery, at a significantly faster rate and lower cost than human-driven discovery. A significant barrier in the application of AI approaches is the quantity and quality of existing data, the lack of negative data,18 as well as the choice of representation of chemical and physical systems.17

12.2 Extracting Data from the Literature

From the perspective of using AI approaches to predict new materials and their properties, it is crucial to have a large quantity of high-quality, machine-readable data for training. Within the entirety of the scientific literature, there is a massive amount of experimental and theoretical data in the form of unstructured text, figures or tables in journal articles, technical documents, and patents.19,20 The manual collection and curation of this data into a machine-readable database becomes intractable on a large-scale. Fortunately, the scientific literature is often written in a formulaic way, which allows for the application of text-mining algorithms to automatically extract data. However, the ambiguity and variability in many conventions in different scientific domains limit the universality of established dictionary and rule-based approaches to text mining.19–21 The current trend for large-scale information extraction is the use of machine learning (ML)-based (or hybrid) text-mining workflows because they are much more flexible than hard-coded methods.19,22–24

Recently, Cole and co-workers developed ChemDataExtractor (CDE), open-source software for the automatic extraction of chemical information.25 CDE implements supervised and unsupervised ML models throughout the entire natural language processing (NLP) and named entity recognition (NER) workflow (see Figure 12.2). NER is used to find named entities within the text, which can include chemical species, processes, synthetic conditions, material properties, and characterisation methods, and can be performed using ML23 and hybrid ML, dictionary, and rule-based approaches.19 A significant challenge of text mining is reliably creating a unique identifier for each entity, i.e. matching synonymous terms, which is called entity normalisation. Weston et al. performed tokenisation using CDE, NER using a neural network (NN) and entity normalisation using word embeddings (a machine-learned map of each word onto a dense vector space based on their co-occurrences in text) on the materials science literature toward a structured and accessible database of materials.22 Similarly, Tshitoyan et al. learned a word embedding using text from scientific abstracts and used this to uncover relationships between materials and their potential properties.24 As a result of its inbuilt flexibility, CDE is useful in many subdomains. In the field of organic materials, Cole and co-workers applied the CDE to the discovery of optimal organic dye pairs for co-sensitised solar cells.26 They text mined 9431 dye candidates into a database that linked chemical structure with optical adsorption peak and molar extinction coefficient. From this initial database, a high-throughput screening workflow was applied to identify suitable candidate dye pairs and improved power conversion efficiency of the resultant top candidates was experimentally validated.

Figure 12.2 Natural language processing pipeline. Text is split into sentences and then into individual tokens. The part-of-speech tagger and entity recogniser outputs are combined to assign a single tag to each token, which is then parsed using a rule-based grammar to produce a tree structure. This tree structure is interpreted to extract individual chemical records for this sentence, which are then combined with records from throughout the document to resolve data interdependencies and produce unified records for depositing in a database. Tags shown: NN=noun, CD=cardinal number, VBZ=verb (third person singular present), DT=determiner, NNS=noun plural, IN=preposition, JJ=adjective, CC=coordinating conjunction, CM=chemical mention. Reproduced from ref. 25 with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2016.

12.3 Building Block Libraries

Developing diverse precursor libraries is an important part of the materials screening process,27 as it defines the chemical space available for examination. While molecular structure libraries such as ZINC,28 GBD,29 and PubChem30 offer a large amount of diverse, synthesisable molecules, they are unfocused, making an exhaustive search of all precursor candidates infeasible, and many molecules in them are not designed with materials in mind. Enumeration of existing molecular libraries, through adding known useful functionalities or systematic processes, is a common method of extending building block libraries. However, hard-coded transformations often limit the chemical space spanned by precursor libraries,27 potentially missing compounds that occupy favourable regions of property space. As part of the Harvard Clean Energy Project, a precursor library was created by enumerating compounds based on combining 26 molecular building blocks using pre-defined chemical transformations, to generate a library of over 1 000 000 molecules.31 Additionally, Gómez-Bombarelli et al. designed a library of 1.6 million candidate materials for light-emitting diodes based on donor-bridge-acceptor molecules, systematically incorporating additional functional groups into the library according to chemical intuition.32

12.4 Predicting Properties

12.4.1 Training Data

Any application of ML requires training data for the model, the quantity and quality of which directly influence the types of algorithms that can be used and the likely accuracy of the trained model. Regression, e.g. Gaussian process and kernel ridge regression (KRR), and decision tree models can be trained with relatively small training datasets, but neural networks require much more data. Both algorithms offer advantages; however, deep neural networks typically outperform traditional ML techniques in property prediction.33 The training data itself can be obtained from experiment or from theory and computation. In the context of property prediction, experimental data-sets are typically rather limited in size; for example, Kim et al. trained models to predict the glass temperature and density of polymers using 451 and 173 experimental data points, respectively.34 Hence experimental training data is often used in combination with regression and decision tree methods. Computational chemistry derived training datasets can be much larger, up to millions of data points, and can be obtained from a range of methods, including semi-empirical, density functional theory (DFT) and quantum chemistry calculations. DFT calculations are the norm, but modern semi-empirical methods, e.g. the xTB family of semi-empirical methods developed by the Grimme group,35,36 can give results with a similar accuracy for a fraction of the computer time and hence allow for the generation of (much) larger training data-sets than feasible with DFT.8,37 Conversely, if one wants to train an ML model to predict data with similar accuracy to quantum chemistry calculations, then one must train it with data from quantum chemistry calculations, which is possible, but time-consuming.38–40

Despite the ongoing progress in database creation for organic materials, there still remains an absence of data compared to other domains, such as in the fields of drug design or inorganic materials, in which automated calculation workflows have fuelled the growth of several inorganic material property databases, such as NOMAD41 and the Materials Project database.42 In the organic materials domain, there are several data repositories, focussing on specific material applications (see Table 12.1). Many datasets contain computational calculation results such as Khazana,43 the Harvard Organic Photovoltaic Dataset,44 the Open Spectral Dataset,45 the dye-sensitised solar cell database46 and the Organic Materials Database.47 From these repositories, new material design principles have been established using both ML48 and data-mining techniques.49 Olsthoorn et al. used the smooth overlap of atomic positions (SOAP) kernel method of crystal structure featurisation to predict the band gap using KRR on data from the Organic Materials database.50 The predictive model was then used to screen the Crystallographic Open Database, containing 30 713 organic crystal structures, and identified 15 candidates that were predicted to have a suitable band gap for solar cells.

Owing to the absence of large datasets, transfer learning has become an increasingly popular option for model training. In transfer learning, a deep neural network updates its initial weights from a large dataset from a similar domain to the target problem. A smaller, more accurate dataset is then used to fine-tune the weights of the model, learning subtle differences in the data from the new dataset. Paul et al. applied a similar methodology to predicting the HOMO of potential organic solar cell candidates.51 The Harvard Clean Energy Project database was used to provide the properties of 2.3 million candidate donor molecules as training data for a convolutional neural network. Network weights were adapted using a combination of 243 experimental values and 344 values obtained at DFT accuracy, reducing the mean absolute error of the prediction by around half. However, as ML algorithms only interpolate from the provided dataset, the model's accuracy is limited to that attained by the property calculation method used.

12.4.2 Descriptors

When identifying new structure–property relationships using AI, the chemical characteristics of the material must be captured in a numerical (often vector) representation. An ideal descriptor for a material would contain sufficient information for the model to identify chemical insight from the vector representation, without containing unnecessary information. Descriptors are usually engineered based on the type of algorithm being used and the property being targeted for prediction.52 For example, electronic properties, originating from the three-dimensional conformational configuration of the molecule, are often poorly described using descriptors based on the underlying two-dimensional graph representation.53 Descriptors are not limited to encoding structural features of the molecule; they can include experimental measures, such as solubility, dipole moments or polarizability (see Figure 12.3). Thousands of molecular descriptors can be calculated using the DRAGON software, which is frequently used in QSAR modelling.54,55

Figure 12.3 A summary of commonly used descriptors in machine learning for organic materials design. Single molecules can be represented using (a) SMILES string text encodings; (b) molecular fingerprints encoding structural fragments present in a molecule; and (c) graph representations, which are a machine-learned representation of atomic environments in relation to their neighbours. Full atomic environments can be described using descriptors based on (d) 3D geometry, such as modelling interatomic interactions using potential energies; (e) SOAP kernels or symmetry functions; (f) the bag-of-bonds representation; and (g) Coulomb matrices.

Many structural descriptors encode the molecular representation, relying on graph-based bonding representations of the molecule as an input vector. Bonding information can be captured in the form of adjacency matrices; however, bonding information alone is unlikely to contain sufficient chemical information to predict properties. Fingerprinting algorithms, such as Extended-Connectivity or Morgan fingerprints,56 encode a hash of different substructures present in a molecule, facilitating property prediction based on fragments present in the single molecule. Descriptors based on the two-dimensional structure of a molecule do not contain information relating to the broader environment of that molecule in the solid state (i.e. in crystalline or amorphous structures). Therefore, there is significant interest in developing new descriptors to predict properties that arise as a result of molecular packing. Descriptors used to model the solid-state often contain geometric information about atomic environments; however, it is a significant challenge to ensure that they are invariant with respect to rotation, translations or reordering of the atoms in the 3D structure. Coulomb matrices,57 containing the nuclear charge and position of atoms, have proven to be effective at predicting crystal structure properties, despite suffering from issues with describing periodicity.58 The Bag of Bonds descriptor, based on bags representing bond types present in the molecule, and their geometric distances, was used to predict total and atomisation energies.59 Elton et al. found the descriptor calculated from the sum over bonds performed best when calculating density, heat of formation, shock velocity, and explosive energy, when using KRR.60

The SOAP kernel function has been used as a descriptor for properties of molecules in the solid state.61 This kernel function is a measure of dissimilarity between atoms in an environment, enabling three-dimensional atomic arrangements to be distinguished. To calculate the SOAP descriptor, atomic environments are represented by Gaussian functions placed on atomic positions. Alternatively, symmetry functions are useful in converting the higher-dimensional Cartesian coordinate representation into a lower-dimensional space.62 These representations were then used to train an NN; however, SOAP performed similarly well at a reduced computational cost.63 These types of descriptors have been used to learn atomic potentials, with no underlying physical assumptions, enabling simulations of a significantly larger number of atoms than can be achieved using ab initio methods.64

More recently, deep learning (DL) algorithms have been used to generate novel representations of underlying chemical structures, relying solely on a graph representation of a molecule.65 Using automatic feature extraction, DL algorithms are able to learn their own representations from the graph of the molecular structure, assuming no domain knowledge about the material. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can learn novel representations based on the graph of a molecule, leading to an increase in the predictive performance and interpretability of the trained ML model.65 Graph CNNs are not limited to a single-molecule graph representation and have been applied to the featurisation of crystal structures using the positions of atoms in the unit cell.66,67 Wu et al. describe a benchmarking test, MoleculeNet, for both learned and fixed molecular descriptors based on their ability to predict QM energies and physical, biophysical and physiological properties of molecules from benchmarking datasets.68 Learned graph representations were shown to perform better on nearly all datasets because the learned representations took into account spatial details of the atomic environment. However, this approach requires significantly more data than conventional ML methods. In materials design, learned representations could potentially establish novel insights that are not captured using traditional descriptors, but the absence of large datasets is a significant drawback to achieving greater predictive power using these methods.

12.4.3 Accelerated Property Prediction

AI approaches, in particular (supervised) ML offer the opportunity for vastly accelerated property prediction, being many orders of magnitude faster than, for example, DFT calculations, taking property prediction from hours or days to seconds. This sort of forward problem is fairly simple compared with inverse design. While the properties of some organic materials, in particular porous materials, may rely only on geometric features that are computationally cheap to calculate, or properties such as diffusion that can be simulated with molecular dynamics, the vast majority of organic materials have properties that depend on an accurate quantum mechanical description of the material. Performing ab initio calculations to calculate properties is computationally demanding and thus inherently limiting to the number of materials that can be studied. Furthermore, there is the potential for missed opportunities, where a material is only tested for a particular property in mind – for example, power conversion efficiency – when it could have excellent ferroelectric properties, but that property is not considered, and even if it was it would require a different set of specialist calculations.

Property prediction acceleration has already been demonstrated for many properties of isolated organic molecules, such as thermochemistry, electronic properties, atomisation energies, electron density, and solvation energies.17,43,69,70 The next step of modelling the properties of solid-state materials is obviously more challenging, but, later in this chapter, case studies across the range of organic materials will describe successes so far and the future potential in this area. As in other areas, key challenges are to have accessible databases of high-quality data in sufficient quantity for supervised ML; or, alternatively, to have algorithms that are effective with smaller quantities of data. Ideally, one might like experimental data on the properties of interest to more accurately reflect the full complexity of features that can influence performance, but thus far the majority of studies have focused on the rapid prediction of properties based on training data from simulations. A future goal would be to not just predict material performance, but to predict the device-level performance, taking into account a multi-component system with macroscopic influences on properties.

12.5 Structure Prediction

As currently there is often no route to do a forward prediction directly from molecular structure or precursor to bulk material properties, to make predictions it is first necessary to predict the solid-state structure of the material, whether that be an amorphous or crystalline structure. It is also a valuable endeavour to assist in the identification of synthesised materials and to explore and mine structure–property relationships. Structure prediction is a large field in its own right, with potential for AI to accelerate the process, as has already been demonstrated for several elements of it. Crystal structure prediction (CSP) for organic molecules has a long history, in large part due to the interest of pharmaceutical companies in understanding and predicting polymorphs of active pharmaceutical ingredients.71,72 These approaches have also been applied to other organic materials, in particular molecular electronics.73,74 The typical key steps of the prediction (as outlined in Figure 12.4), are to first construct an accurate energetic description of the system, for instance by parameterising a tailor-made forcefield, then to conduct a global optimisation search, which requires an accurate relative energy ranking of the hypothetical polymorphs, on the principle that low energy polymorphs are the most likely to be experimentally observed. Further analysis of the packing motifs or properties of the polymorphs can then be conducted. Regular blind tests have demonstrated the increasing ability of the approaches to deal with more complex systems, such as those including molecular flexibility, co-crystals, and hydrates, with the ability to use ab initio calculations for energy ranking proving particularly effective.75

Figure 12.4 The key steps in crystal structure prediction (top) and where AI techniques can improve the process (bottom).

While the typical current approach for CSP does not involve AI, there are multiple opportunities here (see Figure 12.4), in particular with the development of new algorithms, as demonstrated in several studies looking at improving individual elements of the process. Machine-learnt potentials (MLP)76–78 offer an alternative to transferable or tailor-made forcefields, involving a more generalised approach to their fitting and the potential for higher accuracy. A variety of approaches are used for the search for low energy polymorphs, including genetic algorithms,79 random and quasi-random searches.80 Although not yet applied for molecular CSP, neural networks are effective for enhanced sampling or learning of free energy landscapes.81,82 As the relative energetic rankings of polymorphs are extremely sensitive to small differences in intermolecular interactions, the accurate energetic ranking of polymorphs is a significant challenge. Although the inclusion of final energy rankings using DFT calculations with dispersion corrections is valuable, these calculations are currently prohibitively expensive on all but a few structures; hence forcefield calculations are used in the earlier stage of the structure search. Here, improvements in the calculation of accurate free energies using ML can massively accelerate the calculation of accurate energies.77 McDonagh et al. have demonstrated that forcefield energies for CSP can be improved by using ML to correct the two-body terms with second-order perturbation theory, yielding higher accuracy at a five-fold reduced cost.83 The challenge would be to extend this to more flexible molecules, rather than the rigid molecules in this study.

Musil et al. applied a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) based upon the SOAP-REMatch kernel to assess the structural similarity of the crystal packings and then accurately predict the relative energies of packings of pentacene and two azapentacenes.73 For the simplest structure, pentacene, only 50 data points were needed for accuracy below 1 kJ mol−1, but for the azapentacenes, which had more complicated intermolecular interactions, approximately 1000 data points were needed for the equivalent level of accuracy. Next, Musil et al. used SOAP-REMatch to perform unsupervised learning to classify the thousands of crystal structures to assess the diversity of packing motifs, replacing the need for heuristic rules.73 Yang et al. later showed that this packing exploration was possible for a single multi-landscape analysis of 28 different molecular organic semiconductors, although this did require a manual selection of the parameters for the kernel.84 Finally, the benefit of accelerated property calculation through supervised ML is obviously of great use for property calculation across structure-energy-property landscapes of thousands of structures.

In addition to structure prediction to identify promising hypothetical materials for synthesis, structure prediction can also facilitate faster structure identification, which is a potential bottleneck in high throughput automation studies. If low energy hypothetical crystal structures have been calculated, then their powder diffraction patterns can be simulated, but this is often insufficient for conclusive structure identification without significant further effort. The calculation of NMR shifts has proven to be an effective route to structure identification,85 but this requires solid-state ab initio calculations, so it is certainly not feasible for routine use. However, recently Paruzzo et al. have demonstrated that ML can predict chemical shifts from DFT training data to DFT-level accuracy and thus identify molecular solids.86 One could also envisage ML being used to accelerate analysis from a variety of other data, including imaging.87

Not all organic materials adopt crystalline packings in the solid-state and instead form a molecular or polymeric amorphous packing. Approaches to creating simulated models of these systems typically involve the generation of random packings, followed by some sort of annealing procedure. The most obvious application of ML here is in the generation of MLPs that can not only accelerate the molecular dynamics simulations involved in the annealing, but also allow larger, more realistic models to be simulated. This has already been demonstrated for inorganic materials, for example for amorphous silicon.88 Although we are still a long way from being able to rapidly predict the assembly of a molecule from only its molecular structure, there is a lot of promise in the acceleration of parts of the process of structure prediction. The next challenge will be to make these approaches more generalisable and transferable between systems. Of course, along with better crystal representations and algorithms, more training data on molecules and their low energy polymorphs would be required to try to make a significant leap forward towards a more universal structure prediction of organic materials.

12.6 Exploration of Phase Space

Given the vast potential possibilities for molecular building blocks of organic materials, and the fact that only a limited number of these have ever been synthesised, a significant challenge is how to effectively sample that chemical space to find the most promising materials. All too often, computational studies have been limited by initial building block libraries that are extremely limited in size (of the order of 100), significantly restricting the scope of such studies. In the next section, we discuss how to generate new molecules de novo, but for a given search space there are multiple possible options to try to effectively and efficiently sample the vast phase space of possible materials, or rather the building blocks they could be made from. A brute force approach can be used in cases of a small search space and a relatively cheap assessment method, or a random approach, often combined with intuitive rules included by a chemist, could be applied. Moving into AI approaches, genetic algorithms (GAs) are frequently used as efficient approaches to sample phase space and find promising candidates. Flavours of GAs can include, with a SMILES representation, graph-based representation (GB-GA) or Monte Carlo Tree Search (GA-MCTS).89 More recently, ML approaches have also been applied, including variational autoencoders (VAE), deep neural networks (DNN), and recurrent neural networks (RNN). However, recent benchmarking of GA-based approaches compared to ML in the area of molecular design for drug discovery have suggested that GB-GA can outcompete RNNs that use SMILES representations, but RNNs trained on large datasets did outperform the GA in the compound quality.90 This type of benchmarking has not yet been performed for organic materials design, but it should be borne in mind that an NN will not necessarily outperform other methods.

Of course, effective exploration of chemical space is a problem not just limited to computational studies, but is also of increasing importance for experimental studies for materials discovery or material optimisation, particularly with the increase of automation.12,91,92 GAs, simulated annealing, and particle swarm optimisations have been used to guide discovery, find new systems, or find optimal conditions to enhance performance. Design of Experiments (DOE) is a statistical approach for multivariate analysis and is used to test and optimise several variables simultaneously, accelerating optimisation, time and resources. This is obviously valuable for optimisation of materials and devices where there is a high degree of complexity arising from many components and processing conditions. DOE combined with ML was found to be effective by Cao et al. for optimising power conversion efficiency (PCE) in an organic photovoltaic, where they used a support-vector machine learning approach to create phase maps based on sampled points.93 RNNs will likely be increasingly used to select the initial test sets, for automated analysis of outcomes on chemical robots, including classification of results, and the prediction and selection of the next tests to perform. The latter has been achieved for organic synthesis reactions, classifying “reactive” and “non-reactive” outcomes on a robot and predicting future reactivity.94 This will be extended further to the more complex problems of organic materials in the future.

12.7 De Novo Molecular Design of Materials Building Blocks

There has been a significant interest in both ML and, most notably, DL algorithms for de novo molecular library design to assist in exploring larger regions of chemical space than that covered by known building blocks or small libraries. There is typically a trade-off between large chemical space exploration and creating new molecules that are chemically synthesisable. NNs possess the ability to learn novel representations of molecular input representations, transforming input features into machine-interpreted latent space, whilst DNNs can create even more complex representations as they contain a greater number of hidden layers. Many approaches rely on perturbing these learned representations, thereby sampling the machine-learnt chemical space (see Figure 12.5(a)).16

Figure 12.5 A summary of molecular de novo design techniques: (a) variational autoencoder-decoder, in which a neural network is trained to transform molecules into a latent representation; (b) generative adversarial networks, in which a generator neural network creates molecules, that are classified as real compounds using the discriminator network; and (c) reinforcement learning, where a neural network is trained to predict the best possible action to perform on a given state.

The ability of DNNs to transform human-interpretable molecular representations into phase space makes them suitable for molecular design. Gómez-Bombarelli et al. used a DNN as part of a VAE, to create a mapping from the graph-based SMILES representation of a molecule into latent space. Transformations were then applied to a molecule by perturbing the continuous vector representation of the molecule in latent space, which was converted back into SMILES using another DNN as the decoder.16 Both an RNN and CNN were trialled as the encoder, with the CNN performing slightly better. An advantage of this approach is the ability to perform property predictions in latent space, potentially allowing for inverse design when sampling regions of this space.27 Transfer learning has shown to be useful at generating molecules with desirable properties, by adapting a model that has been pre-trained on valid chemical SMILES from large precursor datasets. This is followed by retraining the model to generate compounds with certain properties.95 The ChemTS library uses a Monte Carlo tree search, combined with an RNN to dictate the probabilities of selecting each search path.96 Sumita et al. used ChemTS to generate molecules with desirable excitation energies, combining the reward function of the molecular generator with time-dependent DFT calculations.97 Excitation energies were calculated and fed into the generator model, resulting in the identification of five novel compounds with favourable oscillator strengths.

Reinforcement learning, which aims to learn the best course of action to take based on the prior experiences the model has seen, has been shown to bias the generative model towards creating molecules with favourable properties.98,99 Popova et al. used the ReLeaSE framework to generate molecules with desired properties.99 Consisting of both a generative and predictive NN, combined with reinforcement learning, the generative NN was able to propose molecules that maximised a single-optimisation reward function, which can be tuned to maximise a desired property. Despite the many types of generative algorithms that have been developed, many suffer from significant flaws. A large proportion of the GANs and RNNs often produce invalid SMILES strings, limiting their potential usage. While using a long short-term memory architecture in RNNs has been shown to diminish this issue,27 algorithms that optimise towards a specific goal, often significantly reduce the diversity of the molecules, most notably in GANs.100 The vast number of generative algorithms has resulted in many benchmarking metrics for generated molecules, including quantitative analyses of uniqueness, diversity, and novelty of molecules.90 These standardised benchmarks have been primarily used to evaluate drug molecules space; however, these same measures could be used to evaluate generated molecules for materials use in the future.101

12.8 Predicting Synthetically Accessible Materials

While AI approaches have been shown to successfully identify materials with favourable properties, it is difficult to determine which of those materials are experimentally realisable. The synthetic accessibility (SA) of a material is an important part of the materials screening process, due to the time and costs associated with experimentally validating a potential new material. Several points need to be considered: (i) can the material's precursors be synthesised, (ii) can the material then be synthesised in the correct form using a modular approach in high yield and purity, and (iii) can the material be processed into the correct form to obtain the desired properties. When performing a high-throughput screening procedure, SA of the precursors can be incorporated into the methodology in one of two ways. Precursor libraries can be restricted to those that have previously been synthesised or do not require difficult synthetic procedures to create. Alternatively, the SA of a material can be defined as a numerical property and optimised during material optimisation. Significant challenges arise when calculating SA due to the vast number of factors that can affect it, and the assumptions inherent in its calculation. A molecule that requires several low yielding reaction steps, with several difficult separation processes involved and costly reagents, would be inherently difficult to synthesise. As new reactions are discovered, and chemical prices fluctuate, a material's SA can change with time. Early approaches aimed at computing the SA of an organic molecule focused on penalising molecules exhibiting more complex structural moieties.102 However, medicinal chemists were shown to disagree when selecting a target molecule to easily synthesise, suggesting training data is not often reliable from expert chemists.103

ML has provided an alternative solution to predicting the SA of a molecule, by using a data-driven approach. Reaction data can provide an insight into the type of synthetic transformations that are possible, allowing a prediction to be made as to whether a molecule is synthesisable. Using an NN, reaction databases have been used to predict the SA of a molecule.104 ML has also shown to perform well for retrosynthetic pathway prediction, allowing an understanding of the possible reaction pathways to create a molecule.105,106 While the number of reaction steps is a factor in dictating the SA of a molecule, another important factor, cost, was shown to be linearly dependent on the number of reaction steps to synthesise an organic photovoltaic molecule.107 One challenging factor in this type of ML prediction is the absence of informative reaction data. Organic reaction databases are primarily composed of reactant, product pairs and do not contain yield, solvent or work-up information associated with the reaction. Furthermore, the absence of negative examples of failed reactions makes classification tasks difficult.

O'Boyle et al. used chemical intuition from previously synthesised molecules to create a library of precursors that were used to design polymers for organic photovoltaics.108 Additionally, the symmetry of each monomer was considered when creating tetramers to increase the probability that each polymer could be synthesised at the expense of reducing the size of explored chemical space. Even if the covalent bonding in the organic material can be predicted using the techniques mentioned previously, it is still challenging to predict whether the molecule will form the desired three-dimensional conformation with desirable properties. For example, when considering porous organic cages, the topology and resulting porosity are sensitive to a diverse range of factors, including solvent effects, reaction conditions, and the structural characteristics of precursor molecules.109 Therefore, each of these factors should be considered when determining if a porous organic cage is synthesisable.

12.9 Case Studies

12.9.1 Organic Electronics

In the field of organic electronics, the optoelectronic properties of small molecules, oligomers, and/or polymers are exploited to make solar cells, light emitting diodes, transistors, and thermoelectrics. The potential chemical space of relevant molecules is enormous; for example, even from a limited library of 500 monomers, one could construct up to 250 000 binary ordered co-polymers.37 Therefore, virtual screening of molecules to find promising leads or to understand trends is impossible in the absence of machine learning models. Most, if not all, studies in this area make use of the single-molecule approximation in some way and focus either on training and using ML models for predicting the properties of isolated molecules or on taking the properties of isolated molecules calculated using traditional quantum chemistry and using AI to predict the properties of the bulk or devices.

Application of AI in this area started essentially with the use of simple multivariable linear regression (though Sumpter and Noid already in 1994 showed that NNs could in principle be used to predict properties of polymers including electronic properties such as their dielectric constant, see Section 12.9.3 for more details).110 Olivares-Amaya et al. used multivariable linear regression in combination with classical cheminformatics descriptors, such as molecular mass and logP, to predict the open circuit voltage (Voc), short circuit current (Jsc), fill-factor (FF) and power conversion efficiency (PCE) of organic solar cells based on a combination of organic electron-donor polymers and the electron-acceptor fullerene PCBM,111 while Jabeen et al. use a similar set-up to predict the refractive index of polymers.112 Pyzer-Knapp et al. trained GPR models to correct the energy of the highest occupied molecular orbitals (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMO) of organic electron-donors included in the HOPV15 data-set44 as calculated with DFT, as well as the Voc, Jsc, and PCE of solar cells based upon them, to reproduce the corresponding experimentally measured values.113 Lopez et al. similarly used GPR models but focussed on small-molecule electron acceptors instead as an alternative to PCBM.44 These GPR models take as input the property based on DFT, as well as the Tanimoto similarities between the Morgan fingerprints of the different molecules in the set. Kim et al. used GPR with a mixture of cheminformatics descriptors to predict properties, such as the band gap, refractive index, dielectric constant and glass temperature, for a mixture of conjugated polymers and non-conjugated polymers.34 Mannodi-Kanakkithodi et al. also studied the dielectric properties of polymers but used KRR instead of GPR.114 In contrast to most of these studies, Kim et al. trained their GPR to reproduce a mixture of experimental and DFT predicted properties.34 Finally, Musil et al. used a combination of SOAP descriptors and GPR to accelerate the prediction of electronic transport properties of large numbers of polymorphs of a given organic semiconductor, exploiting the fact that different polymorphs are very similar and that learning properties based on a sub-set of DFT calculations is relatively easy.74

GPR and KRR are mostly used to train models to experimental data, NNs, in contrast, are generally trained to computational data, e.g. from DFT. Pyzer-Knapp et al. as a proof of principle trained an NN using Morgan fingerprints on the DFT predicted HOMO and LUMO energies and PCE values of 200 000 random molecules from the Harvard Clean Energy Project database and used another 50 000 molecules as the test set.115 Gómez-Bombarelli et al. trained an NN using Morgan fingerprints on the thermally assisted delayed fluorescence (TADF) rates, as calculated by TD-DFT, of 200 000 TADF candidate molecules as part of a workflow for discovering new leads for TADF.32 Wilbraham et al. trained an NN using Morgan fingerprints to predict the ionisation potential, electron affinity and optical gap of 350 000 binary conjugated polymers using a training sub-set of only 50 000 polymers, 50% of which were used for the training of the NN and 50% for testing it.37 Instead of using DFT derived-data, Wilbraham et al. generated their training data using the xTB family of semi-empirical, density functional tight-binding methods,35,36 which often provides properties with similar accuracy to DFT but with computational cost reduced by at least three orders of magnitude.

All the NN studies above use standard Morgan fingerprints. In contrast, St. John et al. when training an NN for the optoelectronic properties of conjugated polymers used a message-passing NN for feature selection as input for their property prediction NN.116 However, this does not necessarily seem to result in better predictions. They found that providing an NN with information about the 3D structure of conjugated polymers does not result in improved performance when training it to predict the optoelectronic properties of these polymers relative to only 2D structural information. This is in line with the observation by Wilbraham et al. that such properties generally vary only slightly between conformers of conjugated polymers.8,37,117 While all of the above studies are for very large data-sets, the structures in them belong to a more limited structural family, for example, polymers based on aromatic monomers or TADF candidate molecules consisting of a donor and an acceptor separated by a spacer. Ramakrishnan et al. demonstrated that it is also possible to train an NN that can reproduce the optical spectra of a much wider variety of organic molecules.38 They trained NNs to recover the approximate coupled-cluster low-energy singlet excitation spectra of a very diverse set of 21 800 molecules with up to 8 CONF atoms, including both aromatic and aliphatic molecules. However, to do so, Ramakrishnan et al. used descriptors that contain 3D structural information (Coulomb matrix, bag-of-bonds) as input.

A completely different example of ML in the area of organic electronics is the recent study by Bai et al., where gradient boosted trees were used to study the correlation between a number of predicted and measured properties of polymers and their activity as hydrogen evolution photocatalysts.118,119 Use of these gradient boosted trees allowed the authors to estimate how much of the variation in the experimentally measured hydrogen evolution rates could be explained by these material properties, something that would be difficult using classical linear regression, as there is no good understanding of a model that links them. Finally, Sumita et al.97 and Benjamin Sanchez-Lengeling et al.120 used, as discussed above, molecular generation tools, ChemTS (a combination of GA-MCTS and RNN) and ORGANIC (GAN) respectively, to generate molecules with desired optical properties and non-fullerene acceptors that maximise the PCE of organic solar cells. Yuan et al. also used transfer learning combined with an RNN to generate donor–acceptor oligomers with targeted electronic properties.101

12.9.2 Property Prediction and Phase Space Exploration of Porous Organic Materials

In the last two decades, the field of porous materials has been revolutionised by multiple classes of materials, including metal–organic frameworks (MOFs),121 covalent organic frameworks (COFs),122 porous organic polymers,123 and porous molecular materials (PMMs).124 Through simple modifications of building blocks or synthetic conditions, the diverse chemical and structure space of porous materials can be explored toward fine-tuned materials for a target application. Currently, the most prominent field of porous materials is in the study of MOFs because of their (mostly) crystalline and extended nature (leading to well-defined structures), their structural and chemical diversity, and their interesting hybrid properties (a result of the presence of inorganic and organic building blocks). The existence of large experimental (∼70 000 structures)125,126 and hypothetical (∼150 000 structures)127,128 databases of MOF structures simplifies the development of structure–property relationships for the performance of MOFs in many applications. Large databases of purely organic extended, porous materials (e.g. COFs),129 and porous polymer networks (PPNs)130 do exist. However, their structures are mostly hypothetical or idealised, because COFs and PPNs are commonly semi-crystalline or amorphous materials. Taking advantage of the existence of these structure databases, Thornton et al. used an NN to guide their exploration of the nanoporous materials genome (∼800 000 porous materials) toward hydrogen storage.131 To avoid simulating the adsorption properties of all porous materials, they used an NN to learn which materials to simulate next after only simulating a small subset (1000 materials) of the entire database. After simulating only 3000 materials in total and training their NN three times (one time per 1000 simulations to guide the selection of the next 1000 materials to simulate), they determined the optimal range of material void fraction for hydrogen working capacity, which shows a strong trade-off effect.

Simplified descriptors of the pore networks of extended porous materials (including the solvent-accessible surface area, accessible pore volume, and pore size distributions) are cheap to calculate and are useful as parts of fingerprints in ML representations of extended porous materials.131–133 Bucior et al. used supervised ML to predict hydrogen storage in MOFs from the discretised potential energy inside the pore network.134 Similarly, Lee et al. used topological data analysis to quantify the structure of pores, which allows for the accurate comparison of two porous materials in a barcode-like fashion.135 Furthermore, ML has assisted in speeding up the calculation of more difficult to access properties such as catalyst performance in carbon dioxide reduction,136 MOF band-gap (using transfer learning)137 and mechanical properties.138,139 At present, there are no uses of AI in the design and property prediction of organic, extended porous materials.

PMMs, including porous organic cages (POCs), are a subclass of porous materials that have porosity derived from their internal cavity (intrinsic porosity) and the packing of individual molecules in the solid-state (extrinsic porosity), which is defined by nonbonded interactions.140 Similar to the field of organic electronics, the properties of some PMMs can be inferred from the properties of the single constituent molecules.7 For example, Evans et al. discovered that single-molecule properties could reasonably predict whether a molecule would form a porous crystal using support-vector machine learning.141 Sturluson et al. learned a latent space representation of POCs using unsupervised singular-value decomposition of the 3D shape and size of a POCs intrinsic pore.142 While a proof-of-concept, they were able to show that the nearest neighbours in the latent space had similar intrinsic pores, and that exploration through latent space was possible, which could lead to the efficient exploration of POC phase space. Currently, the prediction of the molecular structure of a new cage from this latent space is not possible, but this work represents an exciting approach to exploring the POC search space. Using a database of ∼60 000 hypothetical and known POCs, Turcani et al. used ML to predict whether a cage would remain shape persistent, and if so, also predict its pore size.143 Importantly, the input to their model is the chemical structure of the building blocks and proposed topology of the cage. Therefore, their ML algorithm could predict cage properties before constructing a model of the cage, which could drastically speed up the exploration of possible POC materials. However, their ML model required training on the target subclass of the cage (e.g. cages of a specific topology formed via imine condensation) to accurately predict the properties of new cages within that subclass.

Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) are efficient methods to explore chemical space. In particular, EAs are well equipped for the exploration of modular porous materials, where: (i) individual building blocks of a given material can be modified using simple methods, toward a new material; (ii) simple descriptors predict material properties, and (iii) material optimisation is a function of multiple variables. EAs have been applied to explore the chemical and structural space of MOFs to find candidate materials for adsorption applications.144,145 Berardo et al. recently implemented an EA for the targeted discovery of POCs.146 They implement a fitness function that focusses on the single-molecule properties of the cage (i.e. pore and window size and window asymmetry) and highlight the ability to present a diverse set of high-ranking candidates in a series of case studies. During the cage discovery process, they monitor the dominant cage topologies and molecular properties in the population, which act as guiding design principles for future experimental work.

12.9.3 Other Functional Organic Materials

Organic polymers can be used for a multitude of other applications, including insulating materials, structural applications, and even information storage.147 Interest in organic polymers for alternative uses has grown as they are cheaper to manufacture, more flexible, and have increased chemical resistance over most of their inorganic counterparts. The ability of NNs to generate complex, non-linear relationships between observables and output make them particularly useful for predicting polymer properties, where structure–property relationships are often complex or unknown. Early work involving polymer informatics by Sumpter and Noid used quantitative descriptors based on graph-theory to predict nine polymer properties simultaneously, including the molecular volume, heat capacity, glass temperature, and thermal conductivity.110 Despite a small dataset of only 357 polymers, the model was able to achieve a maximum error of only 8%, using cross-validation to reduce overfitting. Generating new quantitative structure–property relationships is an effective strategy for predicting the tensile strength at break, providing an insight into the strength of the bulk polymer material. Cravero et al. showed that simplistic descriptors, based on the molecular weight of the polymer, used as input lead to a better predictive model than using automatic feature extraction of the underlying molecular structure.148 Menon et al. were able to overcome the problem of small polymer datasets, using hierarchical machine learning (HML), to predict the stress-at-break, strain-at-break and tan δ using 18 polyurethanes as ground-truth data.149 In HML, an intermediate layer containing physiochemical polymer properties was used to feed into the next layer of the ML architecture. This was shown to perform better than a direct property prediction with polymer composition data using a random forest model. More recently, Wu et al. employed ML to predict polymers with high thermal conductivity.150 A Bayesian molecular design process was employed to generate new candidate polymers, from regions of chemical space known to exhibit favourable properties. Owing to the small experimental thermal conductivity dataset, containing 28 polymers, transfer learning was used, and three candidates were selected and synthesised.

Packing density affects a significant number of properties, including mechanical, optical, and ionic conductivity. Using 197 descriptors from the Dragon 7 library, Atif Faiz Afzal et al. predicted the final packing density of amorphous structures.151 Ground-truth training data was obtained from MD of simulated packed boxes of molecules and used as predictive values for the DNN. While not limited for predicting optoelectronic or mechanical material properties, ML has been applied to predict the redox potential of carbonyl-containing molecules. By calibrating the semi-empirical PM7 using GPR, Jinich et al. generated a model that was more accurate than using the group contribution method to estimate thermodynamic properties.152

12.10 Conclusions

Artificial intelligence is useful for a wide range of tasks in the field of organic materials; from accelerating the prediction of properties, via the de novo design of molecules and hence predicting molecular solids with desired properties, to assessing the likely synthesisability of such molecules. As in all applications of artificial intelligence, one major hurdle in many, if not all, of these tasks, is the availability of sufficient data to train models with. However, for molecular materials where a molecular representation is sensible, training data might be more easily generated or found in the literature than for other materials. The application of artificial intelligence in the area is thus clearly very promising and has surpassed the hype stage, suggesting that there are good reasons to believe that this is just the beginning of a bright future for artificial intelligence in organic materials discovery.
