CHAPTER 15

Representation Learning in Chemistry

JOSHUA STAKER( 0000-0001-6301-5574),*a GABRIEL MARQUES( 0000-0002-4882-563X)b AND J. DAKKAb

a Schrödinger, Inc.101 SW Main Street, Portland, Oregon 97204, United States

b Schrödinger, Inc.120 West 45th Street, New York, New York 10036, United States

*Email: joshua.staker@schrodinger.com

15.1 Introduction

The applications of chemistry are vast. Nearly everything we interact with and consume, from the molecules that make up our medicine or the electronics that power technology, to the materials in our shoes and eyewear, are the result of chemistry. Advances made in chemistry have widespread implications toward generally improved quality of life worldwide. A significant part of working in the field of chemistry is leveraging technology to both increase the rate at which we can design and improve the quality of developed molecules and materials. In many applications, technology is used to build models and simulations of molecules to predict, in silico, how molecules are expected to interact and perform in the real world. The faster and more accurate our models are, the more effective our discovery efforts become.

There are many varieties of models for chemistry, including machine learning models, and those that are mathematically derived from physics. Rigorous physical calculations, such as ab initio methods for estimating the electronic properties in molecules, are difficult to outperform in terms of accuracy.1,2 However, rigorous methods can be expensive to calculate and cost-prohibitive to run over large datasets or chemical systems containing many atoms. Machine learning (ML) is often computationally less expensive relative to physics-based calculations and can be made quite accurate when flexible models are trained with sufficient data.1 Consequently, ML is useful for estimating the properties of large numbers of molecules.

Many ML approaches in chemistry utilize molecules as inputs, though other features describing the chemical environment can be used instead, or included in addition to the molecules. There is one difficulty frequently encountered when using molecules in ML: most machine learning algorithms cannot operate over standard molecular formats, e.g., SMILES or connection tables, and methods often first require molecules to be described in a form understandable by the algorithm. We call this new form its “representation” and the process by which this form is obtained as “featurization.” Unfortunately, many ML algorithms require representations that are fixed-length vectors, which is not a format well suited for the description of molecules in an unambiguous way.

One way to describe molecules as fixed-length vectors is by calculating various properties and descriptors for the molecules and then arranging the calculated outputs into “feature vectors.” In this approach, it is difficult to know which features to calculate, and the choice of features is highly dependent on the endpoint of interest. Another approach is to calculate molecular fingerprints wherein the presence of substructures is determined and then encoded into fixed-length binary vectors. However, binary fingerprints can experience bit collisions with single bits encoding multiple substructures, decreasing the exactness of the representation. Both molecular fingerprints and calculated feature-vectors are coarse-grained representations that irreversibly discard information about the molecules, forcing learning algorithms to rely on incomplete representations of molecules. Additionally, these types of “non-learned” featurizations rely on significant preprocessing external to the predictive model.

Alternatively, flexible ML models capable of accepting more complex data structures as input provide the opportunity to learn over more complete representations of molecules. Having access to more complete information enables learning algorithms to automate the featurization process and leverage data to learn features that are relevant to the task. Recent neural network architectures support learning over more complex inputs, including graphs, 3D grids, and variable-length sequences, which are formats more suitable for representing molecules. Learning representations not only simplify the featurization process by operating on minimally processed data but can lead to more accurate models.

Herein, we make the distinction between learned and non-learned representations as follows: Non-learned representations are derived from molecules using heuristics or physics with the outputs arranged into feature vectors, while learned representations of molecules are intermediate, latent vectors produced by transformations learned directly from data by an ML model. Our definition of learned versus non-learned is not necessarily strict or rigorous from a computational or mathematical standpoint, but it is useful in describing and understanding the various methods that fall within each category and the general advantages and limitations of each.

Recent advances in deep learning have renewed interest across industries in utilizing vast amounts of data to learn the featurization process, in contrast to relying on pre-defined heuristics for feature generation. With the significant amount of chemical data currently available in the literature, public repositories, and internally generated in commercial companies, there is now greater opportunity for scientists to leverage more flexible models. Consequently, deep learning is becoming more popular in chemistry as an approach to learn representations and build more powerful models. Although both learned and non-learned representations can be used in further downstream modeling, including in neural networks, the ability to learn over more complete molecular representations is an important distinction—for many endpoints, such as protein–ligand binding, it is very difficult to construct feature vectors that contain sufficient information to make reliable predictions.

In this chapter, we describe conventional, non-learned featurization methods that are often used in chemistry, along with their several limitations, then discuss how deep learning can help circumvent those limitations. Next, we explore the motivation behind learned representations, namely, how typical molecular data formats, e.g., SMILES or connection tables, can be transformed using a learned set of parameters into a new n-dimensional space that is useful for various forms of analysis and model building. And, finally, we provide overviews of several families of deep learning architectures used to obtain learned representations. It is impossible to review all relevant representation learning approaches recently seen in the literature, even those that relate directly to chemistry. Instead, we provide a high-level overview of several families of architectures as an entry point for understanding, implementing, and improving molecular representations.

Our discussion is specifically interested in the conversion of minimally processed input data into latent forms, and we encourage the reader to explore the literature for details regarding other aspects of model-building, including optimization, the various hyperparameters, and other implementation specifics. Representation learning for molecules is still relatively new, and much work is still needed to find more general-purpose representations. Throughout our discussion, we also cover some of the needs, challenges, and opportunities in developing better representations, especially in the context of the underlying physics.

15.2 Non-learned Molecular Representations

Often, the data available to practitioners in chemical science include a collection of molecules in a standard format such as SMILES, SDF, or connection table, along with some property of interest. One use of such a dataset is to train a model given the molecules and labels, then use the trained model to make property predictions for new molecules that are not previously seen by the model. Common ML methods used in chemistry often rely on relatively simple models, for example, logistic regression or multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), which require fixed-length vectors of features as input. An immediate question that arises before building such a model is: how can one take a collection of molecules and convert them into a format useable by the model? Fortunately, molecules can be converted into fixed-length vectors through several forms of featurization, each with trade-offs, though choosing which features to generate during featurization is not straightforward and requires making assumptions about the types of patterns in molecules expected to correlate with the endpoint. Additionally, many features are expensive to compute; furthermore, it may be non-obvious how to obtain them, such as how to properly characterize specific interactions between proteins and ligands relevant to binding prediction.

From the 1950's onward, molecular featurization has centered around building quantitative structure–activity or property relationship (QSAR/QSPR) models3 and has historically been performed through non-learned transformations. Conventional non-learned featurization methods include hashing molecular fragments into “fingerprints” or calculating various physical properties arranged into “feature-vectors.” Molecular features can be simple, such as molecular weight, or obtained through complex physics-based calculations. Examples of commonly used properties include logP, quantum mechanical calculations, synthetic feasibility, number of rotatable bonds, number of chiral centers, and many others. It is worth noting that many molecular properties used as inputs to machine learning models are themselves approximations, e.g., logP or DFT energies; although one could approximate these input properties using the learned featurizations discussed later, they have historically been obtained either using relatively simple models or through physics-based calculations. We encourage the reader to review Cherkasov et al.3 for a more comprehensive discussion around common forms of featurization and a history of their development in relation to QSAR/QSPR.

Topological molecular fingerprints are another form of featurization with wide adoption.4 Fingerprints are time-tested in the literature and continue to be used as comparative baselines in contemporary deep learning methodologies.5,6 Other forms of non-learned featurization exist, but topological fingerprints and calculated properties are most prevalent and are briefly described in the following subsections.

15.2.1 Molecular Fingerprints

Not every molecule is the same size; indeed, molecules can be small, with just a few atoms, or quite large such as natural products or polypeptides. Molecular fingerprint generation concerns the encoding of 2D or 3D molecular graphs most often into fixed-length, binary strings of bits with “on” bits indicating the presence of a particular substructure, while “off” bits indicate the lack of such substructure. Fingerprint lengths are fixed, regardless of molecule size, providing a suitable form of representation for use in ML.

There is not a single, standard form of fingerprint, and several varieties have been developed. The overarching principle shared across approaches relevant to machine learning is the encoding of molecular fragments into fixed-length vectors. Cereto-Massagué et al. describe various forms of fingerprints and how they are produced.7

Primary differences between methods concern how substructures are detected and which substructures get encoded in the on-bits. For example, the ECFP method considers atom neighborhoods radially outward from central atoms8 while MACCS takes SMARTS patterns provided by the user to define the substructure matching rules.9 The total number of possible substructures is vast. Rather than encoding each substructure independently into an extremely long, sparse vector, substructures can be hashed, constraining the vector into a fixed length, with the length specified by the user. Hashing substructures provides a convenient way to encode molecules into fixed-length vectors of specific lengths regardless of the size, variety, and the number of molecules to be modeled. While longer fingerprints decrease the risk of bit collisions (where single bits encode multiple substructures), the vectors become very sparse, which not all model types handle well, and computational cost almost invariably increases.

Fixed-length fingerprint vectors are well suited to be used directly in ML without the need to make specific assumptions around which properties should be calculated and included as features. Another benefit of fingerprints is their interpretability. Although it is not possible to reconstruct original molecular graphs from fingerprints, the on-bits indicate which substructures are present in the molecule and can be visualized and examined.

Fingerprints have proven extremely useful and are frequently adopted in the literature.6 However, there remain some endpoints that are difficult to model using fingerprints. For example, protein–ligand binding involves the interaction of molecules with proteins in 3D space, and protein information is not typically included in molecular fingerprints. Also, fingerprints discard overall graph connectivity, i.e., they contain information about which substructures are present but not how they are connected to form the whole molecule, making long-range interactions and stereochemistry more difficult to model. Another disadvantage is that fingerprints sometimes need to be very long, and are consequently extremely sparse, to encode large numbers of different substructures; these are less efficient and expressive than distributed representations.10,11 They also ignore many internal degrees of freedom, such as the 3D spatial-relationships between atoms, and do not contain enough information to account for dynamics.

In summary, fingerprints are easy to calculate, have lengths that are fixed and independent of molecule size, are binary and sparse (enabling lightweight storage), and are interpretable. Various forms of fingerprints exist which can be selected and evaluated empirically during experimentation. Nevertheless, these benefits come at the cost of potential bit collisions and the discarding of overall graph connectivity.

15.2.2 Computable Features

Another time-tested approach to feature generation for molecular modeling is the calculation of molecular properties, either through heuristics or physics-based calculations. Desired features are first identified and calculated, then arranged into vectors for training a model. The variety of useful molecular properties is extensive. For example, Ahneman et al.12 used 120 different calculated features, including energetics, electrostatics, vibrational frequency, and molecular shape. Some software packages can generate thousands of descriptors.13,14 The specific features and the number of different features used are part of the modeling design process and are highly dependent on the endpoint type. Some properties are theoretically motivated, such as quantum mechanical approximations, while others are purely empirical or practically defined, e.g., synthetic accessibility or Lipinski rules for drug-likeness.15 Topological descriptors containing information about shape, surface area, volume, and flexibility can also be useful, and even basic physical properties, like molecular weight, may provide a valuable signal. Apart from calculated or heuristically obtained features, properties approximated through independently built models can be used as input features to other models.16

Some features are based on energetics and can contain information about molecular orbitals and charge density.17 Similarly, HOMO and LUMO energies can be calculated and used,18 as well as other properties approximated through DFT and other levels of theory in quantum mechanical calculations.17,19,20 There is some confidence gained when physics is used in models. Utilizing physically derived features may help encourage downstream approximations to follow the physics more closely. Additionally, models relying on physics may improve as our understanding and implementation of physics improves.

The examples mentioned here are just a small sample of the many such features and approaches found in the literature, and detailed resources containing descriptions of features and their uses have been published elsewhere.13,21–23 We encourage the reader to identify and consider which specific properties may be useful for the task at hand.

Computable features, especially those calculated using rigorous physics or simulations, are immensely useful, and the expansive breadth of features grants much flexibility in selecting which to use. Flexibility, in combination with high-quality features, enables researchers to build more robust models with smaller datasets. It is not always clear, however, which features to choose, and the selection process often takes significant expertise and experimentation to determine. In the case of physics-based calculations, the quality of the generated features depends on the correctness of the implementations, which are sometimes bound to a certain level of theory, where higher levels are more costly to compute. Many features are also themselves generated from other models or approximations and provided through black-box implementations in software. Empirical, externally provided features are difficult to validate and may be unreliable outside a specific region of chemical space. The determination of which features to use, the assumptions made regarding applicable chemical space in feature-generation implementations, and the cost to compute physics-based features, make feature-learning an attractive prospect.

15.3 The Need for Learned Representations

Although non-learned featurizations are powerful and have held up well in the literature, they often do not capture important patterns in the data, discarding information necessary to build robust predictive models. Molecular properties can also be expensive to procure, e.g., quantum mechanical calculations. When using the non-learned features described so far, common questions may arise:

  • Which features should be generated for the data?
  • What patterns in the data should features capture?
  • Should all features be used, or only a selection, and if only a selection, which ones?
  • Do features sufficiently encode the input or is useful signal unintentionally discarded?
  • Should expensive quantum mechanical calculations be included, or can they be avoided?
  • How can we be certain features correlate with the output and not just add noise?

Questions like these were primary motivators behind the last decade of breakthroughs in the ML literature, especially within the subdomain of deep learning using neural networks. A primary goal in deep learning is to learn the feature extraction process as part of the model, instead of relying on external preprocessing for feature generation. Compared with traditional approaches, incorporating featurization as part of the model-building process unlocks the ability to learn the featurization in a data-driven manner, granting significantly improved model flexibility at reduced engineering complexity and potentially lower total computational cost.

Learned featurization provides several attractive benefits. Firstly, learning featurization makes it less imperative for researchers to spend engineering effort to generate and validate a variety of features, or for practitioners to have deep expertise knowing which features to use and their implications in model building. Additionally, features that would have been costly to compute may no longer be required. A most significant benefit, however, is that data-driven featurizations can produce more informative representations, leading to improved model performance.

Perhaps, the most well-known example of feature-learning success is the convolutional neural network applied to images. Early in this last decade's renaissance in deep learning, Krizhevsky et al. introduced the convolutional architecture known as “AlexNet” which showed excellent performance over a challenging image dataset using only minimal preprocessing.24 Just a few years later, convolutional models were shown to exceed human performance on that same image dataset.25 In the last decade, deep learning has transformed the world's approaches toward image recognition, game playing, language, audio generation, and many other problems in a variety of domains. More general advancements such as attention,26 generative modeling,27 and reinforcement learning28 are not restricted to specific problem-spaces and provide fresh, new approaches to tackling wide varieties of challenging problems. At the heart of nearly all of these methods is deep learning and its ability to transform relatively raw data into learned representations.

One can imagine how difficult it would be to design a featurization scheme by hand to describe the many nuances in images with all their variations in color, lighting, object shapes, and input quality. Even more difficult to describe by hand are problems requiring the combination of multiple input data modalities or the generation of highly complex output. Some relatively extreme examples include transcribing video into text29 or animating still images.30 Accomplishing any one of these tasks programmatically, or coming up with features by hand that sufficiently describe the input is overwhelming and virtually impossible. While these (and virtually all) deep learning applications are still very narrow—only performing well within the same data distribution seen during training—they remain powerful for many applications. One can appreciate similarly complex and highly non-linear tasks in chemistry such as protein–ligand binding prediction, quantum mechanical energy estimation, devising synthesis routes, and many others.

It is also possible to visualize and analyze learned representations (often called latent representations). Gómez-Bombarelli et al. performed dimensionality reduction and visualized latent representations of molecules in 2 space, and intuitive patterns emerged.31 Latent representations of data points can be compared using any number of similarity metrics to estimate the distance between points in latent space. When conducting analysis or drawing conclusions using learned representations, it is important to remember, however, that the latent space is empirical and a function of both the data and the learning algorithm. Distances are virtually guaranteed to change when retraining the model with different parameters or data. Even with this important caveat, exploring latent representations can be intuitively pleasing and may hint at how a model is learning.

Learned representations are also powerful in the context of generative models. Generative models can use latent representations to produce new data not seen during training.32 In addition to generating new examples, Berthelot et al.33 used a variational autoencoder to smoothly interpolate between one image and another.

Learning representations, instead of relying on rigorous feature engineering and selection, can both simplify the model-building process and lead to more expressive models. However, these benefits do not come for free. Learning useful representations from raw data often requires more data, additional training time, and more computation. It is essential to consider the tradeoffs between simple models and neural networks when attempting new projects. ML for molecules is also very different than for images or text. Often, molecules must be considered holistically; that is, every atom plays a role in the behavior of a molecule in the context of some endpoint. Depending on the task, molecules may contain little discardable noise (atoms or regions of molecules not critical to learning). This is in contrast with natural images or language, where low-level patterns are often less sensitive to subtle variations in the input. For example, in images, not every pixel is individually essential, and an object may still be easily recognizable after changing a few pixels. Similarly, in text, many words can be replaced with other, similar words without significantly changing the meaning of a sentence.

It is not always clear which form of representation is most appropriate for a given application, especially when applied to chemistry. Furthermore, it is important to realize that deep learning is not always the best choice, and non-learned featurizations may be simpler to work with or perform better in some applications, especially when data are limited.6 Choosing which family of algorithms to pursue is often left to intuition and experimentation. When building models, there are many considerations to keep in mind, with only guiding principles to help inform our decisions. Most choices regarding data selection and model design are necessarily based on extensive trial-and-error and need to be rigorously validated using well-designed test sets. Choosing between non-learned and learned featurization, or selecting which types of deep learning models to try, is a balance between flexibility, practicality, engineering complexity, compute cost, and experimentation time required to both build and validate models. For more information regarding the theory and mathematics behind representation learning, and a comprehensive overview of many approaches seen throughout the machine learning community, we highly recommend reviewing Bengio et al.34

15.4 Learning Molecular Representations

Even with its weaknesses, learned featurization is an exciting and powerful paradigm. Defining the representation automatically from relatively raw data helps eliminate the need to make difficult assumptions about which molecular features should be included to predict a given endpoint. Learning representations can also better disambiguate explanatory factors in data and produce representations that are more highly correlated with many endpoints, leading to improved models.

Up until now, we have spoken only rather vaguely about learned representations and how they have been useful in other fields. However, we have not yet talked about, in practical terms and examples, the methods used to produce learned representations of molecules and the architectures best suited for learning such representations. In this section, we review representation learning algorithms explored in the literature, with particular focus on the deep learning architectures used. Whether learning representations from inputs in an unsupervised way or in the context of an endpoint in supervised learning, the heart of representation learning for chemistry is the choice of architecture used to define the learning mechanism and its parameters. When developing and training an ML model, we make certain assumptions about the nature and structure of the data and the model to be learned. These assumptions comprise the “inductive bias” of our model and play a significant role in the effectiveness of learning. The inductive bias affects how fast we can hope to converge and any guarantees of convergence, the parameter space we assume the solution lies within, the generalizability of the final model, and the amount of data required to fit the model. The stronger the inductive bias, especially when assumptions are correct, the more all aspects of learning improve, and the resulting models are usually also of higher quality. The selection of which architecture family to use in an algorithm comprises a significant portion of the inductive bias of the model.

In the following subsections, we outline several families of architectures often seen in the chemistry ML literature. We first consider graph models (often called graph convolutions) that take in 2D representations of molecules and pass “messages” between atoms iteratively until latent representations of atoms and molecules are obtained. Next, we discuss grid models where information is propagated in 3D space without respect to any bonding structure, i.e., atoms are treated as independent particles. We then describe sequence architectures that operate over molecules represented as strings of characters called SMILES. Lastly, we explore architecture designs inspired directly by physics.

Although there are many additional developments and results in the literature related to the discussed architectures, we focus on the representation learning portion of the work and how they enable researchers to learn over molecules with minimal preprocessing and encourage the reader to further investigate the literature for additional details. With an appreciation for both the value of representation learning and its tradeoffs and caveats, we can now consider the different families of architectures used to learn molecular representations.

15.4.1 Graph Models

There is an abundance of graph-structured data in chemistry, from directed graphs of chemical reactions, interaction networks of proteins, to the topological structure of small molecules themselves. Assuming a graphical prior in neural architectures helps improve learning over graphs, encouraging robustness and easing optimization. However, there are several approaches to introducing graphical priors in models, the choice of which is highly dependent on the chemistry to be modeled.

Before discussing graph neural networks (GNNs), let us revisit molecular fingerprints in the context of chemical graphs. The extended-connectivity circular fingerprint (ECFP) algorithm provides a solid basis for understanding graph convolutions wherein both algorithms apply the same operation everywhere within a molecule before integrating information through a global pooling step. Appreciating similar operations in non-learned fingerprints will pave the way for understanding the derivation of their differentiable generalization, Neural Graph Fingerprints,35 an early graph convolutional (GC) method applied to molecules.

The ECFP algorithm is commonly denoted ECFP(N), where N is some positive, non-zero integer denoting the circular radius in number of bonds. As we iterate up to the full bond radius, for each atom in the molecular graph we gather its neighbors up to the current radius then pass the resulting molecular fragment to a hashing function where an index is assigned to the fragment. The hashing function ensures that a change in a fragment results in a change in its index. An indexing function then aggregates all indices into a single, sparse vector of fixed length. In this soup of fragments, there can be collisions, and fingerprints must be large to avoid overlap. Large, sparse vectors are also computationally expensive for downstream processing. These shortcomings motivate the development of more efficient representations that are smaller and denser, only encoding the relevant features for the task at hand. However, it is not trivial to find good hashing and indexing functions that can produce effective, yet dense, representations of chemical space. Furthermore, different prediction tasks may benefit from using different functions, but it is not always easy to anticipate which functions to use and when. Fortunately, the machinery of deep learning provides the ability to learn useful functions from data, diminishing the need to define or select functions manually. Whereas circular fingerprints combine a hashing function and an indexing operation, neural fingerprints replace these with differentiable equivalents. The use of differentiation allows for gradient-based optimization of a loss function, making neural fingerprints learnable. The gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters can be used to steer the neural fingerprint parameters in such a way that predictive performance improves when compared with circular fingerprints. The superior neural-fingerprint prediction performance is primarily due to its ability to learn important features relevant to the predictive task at hand.6,36

Neural fingerprints encode fragments by processing input features through a series of neural network layers. The learned parameters (network weights) and their resulting activations over features provide a learned function that is counterpart to the hashing function in non-learned fingerprints. The learned function is smooth, enabling activations to be similar when molecular structure is similar. The index function is replaced with a softmax over the output vector of the learned hash function. In this way, each atom classifies itself as belonging to some learned category before being summed up across the molecule to produce the learned fingerprint. When this learned fingerprint was trained end-to-end with a deep feed-forward network it outperformed standard fingerprints using the same deep feed-forward architecture on several tasks, including predicting solubility and photovoltaic efficiency.35

In addition to neural graph fingerprints, many other GC approaches exist. There have been a few attempts to generalize GC architectures into a common mathematical framework. One such approach often referenced in the literature is the message passing neural networks (MPNNs).5 The message passing framework generalizes the neural information passing algorithm on chemical graphs by splitting the method into two main phases: a message-passing phase and a readout phase. In the message-passing phase, for each atom in the molecule, the vector representations of neighboring atoms are passed through a learned, differentiable message function then summed, yielding the message vector for that atom. Depending on the choice of message function, messages can incorporate information from the representations of the current atom, neighboring atoms, and the bonds between them. Typically, the same message function is used for all nodes in the neural network. This application of the same function everywhere is what makes it a convolutional network, and grants additional invariance by sharing parameters across the whole input. The message vector for an atom is then passed through a learned differentiable update function, along with the atom's representation, to produce the new representation for that atom. The output of the message passing step is a new representation vector for each atom in the chemical graph and is performed for N iterations, allowing information to propagate over a distance of N bonds. After all iterations of message passing are completed, the learned representations of all atoms in the chemical graph are integrated together using a learned readout function. The readout function produces a molecule-level representation that can be used in further processing. See Figure 15.1 for an illustration of MPNNs.

Figure 15.1 Aggregation of messages for a single node ν in a single step t through message function M and update function U. After T steps, all the node vectors are passed to the readout function R.

For most architectures that fit in the MPNN framework, bond information is not considered. Bond-level representations can be learned but require an additional network. Other implementations such as the Directed MPNN (D-MPNN)6 operate over directed bond-level representations, avoiding loops in message passing that would introduce noise. D-MPNNs also combine computed molecular features with learned representations to overcome performance limitations of learned representations on small datasets to achieve state-of-the-art on many proprietary and public datasets.

However, GNNs are not without their limitations. Care has to be taken when designing certain architectural components of the neural networks. For example, not all GNNs are invariant to permutation of their indices, and in MPNNs, the readout function must be designed to handle such invariance. Networks lacking invariance to graph isomorphism can produce different atom or molecule level outputs for the same compound with different atom indexing. In these cases, canonicalization of the graph, usually through canonicalization of SMILES, should be done before generating graphs to pass to the network. Special consideration must also be taken when working with non-local properties on graphs. GNNs usually have a fixed propagation distance and cannot represent long-range quantum nonlocality.37 Attempts to improve long-range message propagation include using a master atom connected to all other atoms in the molecule.5 The master atom's latent vector acts as a scratchpad the neural network can read and write to during message passing. The authors of MPNN also tried adding a separate virtual edge type to help ease information flow between non-bonded atoms. Another design consideration in GC approaches relevant to capturing long-range interactions is the choice of graph traversal algorithm. Matlock et al. suggest a bond-wise, breadth-first traversal of the whole chemical graph for propagating information from a chosen center atom to the farthest atoms, then back again.37 The forward-then-backward passing of information across the molecule can be repeated multiple times. They demonstrate the efficacy of their method on aromaticity and conjugation in large systems. Stereochemistry is another strong limitation of GNNs. While stereochemical information can be included in atom and bond level features before passing to the graph neural network, it is especially difficult to represent certain types such as conformational or relative stereochemistry. Such stereochemical limitations motivate the use of grid methods for learning molecular representations.

15.4.2 Grid Models

In graph models, propagation of information often only occurs between neighboring, bonded atoms. Additionally, most graph models ignore positional information and the spatial relationships between atoms. The exclusion of spatial information in data leads to learning representations that lack sufficient context for some applications, for example, predicting quantum mechanical energies or protein–ligand binding.36 Attempts to capture non-bonded interactions in a graph-only approach becomes especially difficult in larger systems. Instead of relying solely on the graph, atoms can be positioned in a 3D coordinate space, represented as a grid, granting models access to those spatial relationships. Positioning Cartesian coordinates of inputs into 3D grids essentially discretizes the data and makes the data more suitable for processing using 3D convolutions. The familiar 2D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) often used in image recognition are most effective when used with planar (2D) inputs, e.g., images, and are not well suited for 3D grids, and 3D convolutions are used instead. Similar to CNNs for images, 3D convolutional filters can extract features describing local covariance.

Models with access to spatial information can learn to assess the impact of interacting neighborhoods of atoms, enabling efficient learning of long-range interactions between atoms that are proximal in 3D space but not necessarily close in the graph. In many cases, molecular bonds are not explicitly included in the input data. However, bonding can be ascertained implicitly; the distances and angles between atoms, relative to the strength of their repulsion or attraction, are dependent on whether atoms are bonded. However, relying on the model to infer bonding may lead to ambiguity in some cases, especially when grid resolutions are too low or when data quality is poor and distances are noisy.

An area of strong interest for 3D grid models is predicting small-molecule binding to target proteins in structure-based drug discovery.38,39 An early example of this approach is the AtomNet model,38 which utilizes 3D-convolutions over a 3D grid containing the protein–ligand complex. The 3D grid is centered at the target protein's binding site, and small-molecule conformers are sampled within the site. For an approach like this to work, the location of each atom, both in the binding site and the molecule, is required. The additional 3D-structural information enables the model to learn arbitrary, data-driven 3D features that can lead to better generalization. One goal of learning such a model is to capture favorable and unfavorable interactions between protein and ligand atoms then apply the model to new proteins and ligands not previously seen during training. Though it is difficult to find in the literature compelling examples of 3D grid models applied prospectively to structure-based drug-discovery projects, the approach remains promising. In principle, having access to both the protein and ligand may help 3D models become better at generalizing relative to ligand-only techniques.

Deep learning over 3D space has seen increased interest both in drug discovery and in other 3D applications, e.g., processing point-cloud data or generative design in manufacturing. One challenge in 3D applications is that when operating over 3D grids, representations are often not invariant to rotation and translation. Instead of discretizing 3D data and placing in a grid, the precise 3D coordinate information can be preserved, enabling greater rotation and translation invariance. A particularly notable approach exploiting rotational symmetries in molecules is Tensor Field Networks.40 In their method, geometric tensors are generated using spherical harmonics and Wigner D-matrices. To achieve SO(3)  equivariance, each input (molecular structure) is converted to a set of 3D points with an associated SO(3) group (vectors). Essentially, SO(3) groups are used to describe the possible rotational symmetries of an object, as well as the orientation of an object in space, leading to the preservation of molecular features in 3D space. We further explore strategies for preserving invariances in the Physically inspired Architectures section, introduced later.

15.4.3 Sequence Models

An alternative to computing over molecular graphs with convolutions is to use recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with SMILES strings as input.41 SMILES contain the same graphical information typically expressed in molecular 2D graphs, with the graph encoded in a 1D list of characters. The exact character ordering for a given molecule is determined by a ruleset specific to the implementation used to generate the SMILES. Atoms are represented with a one or two-letter elemental symbol, e.g., “C” for carbon, with additional characters used to signify branching, chirality, and other relationships between atoms in the graph. One reason to use SMILES rather than 2D graphs is that 1D inputs can readily be used in many RNN architectures essentially out-of-the-box. Sequence algorithms used in other domains that leverage attention,26 reasoning,42 or memory43 can be adapted to use SMILES as input. Most often, RNNs are used to read in SMILES, though 1D convolutions have also been tried.44 When generating molecules, it is also more straightforward to use RNNs to output character sequences than to generate 2D graphs.

GNNs usually pass messages along bonds to only immediate neighbors, and it can take several messaging passing steps to propagate information from one end of the molecule to another. In the case of sequence models, there is generally a single hidden state that all atoms have the opportunity to update successively, given the previous state. Having access to the full state when computing an update means that atoms have global access to the whole of the molecule (as encoded by the state), and long-range interactions are capturable. In the Yang et al. approach to GCs,  message passing is centered around bonds instead of atoms, and messages are forced to travel along a directed path across the molecule to avoid totters (messages getting passed back and forth between two atoms, amplifying noise).6 Interestingly, this is in parallel with how RNNs work with SMILES. In RNNs, the state is passed and updated from atom to atom in a directed, ordered fashion. Also, incorporating messages from both forward and backward directions is reminiscent of bi-directional RNNs where both forward and backward passes are made along the sequence.

After encoding a sequence, the RNN state is an intermediate, latent representation of a molecule and can be used to predict an endpoint.45 Making predictions using RNNs is often done in a supervised learning setting, where both SMILES and labels are provided. However, there is also recent interest in using RNNs to learn from SMILES in a self-supervised way. Self-supervision (often called unsupervised learning) is where models are tasked with reproducing their input, often using autoencoders. Briefly, autoencoders work by taking input, learning to compress the input into a latent representation, then decoding the latent representation into a reconstruction of the input. Through the compression process, the model learns the salient features of the data and the structured patterns that best describe the input. One or more constraints are often applied to the learning process to discourage autoencoders from merely learning the identity function. One constraint used to encourage more disentangled latent variables is the use of a Gaussian prior (μ=0, σ=1) applied to the latent vector, enforced through minimizing KL-divergence. This type of constrained autoencoder is called the variational autoencoder (VAE) and is based on Bayesian inference.46

VAEs and other forms of RNNs trained using self-supervision have been successfully applied in chemistry with compelling early examples in de novo applications.31,47 Latent representations produced by autoencoders can be optimized for particular properties, with new molecules then generated from the optimized representations (often generated into SMILES strings).31 A recent example in the literature tested generated molecules in vitro.48 The motivation behind utilizing self-supervision with SMILES is that statistics about the distribution of latent variables describing a region of chemical space can be learned using large datasets without needing specific endpoint labels, e.g., binding affinities. Although not utilizing SMILES as input, another interesting example of the application of VAEs to chemistry is learning reaction coordinates and trajectories.49 Learning latent representations of trajectories enabled researchers to utilize physics in conjunction with ML, providing the ability to switch between the two during sampling.

When considering RNNs for an application, it is important to recognize that using RNNs with SMILES comes at a representational cost compared to GC-like approaches. RNNs are sensitive to input order,50 and in SMILES, some character order must be assumed, i.e., some atom has to come first. Additionally, treating the graph as a sequence requires the model to learn not only the relationship between the molecules and the endpoint (the desired task) but also how to infer graph structures from sequences. SMILES also utilize characters for annotating relationships between atoms, e.g., parentheses for branching, which the model needs to learn in order to understand the graph instead of the model encoding this directly in its architecture (stronger inductive bias toward graphs) as in GC approaches.

15.4.4 Physically Inspired Architectures

Machine learning can be used in conjunction with physics-based calculations, where ML models first identify the most interesting molecules, with a portion then selected for further evaluation in more rigorous simulations. Similarly, empirical models can utilize physical calculations as input features. Though using physical features negates the benefit of avoiding the calculation expense, combining physics with ML can lead to methods that leverage benefits from each paradigm. Another strategy toward improved learning systems is the application of physical constraints on models, ensuring that learned representations capture more of the invariances naturally found in chemistry.

Much of the research within the chemistry ML community has focused on adopting successes seen in other domains, namely image recognition and language modeling, to chemistry. Many similarities can be observed between graph convolutions and the convolutional networks used in image classifiers.51 Similarly, RNNs with SMILES are architected after recent successes in language modeling and other sequence modeling tasks. The rapid progression in the field of deep learning for chemistry with the varieties of approaches and applications seen in the growing body of literature is mainly through analogies drawn and lessons learned from other areas adapted to chemistry. Nevertheless, many challenges still remain.

Chemical space is vast, and, often, not much can be discarded as “noise” or “out of distribution,” depending on the task and the degree of generalization desired. With 1060 molecules in drug-like space alone, datasets of realistic size are necessarily limited in how many relevant patterns they can contain. The difficulty in developing useful and large enough datasets causes many models to exploit biases and learn spurious correlations rather than learning more generally useful and invariant features. Furthermore, metrics often miss these weaknesses, making it difficult to ascertain model and method reliability.52,53 In language modeling, individual words carry significant meaning and rich context, but in molecular data formats, atoms themselves are usually represented as discreet. Consequently, one subfragment in a molecule may have a completely different meaning in virtually all other chemical contexts, for example, the binding of a molecule in one protein versus its interaction with another. The difficulty in finding generally applicable patterns in even small subfragments tends to result in more fragile ML models with significantly narrower reliability and makes transfer learning for chemistry especially difficult.54 This is often referred to as a model's “domain of applicability” and requires researchers to be very aware of the robustness of models relative to chemical space.

A natural research direction toward learning more invariant molecular representations is to explore inductive biases closer to the underlying physics. Finding and applying stronger assumptions tied to physics instead of relying on overly flexible models with priors that are too general can significantly enhance learning and generalizability, and can help in building more robust models when trained with fewer data.

There are two general approaches to leveraging physical priors. The first is to retain significant flexibility in the learning algorithm (weak inductive bias) and learn to approximate generally applicable physical equations, such as those describing quantum mechanics, using large amounts of data. The goal of developing a model that approximates the equations directly is that with sufficient data the learned functions have some degree of transferability. Even with large volumes of data, however, we assume that the data distribution during testing is the same, or at least very similar to the data distribution seen during training. This approach generally leads to sufficiently good interpolation but is unreliable at best when attempting to extrapolate. Mills et al. utilize this data-first approach in approximating the Schrödinger equation.55 When data are more limited, one way to compensate for the lack of invariance built into the model is through data augmentation. For example, randomly rotating molecules in 3D space can help artificially increase data volume.39

The second approach to leveraging physics is to find stronger priors that are closer to our understanding of physics and incorporate these priors and invariances into models directly. Kondor et al., in their body of work around covariance in neural networks for chemistry, state their goal of using ML for molecules as not necessarily to learn the physical laws per se, but to understand and utilize the structure of physical laws to inform the types of invariances in molecules and physical interactions between atoms that can be captured in architectures.56–58 They place particular emphasis on positional invariances (permutation, rotation, and translation) of atoms when computing atom or groups-of-atoms representations and their interactions. They show how expanded invariances baked into the model help outperform similar state-of-the-art ML models using QM9 properties and MD-17 conformational energies. The method in Smith et al. is another example of employing stronger inductive bias where rotation invariance implemented at the model level relieves the network from needing to learn how to encode the same molecules in different orientations.59 In Gomes et al., the authors used the thermodynamics of protein–ligand binding to guide the interactions between components in their architecture.60 Additionally, Levin et al. explore the connection between deep learning and quantum entanglement.61

The work of Schütt et al. emphasizes the importance of atom positions and provides a direction for developing ML models that can compute energies and forces for molecules in non-equilibrium configurations (positions and trajectories outside a local minimum in the potential energy landscape).62 They describe designing their models around assumptions that are physically inspired, such as energy-conserving forces, to encourage the capture of more physically meaningful representations. Molecular physics has no concept of rotation or translation of atoms relative to a fixed coordinate system. Rather than using 3D Cartesian coordinates as part of the atom features, their model utilizes distances between atoms. To ease training, radial basis functions are used to provide additional non-linearity in the distances. Learning models that are robust to rotation relative to a coordinate system would necessitate augmenting the data with different molecular orientations, and with no guarantee that the same molecule in different orientations would produce the same result. Other researchers have also employed similar radial processing.59,60 Schütt et al. additionally utilized a shifted softplus activation function to obtain smooth potential energy surfaces that are continuous in all orders of derivatives. The work by Gilmer et al. and Smith et al., and likely others, show near-chemical accuracy compared with DFT but at a fraction of the computational cost.1,5,59

As a brief aside from chemistry, Lutter et al. used Lagrangian mechanics to learn physics describing robot motion.63 Instead of approximating the inverse dynamics directly from data, as most deep learning systems would do, they implemented the underlying equation explicitly as part of the model then approximated the physical parameters and subequations. Schmidt and Lipson also discuss learning natural physical laws from data.64 The physics of chemistry is deeply rooted in mathematics, and it is not implausible to consider that stronger physical priors in our models may be possible. Nevertheless, physics is very complex. Energies and potentials of molecules are not isolatable atomistically but arise from complex interactions between many subatomic particles. Pfau et al. went beyond atomistic representations and used individual electrons as inputs to their deep neural network.65 In limited hydrogen and nitrogen systems, they produced results that remarkably go beyond the accuracy of coupled-cluster. Although limited in scope thus far, modeling individual particles using deep learning is the beginning of a new and exciting approach compared with the atomistic models mostly explored thus far.

Regardless of whether physics is learned implicitly from data, or implemented directly in models, predicting physical endpoints are valuable benchmarks. Physical benchmarks help the community understand how well our models learn representations directly from data that sufficiently encode physical relationships, energies, and forces. For example, results were compared to DFT-computed ground state energies and electron density, and also compared to coupled-cluster predictions.66 Similarly, Schütt et al. trained a model to learn the wave function describing quantum mechanics, which, if the representation adequately captures the physics, enables the prediction of virtually any ground-state property without the need for any additional training.67 Like Schütt's work, many of the current lines of research assume molecules to be at ground state, and more work will be needed to eventually extend these methods to non-equilibrium conditions.

In a recent talk,68 Dr. Léon Bottou discussed how common learning algorithms employ statistics only as a proxy, and causal relationships are generally not modeled effectively at all. He demonstrated that the removal of spurious correlations in favor of invariant relationships enabled much more effective extrapolation. His talk is not chemistry-specific but prompts valuable questions regarding the application of ML to chemistry. All molecule datasets contain some form of bias, primarily due to the sheer vastness of chemical space, and assumptions need to be made when building a dataset, e.g., the maximum number of atoms allowed. Some chemical datasets are extremely biased, such as in enumerations developed for protein–ligand binding. In enumerations, molecules often contain very similar cores, with only minor structural perturbations between molecules. Most features learned for such a dataset using typical ML methods have little hope of being useful in other learning tasks. The model will likely pick up on the strong bias contained in the dataset, and anywhere that bias is no longer present, the model will fail. Wallach and Heifets showed that many learning approaches employed in the drug discovery space are learning the specific biases contained within the datasets,52e.g., the spurious correlations suggested by Bottou. Perhaps, if models can instead learn features more invariant across datasets, for example, something closer to the physics of chemistry, there is a higher chance of learning representations that are useful in a wide variety of learning tasks. More invariant features enable improved transfer learning (building a model from a large dataset and then fine-tuning the model using a much smaller dataset for another application), or even extrapolation if no additional training data are available. Learning chemical invariances also unlocks the opportunity for improved modeling of larger systems, such as protein-structure-based machine learning, and may increase the viability of ML when applied to biologics endpoints or protein folding prediction.

Although predicting physical endpoints remains a valuable research direction, much work is still needed to validate further the usefulness of deep learning in its current form for adequately approximating physics. The examples mentioned in this section showcase the value of designing architectures that are informed by invariances found in natural chemistry and the improvements toward generalization they can provide. Even stronger inductive biases closer to the underlying physics of chemistry may yet lead to even better performance across a variety of applications and datasets.

15.5 Data Considerations

Data quality and volume are prime concerns for building good models in nearly any application or domain. Apart from influencing the goodness of a model, data directly affects the quality of the learned representation; therefore, it is valuable to at least briefly consider the data's influence on representation quality. Because learned representations are data-driven, their quality is directly dependent on data quality. Care must be taken when curating data to ensure data are correct, and that validation sets remain useful for rigorous testing of models. Wu et al. discuss how the splitting of molecular datasets into training and validation sets must be done with care.69 For example, if molecules with very similar scaffolds appear in both training and validation sets, validation may not catch overfitting on those particular scaffolds. Also, neural networks are incredibly flexible, and the latent representations learned are highly dependent on the volume and variety of molecules presented to the network. Consequently, due to the vastness of chemical space, essentially all chemical libraries will contain some bias. Care should be employed when both selecting training data and when applying a trained model to new data.

Properties of molecules are also extremely dependent on context. For example, the binding of a particular molecule may be very different in one protein compared to another protein, and mixing data from multiple assays may be disastrous. Laboratory experiments can also be notoriously difficult to reproduce due to subtle variations in temperature, pressure, materials, and in nearly any other component or condition of an experiment. Published experiments may also lack sufficient assay details to reproduce.70 Even the same assay performed in different labs, or the same lab at different times, may not be consistent, and expertly measured experimental data may still be noisy. Furthermore, publicly available data are often highly variable in quality. Many principles exist for proper data handling, and we encourage the reader to explore the literature for insights relevant to their particular datasets.70–72

Another question that often arises in drug discovery and other areas of chemical discovery and development relates to the diversity of molecules in datasets. Screening libraries are often developed to contain a diverse sampling of chemical matter to help maximize chances of finding a hit, or finding hits with different scaffolds in the case when multiple hits are found. The challenge, however, is that diversity is loosely defined and can be evaluated in a number of different ways using various metrics. It is also challenging to know if diversity will help in learning a robust model, in the context of an endpoint. One advantage of learned representations is that they are data-driven, and can be compared in the context of the training distribution. Common distance metrics can be calculated for representations produced using the learned featurization methods described in this chapter to measure similarity between molecules. In most cases, the learned representations are continuous, and Tanimoto, Euclidean, and cosine similarity metrics can be used to calculate distances. Dimensionality reduction of learned representations can also be used to visualize similarity. Popova et al. show examples of dimensionality reduction and how molecules with similar properties group together.73 Measuring similarity using learned representations can also inform researchers regarding which molecules may be farthest from the training data and, hence, useful for adding to the training dataset.

15.6 Current Challenges and Directions for Future Research

When applying models, it is important to keep in mind the expectations we place on models regarding interpolation versus extrapolation. Most deep learning is highly interpolative, and a key assumption made when validating or deploying models is that the distribution of chemical space fed to the model is contained within the same distribution as the training data. A strategy for building more robust models includes increasing the size and variety of the training data, but large datasets for many endpoints are not always easy to obtain. Many datasets in chemistry are relatively small, and the ability to leverage other, much larger datasets to improve performance in applications when data is sparing could be transformative. A key benefit of representation learning is its ability to help facilitate transfer learning; yet, transfer learning for chemistry remains challenging.54 In assessing whether transfer learning is a reasonable expectation for chemical datasets, a key question is what patterns can we expect models to learn that are transferable to other systems? In protein–ligand binding, for example, binding mechanisms vary across proteins. Most interactions between protein and ligand that are relevant in one protein system may not be useful in another.

Pretraining over a large corpus of data, then fine-tuning a trained network over a few examples for a new application, has seen success in image recognition. In transfer learning, we assume that patterns are common among tasks, and that learned features are invariant, i.e., they can pick up the same patterns across different data. In the discussion above regarding physically inspired architectures, we mentioned that more closely approximating physics may help with transfer learning. In the extreme case, if we imagine that it is possible to approximate the physics perfectly, then we will have effectively learned a model that could readily perform zero-shot transfer learning. Of course, approximating physics to that extent is not currently possible. However, we can consider cases where approximating physics may help and also consider directions to explore toward improving the approximations.

Building models closer to physics is scientifically interesting and may help with learning more invariant features, but current deep learning approaches may not be sufficient for learning such features. For example, most of the architectures described above produce distributed vectors, which are likely not physically meaningful. Even when disentangling latent variables is especially encouraged, such as in the VAE, we do not have any explicit control over which variables are expressed, nor an adequate way to interpret causal relationships between variables. Learning causality is an exciting branch of ML research currently being pursued. Considering the deeply rooted relationship between causality and physics, similar questions and lines of research may be especially relevant in ML for chemistry. Regardless of the direction taken, a strong emphasis on physics, either learning the physics directly or at least used to help validate ML models, will be important when applying future ML advancements to chemistry.

15.7 Conclusion

Learning molecular representations directly from data both simplifies the development of machine learning models for chemistry and can greatly improve the usefulness of the trained models. There are many ways to represent input molecules, including graphs or points in 3D space, and several different families of architectures, each suited for learning from different forms of input, can be used to learn over minimally processed data. Regardless of the type of architecture used, the goal of deep learning or any other form of modeling for chemistry is to develop more useful tools that aid in the design and application of new chemical matter and the furthering of science. One advantage of deep learning over many other forms of machine learning is its ability to learn representations directly from data without the need to rely on expertly curated features that may lack general applicability or are otherwise difficult to obtain.

Most of the models published in the literature thus far are inspired by models developed in other domains, namely, image recognition and language modeling, and may not always be well suited for chemistry tasks. Transfer learning remains one such area where successes seen in other domains have not been realized to the same extent in chemistry. Physically inspired architectures is a promising line of research that can potentially lead to more robust and powerful models and may also aid in more reliable extrapolation. Currently, physically inspired architectures are mostly conservative in the extent that physics is included or have only been tested in small systems thus far; more work is, therefore, needed.

Deep learning is currently the dominant approach in learning molecular representations. Thus, all the challenges and weaknesses of deep learning are relevant in our chemistry models, including needing large training sets, architecture sensitivity to hyperparameters, and fragility when applied to new data outside the domain of applicability. It is not yet clear if deep learning is the best paradigm for learning molecular representations, as seen by the difficulty in transfer learning, and physics will continue to play a significant role in validating the usefulness of representations and further inspiring future learning algorithms. With the limitations of deep learning aside, the impact of learning representations from raw data is clear, with many new approaches and applications published utilizing these methods that achieve high accuracy at a relatively reduced computational cost.

CHAPTER 16

Demystifying Artificial Neural Networks as Generators of New Chemical Knowledge: Antimalarial Drug Discovery as a Case Study

ALEJANDRO SPECK-PLANCHE( 0000-0002-9544-9016)*a AND VALERIA V. KLEANDROVA( 0000-0002-1928-853X)b

16.1 Introduction

With the advent of machine learning (ML) methods and computational models, which are crucial in most modern scientific projects, drug discovery has undergone a process of constant change and evolution.1 Nowadays, the important role of ML methods in areas such as data mining and virtual screening is well-established.1–3 Among them, artificial neural networks (ANNs) have become a focus of attention, particularly due to the emergence of revolutionary subfields such as deep learning.4 In fact, within early drug discovery, ANNs have found impressive applications in the de novo design of molecules with desired properties.5–8

Nevertheless, the efficiency and success of current ANNs are strongly associated with a very high computational cost, and the advanced degree of programming/codification skills that researchers must have; the latter can take too much time to master. In addition to these limitations, two other handicaps prevent the full exploitation of ANNs in drug discovery. From one side, the computational models based on ANNs continue to be treated as black boxes because they lack interpretability; they are not capable of providing a clear interpretation of the physicochemical properties and/or structural features of the chemicals in the databases, which they intend to design and/or predict. On the other hand, the in silico models focused on ANNs consider a specific stage (usually the pharmacological activity domain) of the drug discovery process. Considering the multi-scale nature of drug discovery and the vast chemical space that needs to be filtered (1060 small to medium-sized organic compounds),9 one of the greatest challenges is the development of models based on ANNs that can integrate multiple biological data and design seemingly new molecular entities with potent activity, low toxicity, and adequate pharmacokinetic properties.

In the last seven years, several research groups have focused their efforts on the creation of a series of computational tools known as multi-scale models for quantitative structure-biological effect relationships (ms-QSBER).10 These models can integrate different sources of data, permitting the simultaneous prediction of multiple biological endpoints against many targets of varying degrees of complexity. In this sense, ms-QSBER models (some of them based on ANNs) have been successfully applied to different fields of research such as cancer research,11 infectious diseases,12–22 nanomedicine and nanotoxicology,23–27 immunology and immunotoxicity,28–31 and neuroscience.32–35 Also, multi-scale de novo drug design36 has emerged as an encouraging paradigm, combining the predictive capabilities of the ms-QSBER models, chemical reasoning, and concepts from fragment-based drug discovery to accelerate the rational design of molecules that virtually exhibit high activity, low toxicity, and very good pharmacokinetics.37 Yet, the applications of ANNs in the context of ms-QSBER models have been restricted to performing virtual screening tasks.

Bearing in mind all the previous ideas, this chapter intends to demonstrate that computational models based on ANNs can be used in a chemistry-friendly manner to accelerate the design of virtually new, potent, and safe therapeutics at the preclinical level. Thus, we report the first ms-QSBER model based on an ensemble of ANNs (ms-QSBER-EL) devoted to performing virtual design and prediction of potentially active and safe antimicrobial agents. Here, antimalarial drug discovery is used as a case study for a number of reasons. First, malaria is one of the oldest diseases known by mankind, which has an elevated mortality and morbidity; 445 000 deaths and 216 million cases of malaria occurred worldwide in 2016.38 Second, the efficacy of antimalarial treatments has diminished because Plasmodium falciparum, widely recognized as the main causal agent of malaria, has become resistant to antimalarial drugs.39 Last, there are serious concerns regarding the adverse reactions associated with the use of antimalarial therapeutics.40

16.2 Materials and Methods

16.2.1 Dataset and Molecular Descriptors

The development of the ms-QSBER models has been widely reported,13–17,37,41 and therefore, only the procedures specific of this work will be explained. All the chemical and biological data employed to build the ms-QSBER-EL model were extracted from the ChEBML database42–44 in the form of a Microsoft Excel-compatible file. The dataset used in this study contained 18 798 different drugs/chemicals belonging to many diverse chemical families. Each molecule was experimentally assayed by considering 1 out of 7 measures of biological effects (activity, cytotoxicity, and pharmacokinetic properties) and against at least 1 out of 20 targets (including proteins, Plasmodium falciparum strains, mammalian cells, and liver microsomes). If a molecule was found to be assayed more than one time against the same target and by considering the same measure of biological effect, its values were averaged. In any case, notice that most of the drugs/chemicals reported in the present dataset were experimentally tested by considering only one measure of biological effect and against only one target. Thus, the dataset used here ended up containing 21 369 statistical cases and so is characterized by a great dispersion of the data. Nevertheless, the great success of the ms-QSBER models mentioned in the previous section is based on their ability to handle greatly dispersed and heterogeneous data.13–17,37,41,45

Each statistical case in the dataset was annotated as positive [BEi(cj)=1] or negative [BEi(cj)=−1], BEi(cj) being a binary categorical variable that described the biological effect of the ith case/chemical under the experimental condition cj. It should be pointed out that a defined experimental condition cj depended on both the qth measure of biological effect (me) reported in a given assay and the rth target (tg) against which the assay was performed. Therefore, each experimental condition can be expressed as cj(me, tg). The dataset employed in this work contained 23 unique experimental conditions (combinations of the elements me and tg).

Assignments of positive and negative cases have been realized by considering different cutoff values that are depicted in Table 16.1; several reasons justify the selection of these rigorous cutoffs. First, an inspection of the dataset extracted from ChEMBL showed that there are FDA-approved drugs reported with biological effects whose values fell either above or below the cutoffs. This aspect highlights the importance of the selected cutoff values because, if a query molecule is predicted as positive (or negative) by a model derived from the present dataset, it will be possible to compare its potential biological effect with those already reported for the clinically relevant drugs. Second, the assignments of the compounds as positive or negative implies that a classification approach was employed instead of a regression one. In contrast to their regression counterparts, classification approaches do not need to predict the exact values of the different properties in a dataset, and, therefore, they do not need to deal with the potentially great uncertainty of the data. Third, the cutoff values selected in this study prevented the imbalance between the number of molecules assigned as positive and the number of molecules annotated as negative. Last, from a phenomenological point of view, even though several clinically relevant antimalarial drugs are present in the dataset, the purpose of the ms-QSBER-EL model is to perform simultaneous predictions and design of new chemicals exhibiting high antimalarial activity, low cytotoxicity, and adequate pharmacokinetic properties. The design of new molecules with chemical structures differing from those present in antimalarial drugs indicates the idea of searching for novel mechanisms of action of antimalarial activity as well as reducing the toxicity and improving the pharmacokinetic profiles not found in most of the current antimalarial drugs.
