To characterize the chemical structures of the molecules present in the dataset, we calculated the molecular descriptors known as the total [TnsAqk(x)] and local [LnsAqk(x)Z] atom-based quadratic indices of the non-stochastic matrix.46 Quadratic indices have been demonstrated to exhibit a greater discriminant power47 than that shown by combining several families of molecular descriptors calculated by popular programs such as DRAGON.48 The quadratic indices can be calculated according to the following mathematical formalism:

(16.1)

(16.2)

In eqn (16.1) and (16.2), the element x accounts for any atomic physicochemical property such as hydrophobicity (HYD), electronegativity (E), atomic weight (AW), polarizability (POL), and polar surface area (PSA). At the same time, in eqn (16.1), the element characterizes the adjacency between any two atoms of the molecule, while in eqn (16.2), has a similar meaning, except for the fact that it focuses on specific types of atoms (Z) such as hydrogen bond acceptors or donors, carbon atoms (both aliphatic and aromatic), and others. Both classes of atom-based quadratic indices consider an atom i and its chemical environment (composed of the jth neighbors) at the topological distance d=k.

To calculate the aforementioned topological indices, the file containing the SMILES codes of all the molecules was manually changed from *.txt to *.smi. After, the software Standardizer v19.18.0 was used to transform the SMILES codes to sdf format.49 The only purpose of converting to sdf format was to obtain the connectivity table for each molecule; no additional standardization actions were used. The sdf file was used as input to calculate quadratic indices by means of the software QuBiLS-MAS v1.047,50 For such a calculation, the software QuBiLS-MAS v1.0 employed a predefined configuration [algebraic form: quadratic; constrains: atom-based; matrix forms: non-stochastic; maximum order: 6; cutoff: keep all; groups: total and local (hydrogen bond acceptors, aliphatic carbon atoms, aromatic carbons, terminal methyl groups, halogens, and heteroatoms); properties: already mentioned in the previous paragraph; aggregation: Manhattan distance].

In eqn (16.1) and (16.2), the quadratic indices cannot differentiate the chemical structure of a molecule when this is tested by considering multiple measures of the biological effects and against different targets. Fortunately, the ms-QSBER models resolve this issue by applying the Box-Jenkins operators17,37,51 to generate new molecular descriptors able to consider both the chemical structure and the set of experimental conditions (e.g., target, the measure of activity, or toxicity, etc.) against which a molecule has been assayed:

(16.3)

In eqn (16.3), n(cj) is the number of molecules annotated as positive, which were assayed under the same experimental condition cj, i.e., by considering both the same measure of biological effect and the same target.52 In addition, QIa refers to any quadratic index (total or local), while avgQI(cj) is the arithmetic mean of the QIa values for all the molecules assigned as positive and tested under the same assay condition cj. In a second step related to the application of the Box-Jenkins operators, the following expression is used:

(16.4)

In eqn (16.4), DQIa(cj) measures how much a molecule structurally deviates from a set of chemicals assigned as positive, all of them being tested under the same assay condition cj. On the other hand, QIMX and QIMN represent the maximum and minimum values for a defined molecular descriptor, respectively; they don't depend on the experimental conditions. Last, p(cj) is the a priori probability of finding a chemical tested under a specific experimental condition cj:

In eqn (16.5), the element n(cj) has been defined in eqn (16.3), and NT refers to the total number of cases/chemicals present in the training set.

16.2.2 Building the Ms-QSBER_EL model

The steps leading to the generation of the present ms-QSBER-EL model are depicted in Figure 16.1. The dataset formed by the 21 369 cases/chemicals was randomly split into two series: training and test sets. The training set was used to search for the best model and was formed by 6591 cases assigned as positive and 9571 annotated as negative, making a total of 16 162 cases (75.63% of the dataset). The purpose of the test set was to validate the model by assessing its predictive power; this set was formed by 5207 cases (24.37%), 2064 annotated as positive and 3143 assigned as negative.

Figure 16.1 Workflow focused on the development and application of the ms-QSBER-EL model. The abbreviation “INTPN” stands for interpretation, which is given for each molecular descriptor from a physicochemical and structural point of view.

To find the best the ms-QSBER-EL model, the two most popular ANN architectures were tested: radial basis function (RBF) and multi-layer perceptron (MLP). The ANN package available in the software STATISTICA v13.5.0.17 was employed to generate the ms-QSBER-EL model.53 When using the ANN package, the first run was performed to assess the appropriateness of three elements: 1) the most significant ANN architectures, 2) the most influential molecular descriptors, and 3) the correlation between the descriptors.

From one side, the most significant ANN architectures were determined by analyzing the training and test errors (as low as possible) and the values of different statistical indices (set to be as high as possible) such as sensitivity [Sn(%)], specificity [Sp(%)], accuracy [Ac(%)], and the Matthews’ correlation coefficient (MCC).54 These statistical indices were used to estimate the internal quality (training set) and the predictive power (test set) of the ms-QSBER-EL model.

On the other hand, the most influential molecular descriptors in the ms-QSBER-EL model were assessed by means of a sensitivity analysis, which was performed by the software STATISTICA v13.5.0.17. This analysis was applied as a variable selection strategy, quantifying the effect of each molecular descriptor by calculating its sensitivity/importance value (SV). In this context, SV was calculated as the error generated in a defined ANN when estimating the value of a molecular descriptor using a missing value procedure, divided by the error generated in that ANN by using the real value of the same molecular descriptor. Only those molecular descriptors with SV>1 were considered to enter in the ms-QSBER-EL model. Also, when selecting the most significant descriptors, the correlation between them was assessed by calculating the Pearson's correlation coefficient (PCC),55 and the cutoff interval used to indicate the lack of redundancy/correlation was −0.7<PCC < 0.7.

As defined in the introductory section, the abbreviation “ms-QSBER-EL” stands for multi-scale model for quantitative structure-biological effect relationships combined with ensemble learning. Therefore, as the final step in the development of the ms-QSBER-EL model, instead of selecting a single ANN, the best ensemble of ANNs was chosen. This comes from the fact that when solving a particular problem, and by providing a consensus response, models based on ensembles of different ANNs can often perform better than the single ANNs from which they were created.56

16.3 Results and Discussion

16.3.1 Ms-QSBER-EL model

The best ms-QSBER-EL model developed in this work was an ensemble comprised of three ANNs with the profiles MLP 8-61-2, MLP 8-67-2, and MLP 8-80-2. The first ANN was constructed by using the logistic function in the hidden layer and softmax function for the output layer. The second and third ANNs had the same activation function in the hidden layer (hyperbolic tangent). For the output layer, the second ANN employed a logistic function while for the third ANN, the softmax function was employed. Notice that all the ANNs contain 8 nodes (molecular descriptors) in the input layer. The number two is the same for all of them in the output layer because they are all predicting the two possible labels (the values −1 and 1) of the categorical variable of biological effect [BEi(cj)]. In any case, the three ANNs have a different number of neurons in their hidden layers. The symbols and definitions of each molecular descriptor present in the ms-QSBER-EL model are reported in Table 16.2, while all the chemical and biological data are available in the Supplementary Information 16.1.† The files corresponding to the three ANNs can be obtained upon request to the author.

One should note that the statistical indices Sn(%) and Sp(%) reflect only the global performance of the model. The magnitudes [Sn(%)]cj and [Sp(%)]cj are the local measures of performance of the ms-QSBER-EL model which depends on each specific experimental condition cj(me, tg). For only 3 out of the 23 experimental conditions reported in the dataset, the local measure of sensitivity [Sn(%)]cj indicated a poor performance. The first two experimental conditions involved cytotoxicity assays (measuring CC50) MRC5 and L929 cells, while the third one focused on determining the half-life in human plasma. In any case, the fact that 20 out of 23 experimental conditions (86.96%) were assessed with high [Sn(%)]cj and [Sp(%)]cj demonstrates the ability of the ms-QSBER-EL model to integrate and accurately predict antimalarial activity, cytotoxicity, and pharmacokinetic profiles of drugs/chemicals.

16.3.2 Applicability Domain

The reliability of the classifications/predictions performed by the ms-QSBER-EL model was estimated by defining its applicability domain according to the descriptor space approach.57 Classically, when using the applicability domain defined by the descriptor space, all the compounds in the training set are used, and the maximum and minimum values of each descriptor present in the model demarcate the boundaries that should not be surpassed; any compound beyond such boundaries will be considered to be outside the applicability domain. Here, the applicability domain derived from the descriptor space approach was applied only to those chemicals correctly classified by the ms-QSBER-EL model in the training set (Supplementary Information 16.31). Using information regarding the maximum and minimum values of the different molecular descriptors in the ms-QSBER-EL model, local scores were assigned to each molecular descriptor. When the descriptor value of a query molecule was between the aforementioned boundaries, the local score was equal to 1; otherwise, the local score was equal to 0. Subsequently, a total score (TSAD) was defined as the sum of the local scores. As the ms-QSBER-EL model was built from eight molecular descriptors, only those compounds with TSAD=8 were considered to be inside the applicability domain.

16.3.3 Gathering Physicochemical and Structural Information from the Molecular Descriptors

Nowadays, it is a common practice to use computational models to perform predictions of large and heterogeneous chemical libraries. As a result, the physicochemical and structural information contained in the molecular descriptors employed to construct the models is often neglected, and no mechanistic interpretation is provided. The ms-QSBER-EL model developed in this work predicts very complex data involving several types of biological effects and different targets. Therefore, it is not possible to gain a mechanistic insight regarding the diverse biological and/or biochemical processes that take place when a molecule interacts with a target, either molecular (e.g., proteins) or non-molecular (cells, subcellular components, and Plasmodium falciparum strains). However, even though stereochemistry is not considered by the molecular descriptors of the ms-QSBER-EL model, interpreting these descriptors can help find 2D-molecular patterns that are common to the different biological effects regardless of the targets on which they were measured. The purpose here is to interpret the different molecular descriptors present in the ms-QSBER-EL model from a physicochemical and structural point of view so that it will be possible to get a better understanding regarding the features that a chemical should possess to increase its antimalarial activity while decreasing its cytotoxicity and improving its pharmacokinetic profile. In this sense, the interpretations given in this subsection will be based on the combination of four aspects: a) the analysis of the influence of each molecular descriptor in the ms-QSBER-EL model, b) the elucidation of the tendency of variation of the different molecular descriptors, c) the information content of the molecular descriptors, and d) the application of a fragment-based analysis. The first aspect is illustrated in Figure 16.2, where the molecular descriptors are represented according to their sensitivity values (SV). The higher the SV of a molecular descriptor, the greater will be its influence in the ms-QSBER-EL model.

Figure 16.2 Relative importance of the molecular descriptors in the ms-QSBER-EL model.

The second aspect is reported in Table 16.4. It is assumed that, by comparing the class-based mean values of each molecular descriptor, one can estimate how a molecular descriptor should vary to cause an increase of the antimalarial activity, a decrease of the cytotoxicity, and/or enhancement of the pharmacokinetic properties. This approach involving the class-based mean values was first applied by Speck-Planche and coworkers as a way to gather information from the molecular descriptors in non-linear models.58 It should be emphasized that the aforementioned approach was applied only to the chemicals that were correctly classified in the training set. Basically, for each molecular descriptor, two means are calculated: one for the set of compounds assigned and correctly classified as positive, and the other for the set of chemicals annotated and properly classified as negative. Comparison of the two means for each molecular descriptor permits us to determine if the descriptor value should be increased or diminished. One must always keep in mind that we are dealing here with a non-linear model, and therefore, these tendencies of variations elucidated from the molecular descriptors will be relative. Consequently, the approach used here will probably not contain the entire chemical space that the ms-QSBER-EL model may cover. Nevertheless, the approach is intended to focus on a defined region of the chemical space where the compounds with the desired properties may be found, in this case, potentially active and safe antimalarial agents.

Regarding the third aspect, as commented before, the ms-QSBER-EL model was built from the deviations of the total and local non-stochastic (atom-based) quadratic indices, which are symbolized as D[TnsAqk(x)]cj and D[LnsAqk(x)Z]cj, respectively. With x being any of the physicochemical atomic properties mentioned above and cj indicating the different experimental conditions, the topological distance (d=k, where k is the kth order of the quadratic index). The topological distance is the number of bonds (without counting the bond multiplicity) that exists between any two atoms. The use of this simple but useful concept helps us to rapidly get an accurate idea of how the different types of atoms (e.g., aliphatic and aromatic carbons, halogens, etc.) should be distributed throughout the entire structure of a molecule.

The last aspect is focused on the fact that any topological (graph-based) descriptor calculated for a molecule can be represented as a linear combination of the frequency with which diverse fragments (connected and disconnected) appear in that molecule.59 Consequently, this property of the topological descriptors allows us to directly define different molecular fragments whose presence contributes positively to variation in the value of any topological index; such fragments can then be used to design new molecules.60–62 The quadratic indices used in the present study are a class of topological descriptors, and therefore, they comply with the aforementioned property. Thus, while interpreting, we will provide a non-exhaustive but useful list of fragments that are suggested to positively contribute to the corresponding variations of each molecular descriptor in the ms-QSBER-EL model (see Figure 16.3). In this illustration, we have focused on small molecular fragments, and therefore, only the descriptors based on topological distance d≤4 are represented. No fragment-based information will be provided for the descriptors focused on d≥4, although the physicochemical and structural interpretations for all of them will be explained.

Figure 16.3 Molecular fragments with favorable contributions with respect to the different molecular descriptors in the ms-QSBER-EL model. Here the symbols refer to: A=F, –OH, or –NH2; X=O or –NH–; Z=–OH or –NH2; Y=O or –NH–; G=F, Cl, or Br; G2=Cl, Br, or I.

Four out of eight descriptors present in the ms-QSBER-EL model are based on the atomic weight, and this already indicates that the most important factors to simultaneously increase the antimalarial activity, decrease the cytotoxicity, and improve the pharmacokinetic profiles are those associated with steric bulk. Notice that, as a property, molecular weight is associated with the size of the molecules. These descriptors based on the atomic weight will depend on the number of atoms in a molecule; they will have a direct impact on the molecular weight, and consequently, on the size of a molecule. We have D[TnsAq6(AW)]cj, which characterizes the decrease of the atomic weight of any two atoms placed at the topological distance equal to six. This is the fifth most significant descriptor in the model, and it indicates a decrease in the number of atoms in the molecule, while the number of heavy atoms (halogens except fluorine) should be reduced as much as possible. In convergence with D[TnsAq6(AW)]cj, the descriptor D[LnsAq4(AW)C]cj (the fourth most important) also indicates the diminution of the atomic weight of any two atoms but at a topological distance equal to four, with at least one of them being an aliphatic carbon. This means that the number of aliphatic carbons should be decreased, and if they are present in a molecule, they should be placed at the topological distance of 4 with respect to other atoms with low atomic weight (carbon, nitrogen, or oxygen). Therefore, as illustrated in Figure 16.3, aromatic and heteroaromatic rings are highly desirable to decrease the presence of aliphatic carbons, decreasing the value of D[LnsAq4(AW)C]cj. A third steric descriptor is D[LnsAq6(AW)M]cj, which provides information regarding the diminution of the atomic weight of any two atoms separated by six bonds (topological distance equal to six), with at least one of these atoms being a carbon from a methyl group. This descriptor has the lowest influence in the ms-QSBER-EL model, and its value can be decreased by reducing the number of methyl groups in the molecules. Last, by analyzing D[LnsAq2(AW)P]cj, we have suggested that the atomic weight of any two atoms (at least one of them being an aromatic carbon) placed at the topological distance equal to two should be diminished. Notice that D[LnsAq2(AW)P]cj is the second most important molecular descriptor, and the presence of aliphatic portions (or rings) and heteroaromatic rings is beneficial for the diminution of the value of D[LnsAq2(AW)P]cj (see Figure 16.3).

Besides the four quadratic indices based on the atomic weights, two other descriptors also provide steric information. One of them is D[LnsAq1(POL)A]cj, characterizing the diminution of the polarizability of the molecules, which depends on the presence of atoms acting as hydrogen bond acceptors (and their adjacent atoms). This descriptor (the seventh most influential) can be diminished by placing fluorine, nitrogen, and oxygen atoms in the periphery of the molecules. In the specific case of the nitrogen atoms, those belonging to primary and secondary aliphatic amine are preferred. The other descriptor that confirms the importance of the steric effect is D[LnsAq1(POL)G]cj, focused on the increase of the polarizability of the molecules by considering only halogens and their adjacent atoms. Notice that this is the most important descriptor in the ms-QSBER-EL model (see Figure 16.2), and that its value can be increased by attaching halogens (specifically Cl, Br, and I) to aromatic carbons (see Figure 16.3).

As described by D[LnsAq1(POL)G]cj, the presence of halogens in certain regions of the molecules is crucial for the increase of antimalarial activity, the diminution of cytotoxicity, and the enhancement of the pharmacokinetic properties. This information is supported by D[LnsAq2(E)G]cj, which has the third greatest influence in the ms-QSBER-EL model. This descriptor indicates the increment of the electronegativity in those regions where the topological distance between any two atoms (at least one of them being a halogen) is equal to two.

Finally, we have D[LnsAq6(HYD)Y]cj, which characterizes the decrease of the joint hydrophobic contribution of any two atoms placed at a topological distance equal to six, with one of these atoms being nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, or phosphorus. This descriptor is the sixth most significant in the ms-QSBER-EL model. It should be pointed out that the term “joint hydrophobic contribution” refers to the product of the hydrophobicity values of any two atoms. In this sense, according to the approach reported by Ghose and Crippen,63 each atom in the molecule is described by its neighboring atoms; hydrogen and halogen atoms are classified by the hybridization and oxidation states of the carbon atom to which they are attached, and for hydrogen atoms, heteroatoms attached to a carbon atom in the α position are further considered. Carbon atoms are classified by their hybridization state and depending on whether their neighbors are carbon or heteroatoms.63

It can be deduced that there are atoms that, depending on their chemical environments, will have a negative hydrophobic contribution, whereas others will have a positive value in that hydrophobicity scale. Examples of atoms with negative contributions are most aliphatic (saturated) carbons, except for those of the form CHX3, CR2X2, CRX3, and CX4, with X being any electronegative atom (O, N, S, P, Se, halogens). Other atoms with negative hydrophobic contributions are almost all nitrogen atoms except for those belonging to pyrrole, amines with at least two aromatic substituents, and tertiary amines. A similar rule can be applied to the oxygen-containing counterparts of the amines mentioned here. The other atoms not mentioned here will have a positive contribution to the hydrophobicity. For the specific case of aromatic carbons, while Ghose and coworkers report different values of hydrophobicities,63 here, the programmers of the software QuBiLS-MAS v1.0 set the hydrophobic contribution to zero for these types of atoms. That being said, a few examples of pairs of atoms (at the topological distance equal to six) whose joint hydrophobic contributions diminish the value of D[LnsAq6(HYD)Y]cj are G with any nitrogen or oxygen (excluding the previous exceptions), where G represents halogen, sulfur, selenium, or phosphorus.

Altogether, the information provided by the molecular descriptors suggests that the presence of halogens is mandatory in the structure of the molecules, but they must be confined to the peripheral regions. In addition, judging by the decrease of the atomic weight characterized by four of the eight descriptors, halogens may be present in the following amount: 1) one iodine, 2) two chlorine, 3) two bromine, 4) one chlorine and one bromine, 5) one fluorine and one bromine, or 6) one fluorine, one chlorine, and one bromine. The presence of heteroaromatic rings substituted with halogen is crucial because they decrease the number of aromatic carbons (decreasing the value of D[LnsAq2(AW)P]cj), and at the same time, they increase the values of the descriptors D[LnsAq1(POL)G]cj and/or D[LnsAq2(E)G]cj. Examples of such fragments are 2-halopyridines, 2-halopyrimidines, and 2-haloazoles. On the other hand, the molecules should not have methyl groups, and aliphatic carbons may be used linkers between the heteroaromatic portions.

16.3.4 Computational Design of Virtually Potent and Safe Antimalarial Chemicals

When predicting external chemical libraries, computational models can perform reliable predictions to some extent. This is because the experimental data often contain uncertainties regarding the conditions under which the assays were carried out. Other factors preventing the full exploitation of the computational models as virtual screening tools are the lack of consensus regarding the definition of the applicability domain, and the non-universality of the molecular descriptors; the latter means that the molecular descriptors can characterize only a reduced fraction of the highly diverse and complex chemical space.

It is also important to keep in mind that most of the models will provide predictions according to predetermined values, which correspond to the descriptors of the molecules that are being predicted. In this context, most of these molecules may not follow the rules of the model. This has nothing to do with the applicability domain or any other method to estimate the reliability of the predictions; it is associated with the fact that in any model, the molecular descriptors in the training set have different degrees of hierarchy, and these embody a phenomenological meaning in the sense of describing the physicochemical and structural features that need to be primarily modified for improving the biological effect under study. Therefore, compounds whose molecular descriptors follow such a degree of the hierarchy/importance in the model are expected to be predicted with a higher accuracy, where the theoretical predictions should better match the experimental results. Although considering the degree of the hierarchy of the molecular descriptors is an aspect neglected by most of the current models devoted to screening vast datasets, recent approaches focused on fragment-based topological design have emphasized its essential role for the optimization of the chemical space.61,64–67 As the molecular descriptors of a predictive computational model are not able to “control” the chemical space to be predicted, it has been proposed that in order to achieve a higher certainty in the predictions, the chemicals must be designed according to the physicochemical and structural interpretations of the molecular descriptors in the models.61,64–67

To prove the veracity of such suggestions and estimate the sensitivity of the ms-QSBER-EL model with respect to small changes in the chemical structures of the molecules, we carried out the following experiment. We designed ten different molecules belonging to different chemical families (see Figure 16.4) according to the following steps. First, for each designed molecule, some of the fragments mentioned above were used as building blocks or seeds. Second, the designed molecules were assembled by fusing or connecting the fragments. Third, when needed, a series of bioisosteric replacements were made, or some atoms or functional groups were added. Last, a series of molecules were designed by rigorously considering the joint interpretation of the molecular descriptors in the ms-QSBER-EL model (from AMA-001 to AMA-004, AMA-008, and AMA-010), while others were designed from the interpretations retrieved from some of the descriptors (AMA-005 to AMA-007, and AMA-009).

Figure 16.4 Chemical structures of the designed molecules.

The results of the predictions (applicability domain included) for all the designed molecules are reported in Supplementary Information 16.4.1 In addition, Table 16.5 illustrates a summary of such predictions, which permits a fast comparison of the different biological profiles of the different molecules. As expected, in general, the molecules from AMA-001 to AMA-004 were predicted as very potent and safe antimalarial agents. Nevertheless, we would like to highlight that although excellent predicted biological profiles of these four molecules were very similar between each other, the molecules AMA-002 and AMA-004 were predicted as negative against the cytotoxicity assay performed on RAW264.7 cells. This happened because, in the case of AMA-002, the presence of the carboxamide group is detrimental to D[TnsAq6(AW)]cj, increasing the value of this descriptor (which must decrease). A similar situation can be found in the molecule AMA-004, which in addition, has pyrimidine instead of 1,2,4-triazine; this slightly increases the values of D[LnsAq2(AW)P]cj and D[LnsAq6(HYD)Y]cj (they both must decrease).

The unfavorable predictions for AMA-005 and AMA-006 are not surprising at all. First, the two halogen atoms appear in a central region instead of being restricted to the periphery of the molecules. These halogens detrimentally increase the value D[TnsAq6(AW)]cj. At the same time, these two halogen atoms are attached to aliphatic carbons, in contrast to the recommendation of attaching them to aromatic carbons, which would favorably increase the value of D[LnsAq1(POL)G]cj. Another important fact is that electronegative atoms such as nitrogen and oxygen appear placed at the topological distance different from two, which decreases the value of the descriptor D[LnsAq2(E)G]cj.

The difference between the predicted biological profiles of AMA-007 and AMA-008 is due to the presence of a fluorine atom in AMA-008, which favorably increases the value of D[LnsAq2(E)G]cj while also desirably decreasing D[TnsAq6(AW)]cj. In the case of AMA-009, as recommended, the three halogen atoms are in the periphery of the molecules. However, the presence of these three chlorine atoms leads to a noticeable increase in the value of D[TnsAq6(AW)]cj. Notice that according to the joint physicochemical and structural interpretation of the molecular descriptors, only two chlorine atoms are recommended instead of three. Finally, AMA-010 is very different from the other nine molecules, and yet, it was predicted to exhibit high activity, low cytotoxicity, and good pharmacokinetic properties except for its half-life against human plasma. Perhaps a simple modification such as switching the positions of the halogens may lead to an analog of AMA-010 with improvements in the predicted biological profiles.

The differences between the predicted biological effects of the designed molecules demonstrate the sensitivity and discriminatory power of the molecular descriptors used to develop the ms-QSBER-EL model. On the other hand, it is clear that each prediction of the biological effect of a molecule does not depend on a single descriptor but in the combination of all the descriptors present in the model. In any case, some physicochemical properties and structural features have more influence than others, and we have explained them by providing the specific descriptors responsible for the observed differences in the chemical structures of the molecules, which translated in different predicted biological profiles.

The most promising molecules are from AMA-001 to AMA-004, AMA-008, and AMA-010. Because of the potentially high antimalarial activity, low cytotoxicity, and adequate pharmacokinetic properties, we searched these molecules in well-known databases such as ChEMBL, ZINC,68 and ChemSpider69 for finding similar molecules. For a similarity cutoff value ≥0.8, only one match was found. In this sense, the molecule ChemSpiderID 51375502 was identified to be similar to AMA-001. However, different structural aspects support the chemical dissimilarity of these two molecules. For instance, ChemSpiderID 51375502 contains a 4-bromopyrimidine ring (instead of the crucial fragment 2-bromopyrimidine reported for AMA-001). Also, ChemSpiderID 51375502 is lacking a second bromine atom in the pyridine ring, instead having an ethyl group. In the end, from the point of view of the physicochemical and structural information extracted from the ms-QSBER-EL model, the 4-bromopyrimidine ring in ChemSpiderID 51375502 is slightly detrimental for the increase of the descriptor D[LnsAq2(E)G]cj. At the same time, the lack of the second bromine atom also unfavorably affects the values of D[LnsAq2(E)G]cj and D[LnsAq6(HYD)Y]cj. Finally, the presence of the methyl moiety in the ethyl group increases the value of D[LnsAq6(AW)M]cj, whose undesirable effect has been explained before. Thus, in principle, ChemSpiderID 51375502, although promising, should be slightly less desirable than AMA-001 in terms of antimalarial activity and/or safety.

16.3.5 Druglikeness

The druglikeness of each molecule was assessed by verifying the compliance with Lipinski's rule of five,70 which establishes that, in order to exhibit a good oral bioavailability, a molecule should have no more than 5 hydrogen bond donors (HBD), 10 or fewer hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), a molecular weight (MW) lower than 500 Da, and an octanol-water partition coefficient (logP) not greater than 5. A variant of the Lipinski's rule of five suggests logP in the range −0.4 to +5.6, molar refractivity in the interval 40–130 cm3 mol−1, MW in the range 180–480 Da, and the number of atoms (nAT) from 20 to70. In addition, Veber and coworkers suggested that only two aspects should be considered when analyzing the potentially good oral bioavailability of a chemical: the polar surface area (PSA) to be lower than ≤140 Å2, and the number of rotatable bonds (RBN) to be ≤10.71 All the properties mentioned above were calculated for the six most promising molecules mentioned above (see Table 16.6) by using the software AlvaDesc v1.0.14.72 From the physicochemical point of view, all the designed molecules were in agreement with the Lipinski's rule of five and its variants.

16.4 Conclusion

Malaria is an emerging and unresolved public health problem that can be halted by using the most advanced in silico approaches in drug discovery. In this context, computational tools are essential for prioritizing the search for novel, potent, and safe antimalarial agents. The predictive models reported to date should go beyond the conventional purpose of screening large chemical libraries. Special attention must be paid to the physicochemical and structural information that can be gathered from the in silico models. The ms-QSBER-EL model developed here is capable of integrating antimalarial activity, cytotoxicity, and pharmacokinetic properties, exhibiting a very good accuracy. The combined use of the physicochemical and structural interpretations of the molecular descriptors and the fragment-based analysis permitted the guided design of virtually new molecules as potent and safe antimalarial chemicals, which are now available to the scientific community as potential leads for future biological testing. This work unveils new horizons for the creation of focused libraries for drug discovery against malaria, with a wide range of applications to other tropical diseases.

CHAPTER 17

Machine Learning for Core-loss Spectrum

T. MIZOGUCHI*a AND S. KIYOHARAa,b

a The University of Tokyo, Institute of Industrial Science, Komaba, Tokyo 153-8505, Japan

b Laboratory for Materials and Structures, Institute of Innovative Research, Tokyo Institute of Technology, Yokohama 226-8503, Japan

*Email: teru@iis.u-tokyo.ac.jp

17.1 Introduction

Unveiling the atomistic configurations, chemical bonding, and vibrational behaviors of molecules and atoms, which are commonly correlated to the functions of a material, is the most important task of materials research. Spectroscopic techniques, such as diffraction, reflection, emission, and absorption, have been used to identify such information because the spectral features are correlated to the material information.

Among existing spectroscopic techniques, core-loss spectroscopy using electrons or X-rays, namely, electron energy-loss near-edge structure (ELNES) and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), offer atomic-scale spatial resolution,1 nanosecond-level time resolution,2 and high sensitivity3 and can be considered the “ultimate analysis” in materials science.4 ELNES and XANES commonly originate from an electron transition from a core orbital to unoccupied states.5,6 As their electron transitions commonly follow an electron dipole transition rule, their spectral features reflect the partial density of states (PDOS) in unoccupied bands. Thus, ELNES and XANES features provide information on the local coordination and chemical bonding of selected elements in the illuminated area.

ELNES and XANES are used as complementary tools. XANES has the advantage of sensitivity, i.e., it can be observed from an element present at ppm-levels,3,7,8 while the main advantage of ELNES is its spatial resolution, i.e., it can be observed from a single atomic column (or even a single atom or buried dopant).1,9–11 The recent emergence of monochromator systems has improved the energy resolution of EELS, which facilitates the identification of vibrational spectra using TEM/STEM systems.12–15 Thus, ELNES/XANES have been used for the characterization of a wide variety of materials systems, such as semiconductors,16–19 ceramics,20–22 batteries,23,24 electrical devices,25–27 and capacitor materials.28–31

Instrument development has accompanied advancements in the theoretical simulation of ELNES/XANES. The most important aspect of ELNES/XANES simulation is the introduction of a core hole, which is generated in the core orbital during the electron transition process.32,33 Depending on the position of the core state and excited electron, ELNES/XANES simulation can be categorized into three methods: one-particle method,34–37 two-particle method,38–41 and multi-particle method.42–45 The fundamentals of ELNES/XANES simulation using the one-, two-, and multi-particle methods have been reviewed elsewhere.46–49 In addition to spectrum simulation, theoretical tools for unveiling the relationships between spectral features and material properties have also been proposed.50,51 By combining experimental and theoretical simulations, one can investigate the valence state,52 local coordination,37 liquid/gas molecular vibration,53–55 lattice vibration,56,57 and van der Waals interaction.58

Recent years have witnessed a rapid increase in spectral data. ELNES/XANES experiments often involve time-resolved and/or spatially resolved observations. For instance, spatially resolved ELNES allows spectral imaging with a resolution of several thousand points in an objective area. In XANES, pico- or nano-second time-resolved observations are possible, and time-resolved experiments for tracing chemical reactions have been performed. Through such spatially/temporally resolved ELNES/XANES observations, up to tens of thousands of spectra can be observed in an experimental session. Individual interpretation through theoretical calculations is infeasible because each ELNES/XANES calculation not only requires extensive experimental and theoretical knowledge but also involves many computations.

Recently, approaches for gaining new insights from big data, namely data-driven approaches, have attracted considerable attention in materials science.59–63 Analysis based on machine learning (ML) can overcome the limitations of manual multi-dimensional big data analysis. ML is extensively used for materials simulations, characterizations, and discoveries. Such data-driven approaches have facilitated the discovery of desired structures with minimum computation,64,65 new materials with high efficiency,66–69 and information that could not be previously determined through experiments70,71 or simulations.72,73 ML has also been applied to experimental observations.74–76 It allows the interpretation of many more spectra compared with manual analysis, as well as the prediction of a scalar value or discrete values in a simple spectrum, such as a chemical shift or peaks in NMR spectra.74–76 In addition, it has been applied to X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) and extended XAFS (EXAFS) spectra.71,77

We have reported the applications of ML for materials characterizations. In particular, we have used ML to investigate crystalline interfaces64,65,78–82 and ELNES/XANES spectra.83,84

This chapter reviews our data-driven approaches for the ELNES/XANES spectrum. First, we review spectrum interpretation and prediction by combining unsupervised hierarchical clustering with supervised decision tree classification.83 In this method, a “two-tree” comprising a dendrogram obtained by hierarchical clustering and another tree for decision tree classification is used to interpret and predict ELNES/XANES spectra. In addition, we use ML to directly quantify the structures and properties of materials from the spectra.84 A feedforward neural network is used to predict the local structures, chemical bonding, and transition energy from only the spectral features. Furthermore, the effect of noise on the prediction accuracy is discussed. Finally, data augmentation is used to construct a prediction model that is robust against noise.

17.2 Methodology

17.2.1 Spectrum Database Construction

This section mainly reviews two tasks: spectral interpretation/prediction and property prediction. To avoid accidental errors and noise, we first constructed the spectrum database via simulation (the experimental spectrum and the effect of noise are discussed later). CASTEP85,86 code was used for the ELNES/XANES calculation, which is based on a first-principles plane-wave-basis pseudopotential method. The oxygen K-edge of oxide materials was simulated. Generalized gradient approximation (GGA) of the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional87 was selected to approximate the exchange–correlation functional, and the cutoff energy was set to 500 eV. To introduce core-hole effects, an excited pseudopotential was generated and applied to the excited oxygen atom in the supercell. To minimize interactions among excited atoms under periodic boundary conditions, sufficiently large supercells (>10 Å) were used in all the cases. The calculated spectrum was obtained by calculating the transition probability based on the Fermi's golden rule. The theoretical transition energy was also simulated similarly to a previous study.86 The details of the calculated spectra are described below.

17.2.2 Spectral Data Clustering

Hierarchical clustering88 was used to categorize the spectral data. Initially, each spectrum was assigned to its own cluster. Then, the two most similar clusters were combined into a single cluster. The clustering process was repeated until a single cluster was obtained. The similarity was estimated based on the cosine distance between a pair of spectra, which is often used for measuring spectral similarity.89,90

The clustering linkage scheme for measuring the cluster similarity was the “completed” method for the “two-tree” method. In this study, as we directly compared the spectral features, the onsets of all the spectra were aligned to each other. The double differential of the spectrum was used to estimate the position of the onset.

17.2.3 Decision Tree for Material Information

A decision tree visualizes classification or regression results using a tree structure. By repeatedly dividing the data into two or more subsets, the decision tree is composed of certain subsets with labels, which are the same as the labels in the training data. As this approach is a type of supervised learning, training labels are necessary. The labels obtained by spectral clustering were used as the training data. The classification and regression tree (CART) algorithm91,92 was used for training.

17.2.4 Feedforward Neural Network

Property prediction from the spectral features was performed using a feedforward neural network. A feedforward neural network is the simplest type of neural network. It was selected for this study because it can accommodate high-dimensional input data, such as spectra, and incorporate interactions between them in a non-linear manner. We used backpropagation, based on the Adam scheme,93 to optimize all the learning parameters in the network, thereby minimizing the mean absolute errors between the model outputs and the training targets. A rectified linear unit (ReLU) was used as the activation function, and the dropout rate was fixed at 0.5 in the hidden layers not linked with the output layer. The hyperparameters, i.e., the number of hidden layers and the regularization parameters, were tuned via five-fold cross-validation using the validation datasets.

17.3 Results and Discussion

17.3.1 Overview of the Data-driven Prediction and Interpretation Method

The proposed data-driven spectral analysis is schematically illustrated in Figure 17.1(a)–(c). First, a spectral database, in which each spectrum has a one-to-one correspondence with its material information, was constructed as shown in Figure 17.1(a).

Figure 17.1 Strategy for data-driven prediction and interpretation of spectra. Schematics of (a) the spectral database and structures, which have one-to-one correspondence, (b) spectral clustering, and (c) structural classification with the spectral groups as the training data. Adapted from ref. 83, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-30994-6, under the terms of the CC BY 4.0 licence, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/.

As described above, we constructed the spectrum database via theoretical simulation. After creating the database, the included spectra are divided into groups according to their “similarity” using hierarchical cluster analysis, which divides spectral data into tree-shaped clusters called “dendrogram”. A dendrogram is schematically shown in Figure 17.1(b); the vertical axis corresponds to the “dissimilarity” of the spectra.

In the final step, the materials are classified into some groups by a decision tree based on the material information, such as the bond length, coordination number, the group in the periodic table, and valency. In the example shown in Figure 17.1(c), the objective materials are classified using the material information such as “trivalent”: true/false and “long bond length”: true/false. The most important aspect of our method is the classification of the materials into spectral groups, which are used as the training labels for classification. As the decision tree for materials is based on the spectral groups, it establishes a correlation between the material information and the spectral features. In the decision tree for material information (see Figure 17.1(c)), the branch points provide the “characteristic” descriptors for classifying the spectra, as discussed later.

Our method uses two trees: the dendrogram (see Figure 17.1(b)) and the decision tree (see Figure 17.1(c)). The two trees, related to spectrum classification and material information, are correlated with each other because the decision tree is constructed based on spectrum classification. After the two-tree is constructed, the ELNES/XANES spectra can be predicted and interpreted. The strategy for the prediction and interpretation of the spectra is schematically shown in Figure 17.2(a) and (b), respectively.

Figure 17.2 Conceptual schemes of (a) “downstream” spectral prediction and (b) “upstream” spectral interpretation. Adapted from ref. 83, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-30994-6, under the terms of the CC BY 4.0 licence, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/.

Consider a situation in which the atomic configuration of an objective material is known, but its ELNES/XANES spectral profiles are unknown. Such situations often occur because we generally predict the spectral profile prior to making observations to validate the experiment and sample conditions. For the prediction, we apply geometric and element information, such as the bond length, angles, and valence state, to the material information decision tree (right side of Figure 17.2(a)).

Hence, the decision tree becomes a true/false diagram (flowchart), e.g., the true/false diagrams for trivalence and the bond length, as shown in Figure 17.2(a). Moving down the true/false diagram using the material (geometric and elemental) information, we arrive at any one of the labels, clusters 1, 2, or 3, as shown in Figure 17.2(a). As the decision tree for the material information is correlated to that for the spectrum, the objective spectrum should be similar to that in the cluster. This “downstream” method corresponds to the “prediction” of the unknown spectrum of a known structure.

Next, we describe the interpretation using the two-tree. First, we define the “interpretation” of ELNES/XANES. ELNES/XANES spectra reflect the atomic and electronic structures; thus, the “interpretation of the ELNES/XANES spectrum” corresponds to the determination of the relationship between the spectrum and the atomic and electronic structures.

Consider a situation in which a spectrum of an unknown area/material is observed. In this case, we need to interpret the spectrum, i.e., the relationship between the spectral profile and the material information, such as the bond length and coordination number, needs to be determined. For such interpretation, we again use the two-tree; however, we move up the decision tree as shown in Figure 17.2(b).

The strategy for the interpretation is schematically shown in Figure 17.2(b). For the ELNES/XANES spectrum of an unknown area/material, the cluster in the spectrum tree that is the most similar to the observed spectrum is first determined. By measuring the dissimilarity between the objective spectrum and all the other spectra in the database, we select the most resembling spectrum to be the most similar to the objective spectrum. In the example shown in Figure 17.2(b), assume that the observed spectrum is the most similar to a spectrum in Cluster 3 (red box). Then, by moving up the material information tree starting from Cluster 3, geometric and elemental information, such as the bond length and valency, can be obtained from the branch of the decision tree. Then, the spectrum is interpreted using such atomic and electronic structure information. In the case of Figure 17.2(b), we can determine that the observed spectrum is obtained from a material that has a “short bond length” and is “trivalent”.

The branching points in a decision tree play a critical role in the interpretation, i.e., when the most similar spectral cluster has been determined, the objective material can be expected to have a structure similar to that of the materials in the cluster. However, the “characteristic” information of the corresponding cluster cannot be obtained. The branching points in the decision tree provide the “characteristic” information of the materials in the corresponding cluster.

In the next section, we describe the use of this two-tree method for the prediction and interpretation of oxygen K-edge (O-K edge) ELNES/XANES. The O-K edges are selected because they can be easily calculated using the one-particle method based on density functional theory (DFT) under the GGA framework, and they basically provide all the information for the conduction band.46,47,50

17.3.2 Demonstration Using the O-K Edges of Mono-metal Oxides

We calculated 39 O-K edges of oxide materials, including 14 of mono-metal oxides (listed in Table 17.1) and 25 of polymorphous SiO2 (listed in Table 17.2). The 14 mono-metal oxides were selected because they do not have “complex” electronic structures, such as partially occupied 3d-orbitals, or magnetic properties. SiO2 was selected because it has several polymorphs and wide applications. The 14 O-K edge spectra of the mono-metal oxides were used to demonstrate our method. The actual interpretation and prediction were performed using the 25 O-K edge spectra of polymorphous SiO2.

First, we applied our approach to the O-K edges of the 14 mono-metal oxides. All the calculated spectra are shown in Figure 17.3. The upper part of Figure 17.3 shows the calculated O-K edges of Al2O3, BeO, CaO, Ga2O3, In2O3, Li2O, MgO, Na2O, SiO2, SnO2, TiO2 (anatase), TiO2 (rutile), Y2O3, and ZrO2. The cluster analysis result for the spectra forms a dendrogram, as shown in Figure 17.4. Starting with no links at the bottom of the dendrogram, similar spectra and/or clusters gradually merge, moving upward in the dendrogram. By cutting the dendrogram horizontally at a certain level, we can obtain a set of clusters. The selection of the cutting level is arbitrary; we selected the level indicated by the dashed line in the dendrogram, resulting in four clusters, Cluster 1 to Cluster 4 (see Figure 17.4). These four clusters have certain characteristic features; for example, Cluster 3 was composed of alkali metal oxides. We attempted to interpret these features using the decision tree.

The label colors correspond to those in the respective dendrograms and decision trees in Figures 17.4 and 17.5. Eight parameters were selected as descriptors for the decision tree: (1) valence of the cation, (2) group and (3) period in the periodic table, coordination number of the (4) anion and (5) cation, and the number of (6) s, (7) p, and (8) d electrons of the cation in the valence and semi-core states. Figure 17.5 shows the constructed decision tree based on supervised learning; the decision tree divided the 14 oxides into two subsets according to whether they initially had d electrons and whether the “1st element or not” divided a subset and the “4th element or not” divided the other. The two constructed trees, shown in Figures 17.4 and 17.5, were used for interpretation.

Figure 17.5 Decision tree based on the training labels in Figure 17.4. Adapted from ref. 83, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-30994-6, under the terms of the CC BY 4.0 licence, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/.

For interpreting the spectra, we moved up the decision tree, as mentioned above. This provides information on each cluster; for example, Cluster 3 was “with 1st elements” and “without d electrons”, which were previously considered from the dendrogram.

For the demonstration, we used the elemental information of the 14 oxides. However, the relationship between the spectral features and certain geometric information, such as the bond length and coordination number, is often important for the interpretation of ELNES/XANES spectra.

To perform the actual interpretation and prediction of the ELNES spectra, we applied this method to the O-K edge spectra of SiO2, as described in the next section.

17.3.3 Interpretation and Prediction of the O-K Edges of Polymorphous SiO2

Next, we considered 13 polymorphs of SiO2, the space groups of which are listed in Table 17.2. Some polymorphs have several oxygen sites, namely 2-1, 2; 3-1–4; 5-1, 2; 6-1, 2; 7-1–3; 8-1–5. Hence, all were calculated separately. Thus, a total of 25 O-K edge spectra were obtained, as shown in Figure 17.3. Because the composition is fixed to SiO2, the atomic configuration is different and the spectral features can be interpreted using geometric information such as the Si–O bond length and the Si–O–Si bond angle. Excluding randomly selected test data, for polymorph 3-4 (middle panel of Figure 17.3), 24 spectra were used for hierarchical clustering and creating the decision tree.

The spectral features of these O-K edges are shown in Figure 17.3, which clearly exhibit a variety of spectral profiles depending on their local structures. The cluster dendrogram for these 24 spectra is shown in Figure 17.6.

Figure 17.6 Dendrogram based on the spectral similarities of the 24 O-K edges of the SiO2 polymorphs. The axis on the right represents the cosine distances. The top (purple in online) and lower (blue in online) arrows are explained in the main text. Adapted from ref. 83, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-30994-6, under the terms of the CC BY 4.0 licence, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/.

The threshold level in Figure 17.6 was set not arbitrarily but in a data-driven manner as described below, and seven clusters were generated. Cluster 4 (purple group), i.e., polymorph 4, is separated from the other spectra at a higher level (as indicated by the upper (purple in online) arrow), indicating that its spectrum is highly dissimilar to those of the other polymorphs. In fact, the spectral features of polymorph 4 differ considerably from those of the others (see Figure 17.3). This result is supported by the fact that the crystal structure of polymorph 4 has higher symmetry than those of the other polymorphs. Polymorphs 7-2, 7-3, 8-4, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13 formed the large Cluster 5 (blue in online), as their spectral features are very similar to each other (see Figure 17.3).

Next, we focus on Cluster 5 (blue in online and indicated by the lower (blue in online) arrow in Figure 17.6). The spectra in this group commonly include a large peak at the spectrum threshold, followed by small peaks, as shown in Figure 17.3 (spectra with blue labels). Their features are visually very similar to those of the spectra in Cluster 6 (yellow in online) and Cluster 7 (green in online). However, our approach indicated that these three groups have some imperceptible differences. A detailed comparison revealed a small distinction, wherein the main peaks of the blue group were slightly sharper than those of the other two groups. The sharper profile of Cluster 5 is ascribed to the more symmetric structures of the included materials. Actually, most of the materials in Cluster 5 have a single oxygen site, whereas those in Clusters 6 and 7 have multiple oxygen sites in their unit cells. Moreover, the spectra in Cluster 7 (green cluster in online) have a sharp first peak, as with the spectra in Cluster 5, but the position of the first peak is slightly different (slightly toward the lower energy side) from that in Cluster 5. These small spectral differences may be imperceptible to the human eye; however, the proposed clustering method has the potential to discern such small differences.

Next, we constructed the decision tree based on the structural information of these polymorphs. To this end, we selected 32 geometric features as descriptors. These 32 descriptors are listed in Table 17.3.

As mentioned previously, the decision tree was constructed via supervised learning. Figure 17.7 shows the constructed decision tree based on the threshold level indicated by the dashed line in Figure 17.6. To determine the threshold, we evaluated the accuracy rate for the training data at each threshold. Decision trees with thresholds higher than the current line had a prediction accuracy of 100% for the training dataset.

Adapted from ref. 83, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-30994-6, under the terms of the CC BY 4.0 licence, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/.

To evaluate the constructed decision tree, the test data, namely polymorph 3-4, was used for prediction and interpretation. First, we attempted to predict the spectrum of the test data (polymorph 3-4). In this case, the geometric information of polymorph 3-4 is known, as summarized in Table 17.4. As mentioned above, we move down the decision tree (see Figure 17.7) for prediction, using the geometric information of the polymorph 3-4 site; the decision tree starts from “minimal Si–O bond length in small tetrahedron≤1.6 Å”. The site for polymorph 3-4 has a minimal Si–O bond length in the small tetrahedron of 1.53 Å; thus, it is “true”. The next true/false decision is the “number of bonds between 4.5–5.0 Å≤4”. For polymorph 3-4, this value is 15; thus, it is “false”. Furthermore, as per the information of polymorph 3-4, presented in Table 17.4, Cluster 2 (red group) is reached.

Table 17.4 List of geometric characteristics of polymorphs 3–4.

Descriptor Polymorph 3-4
Minimal Si–O bond length in small tetra. 1.53 Å
Number of bonds (4.5–5.0 Å) 15
Maximum Si–O* bond length 1.60 Å
Maximum Si–O bond length in small tetra. 1.59 Å

Based on the geometric information of the site, the proposed method suggests that the spectral features of polymorph 3-4 are similar to those of Cluster 2, which consists of polymorph 2-2, 3-1, and 3-2. The actual spectrum for polymorph 3-4 is shown in Figure 17.8(a) along with the spectrum for polymorph 3-1, which is the most similar to polymorph3-4 in terms of the cosine distance (see Figure 17.8(b)). Our method predicted that the test data belonged to Cluster 2, and the spectral features of polymorph 3-4 are indeed very similar to those of polymorph 3-1, indicating that this method can predict the spectral features correctly.

Figure 17.8 Calculated O-K edge spectra of (a) polymorph 3-4 and (b) polymorph 3-1. Adapted from ref. 83, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-30994-6, under the terms of the CC BY 4.0 licence, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/.

Next, our method is used for interpreting the spectrum. We considered a different situation in which we know the spectral features but not the material information of polymorph 3-4. First, we measured the cosine distance between the objective spectrum (in this case, the spectrum of polymorph 3-4) and all the other spectra in the database. In this case, the cosine distance to polymorph 3-1 is the shortest, indicating that this spectrum is the most similar to that of polymorph 3-4. Through this process, the class of the objective spectrum can be determined. In this test case, the objective spectrum is categorized as Cluster 2 because polymorph 3-1 belongs to Cluster 2.

The spectrum is interpreted using the decision tree in Figure 17.7. As the objective spectrum is the most similar to that of polymorph 3-1, the material information of the objective material is expected to be similar to that of polymorph 3-1 and the other polymorphs in Cluster 2. However, as mentioned above, the “characteristic” features of the materials in Cluster 2 cannot be determined. To obtain the “characteristic” feature, we need to travel up the decision tree in Figure 17.7.

We can obtain the initial information, “maximum Si–O bond length in the small tetrahedron ≤1.6 Å”, and the next branch points, “max. Si–O* bond length ≥1.54 Å” and “number of bonds between 4.5 and 5.0 Å≥4”, from the decision tree (see Figure 17.7). This information is in agreement with the geometric information of polymorph 3-4 (as summarized in Table 17.4). Thus, we can obtain the “characteristic” features of the materials in Cluster 2 from the branching points of the decision tree, and the spectrum can be interpreted using these “characteristic” features.

In this section, we proposed a data-driven approach for predicting and interpreting ELNES/XANES spectra. Our method is based on hierarchical clustering and a decision tree. The calculated O-K edges of 14 metal oxides and 25 SiO2 polymorphs were used to demonstrate the proposed method. Our method was effective in predicting the spectral features from the material information.

17.3.4 Machine Learning to Quantify Structures and Properties from ELNES/XANES

Although ELNES/XANES is effective for investigating local atomic and electronic structures, “direct” determination of the material properties using core-loss spectroscopy is more attractive for atomic-resolution function measurements. However, the relationship between the core-loss features and the material functions is ambiguous; hence, extracting it requires theoretical expertise and calculations. Therefore, only a few studies have realized quantification of properties using core-loss spectroscopy.21,50,94,95 Determining the direct relationship between the core-loss features and the material properties could facilitate a nano-scale understanding of the material properties.

Here, we employed a feedforward neural network to quantify the structures and properties from the ELNES feature.84 The schematic diagram of the constructed neural network for predicting properties from the spectrum is shown in Figure 17.9.

Figure 17.9 Schematic of a feedforward neural network model. The input layer (located in the lower position in this figure) accepts intensities of ELNES/XANES spectra at each energy and transfers that information toward the output layer (located in the highest position in this figure). Adapted from ref. 84, https://doi.org/10.1088/2515-7639/ab0b68, under the terms of the CC BY 3.0 licence, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/.

The input data consisted of the intensities of the core-loss spectrum, which were in the range of −1 to 15 eV in increments of 0.1 eV, i.e. 160 dimensional inputs, and the output data were the objective properties. Thus, the theoretical transition energy was not considered in the input data. The properties of individual atomic sites, including local geometrical and bonding properties, such as bond length, bond angles, Voronoi volume, bond overlap population, and Mulliken charge, were calculated by the CASTEP code.85,86 In addition, the transition energy of the respective spectra was selected as the output. Thus, prediction of the transition energy was attempted using only the spectral feature. The average bond length, average bond angle, and Voronoi volume are geometrical features; the first two provide short-range information and the third provides short- and middle-range information. The bonding properties, bond overlap population, Mulliken charge, and excitation energy are related to the valence and core states. Although prediction of the excitation energy is not necessary because it is observed with the experimental spectrum, prediction of the excitation energy based solely on the spectral features was attempted to demonstrate the ability of the present method to predict a core-electron-related property.

Considering these six properties as the objective variables, regression analysis was conducted via a neural network. The best hyperparameters were determined by grid search. The correct and predicted values of the training and test data are plotted in Figure 17.10(a)–(f).

Figure 17.10 Accurate and predicted values of six types of properties: (a) average bond length, (b) average bond angle, (c) Voronoi volume, (d) bond overlap population, (e) Mulliken charge, and (f) transition energy. The gray and dark gray (colored in online) dots represent training and testing data, respectively. The gray diagonal lines indicate that the predicted values are equal to the actual ones. The arrows indicate the spectra with large errors. Adapted from ref. 84, https://doi.org/10.1088/2515-7639/ab0b68, under the terms of the CC BY 3.0 licence, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/.

The gray and colored circles represent the training and testing data, respectively. The circles on the diagonal gray line imply that the predicted values are equal to the actual values. As most of the colored circles are on the gray line in Figure 17.10(a)–(f), our neural network model can predict these local properties accurately, indicating that the information about both geometrical and bonding properties is implicitly contained in the spectral features of the core-loss spectrum. Moreover, the prediction model works well not only for bond lengths and bond angles but also for the Voronoi volume. Core-loss is often believed to reflect very localized information (such as bond lengths and angles); however, the present result implies that middle-range information (such as Voronoi volume) is also included implicitly, and it can be extracted by machine learning.

In addition to the geometrical properties, the same argument can apply to bonding properties. The neural network can correctly predict all the bonding properties (see Figure 17.10(d)–(f)). Note that the present method can correctly predict the excitation energy using “only” the spectral features.

In core-loss spectra, the spectral features and excitation energy are often discussed separately; for instance, the excitation energy, i.e., the chemical shift, is related to the oxidization state, whereas the spectral profile reflects the more detailed and fine structure of the partial density of states (PDOS) of the conduction band. However, the present results indicate that the spectral features themselves contain information on the excitation energy, and the excitation energy can be predicted solely by the spectral features. Furthermore, the present method can correctly predict the valence band information in ground states, i.e., the Mulliken charge and bond overlap population. The core-loss spectrum is known to reflect the PDOS of the conduction band in the excited state and it has no direct relationship with the valence states; however, the present results indicate that spectral features definitely contain information on the valence states. By using a neural network, geometrical and bonding information was extracted from the spectral features of the core-loss spectrum.

A detailed inspection of Figure 17.10 reveals some circles located away from the diagonal lines (denoted by arrows), indicating that the prediction with the neural network fails for some materials/sites. On careful examination of these circles, i.e. the spectra with large errors, it was found that the spectra with large errors for one property tend to have similar large errors for other properties. Specifically, 13 spectra have errors ranked in the worst ten with more than two properties, and 6 spectra have errors ranked with more than four properties. The spectra with large errors are indicated by arrows in Figure 17.10(a)–(f).

A detailed analysis showed two causes of misprediction. First, no similar spectrum was included in the training data. Second, when similar spectra were included in the training data, the corresponding properties differed from each other. Both these causes can be attributed to unique electronic structures, which cannot be learned from the training data.84

17.3.5 Quantification of Structures and Properties from Noisy Spectra

We showed that ELNES/XANES can be used to quantify the structures and properties based on a neural network. However, these investigations were performed using a spectral dataset constructed by theoretical simulation. Specifically, noise was not considered even though an experimental spectrum must contain noise. To apply our method to the experimental spectra, we must investigate the effect of noise on the prediction accuracy.

Figure 17.11 shows the effect of noise on the prediction accuracy. Noise was applied to the original calculated spectra, which do not include noise, based on the Poisson distribution, and the noise intensity was changed and eight types of spectra with different noise levels were generated (black lines from top to bottom in Figure 17.11(a)). Figure 17.11(a) shows the spectra without noise (blue line in online) and with noise (black lines in online). As the distribution of noise differs randomly, 10 spectra with each noise level were generated.

Figure 17.11 (a) The top (blue) and lower black spectra correspond to no-noise and noise-added spectra, respectively. Eight different noise levels were generated based on a Poisson distribution (bottom–top correspond to high–low noise levels). (b)–(g) Prediction accuracy measured by mean absolute error (MAE) of each property with different noise levels. The square and circle symbols correspond to the prediction accuracies without and with data augmentation (DA).

First, the spectra with noise were employed for the prediction model constructed by the spectra without noise. The square symbols in Figure 17.11 (b)–(g) show the prediction accuracies estimated by the mean absolute error (MAE) of the respective properties. The gray dashed lines in these figures represent the prediction accuracies using the spectra without noise. The square symbols are basically located at a higher MAE than the gray dashed lines, indicating that the prediction model constructed by the spectra without noise is not robust against noise.

To construct a more robust prediction model against the noise, a data processing method, data augmentation (DA), was adopted. DA is used to increase the number of training data and create a robust prediction model. In the case of data augmentation of image data, noise-added and/or rotated images were included in the training data, which is effective in constructing more versatile prediction models. In the present case, DA was performed using noise-added spectra. In addition to the no-noise spectra, the noise-added spectra were used as the training data. As mentioned above, the spectra with eight noise levels were separately generated. As the noise distribution is random, 10 spectra were separately generated for the respective noise levels, and the prediction models were constructed for the respective noise levels. Thus, the number of the training data for the respective noise levels becomes 10 times greater than that of previous models without DA.

The prediction accuracy with DA is shown in Figure 17.11(b)–(g) by circles. Clearly, the MAE with DA (circle symbols) is usually lower than that without DA (square symbols) even for spectra with large noise, indicating that DA is highly effective in constructing a prediction model that is robust against noise.

In terms of the bond length, bond angle, Mulliken charge, and transition energy, the prediction accuracy becomes higher (lower MAE) than that for the no-noise spectra (gray dashed lines) (see Figure 17.11(b)(c)(f)(g)). This higher accuracy may be due to the larger number of training data than that without DA. Furthermore, the prediction accuracy for the bond overlap population was not improved by DA (see Figure 17.11(e)). Although this worse prediction was not clear, we can expect that the information on the bond overlap population in the spectrum is small and is hidden by noise. Thus, high-quality spectra with small noise are indispensable for quantifying the bond overlap population by ELNES/XANES.

Finally, we applied our model to an experimental spectrum. We measured the O-K edge of a α-quartz sample. We used an aberration-corrected STEM (JEM-ARM200F, JEOL Ltd.) equipped with a monochromator. As the O-K edge is broadened by the electron–hole lifetime, by approximately 0.1 eV, the energy resolution of the instrument can be ignored. We retrained the model by the database broaden by Gaussian with 0.1 eV and predicted the properties of the experimental spectrum. Figure 17.12(a) and (b) show the theoretical and experimental spectra and both of the properties.

Figure 17.12 (a) Experimental and theoretical O-K edge spectra of α-quartz. (b) Theoretical and predicted values from the experimental spectrum. Adapted from ref. 84, https://doi.org/10.1088/2515-7639/ab0b68, under the terms of the CC BY 3.0 licence, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/.

The experimental spectrum has a profile similar to that of the calculated spectrum; however, it includes some noise. Nevertheless, the predicted properties of the experimental spectrum are extremely similar to the accurate values. Therefore, we can conclude that the model constructed using the simulated spectra is considerably robust against noise and it can predict properties accurately even from the experimental spectrum.

17.4 Conclusions

In this study, we reviewed “data-driven” approaches for ELNES/XANES spectra. First, we applied unsupervised hierarchical clustering and a supervised decision tree to the spectra. A two-tree comprising a dendrogram and a decision tree was constructed, and it was used to interpret and predict the spectra. The calculated oxygen K-edges of 14 metal oxides and 25 SiO2 polymorphs were used to demonstrate the proposed method. With this method, the ELNES/XANES spectra can be interpreted in accordance with material information, such as chemical, elemental, and geometric information. Furthermore, our method is effective in predicting the spectral features from the material information.

Further, hidden information was extracted from core-loss spectra via a feedforward neural network. Thus, three types of geometrical properties, namely average bond length, average bond angle, and Voronoi volume, were successfully predicted. This implies that the spectral features reflect not only short-range information but also relatively middle-range information. Furthermore, our method could simultaneously predict three types of bonding properties, namely bond overlap population, Mulliken charge, and transition energy. Although these chemical bonding properties mainly originate from the valence band, the present method can correctly predict this bonding information, indicating that the core-loss spectra, which reflect the conduction band, contain information pertaining to the valence bands in the ground states.

In addition, the effect of noise on the prediction accuracy was investigated. We showed that data augmentation can be used to construct a prediction model that is robust against noise. We also confirmed that our method can correctly predict the material properties from the spectral features in most cases, and it can be applied to an experimental spectrum with some noise.

We emphasize that the proposed machine learning method is not spectroscopy-dependent and should thus work well in terms of interpreting and predicting any spectral data as well as diffraction, emission, and experimental data. A substantial database of over 500 000–800 000 calculated spectra was recently constructed.82,96 Combining this database or others similar to this method could facilitate versatile and accurate predictions and interpretations. In summary, we believe that our method can pave the way for data-driven spectral interpretation and prediction and local measurements of material properties.
